title: BHM 2026 Hub items and sourced points

points.heading: 1507: John Blanke plays at the Tudor court
points.text: A Black trumpeter, John Blanke, is recorded in the royal accounts of Henry VII and Henry VIII. He is one of the earliest named Black people in English records.

points.heading: 1900: First Pan-African Conference, London
points.text: Organised by the Trinidadian barrister Henry Sylvester Williams at Westminster Town Hall, it laid early foundations for organised Pan-Africanism.

sources.title: History Workshop: The Fifth Pan-African Congress 75 years on

points.heading: 1917: Walter Tull commissioned as an officer
points.text: The footballer Walter Tull becomes one of the first Black officers in the British Army, despite rules that barred people not of 'pure European descent'. He was killed in 1918.

points.heading: 1945: Fifth Pan-African Congress, Manchester
points.text: From 15 to 21 October, around 200 delegates met at Chorlton-on-Medlock Town Hall. Future leaders of Ghana, Kenya and Nigeria attended; its resolutions shaped independence movements.

sources.title: Tribune: The Fifth Pan-African Congress, Manchester 1945
Manchester Metropolitan University: 80th anniversary of the Fifth Pan-African Congress
People's History Museum: Africa Speaks in Manchester

points.heading: 1948: The Empire Windrush arrives at Tilbury
points.text: On 22 June, the Empire Windrush docks with passengers from the Caribbean. Many joined the new NHS, transport and other public services. Their arrival gives the Windrush generation its name.

points.heading: 1948: British Nationality Act
points.text: Creates the status of Citizen of the United Kingdom and Colonies, under which many Caribbean and African people came to Britain as citizens.

sources.title: The National Archives: Black British social and political history in the 20th century

points.heading: 1959: Claudia Jones's Caribbean Carnival
points.text: The journalist and activist Claudia Jones organises an indoor Caribbean carnival at St Pancras Town Hall after the 1958 Notting Hill riots, a forerunner of today's Notting Hill Carnival.

points.heading: 1963: Bristol Bus Boycott
points.text: Led by Paul Stephenson and the West Indian Development Council, a four-month boycott forces the Bristol Omnibus Company to end its refusal to employ Black and Asian crews.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Bristol Bus Boycott
Wikipedia: Paul Stephenson (civil rights campaigner)

points.heading: 1965: Race Relations Act 1965
points.text: The first UK law against racial discrimination, covering public places. The Bristol campaign is widely credited with helping to bring it about.

points.heading: 1966: Notting Hill Carnival takes to the streets
points.text: A local street festival in Notting Hill grows into one of the largest street carnivals in Europe.

points.heading: 1976: Race Relations Act 1976
points.text: Extends protection against discrimination and creates the Commission for Racial Equality.

points.heading: 1987: The first UK Black History Month
points.text: Akyaaba Addai-Sebo, a Ghanaian-born special projects officer at the Greater London Council, founds Black History Month in London.

sources.title: Imperial College London: Honouring our Communities
Senedd Cymru: Black History Month, a special anniversary

points.heading: 1987: First Black MPs of the modern era
points.text: Diane Abbott, Paul Boateng and Bernie Grant are elected to the House of Commons at the general election.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 1987 United Kingdom general election

points.heading: 1999: The Stephen Lawrence Inquiry report
points.text: The Macpherson report into the police response to the 1993 murder of Stephen Lawrence finds institutional racism and makes 70 recommendations for public bodies.

points.heading: 2000: Race Relations (Amendment) Act
points.text: Places a duty on public authorities to promote race equality, the forerunner of today's Public Sector Equality Duty.

points.heading: 2010: Equality Act 2010
points.text: Brings discrimination law together and introduces the Public Sector Equality Duty, which applies to public bodies in Great Britain.

points.heading: 2018: Windrush scandal; Stephen Lawrence Day announced
points.text: The government apologises after people of the Windrush generation are wrongly denied rights. The same month, 22 April is announced as Stephen Lawrence Day; Windrush Day on 22 June follows.

sources.title: ITV News: April 22 to become Stephen Lawrence Day

points.heading: 2025: Standing Firm in Power and Pride
points.text: The 2025 national theme. The Civil Service Race Champion reports ethnically diverse representation in the Civil Service rising from 10.1% in 2014 to 18%.

sources.title: Civil Service blog: Black History Month 2025 (Cat Little)

points.heading: 2026: Honouring Our Communities
points.text: Black History Month UK, about 40 years after the first in 1987, asks the country to recognise the everyday contributors who sustain Black life across the UK.

sources.title: University of York: Black History Month 2026
University of the Arts London: Black History Month 2026

points.heading: 1845: Frederick Douglass speaks in Belfast
points.text: The formerly enslaved American abolitionist gives more than 50 speeches in Ireland in 1845–46, including in Belfast, which he visits five times. A statue in Lombard Street now marks his visits.

sources.title: Belfast Media: Frederick Douglass takes pride of place in Belfast

points.heading: 1881: Andrew Watson captains Scotland
points.text: Born in Demerara, British Guiana, Andrew Watson captains Scotland to a 6–1 win over England on 12 March. He is widely considered the first Black international footballer.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Andrew Watson (footballer, born 1856)

points.heading: 2022: Wales makes these histories mandatory
points.text: The Curriculum for Wales requires schools to teach the histories and contributions of Black, Asian and minority ethnic people, the first UK nation to do so.

points.heading: 2025: England's Curriculum and Assessment Review
points.text: The review, chaired by Professor Becky Francis, reports in November. The government accepts that teachers should be able to reflect the innate diversity of British history, including British Black and Asian history. A revised curriculum is due in 2027.

sources.title: GOV.UK: Government response to the Curriculum and Assessment Review
Historical Association: response to the Curriculum and Assessment Review
The Black Curriculum: response to the Curriculum and Assessment Review

points.heading: 2026: UN resolution on the transatlantic trade in enslaved Africans
points.text: On 25 March the UN General Assembly declares the trafficking of enslaved Africans the gravest crime against humanity and calls for reparations. 123 states vote for, 3 against and 52 abstain, including the UK. It is not binding.

sources.title: OPB / NPR: UN calls for reparations to remedy historical wrongs
AllAfrica / Premium Times: Badenoch on the UN resolution

points.heading: c. 75,000 years ago: Engraved ochre at Blombos Cave
points.text: Pieces of ochre engraved with cross-hatched patterns, found in South Africa, are among the oldest known deliberate designs made by humans.

points.heading: c. 42,000 years ago: The Lebombo bone
points.text: A notched baboon fibula from the Lebombo Mountains of southern Africa, often described as one of the oldest counting tools.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ishango bone

points.heading: c. 20,000 years ago: The Ishango bone
points.text: A bone tool from what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo with 168 marks in three columns. Readings as a counting tool or calendar are debated.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ishango bone

points.heading: 1721: Onesimus and smallpox inoculation
points.text: An enslaved West African man in Boston, Onesimus, described inoculation to Cotton Mather. During the 1721 epidemic about 2% of those inoculated died, against about 14% of those infected naturally.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Onesimus (Bostonian)

points.heading: 1855: The Moçâmedes slave register, Angola
points.text: A register of late 1855 records 850 people enslaved in the Angolan port town of Moçâmedes, held by 111 owners; 19 men held 605 of them. Their labour sustained farming, orchil harvesting, street trades and fishing.

sources.title: Curto, J. C. (2023), 'Uma vila esclavagista: proprietários e seus cativos em Moçâmedes, 1855', Revista Brasileira de História 43(93): 225–263

points.heading: 1923: Garrett Morgan's traffic signal patent
points.text: Morgan patents a signal with a warning phase between stop and go, giving traffic time to clear. He did not invent the first traffic signal, a common myth.

sources.title: Suiter Swantz: Patent of the week, traffic signal

points.heading: 1961: Portugal ends the indigenato regime
points.text: A decree of 6 September abolishes the statute that classed most Africans in Angola, Mozambique and Guinea as 'natives' without citizens' rights, which had underpinned forced labour.

points.heading: 1969: A home security system is patented
points.text: Marie Van Brittan Brown and Albert Brown receive a patent for a door camera, video monitor, intercom and remote lock, filed in 1966.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Marie Van Brittan Brown and Albert L. Brown

points.heading: 1975: Angola, Mozambique and Cabo Verde become independent
points.text: After long liberation struggles, Portugal's African colonies gain independence; Angola on 11 November.

points.heading: 1976: Jerry Lawson's cartridge games console
points.text: Lawson leads the team behind the Fairchild Channel F, the first home console built around swappable game cartridges, with the first pause button.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Jerry Lawson (engineer)

points.heading: 1981: The New Cross fire
points.text: Thirteen young Black people die after a house fire at a birthday party in New Cross, south London, on 18 January. The response led to the Black People's Day of Action in March.

points.heading: 2007: M-Pesa launches in Kenya
points.text: Mobile money by text message reaches millions without bank accounts, and becomes a model copied around the world.

points.heading: 2016: Drone delivery of blood in Rwanda
points.text: On 14 October Rwanda launches the world's first national drone delivery service, flying blood to hospitals with the company Zipline.

sources.title: Gavi: Rwanda launches the world's first national drone delivery service

points.text: The national theme invites people to share, in their own words, what they are proud to be and their pride in their heritage and culture.

points.heading: 2022: Theme: Time for Change: Action Not Words

points.heading: 2023: Theme: Saluting Our Sisters

points.heading: London and British cities
points.text: Caribbean and African communities built since the war, alongside a Black presence recorded since at least Tudor times.

points.heading: Lisbon, Portugal
points.text: A Black presence since the 15th century; today home to communities from Angola, Cabo Verde, Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique and São Tomé and Príncipe.

points.heading: Paris, France
points.text: West and Central African and Caribbean communities; the Négritude movement began here in the 1930s.

points.heading: Amsterdam, Netherlands
points.text: Surinamese and Caribbean communities. Keti Koti on 1 July marks the end of slavery in Suriname and the Dutch Caribbean in 1863.

points.heading: Harlem, New York, USA
points.text: Centre of the Harlem Renaissance in the 1920s and of African American and Caribbean life.

points.heading: Sea Islands, South Carolina and Georgia, USA
points.text: Gullah Geechee communities keep a creole language and West African traditions.

points.heading: Birchtown, Nova Scotia, Canada
points.text: Founded by Black Loyalists who left the United States after the American Revolution, in 1783.

sources.title: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Black Loyalists in British North America

points.heading: Havana, Cuba
points.text: Afro-Cuban music, faith and culture shaped the island's identity.

points.heading: Accompong, Jamaica
points.text: A Maroon town whose people won a treaty with the British in 1739. Jamaica is also home to much of Britain's Windrush generation.

points.heading: Port-au-Prince, Haiti
points.text: Haiti's revolution created the first independent Black republic in 1804.

points.heading: Bridgetown, Barbados
points.text: London Transport recruited staff directly from Barbados from 1956; similar schemes were run with British Rail and the NHS.

points.heading: Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago
points.text: Carnival traditions, and the home of Henry Sylvester Williams, who organised the 1900 Pan-African Conference in London.

sources.title: History Workshop: The Fifth Pan-African Congress 75 years on

points.heading: Garifuna coast, Honduras and Belize
points.text: The Garifuna, of African and Indigenous Caribbean descent, whose language, dance and music are recognised by UNESCO.

points.heading: Costa Chica, Guerrero and Oaxaca, Mexico
points.text: Afro-Mexican communities. Mexico's constitution recognised Afro-Mexican peoples in 2019; the 2020 census counted about 2.6 million.

sources.title: Minority Rights Group: Afro-Mexicans

points.heading: San Basilio de Palenque, Colombia
points.text: Founded around 1600 by people led by Benkos Biohó, described as the first free African town in the Americas. Its Palenquero creole is endangered.

sources.title: Wikipedia: San Basilio de Palenque

points.heading: Esmeraldas, Ecuador
points.text: The heart of Afro-Ecuadorian culture, including marimba music.

points.heading: Suriname interior
points.text: Maroon peoples such as the Saamaka and Ndyuka, descended from people who escaped plantations.

points.heading: Salvador, Bahia, Brazil
points.text: The centre of Afro-Brazilian culture. Brazil has the largest population of African descent outside Africa.

points.heading: El Carmen, Chincha, Peru
points.text: A centre of Afro-Peruvian music and dance.

points.heading: Izmir, Turkey
points.text: Afro-Turkish communities, many descended from Africans brought into the Ottoman Empire.

points.heading: Basra, Iraq
points.text: Afro-Iraqi communities, many descended from East Africans brought through Gulf and Indian Ocean trade.

points.heading: Karachi, Pakistan
points.text: Sheedi communities of African descent.

points.heading: Gujarat and Karnataka, India
points.text: Siddi and Habshi communities of diverse African origins. Siddi rulers governed the state of Janjira for centuries, until 1948; sources give different start dates.

sources.title: Sahapedia: Who are the Siddis?

points.heading: Le Morne, Mauritius
points.text: A mountain refuge for people escaping slavery, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2008) and a symbol of the fight for freedom.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage: Le Morne Cultural Landscape

points.heading: Andaman Islands, India
points.text: The Great Andamanese, Onge and Jarawa, among the oldest populations outside Africa, were labelled "Negrito" by colonial writers. They are not an African diaspora.

points.heading: Luzon, Philippines
points.text: The Aeta and related peoples were given the same colonial label. Use the names they use.

points.heading: Papua New Guinea and Melanesia
points.text: "Melanesia" comes from the Greek for "black islands", a name given by a French explorer in 1832.

points.heading: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, Australia
points.text: Classed as "Black" under colonial law. Many Aboriginal people use "Blak" as a self-chosen identity.

points.heading: Black history in Britain starts with Windrush in 1948.
points.text: People of African origin have been in Britain for at least 1,700 years. In the 3rd century AD a Roman unit called the Aurelian Moors was stationed at Aballava on Hadrian's Wall. A wealthy woman of likely North African descent, the 'Ivory Bangle Lady', was buried in York in the late 4th century. John Blanke was a paid royal trumpeter to Henry VII and Henry VIII from 1507 to 1512.

sources.title: Cumbria County History Trust: The first recorded African community in Britain
Yorkshire Museum: Ivory Bangle Lady
Historic Royal Palaces: John Blanke

points.heading: The Windrush generation came to Britain illegally, or were not British.
points.text: The British Nationality Act 1948 made people born in the UK and its colonies Citizens of the United Kingdom and Colonies, with the right to live here. The government's own review found the Windrush generation 'had every right to be here' and blamed the Home Office's 'institutional ignorance and thoughtlessness towards the issue of race'.

sources.title: Home Office: Windrush Lessons Learned Review (Wendy Williams)
The National Archives blog: Empire Windrush, 70 years on

points.heading: Africa had no written history or great civilisations before Europeans arrived.
points.text: Great Zimbabwe, a stone city built between 1100 and 1450, was the capital of a large state. Timbuktu was an intellectual and spiritual capital in the 15th and 16th centuries, and its libraries hold several hundred thousand manuscripts. Guinness World Records lists the University of al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, founded in 859, as the oldest higher-learning institution; its founding is traditionally credited to Fatima al-Fihri.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Great Zimbabwe National Monument
UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Timbuktu
Guinness World Records: Oldest higher-learning institution

points.heading: Africa is one country, with one culture.
points.text: Africa is a continent of 54 United Nations member states (the African Union has 55 members). Estimates of the number of languages range from about 900 to 2,000, depending on how languages and dialects are counted.

sources.title: Africa Check: How many countries in Africa?
Encyclopaedia Britannica: African languages

points.heading: When Britain abolished slavery, the enslaved were compensated.
points.text: The £20 million compensation went to enslavers (‘slave-owners’ in the law of the time), not to the people they had enslaved. HM Treasury says it was about 40% of government spending in 1833. Freed people were made to work unpaid as 'apprentices' until 1838. The borrowing became part of a government loan that was only finally redeemed in 2015.

sources.title: The National Archives: 1833 Abolition of Slavery Act and compensation claims
HM Treasury: FOI2018/00186, Slavery Abolition Act 1833
The Gazette: Samuel Sharpe and the Christmas Rebellion

points.heading: Enslaved Africans did not resist.
points.text: Resistance was constant, from daily defiance to revolution. The Haitian Revolution of 1791 to 1804 created the first country founded by formerly enslaved people. Nanny led Jamaica's Maroons against the British in the 1720s and 1730s. Samuel Sharpe's rising in 1831 and 1832 drew in up to 60,000 people.

sources.title: Britannica: Haitian Revolution
Jamaica Information Service: Nanny of the Maroons
The Gazette: Samuel Sharpe and the Christmas Rebellion

points.heading: Black people did not fight for Britain in the world wars.
points.text: About 15,600 men served in the British West Indies Regiment in the First World War, and more than a million African troops served in the Second. In 2021 the Commonwealth War Graves Commission found that 45,000 to 54,000 casualties had been commemorated unequally, and at least 116,000, possibly 350,000, were not commemorated by name. It attributed this to 'pervasive racism'.

sources.title: Imperial War Museums: How the West Indies helped the war effort in the First World War
History Workshop: African soldiers in World War II
Commonwealth War Graves Commission: Non-commemoration report

points.heading: Positive action is the same as positive discrimination, and it is illegal.
points.text: The Equality Act 2010 allows proportionate positive action to help people who are disadvantaged, have different needs or are under-represented. In hiring or promotion, an employer may prefer someone from an under-represented group only when candidates are 'as qualified as' each other, and not as a blanket policy. Appointing someone mainly because of a protected characteristic is generally unlawful.

sources.title: legislation.gov.uk: Equality Act 2010, section 158
legislation.gov.uk: Equality Act 2010, section 159

points.heading: Discrimination in hiring is a thing of the past.
points.text: In a 2019 field experiment covering nearly 3,200 real UK vacancies, applicants from ethnic minority backgrounds had to send 60% more applications to get the same positive response as white British applicants with the same CVs. The researchers found discrimination against Black British and Pakistani-heritage applicants unchanged since the late 1960s and 1970s.

sources.title: Nuffield College CSI: New report on ethnic minority job discrimination

points.heading: Race is a fixed biological category.
points.text: There is more genetic variation within self-identified racial groups than between them, and the American Association of Biological Anthropologists states that race does not accurately represent human biological variation. Race is a social classification, and racism has real effects.

sources.title: NHGRI: Race (genetics glossary)
American Association of Biological Anthropologists: Statement on race and racism

points.heading: 'BAME' is the right umbrella term.
points.text: Government guidance says not to use ‘BAME’ or ‘BME’. They emphasise some groups and leave others out, and can hide real differences between groups. Name specific ethnic groups wherever you can.

sources.title: Ethnicity facts and figures: Writing about ethnicity

points.heading: Black History Month is only for Black people.
points.text: UK Black History Month began in London in October 1987, conceived by Akyaaba Addai-Sebo at the Greater London Council. It marks contributions to British society, science, economy and culture that are shared history for everyone, with events in schools, libraries, museums and workplaces open to all.

points.heading: Afro hair is unprofessional, and banning it is fine.
points.text: Race is a protected characteristic, and treating someone badly because of a hairstyle linked to their race can be unlawful. In 2022 the Equality and Human Rights Commission said pupils should not be stopped from wearing natural Afro styles, and that bans without exceptions are likely to be unlawful. The Halo Code is a voluntary pledge for schools and workplaces.

The 'angry Black woman'
points.text: In experiments, when a Black woman expressed anger at work, observers put it down to her personality rather than the situation, and rated her a worse performer and a less capable leader. The same anger from others was judged differently.

sources.title: University of Arizona Eller College (via Newswise): the cost of the 'angry Black woman' stereotype at work

points.heading: 'Black pupils don't aim high'
points.text: In 2024, 48.0% of Black pupils in England entered higher education by age 19, against 29.8% of White pupils. In 2022/23 Black African pupils' average Attainment 8 score (48.7) was above the national average (46.3).

sources.title: Ethnicity facts and figures: Entry rates into higher education

points.heading: 'Black people aren't interested in science and tech'
points.text: More Black students have entered STEM study over the past decade, but Black people are more likely to leave science at every stage of the career path. The problem is retention and progression, not interest.

points.heading: 'Black people commit more crime'
points.text: In the year to March 2026, people identifying as Black or Black British in England and Wales were stopped and searched at 4.1 times the rate of White people; for males aged 18 to 34 the rates were 148.2 and 25.2 per 1,000. The year before, the rates were 22.4 and 5.9 per 1,000 (3.8 times). These figures measure police activity, not offending.

points.heading: 'Black candidates lack leadership qualities'
points.text: At 31 March 2025, 18.0% of civil servants were from ethnic minority backgrounds, a record high, but only 10.5% of the Senior Civil Service. The gap is at the top, not in the talent pool. In the Senior Civil Service, 105 of 7,775 staff were Black: about 1.4%, or 1.5% of those with a known ethnicity.

Cabinet Office: Civil Service Statistics 2025 data browser, ethnicity by responsibility level

points.heading: 'Black people feel less pain' or 'are stronger'
points.text: In a US study, about half of a sample of white medical trainees endorsed false beliefs such as Black people having thicker skin, and those who did rated a Black patient's pain lower. Separately, in England in 2022 to 2024, women from Black ethnic backgrounds had a maternal death risk about 2.7 times that of White women.

sources.title: Hoffman and others, PNAS (2016): racial bias in pain assessment and false beliefs about biological differences
MBRRACE-UK: Maternal mortality 2022 to 2024 data brief

points.heading: 'It's just banter'
points.text: In a 2022 TUC poll, two in five Black and minority ethnic workers had experienced racism at work in five years. Racist jokes or 'banter' was the most common form (27%); after the latest incident 35% felt less confident at work and 31% said it harmed their mental health. Psychologist Monnica Williams links microaggressions to prejudice in those who commit them and to harm to the mental health of those targeted.

sources.title: TUC: Still rigged, racism in the UK labour market (2022)
Williams (2020), Microaggressions: clarification, evidence and impact, Perspectives on Psychological Science 15(1)

points.heading: Kente-inspired strip weave
points.text: Narrow strips woven on a loom and sewn edge to edge into one cloth. Colours and named designs carry meanings, and some were reserved for royalty.

points.heading: Adinkra stamped cloth
points.text: Symbols stamped on cloth with carved calabash stamps; each carries a proverb or idea.

points.heading: Sankofa
points.text: Often read as "go back and fetch it": return to the past to carry forward what you need.

points.heading: Nkonsonkonson
points.text: Chain links: unity, human relations and shared responsibility.

points.heading: Bògòlanfini-inspired mud cloth
points.text: Cotton cloth dyed with plant dyes and fermented mud. Motifs can record events, proverbs and status.

points.heading: Kuba-inspired raffia cloth
points.text: Raffia textiles embroidered and appliquéd with interlacing geometric patterns, used as prestige cloth and in ceremonies.

points.heading: Ndebele-inspired painting
points.text: Bold geometric house painting and beadwork, traditionally made by women, with strong black outlines.

points.heading: East African beadwork-inspired rows
points.text: Colour and arrangement can signal age set, marital status and community.

points.heading: Tibeb-inspired woven border
points.text: Colourful woven borders on cotton garments such as the habesha kemis and netela.

points.heading: Ge'ez script
points.text: An African writing system used for Ge'ez, Amharic and Tigrinya. The word shown is "Ge'ez".

points.heading: Amazigh-inspired lozenges
points.text: Lozenges, chevrons and lines found in weaving, pottery, jewellery and tattoos.

points.heading: Yaz (ⵣ)
points.text: The letter yaz, used as a symbol of the Amazigh people and often read as "free person".

points.heading: Ankh
points.text: The hieroglyph for life. Widely used across the diaspora as a sign of African heritage.

points.heading: Baobab
points.text: A long-lived tree that is often a meeting place where communities gather, talk and settle disputes.

points.heading: Cowrie shell
points.text: Shells used as currency and in divination. Their trade linked the Indian Ocean and Atlantic worlds.

points.heading: Improvisational quilt blocks
points.text: Patchwork built from available cloth with bold, improvised geometry, passed down through families.

points.heading: Naming ceremonies
points.text: Many communities name a baby around a week after birth, when elders give names that carry meaning, family history or hopes. Akan families hold an 'outdooring' on the eighth day.

points.heading: Libation
points.text: Pouring a drink on the ground to honour the ancestors and ask their blessing at gatherings. Ask before including it; it is sacred to many.

points.heading: Griots (jeliw)
points.text: Hereditary historians, musicians and praise singers who keep genealogies and history alive in song, often with the kora.

points.heading: Indaba
points.text: A gathering of leaders to discuss important matters. The word is now used for conferences, such as the Deep Learning Indaba.

points.heading: Coffee ceremony (buna)
points.text: Green beans are roasted, ground and brewed in a clay jebena, then served in three rounds. It is a daily way of gathering with relatives, neighbours and visitors.

points.heading: New Yam Festival (Iri Ji)
points.text: A thanksgiving for the harvest, when the first yams are offered and shared before the community eats the new crop.

points.heading: Homowo
points.text: A harvest festival whose name means 'hooting at hunger', remembering a famine overcome long ago.

points.heading: Gerewol
points.text: A yearly gathering where young men in elaborate make-up and dress dance to be chosen by young women.

points.heading: Carnival
points.text: Masquerade, steel pan, calypso and soca, with deep roots in emancipation celebrations.

points.heading: Junkanoo and Jonkonnu
points.text: Street parades with costumes and drums at Christmas and New Year, begun by enslaved Africans.

points.heading: Crop Over
points.text: A festival marking the end of the sugar cane harvest, now the island's biggest celebration.

points.heading: Nine Night
points.text: Several nights of gathering after a death, ending on the ninth with songs, stories and food to send the spirit on.

points.heading: Kwanzaa
points.text: A week-long celebration from 26 December to 1 January, created in 1966, built on seven principles including Umoja (unity) and Kuumba (creativity).

points.heading: Jumping the broom
points.text: Couples jump over a broom at their wedding, a custom remembered from slavery, when marriages were not legally recognised. Its origins are debated.

points.heading: Black History Month
points.text: An annual commemoration in October in the UK of the history, achievements and contributions of Black people in Britain. First held in London in 1987. In the US and Canada it is held in February.

points.heading: Honouring Our Communities
points.text: The 2026 national theme, which asks people to recognise the everyday contributors who sustain Black life across the UK.

points.heading: Windrush generation
points.text: People who came to the UK from Caribbean countries between 1948 and 1971, named after the Empire Windrush.

points.heading: Public Sector Equality Duty
points.text: The duty in section 149 of the Equality Act 2010 for public bodies to have due regard to eliminating discrimination, advancing equality of opportunity and fostering good relations.

points.heading: Race Relations Acts
points.text: UK laws of 1965, 1968 and 1976 against racial discrimination, later brought into the Equality Act 2010.

points.heading: Institutional racism
points.text: As defined in the 1999 Macpherson report: the collective failure of an organisation to provide an appropriate and professional service to people because of their colour, culture or ethnic origin.

points.heading: Race champion
points.text: A senior leader who sponsors race equality across an organisation and works with staff networks.

points.heading: Staff network
points.text: An employee-led group that supports members and advises the organisation. Network work should be recognised in objectives and time.

points.heading: Adinkra
points.text: Visual symbols of the Akan people of Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire, each carrying a proverb or concept.

points.heading: Sankofa
points.text: An Adinkra symbol meaning, roughly, go back and fetch it: learn from the past to build the future.

points.heading: Nkonsonkonson
points.text: An Adinkra chain-link symbol of unity and human relations.

points.heading: Kente
points.text: Strip-woven cloth associated with the Asante and Ewe peoples of Ghana and Togo. Specific patterns have names and meanings.

points.heading: Pan-Africanism
points.text: A movement for the unity and self-determination of African peoples on the continent and in the diaspora.

points.heading: Tokenism
points.text: Visible gestures towards inclusion without real change, such as asking one person to represent a whole group.

points.heading: Special category data
points.text: Under UK GDPR, data revealing racial or ethnic origin needs extra protection and a lawful condition to process. Get consent and advice before publishing it.

points.heading: Diaspora
points.text: People living outside the homeland of their ancestors who keep a connection to it. The African diaspora was shaped by forced removal as well as by migration.

points.heading: Maroon
points.text: A person who escaped slavery and joined a free settlement, or a descendant of such communities, as in Jamaica, Suriname and Colombia.

points.heading: Creole language
points.text: A language formed from contact between languages that becomes a community's first language, such as Haitian Creole, Jamaican Patwa or Palenquero.

points.heading: Reparations
points.text: Measures to repair a serious wrong. In international law they can include restitution, compensation, rehabilitation, satisfaction (such as an apology) and guarantees that it will not happen again.

points.heading: Equality
points.text: Treating people fairly and giving them the same rights and opportunities. In law, protection from discrimination.

points.heading: Equity
points.text: Giving people what they need to reach fair outcomes, which can mean different support for different people.

points.heading: Inclusion
points.text: Making sure people can take part fully and feel they belong, not only that they are present.

points.heading: Accessibility
points.text: Designing so that as many people as possible can use something, including disabled people. Public sector websites must meet WCAG accessibility standards.

points.heading: Intersectionality
points.text: How different parts of a person's identity, such as race, sex, disability and class, combine to shape their experience of advantage or discrimination.

points.heading: Digital exclusion
points.text: Not being able to use online services because of cost, skills, access, disability or confidence.

points.heading: Section 75 duty
points.text: The equality duty on public authorities in Northern Ireland under section 75 of the Northern Ireland Act 1998.

points.heading: Socio-economic duty
points.text: A duty to consider how decisions can reduce inequalities caused by socio-economic disadvantage. In force in Scotland (Fairer Scotland Duty) and Wales.

points.heading: Griot (jeli)
points.text: A West African hereditary historian, musician and praise singer who keeps family and community history in song.

points.heading: Indaba
points.text: A gathering of leaders to discuss important matters, from Zulu and Xhosa tradition.

points.heading: Libation
points.text: Pouring a drink on the ground to honour ancestors at a gathering. Sacred in many communities; ask before including it.

points.heading: Ubuntu
points.text: A Nguni Bantu idea of shared humanity, often glossed as "I am because we are".

points.heading: Race
points.text: A way of grouping people, mostly by appearance and supposed ancestry, that societies created. Scientists regard it as a social category, not a biological one. In UK law it is a protected characteristic that includes colour, nationality and ethnic or national origins.

points.heading: Ethnicity
points.text: Belonging to a group with shared ancestry, culture, language, history or nationality. It is self-defined: in UK statistics a person's ethnic group is the one they say they belong to.

points.heading: Enslaved person
points.text: Preferred to 'slave', because it describes what was done to a person rather than defining them by it. 'Enslaver' is preferred to 'slave owner' or 'master'.

points.heading: Amazigh (Imazighen)
points.text: The name the Indigenous peoples of North Africa use for themselves; often called 'Berber', a name many regard as an outsider's label.

points.heading: NEET
points.text: Not in education, employment or training. The official measure covers 16 to 24 year olds; councils in England also track 16 and 17 year olds. It describes a status, not a person.

points.heading: BEET
points.text: Being in Education, Employment or Training: the default engaged state, not tracked individually once things go well. A term used in public-sector work on young people's journeys.

points.heading: CHEET
points.text: Child Held in Early years, Education or Training: a child held by the state or by someone other than their parents, such as in care, custody or treatment. A term used in public-sector work on young people's journeys.

points.heading: Departure event
points.text: The point where a child leaves a system, or a system stops seeing them: for example exclusion, deregistration for home education, leaving care at 18 or leaving custody.

points.heading: Adultification
points.text: When children, often Black children, are not given the presumption of innocence and vulnerability that childhood should bring, and are treated as older than they are.

points.heading: Political blackness
points.text: The use of 'Black' in 1960s to 1980s Britain as a shared political identity for people of African, Caribbean and South Asian heritage organising against racism. It has since largely fallen out of use.

points.heading: Négritude
points.text: A literary and cultural movement begun in Paris in the 1930s by French-speaking African and Caribbean writers, affirming Black culture against colonial assimilation.

points.heading: Pan-Africanism
points.text: The idea that people of African descent share common interests and should unite. The Fifth Pan-African Congress met in Manchester in 1945.

points.heading: Hypodescent ('one-drop rule')
points.text: A custom, later written into some US laws, of classing anyone with any African ancestry as Black.

points.heading: Preto and pardo
points.text: Census categories in Brazil: preto (Black) and pardo (brown, often of mixed heritage). Together they are often called negros.

points.heading: Pardner
points.text: A rotating savings scheme: members pay in together and take turns to receive the pot. Caribbean communities in Britain used it when banks shut them out.

points.heading: The diaspora as Africa's 'sixth region'
points.text: The African Union's description of the African diaspora, alongside its five regions on the continent.

points.heading: DEEIA
points.text: Diversity, equity, equality, inclusion and accessibility: five related but different ideas. See the DEEIA lens page.

points.heading: Positive action
points.text: Steps the Equality Act 2010 allows to help under-represented or disadvantaged groups, such as targeted training. Positive discrimination, such as quotas, is generally unlawful.

points.heading: WRES
points.text: The NHS Workforce Race Equality Standard: indicators that compare the experience of staff from Black and minority ethnic groups with White staff in NHS trusts.

points.heading: Senior Civil Service (SCS)
points.text: The most senior grades of the UK civil service, from deputy director upwards.

points.heading: Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard
points.text: A government standard for publishing records of the algorithmic tools public bodies use. It is mandatory for central government.

points.heading: African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA)
points.text: A free trade area among African Union member states; trading under it began on 1 January 2021.

points.heading: Developing Countries Trading Scheme
points.text: The UK scheme, since 19 June 2023, giving preferential access for imports from eligible developing countries, many in Africa.

points.heading: Self-verify
points.text: Runs every in-page check and its negative proof.

points.heading: Self-repair
points.text: Fills gaps in card grids and repairs accessibility attributes, then re-measures.

points.heading: Self-assess
points.text: Scores the hub against its traced requirements.

points.heading: Staleness check
points.text: Flags sources not checked in the last 12 months and calendar dates already past.

points.heading: Accessibility self-audit
points.text: Looks for images without text, unnamed buttons, unlabelled fields and skipped heading levels.

points.heading: Privacy self-scan
points.text: Scans the page for email addresses, phone and National Insurance numbers, and lists what this browser stores.

points.heading: Performance self-measure
points.text: Measures page size, elements and start-up time against budgets.

points.heading: Balance self-check
points.text: Checks that group pages show strengths as well as gaps, that disputed firsts are labelled and that debates show opposing views.

points.heading: Link self-audit
points.text: Counts external links, insecure links and sources that share a web address.

points.heading: Data self-heal
points.text: Finds items citing sources that do not exist, duplicate IDs and in-page links that go nowhere.

points.heading: Self-report
points.text: Writes a plain-English status report of every routine, ready to download or paste.

points.heading: Self-explain
points.text: Confirms that every dataset can show where its items come from, which page shows them and which check covers them.

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: How many countries?
points.text: The African Union has 55 member states, including the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic (Western Sahara). Morocco rejoined the AU on 31 January 2017. Somaliland governs itself but is not a recognised state.
points.note: The count depends on who is counting: Western Sahara's status is contested between Morocco and the Sahrawi Republic, and Somaliland is not recognised as a state.

sources.title: Member States | African Union
Africa Check: How many countries in Africa?

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Mainland and island states
points.text: Six AU members are island states: Madagascar, Comoros, Mauritius and Seychelles in the Indian Ocean; Cabo Verde and São Tomé and Príncipe in the Atlantic. Several other African islands belong to European states or are part of mainland African countries (see islands list).

sources.title: Member States | African Union

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: How many languages?
points.text: Linguists estimate that Africa has around 2,000 or more languages, roughly a third of the world's total. An Ethnologue-based count from 2009 gave 2,110 (31%), second only to Asia (2,322; 34%). Lower figures exist because experts disagree on where a dialect ends and a language begins.
points.note: Britannica gives a much lower range (900 to 1,500); counts depend on where a dialect ends and a language begins. 'About a third of the world's languages' is the safest statement.

sources.title: African languages: From Cape to Cairo, via Colchester (Dr Hannah Gibson, University of Essex)
Encyclopaedia Britannica: African languages

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Afro-Asiatic family
points.text: Spoken across North Africa, the Horn and parts of the Sahara and Sahel. It includes Arabic, Amazigh (Berber) languages, Hausa (Chadic), Somali and Oromo (Cushitic) and Amharic (Semitic).
points.note: Language count from Wikipedia: 'about 400' (Almansa-Villatoro & Štubňová Nigrelli) and 'Ethnologue lists 375'. These include Semitic languages spoken in Asia. Family counts on this page come from different sources and editions; do not add them up.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica: African languages
Afroasiatic languages (Wikipedia)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Niger-Congo / Atlantic-Congo family
points.text: The largest family in Africa by number of languages, covering most of West, Central, East and Southern Africa, including the Bantu languages such as Swahili, Zulu and Lingala. Linguists accept the Atlantic-Congo core; the wider Niger-Congo grouping is not proven.
points.note: The full Niger-Congo family is a hypothesis, not a proven grouping.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica: African languages
Niger-Congo languages (Wikipedia)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Nilo-Saharan family
points.text: A proposed family of around 210 languages along the Nile basin and central Sahara, including Kanuri, Dinka, Luo, Maasai and Songhay.
points.note: Not all linguists accept that these languages are related.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica: African languages
Nilo-Saharan languages (Wikipedia)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Click languages (Khoe, Kx'a, Tuu)
points.text: Click consonants are typical of the languages once grouped as 'Khoisan'. Linguists now see them as three separate families plus two isolates (Sandawe and Hadza in Tanzania). Clicks have also passed into Bantu languages such as Zulu and Xhosa.
points.note: Britannica's overview of African languages still says 'Khoisan family', but its own Khoisan article says the term should be used 'only in a loose typological sense' and not as a family in the strict sense.

sources.title: Khoisan languages (Wikipedia)

Khoisan languages, Encyclopaedia Britannica

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Austronesian Malagasy
points.text: Malagasy, spoken across Madagascar, belongs to the Austronesian family. Its closest relative is Ma'anyan, spoken on Borneo. Madagascar's people mainly descend from settlers who crossed the Indian Ocean, mixed with people of African descent.
points.note: Settlement dates vary (from the 5th century AD to the 7th to 13th centuries).

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Most linguistically diverse countries
points.text: Nigeria has over 520 native languages. Cameroon has at least 250 (Ethnologue has given 279; some accounts say around 600). The Democratic Republic of the Congo has an estimated 242, of which Ethnologue lists 215 as living languages.
points.figure: Nigeria 520+; Cameroon 250-279 (some accounts c. 600); DR Congo 215-242
points.note: Counts differ by source and edition. Cameroon estimates range from 247 to 279. These figures come from Wikipedia and an academic chapter, not from Ethnologue directly.

points.heading: Lingua francas
points.text: Shared languages help across these divides: Swahili in East Africa, Hausa in West Africa, Lingala in the two Congos, Nigerian Pidgin, Arabic in the north, plus English, French and Portuguese from colonial rule.

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Greatest human genetic diversity
points.text: Africa has more human genetic diversity than anywhere else. The usual explanation is that modern humans have lived there longest. One major study sampled 121 African populations.
points.note: Tishkoff and others, Science, 2009, as reported by Dartmouth.

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: How many ethnic groups?
points.text: There is no reliable count. Groups have subgroups, and sources disagree on whether a subgroup counts as its own group. Popular claims such as 'over 3,000 tribes' could not be traced to an authoritative source.
points.note: There is no reliable count. Groups have subgroups, and sources disagree on whether a subgroup counts as its own group. Popular claims such as 'over 3,000 tribes' have no authoritative source.

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Population and age
points.text: About 1.55 billion people lived in Africa in 2025, nearly one in five of the world's population. Africa is the youngest continent, with a median age of about 19.
points.figure: c. 1.55 billion; median age 19.3; 18.8% of world
points.note: Secondary source (Worldometer) reworking UN DESA World Population Prospects 2024; the UN DESA data portal itself was not opened. Quote these as 'about 1.5 billion' and 'median age about 19'.

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: The East African Rift Valley and human origins
points.text: Olorgesailie, a sedimentary basin in the East African Rift Valley in southern Kenya, is a long-studied site of human evolution: early humans lived between 1.2 million and 490,000 years ago and left large numbers of handaxes. Smithsonian research there links a period of landscape instability in the rift with a major shift in human behaviour and technology around 320,000 years ago. Tectonic activity also changed the size and location of the lakes and rivers early humans depended on.
points.note: The rift's length and extent, and wider claims that humans originated only in the rift, are not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Olorgesailie, Kenya | The Smithsonian Institution's Human Origins Program
Olorgesailie Drilling Project | The Smithsonian Institution's Human Origins Program
Climate Effects on Human Evolution | The Smithsonian Institution's Human Origins Program

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Africa's share of the world's population
points.text: In 2024 Africa had about 1.51 billion of the world's 8.16 billion people, about 18.5 per cent. On the UN's medium projection, Africa's share rises to about 25.5 per cent by 2050 and about 37.4 per cent by 2100.
points.note: Shares are calculated from UN World Population Prospects 2024 figures summed to continents by Our World in Data (2024: 1.514 billion of 8.162 billion). Figures for 2024 and later are medium-scenario projections, so they are modelled, not counted. The latest estimate, for 2023, gives about 18.3%.

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: The Berlin Conference, 1884-85
points.text: Fourteen states met in Berlin from November 1884 to February 1885. No African ruler was represented. They agreed rules for claiming African coasts ('effective occupation' and notifying other powers) and discussed the boundaries of the Congo Free State.

sources.title: Berlin West Africa Conference, Encyclopaedia Britannica
Berlin Conference 1884-5: Establishing the Rules of the Scramble for Africa (World History Encyclopedia)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Berlin did not draw the map
points.text: Despite the popular claim, the conference did not divide the continent. It set the rules. Most borders were set through hundreds of treaties over some 40 years from the 1860s, many of them after Berlin, and surveyed on the ground later still.
points.note: Corrects the common myth that 'Berlin drew Africa's borders'.

sources.title: Berlin Conference 1884-5: Establishing the Rules of the Scramble for Africa (World History Encyclopedia)
Michalopoulos & Papaioannou, The Long-Run Effects of the Scramble for Africa (CAGE working paper 162, 2013; published AER 2016)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Speed of the Scramble
points.text: European control grew from about 10% of Africa around 1870 to about 90% by 1914, by which time only Ethiopia and Liberia (and, by some accounts, the Dervish state in Somaliland) were still independent. Italy occupied Ethiopia from 1936.
points.note: Round figures from an openly licensed teaching text; they are widely repeated but are not precise measurements.

sources.title: Involvement in Africa before 1884 (Lumen Learning / SUNY World History)
Scramble for Africa (Wikipedia)

points.heading: Seven colonial powers
points.text: Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, Portugal, Spain and the United Kingdom took territory.

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Straight-line borders
points.text: Many African borders follow straight lines of latitude and longitude. One widely cited estimate (Alesina, Easterly and Matuszeski, as cited by Michalopoulos and Papaioannou) puts this at 80%, more than in any other part of the world. A '44%' figure is also often repeated, but we could not trace it to a source.
points.figure: 80% (as cited by Michalopoulos & Papaioannou from Alesina et al.)
points.note: Figures vary with the method: share of border length or number of segments, and how 'straight' is defined.

sources.title: Michalopoulos & Papaioannou, The Long-Run Effects of the Scramble for Africa (CAGE working paper 162, 2013; published AER 2016)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Partitioned peoples
points.text: In one major study, 231 ethnic groups had at least 10% of their homeland split between modern states. That is just over a quarter (about 28%) of the 834 groups mapped.
points.note: Based on Murdock's 1959 ethnographic map, which has its own limits. With a 5% threshold the count rises to 267; the paper's baseline sample has 826 populated areas, 230 of them partitioned.

sources.title: Michalopoulos & Papaioannou, The Long-Run Effects of the Scramble for Africa (CAGE working paper 162, 2013; published AER 2016)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Partition and conflict
points.text: The study found more violence in the homelands of partitioned groups, including about 40% more violence against civilians.
points.note: The authors treat the Scramble as a 'quasi-natural experiment' and argue the effect is causal. The finding rests on Murdock's 1959 map and conflict data for 1997-2010, and it is an average across areas, not a rule for any one border. Conflict has many causes; borders are one factor among several.

sources.title: Michalopoulos & Papaioannou, The Long-Run Effects of the Scramble for Africa (CAGE working paper 162, 2013; published AER 2016)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Not all borders were arbitrary
points.text: The same authors say not every border was random. In a few cases Europeans took existing political units into account (for example Eswatini, then Swaziland, Burundi and parts of Uganda), and referendums were held on the Cameroon-Nigeria and Ghana-Togo borders.
points.note: The same paper finds that 'in the overwhelming majority of cases, European powers drew borders without taking into account local conditions'.

sources.title: Michalopoulos & Papaioannou, The Long-Run Effects of the Scramble for Africa (CAGE working paper 162, 2013; published AER 2016)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: OAU Cairo resolution, 1964
points.text: In July 1964 African heads of state agreed to keep the borders they had at independence, judging that border problems were 'a grave and permanent factor of dissention'; the legal idea is known as uti possidetis. Somalia and Morocco did not accept the colonial borders, and Ghana and Togo objected to the line dividing the Ewe.
points.note: The term 'uti possidetis' does not appear in the resolution text.

sources.title: AHG/Res. 16(I) Border Disputes Among African States (OAU, Cairo 1964)
Michalopoulos & Papaioannou, The Long-Run Effects of the Scramble for Africa (CAGE working paper 162, 2013; published AER 2016)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Later border changes
points.text: Borders have changed only rarely since independence. Eritrea joined the UN in 1993 after a referendum, and South Sudan in 2011.
points.note: Years are UN admission dates.

sources.title: Member States | United Nations

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Settling disputes by law: Bakassi
points.text: In 2002 the International Court of Justice ruled that the Bakassi peninsula belongs to Cameroon, based on a 1913 Anglo-German agreement.

sources.title: International Court of Justice gives judgment in Cameroon-Nigeria boundary dispute (UN press release ICJ/603, 2002)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Transatlantic trade in enslaved Africans
points.text: From 1501 to 1875 about 12.5 million Africans were forced onto ships bound for the Americas. About 10.7 million survived the Middle Passage.
points.figure: c. 12.5 million embarked; c. 10.7 million arrived
points.note: These estimates come from the Slave Voyages database, built from surviving records, so the true numbers may be higher.

sources.title: Gross Injustice (HUMANITIES, NEH, Sept/Oct 2010)
Global African Diaspora of Slave Origin: slave trade tables (Boston University African Studies Center, 2023)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Trans-Saharan trade
points.text: Enslaved people were also taken north across the Sahara over more than a thousand years. One estimate is about 7.4 million between 650 and 1900.
points.note: Lovejoy's estimate. Records are much thinner than for the Atlantic trade, so the uncertainty is large.

sources.title: Global African Diaspora of Slave Origin: slave trade tables (Boston University African Studies Center, 2023)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Red Sea and Indian Ocean trades
points.text: Others were taken from the Red Sea and East African coasts to Arabia, the Gulf and India, about 3.3 to 4 million between 800 and 1896.
points.note: Wide ranges reflect sparse records (Lovejoy; Allen).

sources.title: Global African Diaspora of Slave Origin: slave trade tables (Boston University African Studies Center, 2023)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Congo Free State
points.text: Leopold II ran the Congo Free State as his personal venture until Belgium annexed it in 1908, amid protests over killings and atrocities carried out on a mass scale by his agents. The number of deaths is not confirmed by the sources cited.
points.note: Death toll estimates vary widely; avoid quoting a single figure.

sources.title: Congo Free State (Wikipedia)
DR Congo country profile - BBC News

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Herero and Nama genocide, 1904-08
points.text: German colonial forces killed tens of thousands of Herero and Nama people in present-day Namibia between 1904 and 1908. Estimates suggest about 80% of the Herero died; South African History Online gives 65,000-80,000 Herero and around 10,000 Nama deaths. In 2021 Germany said it would recognise the killings as genocide.
points.note: Shares are estimates. NPR reported a commitment of '$1.3 billion, largely on development projects'; others report €1.1 billion. Namibian groups have criticised the agreement.

sources.title: Germany Officially Recognizes It Committed Genocide In Present-Day Namibia (NPR, 28 May 2021)
Herero Revolt 1904-1907 (South African History Online, updated 20 Jul 2026)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Kenya: the Emergency, 1952-60
points.text: During the Mau Mau uprising, British authorities detained tens of thousands of people and forced over a million Kikuyu into guarded villages. In 2013 the UK government recognised that 'Kenyans were subject to torture and other forms of ill treatment at the hands of the colonial administration', and settled claims from 5,228 people for £19.9 million while continuing to deny legal liability.
points.note: The total number detained is disputed. The figure of over a million people moved into guarded villages rests on Wikipedia.

sources.title: Statement to Parliament on settlement of Mau Mau claims (Foreign and Commonwealth Office, GOV.UK, 6 June 2013)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Apartheid forced removals
points.text: Over 3.5 million people were forcibly removed in South Africa under apartheid laws, including the Group Areas Act (1950-1991).
points.note: Surplus People Project count (1983 report), covering removals up to about 1982.

sources.title: Forced Removals in South Africa (South African History Online)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Biafra, 1967-70
points.text: During Nigeria's civil war, starvation and disease followed the fighting; estimates of deaths generally range from 500,000 to 3 million. Many people were displaced.
points.note: Estimates range widely.

sources.title: Biafra | Britannica

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Rwanda, 1994
points.text: More than a million people are estimated to have died in the genocide against the Tutsi. Afterwards, officials, soldiers and militia who had taken part fled into what is now DR Congo, taking 1.4 million civilians with them, most of them Hutu.
points.note: Death toll estimates vary (often 500,000 to over 1 million).

sources.title: Outreach Programme on the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda: historical background (UN)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Ethiopia: Tigray war, 2020-22
points.text: Tension between the federal government and the Tigray region led to armed conflict in 2020, with Eritrean troops intervening; a peace deal was signed in 2022. Death and displacement estimates are not confirmed by the sources cited.
points.note: Very uncertain.

sources.title: Tigray war (Wikipedia)
Ethiopia country profile - BBC News

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Sudan, 2023 onwards
points.text: The war that began in April 2023 created the world's largest internal displacement crisis, with over 12 million people displaced by the end of 2024. At the end of 2025 about 9.1 million were still internally displaced.
points.note: The figures measure different things: total displaced including refugees, versus people still internally displaced.

sources.title: Regional update - East and Horn of Africa and the Great Lakes (UNHCR, 24 Feb 2025)
IDMC GRID 2026 Global Report on Internal Displacement (PDF, May 2026)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Sub-Saharan Africa today: internal displacement
points.text: At the end of 2025, 31.7 million people were internally displaced in sub-Saharan Africa, almost 39% of the world total. Of 17.3 million new movements in 2025, conflict caused 14.5 million (83%) and disasters about 2.9 million.
points.note: Movements count events, not people; one person can be displaced more than once.

sources.title: IDMC GRID 2026 Global Report on Internal Displacement (PDF, May 2026)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: DR Congo, 2025
points.text: The Democratic Republic of the Congo recorded a record 9.7 million displacement movements in 2025, two-thirds of all conflict displacement in the region.

sources.title: IDMC GRID 2026 Global Report on Internal Displacement (PDF, May 2026)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Disasters: floods, cyclones, drought
points.text: Cyclone Idai (2019) killed at least 1,593 people across south-east Africa. Freddy (2023), at 36 days, was the longest-lasting tropical cyclone on record, according to the World Meteorological Organization. In 2025, back-to-back cyclones caused 826,000 movements and South Sudan's floods over 487,000.
points.note: IDMC notes that drought displacement in the Horn of Africa fell in 2025 after several severe years.

sources.title: Cyclone Idai (Wikipedia)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Regional totals (UNHCR)
points.text: West and Central Africa: a record 12.7 million forcibly displaced or stateless (June 2025). East, Horn and Great Lakes: 26.3 million (end 2024). Southern Africa: 11.5 million people covered by UNHCR (May 2025).
points.note: Regional groupings and dates differ, so these cannot be added into a single Africa total.

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Most Africans move within Africa
points.text: Measures differ. UNDP says over 80% of African migration happens within the continent. The IOM and African Union put intra-African migration at 51% of emigration from African countries and 83% of immigration into them. Most refugees worldwide stay in neighbouring countries.
points.note: Counters the impression that most African migrants go to Europe.

sources.title: Africa Migration Report, second edition (IOM and African Union, 2024)
Common misconceptions about African migration (UNCTAD)
Scaling Fences: Voices of Irregular African Migrants to Europe (UNDP, 2019)
Global Trends (UNHCR; page served the 2023 edition)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Frame: the AU's five regions
points.text: The African Union groups its 55 members into five regions: North (7), West (15), Central (9), East (14) and Southern (10). The island states are split between them: Madagascar, Mauritius, Seychelles and Comoros are in East; Cabo Verde is in West; São Tomé and Príncipe is in Central.

sources.title: Member States | African Union

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: How the UN M49 scheme differs
points.text: The UN statistical scheme puts Sudan in Northern Africa (the AU puts it in East) and Mauritania in Western Africa (the AU puts it in North). Malawi, Mozambique, Zambia and Zimbabwe are 'Eastern Africa' in M49 but Southern in the AU. Angola, Chad and Cameroon are 'Middle Africa'. The UN says its groupings imply no political meaning.
points.note: M49 also places Réunion and Mayotte in Eastern Africa and Saint Helena in Western Africa.

sources.title: UN Statistics Division: Standard country or area codes (M49)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: 'North Africa' versus 'sub-Saharan Africa'
points.text: 'Sub-Saharan Africa' means the parts of Africa south of the Sahara. It is a standard grouping in UN (M49) and World Bank statistics. Some African scholars argue it has 'racialist origins and racist undertones' and implies a false divide between North Africa and the rest of the continent. Others keep it for statistical convenience. Its membership varies from 46 to 48 countries.
points.note: The criticism comes from the CODESRIA Bulletin (2022), an advocacy piece citing the scholars Adébísí, Chachage, Ekwe-Ekwe and Zeleza. The UN M49 scheme uses 'Sub-Saharan Africa' (code 202) as an official grouping; the AU organises its members in five regions.

sources.title: Whither 'Sub-Saharan Africa': Can We Use the Compass Instead? (CODESRIA Bulletin, No. 3, 2022, p. 57)
UN Statistics Division: Standard country or area codes (M49)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: The Sahara as a connector
points.text: The Sahara linked people as well as dividing them. Caravans crossed it along chains of oases, and towns such as Timbuktu and Agadez grew rich from the trade and became centres of Islamic learning.

sources.title: Sub-Saharan Africa (Wikipedia)
Timbuktu | Britannica
Historic Centre of Agadez (UNESCO WHC)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Religion across the continent
points.text: Northern Africa is mainly Muslim and southern Africa mainly Christian, and they meet in a broad belt from Senegal to Somalia. In sub-Saharan Africa, Christians grew from about 7 million in 1900 to 470 million in 2010, and Muslims from 11 million to 234 million. Traditional beliefs persist alongside both.
points.note: Figures are from 2010.

sources.title: Tolerance and Tension: Islam and Christianity in Sub-Saharan Africa, Pew Research Center, 2010

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Mediterranean Sea
points.text: Phoenician Carthage, Rome, Byzantium, the Arab caliphates and the Ottomans all linked Africa's north coast with Europe and the Levant. Today IOM records more migrant deaths there than in any other region it tracks.
points.note: See the Mediterranean region entry for details.

sources.title: Archaeological Site of Carthage (UNESCO WHC)
Missing Migrants Project (IOM) home page

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Strait of Gibraltar
points.text: The strait, about 13 km wide at its narrowest, links the Atlantic and the Mediterranean and separates Spain from Morocco.

sources.title: Strait of Gibraltar (Wikipedia)
Strait of Gibraltar | Britannica

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Suez Canal
points.text: The Suez Canal, completed in 1869, joins the Mediterranean and Red Seas across 193 km of Egypt. It cut Africa off from Asia by water and transformed sea routes around the continent.
points.note: Its nationalisation in 1956 is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Suez Canal | Britannica

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Red Sea, Bab-el-Mandeb and Gulf of Aden
points.text: Aksum controlled Red Sea trade through Adulis. The Bab-el-Mandeb strait, between Yemen and Djibouti/Eritrea, links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. On the 'Eastern Route' from the Horn to Yemen and the Gulf, 922 migrants died in 2025, almost all Ethiopian.
points.note: Reuters' wording ('from Yemen to the Gulf States') may refer only to the onward stage of the journey.

sources.title: Aksum (UNESCO WHC)
Bab-el-Mandeb (Wikipedia)
Almost 8,000 died on migration routes in 2025 but toll likely far higher, says UN agency (Reuters via AOL, 26 Feb 2026)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Indian Ocean and the Swahili coast
points.text: Monsoon winds made seasonal sailing between East Africa, Arabia and India possible. Swahili ports such as Kilwa and Zanzibar mixed African, Arab, Persian and Indian influences, and Austronesian sailors settled Madagascar.
points.note: Zanzibar was also a major East African slave-trading port.

sources.title: Indian Ocean trade (Wikipedia)
Stone Town of Zanzibar (UNESCO WHC)
Island of Mozambique (UNESCO WHC)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Mozambique Channel
points.text: The channel runs about 1,600 km between Madagascar and Mozambique. The Comoros mark its northern entrance, and Cyclone Idai formed over it in March 2019.

sources.title: Mozambique Channel (Wikipedia)
Mozambique Channel | Britannica
Tropical Cyclone Idai - Mar 2019 | ReliefWeb (UN OCHA)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Atlantic: Gulf of Guinea
points.text: The Gulf of Guinea coast was a centre of the Atlantic trade in enslaved Africans; the Portuguese built São Jorge da Mina (Elmina) in 1481. Its islands are Bioko, Príncipe, São Tomé and Annobón. Piracy and kidnapping remain a concern.
points.note: The Gorée claim is disputed (see West Africa). Elmina 1481 is confirmed on the Gulf of Guinea Wikipedia page.

sources.title: Gulf of Guinea (Wikipedia)
Island of Gorée (UNESCO WHC)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Atlantic: Canary Current coast and the Canaries route
points.text: The cool Canary Current runs past Morocco, Western Sahara and the Canaries. Today boats from Senegal, Mauritania and Morocco take the Atlantic route to the Canaries: over 1,000 people died on it in 2025.
points.note: Two IOM-based figures (1,047 in February 2026; 1,200+ in April 2026) reflect later updates. Use 'over 1,000'.

sources.title: Canary Current (Wikipedia)
Almost 8,000 died on migration routes in 2025 but toll likely far higher, says UN agency (Reuters via AOL, 26 Feb 2026)
The IOM reports nearly 8.000 migrant deaths or disappearances worldwide in 2025 (EMN Belgium, 21 April 2026)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: The Cape: where oceans meet
points.text: Cape Agulhas, Africa's southernmost point, marks the official boundary between the Atlantic and Indian Oceans.

sources.title: Cape Agulhas (Wikipedia)
Cape Agulhas | Britannica

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Myth: 'Berlin drew the map of Africa'
points.text: The conference set rules and settled Congo questions. Most borders came from later treaties and surveys, some of which continued into the 20th century.

sources.title: Berlin Conference 1884-5: Establishing the Rules of the Scramble for Africa (World History Encyclopedia)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Claim: 'borders alone explain Africa's conflicts'
points.text: Partitioned areas do see more violence, and the main study argues this is a causal effect. The same research says not all borders were arbitrary. Conflict also has causes in governance, resources, inequality and outside involvement. Few borders have changed since 1964, though some have been fought over and others settled in court (Bakassi, 2002).
points.note: Base rate: since 1964 only two new states (Eritrea and South Sudan) have been created by separation.

sources.title: Michalopoulos & Papaioannou, The Long-Run Effects of the Scramble for Africa (CAGE working paper 162, 2013; published AER 2016)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Claim: 'Africa has over 3,000 tribes'
points.text: No authoritative source for this number was found. Counts depend on definitions, and 'tribe' is widely seen as a loaded colonial term.

sources.title: Ethnic groups in Africa (Wikipedia)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Language counts vary
points.text: Estimates for Africa range from about 900-1,500 (Britannica) to over 2,000 (Ethnologue-based).

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica: African languages
African languages: From Cape to Cairo, via Colchester (Dr Hannah Gibson, University of Essex)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Slave trade figures are estimates
points.text: The transatlantic figures come from well-documented ship records. Saharan and Indian Ocean figures rest on far thinner evidence and come as wide ranges.

sources.title: Global African Diaspora of Slave Origin: slave trade tables (Boston University African Studies Center, 2023)

points.datasetTitle: Africa: peoples, regions, borders and displacement
points.heading: Displacement figures measure different things
points.text: IDMC counts movements (events) and stocks of internally displaced people; UNHCR counts refugees, asylum-seekers, IDPs and stateless people within its own regions; IOM counts recorded deaths, which are minimums. Do not add them together.

sources.title: 2026 Global Report on Internal Displacement (IDMC)

points.heading: Africa holds the most human genetic diversity
points.text: The 1000 Genomes Project (2015) found that people from African-ancestry populations carry the greatest number of variant sites. The H3Africa consortium describes Africa as containing more genetic diversity than any other continent.
points.note: Diversity is a property of populations, not a ranking of people. More variation means existing reference data, built mostly from European-ancestry samples, misses more of what is in African genomes.

sources.title: A global reference for human genetic variation (Nature, 2015)
Three Million African Genomes: A New Project for A New Generation (H3Africa)

points.heading: Tishkoff et al. 2009: 121 African populations
points.text: A major study of African genetic structure (Science, 2009) looked at 121 African populations, four African American populations and 60 non-African populations. It found 14 ancestral clusters in Africa that broadly match self-described ethnic, cultural and language groups. It estimated that, on average, African American ancestry was mostly from the Niger-Kordofanian cluster (about 71%, largely West and west-central African), with about 13% European and about 8% other African. Levels of mixed ancestry varied widely between individuals.
points.figure: 121 African populations; 14 ancestral clusters; ~71% Niger-Kordofanian, ~13% European, ~8% other African ancestry in African Americans (average)
points.note: The averages hide wide individual variation, which the paper itself notes. The suggested origin point near the Namibia–Angola coast comes from present-day diversity patterns and is a model estimate, not a fixed fact.

sources.title: The Genetic Structure and History of Africans and African Americans (Tishkoff et al., Science 2009)

points.heading: The deepest population splits: southern African ancient genomes
points.text: Schlebusch, Jakobsson and colleagues (Science, 2017) sequenced ancient southern Africans, including a Stone Age boy from Ballito Bay, South Africa. They estimated that modern human populations began to diverge 350,000 to 260,000 years ago. The oldest individuals were related to the descendants of southern Khoe-San groups.
points.note: Divergence dates are model-based estimates and differ between studies and methods. Khoe-San populations are often described as carrying the deepest-branching lineages among living people; that wording is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Modern humans emerged more than 300,000 years ago, new study suggests (Uppsala University, 28 Sep 2017)

points.heading: Ancient DNA from Africa
points.text: Skoglund et al. (Cell, 2017) analysed 16 prehistoric Africans and showed that the spread of farmers from western Africa replaced local hunter-gatherer populations entirely in some regions. Lipson et al. (Nature, 2022) added ancient DNA from eastern and south-central Africa covering about 18,000 years, and found deep structure going back to interactions roughly 80,000 to 20,000 years ago.
points.figure: 16 prehistoric individuals (2017); 6 new individuals plus 28 previously published, spanning ~18,000 years (2022)
points.note: Africa's heat and humidity degrade DNA, so ancient African genomes are still few. Lipson et al. reported six new individuals and re-analysed or drew on data from 28 previously published ancient individuals.

sources.title: Reconstructing Prehistoric African Population Structure (Skoglund et al., Cell 2017)
Ancient DNA and deep population structure in sub-Saharan African foragers (Lipson et al., Nature 2022)

points.heading: HapMap and 1000 Genomes African-ancestry samples
points.text: The International HapMap Project (from 2002) included 30 parent–child trios from the Yoruba in Ibadan, Nigeria.
