The 1000 Genomes Project (final paper 2015) included seven African-ancestry groups: Yoruba in Ibadan, Nigeria (YRI); Luhya in Webuye, Kenya (LWK); Gambian in Western Division, The Gambia (GWD); Mende in Sierra Leone (MSL); Esan in Nigeria (ESN); African Ancestry in Southwest US (ASW); and African Caribbean in Barbados (ACB).
points.note: A handful of groups cannot represent a continent of more than 2,000 ethnolinguistic groups. The Barbados (ACB) sample is one of the few Caribbean reference sets in widely used public data.

sources.title: About the International HapMap Project (NHGRI)
Population frequencies & genotypes (Ensembl)

points.heading: African Genome Variation Project (2015)
points.text: Led by the Wellcome Sanger Institute and African partners, the project (Nature, 2015) produced dense genotype data on 1,481 people and whole genomes for 320 people from 18 ethnolinguistic groups across sub-Saharan Africa.

sources.title: The African Genome Variation Project shapes medical genetics in Africa (Gurdasani et al., Nature 2015)

points.heading: H3Africa (Human Heredity and Health in Africa)
points.text: H3Africa grew out of a March 2009 meeting in Yaoundé, Cameroon, involving the African Society of Human Genetics, the NIH and the Wellcome Trust. It was announced in June 2010 and is supported by the NIH Common Fund and Wellcome, to fund African-led research on genetics, health and disease.
points.note: First funding awards followed the 2010 announcement; the year of the first awards is not confirmed by the sources cited. Nature News reported in 2018 that H3Africa was spending US$188 million over 10 years.

sources.title: Our History (H3Africa)

points.heading: Choudhury et al. 2020: 426 high-depth African genomes
points.text: An H3Africa study (Nature, October 2020) sequenced 426 people from 50 ethnolinguistic groups, including groups never sampled before, and found more than 3 million variants not previously described.
points.figure: 426 genomes; 50 groups; >3 million new variants (H3Africa press release: ~3.4 million; 13 countries)
points.note: The paper says 'more than 3 million'; the H3Africa press release says about 3.4 million and 13 countries.

sources.title: High-depth African genomes inform human migration and health, Nature, 2020
Genome Data from Africa Reveal Millions of New Variants (H3Africa)

points.heading: Uganda Genome Resource (2019)
points.text: A study in Cell (2019) used genome-wide data from 6,400 people in rural Uganda, including whole genomes for 1,978. LSHTM reported ten new disease associations, nine of which are found only in Africans. One variant, present in about 22% of Africans, is associated with glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c), a marker used to diagnose diabetes, so diabetes may be misdiagnosed in some Africans.
points.note: Partners included LSHTM, the MRC/UVRI and LSHTM Uganda Research Unit and the Wellcome Sanger Institute. Details are from LSHTM's announcement and the Cell abstract.

sources.title: Largest ever genome study of Africans could lead to new disease treatments (LSHTM)

points.heading: Three Million African Genomes (3MAG) proposal
points.text: In Nature (February 2021) Ambroise Wonkam (University of Cape Town) proposed sequencing three million African genomes over about a decade. He noted that fewer than 2% of human genomes analysed so far were from African people.
points.figure: 3 million genomes; ~10 years; ~$450 million a year
points.note: This is a proposal, not a funded or completed project.

sources.title: Sequence three million genomes across Africa (Wonkam, Nature 2021)

points.heading: African BioGenome Project (not about human DNA)
points.text: AfricaBP, started in 2021, sequences the genomes of African plants, animals and other species for conservation and sustainable use. It is affiliated with the Earth BioGenome Project. It is about biodiversity, not human genomes.
points.note: Included because it was in the brief; it should not be presented as human-genome research.

sources.title: African BioGenome Project

points.heading: 54gene: rise and collapse
points.text: 54gene, a Nigerian genomics company founded in 2019 by Dr Abasi Ene-Obong, aimed to supply genetic data on Africans for drug research. It raised $45 million but began shutting down in July 2023. In 2025 a Federal High Court in Lagos granted an injunction blocking the sale of its assets, which reportedly included biodata on 100,000 Nigerians.
points.note: Sources are tech news reports, not official records. The reasons for its failure and the status of the samples are contested in court.

sources.title: TechCabal Daily: 54gene shuts down
Nigerian court blocks sale of 54gene's assets, as founder claims investor wrongdoing (TechCabal)

points.heading: Large cohorts in the US
points.text: The NIH All of Us programme released nearly a quarter of a million whole genomes in 2023. About 45% of the data came from people who self-identify with a racial or ethnic group historically under-represented in medical research. The US Million Veteran Program has more than one million participants.
points.figure: ~250,000 genomes, ~45% from under-represented groups (All of Us, 2023); >1 million (MVP)
points.note: The All of Us figure covers all under-represented groups, not only people of African ancestry. The MVP page gave no ancestry breakdown.

sources.title: All of Us genomic dataset is world's largest and most diverse dataset of its kind (NIH)
MVP Home (US Department of Veterans Affairs)

points.heading: UK cohorts and initiatives
points.text: UK Biobank recruited 500,000 people aged 40 to 69 between 2006 and 2010. Our Future Health aims to bring together up to five million people and says it is building a community that reflects the UK population. Genomics England launched its Diverse Data initiative in September 2021 to tackle under-representation in genomic data.
points.figure: UK Biobank 500,000; Our Future Health up to 5 million
points.note: The sources cited do not give the number or share of participants of Black African or Black Caribbean ancestry.

sources.title: About us (UK Biobank)
Our Future Health
Health Secretary participates in Diverse Data Initiative aimed at reducing health inequalities (Genomics England, 20 Sep 2021)

points.heading: Caribbean and Black British data
points.text: Published, open reference data for Caribbean ancestry is thin. The main public sample is African Caribbean in Barbados (ACB) in 1000 Genomes. In the UK, the Sickle Cell Society reports sickle cell trait in about 1 in 4 West Africans and 1 in 10 Afro-Caribbeans, and notes it is also found in people with Mediterranean, Asian and Middle Eastern origins.
points.figure: Trait: 1 in 4 West Africans; 1 in 10 Afro-Caribbeans
points.note: The sources cited give no count of Black British participants in UK genomic cohorts.

sources.title: Population frequencies & genotypes (Ensembl)
About Sickle Cell and Trait (Sickle Cell Society)

points.heading: Popejoy and Fullerton 2016
points.text: In Nature (October 2016), Popejoy and Fullerton reported that the share of genome-wide association study (GWAS) participants of European descent fell from 96% in 2009 to about 81% in 2016 (non-European participants rose to nearly 20%). Much of the rise came from studies in Asia of people of Asian ancestry. African-ancestry samples were about 3%.
points.note: The 96% and 'nearly 20%' figures are from the authors' manuscript. The 81% and 3% figures are from reports of the article's chart (MIT Technology Review, Bio-IT World). In the text, African, Hispanic/Latin American and Indigenous samples together are under 4%. Percentages depend on whether studies, participants or samples are counted.

sources.title: Solving the lack of diversity in genomic research (MIT Technology Review)
Among the Multitude: A Look At The Complexity Of Diversity In Genetics (Bio-IT World)
Genomics is failing on diversity (Popejoy & Fullerton, Nature 2016; author manuscript, PubMed Central)

points.heading: Later estimates
points.text: Genomics England states that about 80% of GWAS participants are of European ancestry and only 2% of African ancestry. Mills and Rahal (Communications Biology, 2019) found GWAS participants were still mostly of European ancestry (88% in 2017). A 2021 King's College London blog notes that more than 70% of GWAS participants are both of European descent and recruited in just three countries: the US, the UK and Iceland. Fatumo et al. (Nature Medicine, 2022) set out a roadmap to increase diversity.
points.figure: ~80% European; ~2% African (Genomics England); 88% European in 2017 (Mills and Rahal)
points.note: Estimates differ (roughly 1% to 3% African ancestry; 78% to 88% European) because of different counting methods and dates. The exact Fatumo 2022 figures are not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Diverse Data (Genomics England)
A roadmap to increase diversity in genomic studies (Fatumo et al., Nature Medicine 2022)
A scientometric review of genome-wide association studies (Mills & Rahal, Communications Biology 2019)

points.heading: Consequences: risk scores, uncertain variants, misdiagnosis
points.text: Genomics England reports that some polygenic risk scores are about four times more accurate for people of European ancestry than for people of African ancestry. A 2026 Genomics England study of over 29,000 people with rare conditions found that, compared with people of European ancestry, people of East African ancestry had almost three times as many genetic changes flagged for review. Diagnosis rates were similar across ancestry groups once other factors were taken into account.
points.figure: Risk scores ~4x more accurate for European ancestry; ~3x more flagged variants for East African ancestry
points.note: Flagged variants that cannot be classified are often called variants of uncertain significance. They create extra work and uncertainty for patients.

sources.title: Diverse Data (Genomics England)
More diverse genomic datasets could improve equity in rare conditions diagnoses (Genomics England)

points.heading: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy misclassification (Manrai et al. 2016)
points.text: A Harvard study (New England Journal of Medicine, August 2016) found that genetic tests for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a heart condition, had misclassified variants as disease-causing in patients of African or unspecified ancestry. All the reported variants were later reclassified as benign. The variants were more common among Black Americans than white Americans, and including even small numbers of Black Americans in control groups would probably have prevented the errors.
points.note: The study used a single testing laboratory's records. Its findings show the risk of reference data that lacks diversity, not a difference in disease between groups.

sources.title: Imprecise Diagnoses (Harvard Medical School DBMI, 16 Aug 2016)
Genetic Misdiagnoses and the Potential for Health Disparities (Manrai et al., NEJM 2016; abstract)

points.heading: Sickle cell and malaria
points.text: Sickle cell disease is inherited and is more common in people with African, Caribbean, Mediterranean, south and southeast Asian, and Middle Eastern backgrounds. Carrying one copy (sickle cell trait) gives some protection against malaria. A CDC birth cohort study in western Kenya found the trait gave 60% protection against overall mortality, mostly between 2 and 16 months of age.
points.figure: Trait 1 in 4 West Africans, 1 in 10 Afro-Caribbeans; 60% protection against overall mortality (Kenya study)
points.note: Figures for the number of people living with sickle cell disease are under Intersections: disabled people, on the Life stages and identities page.

sources.title: Sickle cell disease (NHS)
Protective Effect of Sickle Cell Trait Against Malaria-Associated Mortality And Morbidity (CDC)
Sickle cell disease (MedlinePlus Genetics)

points.heading: APOL1, kidney disease and sleeping sickness
points.text: In 2010 NIH-funded researchers (Science) found that two APOL1 variants, common in people with African ancestry and absent from European chromosomes, raise the risk of kidney disease. Only the risk variants destroyed a parasite that causes African sleeping sickness in laboratory tests, so they are thought to protect against that infection.
points.note: Most people who carry two risk variants do not develop kidney disease (NIDDK); other factors are involved.

sources.title: Association of trypanolytic ApoL1 variants with kidney disease in African Americans (Genovese et al., Science 2010; abstract)
Story of Discovery: APOL1 Gene Variants (NIDDK, NIH)

points.heading: G6PD deficiency
points.text: About 400 million people worldwide have G6PD deficiency. It is most frequent in parts of Africa, Asia, the Mediterranean and the Middle East, and may give partial protection against malaria.
points.note: UK prevalence figures are not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency (MedlinePlus Genetics)

points.heading: Duffy-null and neutrophil counts (DANC)
points.text: People with the Duffy-null blood type often have lower neutrophil (white blood cell) counts but no illness. Duffy-null is most common in people with African or Arabian Peninsula genetic ancestry but is not exclusive to them. In the US, about two in three people who identify as Black are expected to have it. Standard reference ranges can wrongly label them as neutropenic, causing unnecessary tests or delayed chemotherapy. The American Society of Hematology runs a project to redefine reference ranges by Duffy status, and has published Duffy-null-specific ranges.
points.figure: ~2 in 3 people identifying as Black in the US expected to be Duffy-null
points.note: The older label 'benign ethnic neutropenia' is being replaced by 'Duffy-null associated neutrophil count', the term ASH uses. The date and origin of the renaming are not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Duffy-null Associated Neutrophil Count (DANC) (American Society of Hematology)

points.heading: Pharmacogenomics and the BiDil caution
points.text: Variants in genes such as CYP2C19, which processes at least 10% of commonly prescribed drugs, change how people respond to medicines such as clopidogrel. These variants occur in all populations at different frequencies, so testing the person works better than guessing from ancestry. BiDil, approved in the US in 2005 for heart failure in self-identified Black patients, was criticised as race-based medicine. FDA staff defended the approval on the basis of a trial in which self-identified Black patients had a 43% reduction in mortality.
points.figure: CYP2C19 processes at least 10% of common drugs
points.note: The approval date is from secondary sources citing the FDA's June 2005 announcement. Population frequencies of CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 variants by ancestry are not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: CYP2C19 gene (MedlinePlus Genetics)
BiDil for heart failure in black patients: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration perspective (Annals of Internal Medicine, 2007; abstract)

points.heading: Moving away from race-based clinical formulas
points.text: In September 2021 a joint task force of the US National Kidney Foundation and American Society of Nephrology recommended a new CKD-EPI kidney function (eGFR) equation without a race variable. In England, NICE guideline NG203 (2021) recommends the CKD-EPI creatinine equation and says not to use ethnicity as a risk factor for deciding who to test.
points.note: NICE NG203 says ethnicity should not be used as a risk factor for deciding who to test for CKD. NICE also removed its 2014 recommendation to adjust the eGFR equation for adults of African-Caribbean or African family origin, finding that adding an ethnicity adjustment may not be valid or accurate.

sources.title: Chronic kidney disease: assessment and management, NG203: rationale and impact (NICE)
NKF-ASN task force issues final report on use of race in diagnosing kidney disease (ACP Internist)
Chronic kidney disease: assessment and management, NG203 Recommendations (NICE)
NKF and ASN Release New Way to Diagnose Kidney Diseases (National Kidney Foundation, 23 Sept 2021)

points.heading: Genetic legacy of the transatlantic slave trade (Micheletti et al. 2020)
points.text: A 23andMe-led study (American Journal of Human Genetics, July 2020) analysed genetic data from 50,281 research participants and compared it with historical shipping records. African women contributed more than African men to present-day ancestry, although most enslaved people were men. Nigerian ancestry is over-represented in African Americans in the US, which the authors link largely to onward transport of enslaved people from the Caribbean.
points.note: The authors link the female bias to sexual exploitation of enslaved women. The research was done by a commercial company using its customers' data.

sources.title: Exploring the History of Slavery Through Genetic African Ancestry Data (Technology Networks, 24 Jul 2020)
Genetic Consequences of the Transatlantic Slave Trade in the Americas (Micheletti et al., AJHG 2020; abstract)

points.heading: Admixture in African Americans and Caribbean people
points.text: African Americans typically have mixed African and European ancestry in varying proportions. Tishkoff et al. 2009 estimated averages of about 71% Niger-Kordofanian (largely West and west-central African), 13% European and 8% other African, with wide variation between individuals. Caribbean populations also show mixed African, European and other ancestries, which is why 1000 Genomes includes an African Caribbean sample from Barbados.
points.figure: ~71% Niger-Kordofanian, ~13% European, ~8% other African (African American average, 2009)
points.note: The sources cited give no admixture proportions for Caribbean or Black British populations.

sources.title: The Genetic Structure and History of Africans and African Americans (Tishkoff et al., Science 2009)

points.heading: Limits of commercial ancestry tests
points.text: Ancestry tests compare your DNA with reference databases that differ between companies and do not represent all populations equally. Results can differ between companies and show where a family originated rather than where it lived. With few African reference samples, tests cannot reliably name a particular ethnic group, town or village.
points.note: The final sentence is an inference from the reference-database limits; MedlinePlus does not say 'cannot name a village' in those words.

sources.title: What is genetic ancestry testing? (MedlinePlus Genetics)

points.heading: Scientific racism and what genetics actually shows
points.text: Britannica describes scientific racism as false or pseudoscientific claims used to justify European colonial rule. Genetic studies in the late twentieth century refuted the existence of biologically distinct races. NHGRI describes race as a social construct, with more genetic variation within self-identified racial groups than between them.
points.note: The American Society of Human Genetics also published a report on the field's history in 2023. Its content is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Scientific racism (Britannica)
Race | Definition, Ideologies, Constructions, & Facts | Britannica
NHGRI: Race (genetics glossary)

points.heading: Henrietta Lacks and HeLa cells
points.text: In 1951 doctors at Johns Hopkins took cells from Henrietta Lacks, a Black woman being treated for cervical cancer, without her knowledge or permission. Her cells, HeLa, became widely used in research. Johns Hopkins says it should have done more to work with her family, and that it has never sold or profited from HeLa cells. In August 2023 her family reached a confidential settlement with Thermo Fisher Scientific.

sources.title: Henrietta Lacks' descendants reach a settlement over the use of her 'stolen' cells (OPB/NPR, 1 Aug 2023)
The Legacy of Henrietta Lacks (Johns Hopkins Medicine)

points.heading: 'Helicopter research' and the H3Africa ethics guidelines
points.text: In 2018 the H3Africa ethics working group issued voluntary guidelines to counter 'helicopter research', where foreign scientists take samples and data from communities without lasting involvement. The guidelines say research should respect African values and benefit African citizens.

sources.title: African scientists call for more control of their continent's genomic data (Nature news via BioEd Online, 18 Apr 2018)

points.heading: Benefit-sharing, data sovereignty and capacity building
points.text: H3Africa's biospecimen sharing policy (2021) balances protecting participants with enabling research, and aims to make African researchers competitive in genomics. The contested 54gene asset sale raised concerns, reported by TechCabal from the founder's side of the dispute, that Nigerians' genomic data could pass to the highest bidder.
points.note: Details of Wellcome Sanger-funded training programmes are not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: H3Africa Biospecimen Sharing, Access and Release Policy (1 March 2021)
Nigerian court blocks sale of 54gene's assets, as founder claims investor wrongdoing (TechCabal)

points.heading: UK context: NHS Race and Health Observatory
points.text: In June 2024 the NHS Race and Health Observatory and the University of Nottingham published a review finding that Black, Asian and minority ethnic communities are poorly represented in genetic medicine research. It examined 70 policy and guidance documents (2017–2022). Its key recommendations include making research databases representative of the population and monitoring access to genetic services by ethnicity. Historical abuses by medical institutions have reduced trust.

sources.title: NHS Race and Health Observatory, genetic research report news (5 June 2024)

points.heading: Myth: genetics proves races exist
points.text: Genetic differences between populations are real but small, gradual across geography, and mostly found within groups rather than between them. No genes mark out the conventional race categories. Ancestry is a better description than race.
points.figure: Widely separated populations differ in about 6–8% of genes (Britannica)
points.note: Self-identified race can correlate loosely with ancestry, which is why it was used as a stand-in in medicine; this is a proxy, not a biological category.

sources.title: Race | Definition, Ideologies, Constructions, & Facts | Britannica
NHGRI: Race (genetics glossary)

points.heading: Myth: one gene decides a complex trait
points.text: Even well-known variants such as APOL1 raise risk rather than decide outcomes: most people with two APOL1 risk variants do not develop kidney disease. The Duffy-null example shows a normal variation being mistaken for illness. Complex traits also depend on environment and social factors.

sources.title: Duffy-null Associated Neutrophil Count (DANC) (American Society of Hematology)

points.heading: Where estimates differ
points.text: Shares of African-ancestry participants in GWAS range from under 1% to about 3%, and European-ancestry shares from about 78% to 88%, depending on source and year. New-variant counts for the 2020 H3Africa study are given as 'more than 3 million' (paper) and 'about 3.4 million' (press release). Dates for the emergence of modern humans are model estimates.

sources.title: Diverse Data (Genomics England)
Genome Data from Africa Reveal Millions of New Variants (H3Africa)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: Self-identification
points.text: Official statistics in the UK and the USA count ethnicity or race by asking people how they identify. The ONS describes ethnicity as multi-dimensional and subjective; the US Census Bureau says its race categories reflect a social definition, not a biological one.
points.note: Self-identification means the same person can answer differently over time or on different forms.

sources.title: ONS: Ethnic group, England and Wales, Census 2021
About the topic of race (US Census Bureau)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: A political and cultural identity
points.text: 'Black' has been used as a shared identity for people of African descent across many countries, and as a political banner. It is not a biological category (see the hub's DNA page). Some researchers study how African migrants take on, or resist, a Black identity after moving to Europe.

sources.title: Being and becoming black (Max Planck Institute for the Study of Religious and Ethnic Diversity)
The decision to capitalize Black (Associated Press)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: 'Political blackness' in Britain
points.text: From the 1960s to the 1980s, many activists of African Caribbean, South Asian and African heritage organised together under the word 'Black' to fight racism in housing, work, policing and schools. Groups such as Southall Black Sisters (mainly South Asian women, founded 1979) used the 'Black' banner.

sources.title: South Asian political Blackness in 1970s Britain (History Workshop, Saffron East)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: Why 'political blackness' fell out of use
points.text: Historians give several reasons. Some South Asian writers say claiming Blackness can feel like appropriating histories, such as enslavement, that are not shared. Others argue the umbrella could hide the specific experiences of Black women and people of African descent. Some trade unions still use 'Black' in the political sense.
points.note: Views differ: some see political blackness as a lasting model of solidarity; others think it has run its course. Both views are reported here.

sources.title: South Asian political Blackness in 1970s Britain (History Workshop, Saffron East)
To Be (Politically) Black and British (AAIHS Black Perspectives, Nicole M. Jackson)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: Négritude
points.text: Négritude was a literary and cultural movement that began in Paris in the 1930s among French-speaking African and Caribbean writers, led by Black students from French colonies including Aimé Césaire (Martinique) and Léon-Gontran Damas (French Guiana). It affirmed Black culture against French colonial assimilation.

sources.title: Négritude (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
Negritude (Britannica)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: Pan-Africanism
points.text: Pan-Africanism is the idea that people of African descent share common interests and should unite. The Fifth Pan-African Congress met in Manchester from 15 to 21 October 1945, with some 200 people attending and 87 delegates representing about fifty organisations.

sources.title: Pan-Africanism (Britannica)
Remembering the Fifth Pan-African Congress (LUCAS, University of Leeds, Christian Høgsbjerg)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: Black Consciousness (South Africa)
points.text: Steve Biko founded the Black Consciousness Movement in apartheid South Africa. It encouraged Black people to recognise their own dignity and self-worth. Biko died from injuries suffered in police custody in 1977.
points.note: Whether Black Consciousness included Coloured and Indian South Africans as 'Black' is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Steve Biko (Britannica)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: Capitalising 'Black'
points.text: Many publishers now write 'Black' with a capital B when it refers to people, to signal a shared identity rather than a colour. The Associated Press changed its style in 2020. UK government statistics guidance uses 'Black people' and advises against 'Blacks'.
points.note: Practice varies between publishers and countries, and whether to capitalise 'white' is still debated.

sources.title: The decision to capitalize Black (Associated Press)
PBS, other media companies, capitalize Black (PBS Standards)
Writing about ethnicity (Ethnicity facts and figures, GOV.UK)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: United Kingdom: census categories
points.text: In England and Wales, people first choose one of five high-level ethnic groups, including 'Black, Black British, Black Welsh, Caribbean or African', then a more detailed option such as African, Caribbean or Other Black. Mixed groups include 'White and Black Caribbean' and 'White and Black African'. Scotland's 2022 census used separate headings for 'African' and 'Caribbean or Black'.
points.note: Northern Ireland's census figures are not included here: they are not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: ONS: Ethnic group, England and Wales, Census 2021
Scotland's Census 2022: Ethnic group, national identity, language and religion

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: United Kingdom: 2021 numbers
points.text: In 2021, 2.4 million people in England and Wales (4.0%) identified as Black: 1.49 million Black African (2.5%), 623,000 Black Caribbean (1.0%) and 298,000 Other Black (0.5%). A further 513,000 identified as Mixed White and Black Caribbean (0.9%) and 250,000 as Mixed White and Black African (0.4%).
points.note: Totals differ by a handful of people between census tables because ONS adds small random changes to protect confidentiality.

sources.title: Ethnicity facts and figures: Population of England and Wales (Census 2021)
Census 2021 TS021 Ethnic group, England and Wales (ONS via Nomis)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: USA: the one-drop rule
points.text: For generations in the USA, a custom and later laws treated anyone with any African ancestry as Black (the 'one-drop rule', or hypodescent). Scholars say this limited people's ability to define themselves.
points.note: The exact dates of particular state laws are not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: The Devil and the One Drop Rule (Michigan Law Review, Christine B. Hickman, 1997)
Hypodescent (EBSCO Research Starters)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: USA: census categories today
points.text: The US census asks about race and Hispanic origin separately. 'Black or African American' is one of five minimum race categories, and since 2000 people can choose more than one race.

sources.title: About the topic of race (US Census Bureau)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: USA: a diverse Black population
points.text: Pew Research Center estimates 48.3 million people in the USA identified as Black in 2023 (14.4%). More than 5 million (about 11%) were born abroad. The total includes 5.6 million multiracial Black people and 3.0 million Black Hispanic people.
points.note: Pew warns that immigrants are slightly undercounted in the survey these figures use.

sources.title: Facts about the U.S. Black population (Pew Research Center)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: Brazil: preto and pardo
points.text: Brazil's census asks people to choose a 'cor ou raça' (colour or race): branca, preta, parda, amarela or indígena. In the 2022 census, pardo (brown, often of mixed heritage) became the largest group for the first time since the current series began in 1991, at 45.3% (92.1 million). 10.2% (20.6 million) identified as preto (Black). The Black movement in Brazil has long grouped pretos and pardos together as negros.
points.note: These figures are as reported by Brazilian news media from the national statistics office (IBGE) release; they are not confirmed directly from IBGE's own release.

sources.title: Número de brasileiros que se declaram pardos supera pela 1ª vez o de brancos (IstoÉ Dinheiro, reporting IBGE, 2023)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: The Caribbean and Canada
points.text: Caribbean migration shaped Black communities across the Atlantic. In Canada in 2021, Jamaica and Haiti were the top birthplaces of Caribbean-born Black people, and Statistics Canada stresses there is 'not one, but many' Black populations.
points.note: Detailed census definitions for individual Caribbean countries are not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Black History Month: celebrating diversity in Canada (Statistics Canada)
The Diversity of the Black Populations in Canada, 2021 (Statistics Canada)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: France: no ethnic statistics
points.text: France follows a 'colour-blind' model. A 1978 law restricted collecting race-based data, and France does not collect census data on race or ethnicity.
points.note: This source dates from 2001; debate in France about ethnic data has continued since, and current rules are not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Race policy in France (Brookings, Erik Bleich, 1 May 2001)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: South Africa: apartheid categories and their legacy
points.text: Under apartheid, the Population Registration Act of 1950 classified every South African by race. Statistics South Africa still reports 'population groups': in its 2022 census, Black African people were the largest group, followed by people classified as ‘Coloured’ at 8.2%. Some MPs have questioned continuing to use these terms.
points.note: The year the Act was repealed is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Population Registration Act (Britannica)
Briefing by Statistician-General on the Census 2022 results (Parliamentary Monitoring Group, South Africa)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: Afro-Latin Americans
points.text: About 130 million people of African descent live in Latin America, roughly a quarter of the population, according to Princeton's PERLA project as reported by Pew. Many Latin American countries only recently began counting race in their censuses.
points.note: Country figures for Colombia, Cuba and the Dominican Republic are not confirmed by the sources cited; estimates vary widely with how questions are asked.

sources.title: Afro-Latino: a deeply rooted identity among U.S. Hispanics (Pew Research Center, 2016)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: Afro-descendants in Asia and the Middle East
points.text: Communities of African descent live in India (Siddis, in Gujarat, Maharashtra, Telangana and Karnataka), Türkiye (Afro-Turks, descendants of enslaved Africans in the Ottoman Empire) and Iraq (Afro-Iraqis, mainly around Basra).
points.note: Population estimates for these communities are very uncertain; the Basra range is wide.

sources.title: Sahapedia: Who are the Siddis?
The Making and Unmaking of the African Community of Ottoman Izmir, 1870-1922 (University of Arizona)
Afro-Iraqis, climate change and environmental injustice in Basra (Carnegie Endowment, 2026)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: Within Africa
points.text: In Africa, most people are part of the majority, so 'Black' is rarely the main way they describe themselves. Afrobarometer surveys in 2021–2023 found 41% felt more connected to their national than their ethnic identity, 45% felt equally attached to both, and 14% put ethnic identity first.
points.note: The survey asked about national and ethnic identity, not about 'Black' identity; that Africans rarely use 'Black' at home is an interpretation, not a survey finding. North African experiences differ again.

sources.title: Africans struggle with interethnic trust but embrace coexistence (Afrobarometer, 2025)
Being and becoming black (Max Planck Institute for the Study of Religious and Ethnic Diversity)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: Growth since 2011
points.text: Between 2011 and 2021 in England and Wales, the Black African group grew from 990,000 to 1.49 million (about +50%). The Black Caribbean group grew from 595,000 to 623,000 (about +5%). The Black groups together grew from 1.86 million (3.3%) to 2.41 million (4.0%).
points.note: Percentage changes are calculated from the census counts. ONS says 2021's new write-in option for Black African means the two years are not perfectly comparable.

sources.title: ONS: Ethnic group, England and Wales, Census 2021
Census 2011 KS201EW Ethnic group, England and Wales (ONS via Nomis)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: African backgrounds people wrote in
points.text: The new write-in option showed the largest specific African backgrounds were Nigerian (271,000), Somali (151,000) and Ghanaian (113,000).

sources.title: ONS: Ethnic group, England and Wales, Census 2021

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: Country of birth
points.text: 1.59 million residents of England and Wales were born in Africa (2.7%). The largest countries of birth were Nigeria (270,768), South Africa (217,180), Kenya (134,944), Ghana (132,577), Zimbabwe (124,146) and Somalia (108,921).
points.note: Country of birth is not ethnicity. Not everyone born in an African country identifies as Black, and most Black people in the UK were born here. A breakdown of Africa-born people by ethnic group is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Census 2021 TS012 Country of birth (detailed), England and Wales (ONS via Nomis)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: Languages
points.text: Most people speak English as their main language. Among people whose main language is an African language, the largest were Somali (62,240), Tigrinya (22,825), Akan (19,757), Igbo (11,074), Amharic (10,834), Shona (10,773), Swahili (10,154) and Yoruba (9,942).
points.note: The census asked only for a person's main language, so it undercounts people who speak an African language alongside English.

sources.title: Census 2021 TS024 Main language (detailed), England and Wales (ONS via Nomis)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: Religion
points.text: Of people in the Black groups in England and Wales, about 67% said they were Christian, 17% Muslim and 8.5% no religion; 6.4% did not answer.
points.note: Percentages are calculated from census counts. The religion question was voluntary.

sources.title: Census 2021 RM031 Ethnic group by religion, England and Wales (ONS via Nomis)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: Where people live
points.text: About half (49.3%) of people in the Black groups in England and Wales live in London, where they make up 13.5% of residents. Outside London, the largest shares are in Manchester (11.9%), Birmingham (11.0%) and Nottingham (10.0%). In Lewisham the share is 26.8%.
points.note: The London share of 49.3% is calculated from the census counts.

sources.title: Census 2021 TS021 Ethnic group by region (ONS via Nomis)
Census 2021 TS021 Ethnic group by local authority (ONS via Nomis)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: Roman Britain: the Ivory Bangle Lady
points.text: A wealthy young woman buried in Roman York in the later 4th century AD had ancestral links to North Africa, according to scientific study of her remains.
points.note: Her ancestry was assessed from skull measurements; such methods have limits, and the finding is about ancestry, not how she saw herself.

sources.title: Celebrating Ivory Bangle Lady (York Museums Trust)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: Tudor England: John Blanke
points.text: John Blanke was a Black African trumpeter at the courts of Henry VII and Henry VIII, recorded in 1507 and pictured in the Westminster Tournament Roll of 1511.

sources.title: John Blanke: investigating a life (The National Archives)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: The Windrush generation
points.text: The Empire Windrush docked at Tilbury on 22 June 1948, bringing Caribbean passengers who, as citizens of the United Kingdom and Colonies, had the right to live and work in Britain.
points.note: The National Archives page gives two different passenger figures (1,072 total and 492); the number of Caribbean passengers is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Empire Windrush: Caribbean migration (The National Archives)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: African migration and refugees
points.text: African migration to the UK grew after many African countries became independent, and again from the 1990s. Somalia's civil war, from 1988, produced a large flow of refugees, many of whom came to Britain.
points.note: Dates and numbers for post-1960s African migration, and for Eritrean and Sudanese refugees, are not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Resilient women: what we can learn from Somali refugees in Britain (LSE, Joanna Lewis, 2021)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: UN Decades for People of African Descent
points.text: The UN's International Decade for People of African Descent ran from 2015 to 2024. A Second International Decade runs from 1 January 2025 to 31 December 2034, with the theme 'Recognition, Justice and Development'. The first decade led to the UN Permanent Forum on People of African Descent.

sources.title: International Decade for People of African Descent - Background

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: The African Union and the diaspora as a 'sixth region'
points.text: The African Union defines the African diaspora as people of African origin living outside the continent, whatever their citizenship, who are willing to contribute to Africa's development. The AU has recognised the diaspora as the 'sixth region' of Africa, alongside the North, South, East, West and Central regions.
points.note: The date of the AU decision is not confirmed by the sources cited; the 'sixth region' source is a 2016 Ghanaian news report.

sources.title: African Union Diaspora Division (CIDO)
African Diaspora acknowledged as 6th region in Africa by AU (MyJoyOnline, 2016)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: Black British Voices Project: belonging
points.text: The Black British Voices Project (University of Cambridge with The Voice and I-Cubed, 2023) surveyed over 10,000 Black Britons. 81% described themselves as British, but pride was split: 49% were proud to be British and 45% were not.

sources.title: Black British Voices: the findings (University of Cambridge, 28 September 2023)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: Black British Voices Project: work, health, education, policing
points.text: 88% reported racial discrimination at work. 95% said the school curriculum neglects Black lives. 87% expected worse healthcare because of their race, and 87% had little or no trust in the criminal justice system. 74% were uncomfortable with the label 'BAME'.
points.note: Participants volunteered to take part, so results may not represent all Black Britons exactly.

sources.title: Black British Voices: the findings (University of Cambridge, 28 September 2023)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: Faith and identity
points.text: 84% of Black British Voices participants described themselves as religious or spiritual. This fits census findings that most people in the Black groups report a religion.

sources.title: Black British Voices: the findings (University of Cambridge, 28 September 2023)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: EVENS survey (2023)
points.text: The Evidence for Equality National Survey, led by the Centre on the Dynamics of Ethnicity, found 40–50% of Black Caribbean, Any other Black, and White and Black Caribbean respondents reported racist abuse in public places. Over a third of Black Caribbean and Any other Black respondents reported discrimination from the police.

sources.title: Over a third of people from minority groups have experienced racist assaults, survey finds (University of Manchester, April 2023)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: Census 2021 on identity
points.text: The census lets people describe themselves. A new write-in option for Black African and an online search-as-you-type tool made it easier to self-define, which ONS says may partly explain some of the increases.
points.note: ONS or EHRC surveys on belonging and discrimination specific to Black groups are not confirmed by the sources cited here.

sources.title: ONS: Ethnic group, England and Wales, Census 2021

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: Categories are imperfect
points.text: Census categories mix race, nationality and culture, and change over time. People with the same family history may tick different boxes. The US Census Bureau says its categories include national origin and sociocultural groups.

sources.title: About the topic of race (US Census Bureau)
Facts about the U.S. Black population (Pew Research Center)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: Grouping African and Caribbean people
points.text: Combining Black African and Black Caribbean people into one 'Black' figure can hide big differences. For example, between 2011 and 2021 the Black African group grew by about 50% while the Black Caribbean group grew by about 5%. Government guidance prefers to refer to groups individually where possible.
points.note: Others argue a shared 'Black' figure is still useful for tracking racism that affects both groups. Both views are reported here.

sources.title: Writing about ethnicity (Ethnicity facts and figures, GOV.UK)
Ethnicity facts and figures: Population of England and Wales (Census 2021)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: Critiques of 'BAME'
points.text: The UK government no longer uses 'BAME' or 'BME' because they emphasise some groups and leave out others. The Commission on Race and Ethnic Disparities recommended stopping its use in March 2021. See the hub's Words matter page.

sources.title: Writing about ethnicity (Ethnicity facts and figures, GOV.UK)
Black British Voices: the findings (University of Cambridge, 28 September 2023)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: Where figures differ
points.text: Figures for the same group can differ slightly between tables, because of rounding and ONS's confidentiality adjustments. For example, the total Black population is 2,409,278 in one 2021 table and 2,409,280 in another. In 2011, the Black share was 3.3% when calculated from the total but 3.4% when rounded subgroup shares are added.
points.note: Differences are small and do not change the overall picture.

sources.title: Census 2021 TS021 Ethnic group, England and Wales (ONS via Nomis)
Census 2021 RM031 Ethnic group by religion, England and Wales (ONS via Nomis)

points.datasetTitle: What it means to be Black
points.heading: Survey limits
points.text: Large community surveys such as the Black British Voices Project give voice to many people, but they rely on volunteers. The researchers note that Black communities have historically been wary of reports on race.

sources.title: Black British Voices: the findings (University of Cambridge, 28 September 2023)

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: £25 billion a year from around 250,000 firms
points.text: The FSB estimated that in 2018 around 250,000 firms were led by ethnic minority entrepreneurs, generating £25 billion of gross value added.
points.note: Based on the government Small Business Survey. The figure covers all ethnic minority groups, not Black-led firms alone.

sources.title: Federation of Small Businesses: Unlocking opportunity: the value of ethnic minority firms to UK economic activity and enterprise (2020), hosted by the Enterprise Research Centre

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: The fastest-growing self-employed group
points.text: Across ethnic groups, Black and Black British self-employment grew fastest between 2011 and 2018.
points.note: Growth rate, not overall level: Pakistani and Bangladeshi workers had the highest self-employment shares.

sources.title: Federation of Small Businesses: Unlocking opportunity: the value of ethnic minority firms to UK economic activity and enterprise (2020), hosted by the Enterprise Research Centre

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: Higher entrepreneurial activity
points.text: Since 2002, ethnic minority entrepreneurs have typically reported higher rates of early-stage entrepreneurial activity than other people.
points.note: A pattern across survey years, reported by the FSB.

sources.title: Federation of Small Businesses: Unlocking opportunity: the value of ethnic minority firms to UK economic activity and enterprise (2020), hosted by the Enterprise Research Centre

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: Innovative and exporting
points.text: Ethnic minority businesses were more likely than other firms to have innovated recently and, in every UK region, more likely to export.
points.figure: 30% engaged in recent product or service innovation

sources.title: Federation of Small Businesses: Unlocking opportunity: the value of ethnic minority firms to UK economic activity and enterprise (2020), hosted by the Enterprise Research Centre

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: About 6% of SME employers are ethnic minority-led
points.text: In the government's 2024 survey, about 6% of small and medium employers were led by a team at least half from minority ethnic groups. That is little changed since 2015.
points.note: 2023 was 7%. The survey does not give a separate figure for Black-led businesses.

sources.title: Department for Business and Trade: Longitudinal Small Business Survey 2024: SME employers (published 25 September 2025)

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: Firms with no employees
points.text: In 2021, 4.9% of SMEs with no employees and 6.1% of SME employers were majority-led by people from an ethnic minority.
points.note: Groups all ethnic minority groups together as "All Other Ethnic Groups Combined". No Black-only figure is given.

sources.title: Ethnicity facts and figures: Leadership of small and medium enterprises (2021 data, updated 8 August 2023)

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: Black founders start up as successfully as white founders
points.text: The British Business Bank found that Black and white entrepreneurs succeed in starting a business at similar rates. The gaps appear after launch.
points.note: Quoted from the full report PDF, a copy hosted by a third party because the Bank's own page blocks automated reading. The report notes small sample sizes for some groups.

sources.title: Alone, together: entrepreneurship and diversity in the UK, full report PDF (British Business Bank and Oliver Wyman, 2020; copy hosted by Diversity UK)
Oliver Wyman press release on the British Business Bank report, 21 October 2020

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: More preparation, and spotting unmet demand
points.text: Black, Asian and other ethnic minority entrepreneurs invest more time and money developing their ideas than white entrepreneurs. One in six Black entrepreneurs starts a business after spotting a gap in products suited to them.

sources.title: Alone, together: entrepreneurship and diversity in the UK, full report PDF (British Business Bank and Oliver Wyman, 2020; copy hosted by Diversity UK)

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: Lower median turnover
points.text: Black business owners reported median turnover of £25,000, against £35,000 for white owners. For owners from a Black African background the figure was £17,000.
points.note: From the Bank's 2020 entrepreneur survey, taken during the first year of COVID-19. Median turnover only, not profit or growth.

sources.title: British Business Bank: Alone, together: entrepreneurship and diversity in the UK (2020)
Alone, together: entrepreneurship and diversity in the UK, full report PDF (British Business Bank and Oliver Wyman, 2020; copy hosted by Diversity UK)

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: Profit and aims
points.text: 72% of Black business owners reported making a profit the previous year, against 84% of white owners. About half of Black entrepreneurs met their non-financial aims, against nearly 70% of white entrepreneurs.
points.note: The Bank's later factsheet puts the non-financial aims figure at 49%.

sources.title: Alone, together: entrepreneurship and diversity in the UK, full report PDF (British Business Bank and Oliver Wyman, 2020; copy hosted by Diversity UK)
Unlocking the potential of diverse entrepreneurs – Factsheet

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: Gender and ethnicity compound
points.text: 37% of Black female entrepreneurs did not make a profit the previous year, against 16% of white male entrepreneurs.

sources.title: Alone, together: entrepreneurship and diversity in the UK, full report PDF (British Business Bank and Oliver Wyman, 2020; copy hosted by Diversity UK)

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: Finance stops ideas
points.text: Difficulty getting finance was the reason 39% of Black aspiring entrepreneurs, and 49% of Asian and other ethnic minority ones, gave for stopping work on a business idea.

sources.title: British Business Bank: Alone, together: entrepreneurship and diversity in the UK (2020)

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: Higher rejection and discouragement
points.text: Between 2018 and mid-2020, 52% of ethnic minority-led businesses that applied for finance were turned down, against 22% of white-led businesses. In 2021, 20% wanted to apply but were put off, against 8%.
points.note: Covers all ethnic minority-led businesses, not Black-led alone. The white-led comparison figures were read on the factsheet but are not in the quoted text.

sources.title: British Business Bank: Small Business Finance Markets Report 2021/22, factsheet

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: Systemic disadvantage, not only circumstance
points.text: After controlling for sector, money, human and social capital and access to finance, some disparities remain. The British Business Bank attributes this to systemic disadvantage.

sources.title: Alone, together: entrepreneurship and diversity in the UK, full report PDF (British Business Bank and Oliver Wyman, 2020; copy hosted by Diversity UK)

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: Discrimination and distance from formal support
points.text: The FSB reported that ethnic minority entrepreneurs sometimes face discrimination, and are often detached from formal support networks. They rely more on informal networks, especially in Black-led and mixed-led businesses.
points.note: Reliance on informal networks is also a strength: it is community infrastructure.

sources.title: Federation of Small Businesses: Unlocking opportunity: the value of ethnic minority firms to UK economic activity and enterprise (2020), hosted by the Enterprise Research Centre

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: Household wealth matters for everyone
points.text: Regardless of ethnicity, entrepreneurs with household income of £75,000 or more were more likely to make a profit than those under £20,000. Lower household income is more common among Black Caribbean and Black African entrepreneurs.

sources.title: Alone, together: entrepreneurship and diversity in the UK, full report PDF (British Business Bank and Oliver Wyman, 2020; copy hosted by Diversity UK)

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: Start Up Loans: up to £25,000 with mentoring
points.text: Government-backed personal loans of up to £25,000, with 12 months of free mentoring for first-time recipients. From 6 April 2026 the fixed rate is 7.5% and businesses trading for up to five years can apply.
points.figure: up to £25,000; 7.5%; up to 60 months trading
points.note: Terms change; check the live page before relying on them.

sources.title: Start Up Loans (British Business Bank): Start Up Loans
Start Up Loans: changes to interest rate and eligibility criteria

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: One in five Start Up Loans to ethnic minority founders
points.text: Of the first £1 billion lent since 2012, 20% (£201 million) went to people from Black, Asian and other ethnic minority backgrounds. The British Business Bank compares its 21% share with 4% of the overall SME population.
points.note: "Black, Asian and Other Ethnic Minority" excludes white minorities. No Black-only figure was found. The milestone release is undated on the page; press coverage dates it 13 September 2023. The Bank's factsheet uses 21% and is undated.

sources.title: Start Up Loans: Start Up Loans hits £1bn milestone of loans to UK small businesses (September 2023)
Unlocking the potential of diverse entrepreneurs – Factsheet

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: Almost half of London's Start Up Loans
points.text: In London, 7,366 loans worth more than £50 million, almost half of all loans issued in the capital since 2012, went to people from ethnic minority backgrounds.
points.note: Data to end of October 2019. The release uses the term ‘BAME’.

sources.title: Start Up Loans: £50 million of Start Up Loans in London go to ethnic minority entrepreneurs (data to end October 2019)

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: Mayor of London: Ascend programme
points.text: A 12-week programme funded by the UK Shared Prosperity Fund (£748,000) and run by Foundervine, for under-represented founders including women and ethnic minorities. It addresses barriers to raising investment.
points.note: Foundervine is described here as the delivery body only, not endorsed. UKSPF activity ends on 30 September 2026, according to the whole-journey page.

sources.title: Mayor of London: UK Shared Prosperity Fund case study: Ascend programme

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: Mayor of London: Investment Readiness Programme (2020)
points.text: A one-year grant of up to £44,000 to Funding London to help women-owned and ethnic minority-owned SMEs understand the finance available to them.
points.note: A historical example; check whether it is still running before linking to it.

sources.title: Mayor of London: ADD2434 Investment Readiness Programme (decision of 3 March 2020)

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: Innovate UK Women in Innovation
points.text: In 2026, Innovate UK backed 100 women founders: 61 award winners each received a £75,000 grant plus 12 months of support. 29% of the cohort identify as being from an ethnic minority background.
points.note: No dedicated ethnic minority strand was found. Whether one exists is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: UKRI: Innovate UK backs 100 women founders shaping the UK’s future industries (5 August 2026)

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: Regional example: START, West of England
points.text: A free early-stage programme for tech and digital start-ups in the West of England. The provider states it wants to support community-led and ethnic minority-led entrepreneurship.
points.note: Applicants must be over 18 and live in the combined authority area.

sources.title: TechSpark: START (West of England)

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: Equal treatment in services and lending
points.text: A provider of services to the public, including finance, must not discriminate by refusing the service or by the terms it offers.
points.note: Section 13 defines direct discrimination; section 29 applies it to services.

sources.title: Equality Act 2010, section 29 (provision of services)

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: Networks led by and for Black business
points.text: Black business networks exist across the UK. Examples include the London Chamber of Commerce and Industry's Black Business Association (launched 2020), Coding Black Females and Colorintech, which runs Black Tech Fest.
points.note: Described, not endorsed; no government register of such networks exists. The Black Business Network is not described, as no authoritative source for it is cited.

sources.title: London Chamber of Commerce and Industry: LCCI to launch Black Business Association (19 October 2020)
Coding Black Females
Black Tech Fest (BTF); blacktechfest.com now redirects here

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: Appetite for growth finance
points.text: Half of ethnic minority-led businesses are open to using finance for growth, against around three in ten white-led businesses.
points.note: From the 2021/22 Small Business Finance Markets factsheet.

sources.title: British Business Bank: Small Business Finance Markets Report 2021/22, factsheet

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: Alternative finance is recognised in tax law
points.text: UK tax law treats returns under alternative (for example Sharia-compliant) finance arrangements as interest for tax purposes.

sources.title: Income Tax Act 2007, Part 10A: alternative finance arrangements

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: Sharia-compliant Start Up Loans route has closed to new applicants
points.text: Start Up Loans offered Sharia-compliant funding through Financing Sharia Enterprise. It stopped taking new applications from 29 December 2025, and the standard Start Up Loan is not Sharia compliant.
points.note: Relevant to Black Muslim founders, including many of Somali, Nigerian and other African heritage; no source gives numbers. Whether a replacement route exists is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Start Up Loans: Sharia compliant finance

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: Pardner: community savings as a response to exclusion
points.text: Pardner is a rotating savings and credit arrangement. Members pay in together and take turns to receive the pot. Caribbean communities used it when Windrush-generation migrants faced barriers to UK banking.
points.note: Similar rotating schemes exist in many African communities (for example susu or esusu), but the sources cited do not confirm this.

sources.title: Bank of England Museum: Pardner Hand: a Caribbean answer to British banking exclusion (exhibition with Museumand, closed 20 December 2024)
Bank of England Museum: Community savings and the Pardner Hand (16 June 2023)

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: International networks as an asset
points.text: The FSB described ethnic minority and migrant communities as forging trading links by drawing on international networks.

sources.title: Federation of Small Businesses: Unlocking opportunity: the value of ethnic minority firms to UK economic activity and enterprise (2020), hosted by the Enterprise Research Centre

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: Developing Countries Trading Scheme
points.text: Since 19 June 2023, the UK's Developing Countries Trading Scheme has given preferential access to UK imports from 65 eligible countries, many of them in Africa. It replaced the UK Generalised Scheme of Preferences.
points.note: The scheme benefits UK importers buying from eligible countries. Tier and tariff details are on linked GOV.UK guidance and are not covered here here.

sources.title: GOV.UK: Developing Countries Trading Scheme (DCTS)

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: African Continental Free Trade Area
points.text: Trading under the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) started on 1 January 2021. 54 African Union member states have signed the agreement.
points.note: Ratification figures are from January 2021 (30 countries) and have since changed; the current count is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: African Union: press briefing on the status of the AfCFTA (12 January 2021)

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: UK trade with African partners: an example
points.text: UK–Kenya trade in goods and services was £2.1 billion in the four quarters to the end of the first quarter of 2026. The Department for Business and Trade publishes a factsheet like this for each partner country.
points.note: One country shown as an example. A total for UK–Africa trade is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Department for Business and Trade: Trade and investment factsheet, Kenya (24 September 2026)

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: Remittances and money service businesses
points.text: Remittances from diaspora communities are a major economic link, and money service businesses that carry them are themselves diaspora enterprises. A 2015 government factsheet estimated at least US$1.3 billion a year was remitted to Somalia, mainly through such businesses.
points.figure: at least US$1.3 billion a year (Somalia)
points.note: Dated, single-country and quoting an Oxfam estimate. No current official figure for UK remittances to Africa as a whole was confirmed.

sources.title: HM Government: UK-Somalia Remittance Factsheet (March 2015)

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: Dr Harold Moody's practice, Peckham, 1913
points.text: Refused hospital work because of his colour, Harold Moody set up his own medical practice in Peckham in February 1913. He later co-founded the League of Coloured Peoples in 1931.

sources.title: King’s College London: Dr Harold Moody

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: Brixton's markets in the Windrush years
points.text: In the 1950s, Brixton became a hub for the African Caribbean community, and its markets became the community's commercial and social heart, selling Caribbean produce.
points.note: Historic England does not say who owned the stalls or shops. Black ownership of specific Windrush-era Brixton businesses is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Historic England blog: Places that tell stories of the Windrush generation (22 June 2020)

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: Pardner and Caribbean entrepreneurship
points.text: The Bank of England Museum and Museumand presented pardner as Caribbean entrepreneurship in the face of financial discrimination: Windrush-generation migrants were often denied basic banking services.
points.note: Exhibition closed 20 December 2024.

sources.title: Bank of England Museum: Pardner Hand: a Caribbean answer to British banking exclusion (exhibition with Museumand, closed 20 December 2024)
Bank of England Museum: Community savings and the Pardner Hand (16 June 2023)

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: New Beacon Books, 1966
points.text: New Beacon Books, established in 1966, describes itself as Britain's first Black publisher and bookshop.
points.note: The "first" claim is the organisation's own and was not independently verified.

sources.title: New Beacon Books: The George Padmore Institute

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: Black-specific data is thin
points.text: Official surveys mostly report "ethnic minority" as one group. The British Business Bank's 2020 study is the main source with Black-specific figures, and it notes small samples for some groups.
points.note: Treat Black African and Black female figures as indicative.

sources.title: Alone, together: entrepreneurship and diversity in the UK, full report PDF (British Business Bank and Oliver Wyman, 2020; copy hosted by Diversity UK)

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: Much of the evidence dates from 2018 to 2021
points.text: The key studies use data from before or during COVID-19. No newer study with comparable Black-specific outcome figures is cited here.

sources.title: Department for Business and Trade: Longitudinal Small Business Survey 2024: SME employers (published 25 September 2025)

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: No immigration advice
points.text: Whether a person may work or run a business in the UK depends on their immigration status. This page gives no immigration advice and says nothing about any individual's status. Employers must check that a job applicant is allowed to work in the UK before employing them.

sources.title: Check a job applicant's right to work

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: Naming is not endorsing
points.text: Networks, programmes and private bodies are described so people can find them. No government register of community networks exists, and inclusion here is not a recommendation.

points.datasetTitle: Black enterprise: starting and growing a business
points.heading: Unconfirmed items
points.text: These items are not confirmed by the sources cited: the Pathways recommendation on ethnicity data; the Black Business Network; any Innovate UK ethnic minority strand; Black ownership of named Windrush-era Brixton businesses; the minimum Start Up Loan amount; a current UK–Africa trade or remittance total.

points.datasetTitle: Young lives: NEET, BEET and CHEET
points.heading: BEET
points.text: Being in Education, Employment or Training: the default engaged state, universal and not individually tracked once things go well.
points.note: A term used by this hub; no external source.

points.datasetTitle: Young lives: NEET, BEET and CHEET
points.heading: CHEET
points.text: Child Held in Early years, Education or Training: held by the state or someone other than their parents, such as care, guardianship, treatment, custody of a parent, or licensed work.
points.note: A term used by this hub; no external source.

points.datasetTitle: Young lives: NEET, BEET and CHEET
points.heading: NEET
points.text: Not in Education, Employment or Training, officially measured at 16 to 24 from the Labour Force Survey. DfE also tracks 16 and 17 year olds.

points.datasetTitle: Young lives: NEET, BEET and CHEET
points.heading: Departure events
points.text: The point where a child leaves a system, or a system stops seeing them: for example exclusion, deregistration for home education, leaving care at 18, or leaving custody. This page uses them to show where Black, African and Caribbean young people's experiences differ.
points.note: Linking statement is an editorial synthesis, based on the sections below.

points.datasetTitle: Young lives: NEET, BEET and CHEET
points.heading: Suspensions: Mixed White and Black Caribbean
points.text: Pupils from the Mixed White and Black Caribbean group had a suspension rate of 17.36 (per 100 pupils), almost twice the England rate of 9.33.
points.note: Rate = suspensions per 100 pupils; one pupil can be suspended more than once.

sources.title: Pupil exclusions (suspensions)

points.datasetTitle: Young lives: NEET, BEET and CHEET
points.heading: Suspensions: Black Caribbean
points.text: Black Caribbean pupils had a suspension rate of 13.58, above the England rate. Black African pupils had a rate of 5.54, below it.
points.note: Black African figure is from the page's data table, not its text.

sources.title: Pupil exclusions (suspensions)

points.datasetTitle: Young lives: NEET, BEET and CHEET
points.heading: Permanent exclusions
points.text: The England rate was 0.11. In the data table, Mixed White and Black Caribbean was 0.24 and Black Caribbean 0.18; Black African was 0.06, below average. Highest rates were for Gypsy or Roma and Irish Traveller pupils.
points.note: Group rates are table values; the page warns they rest on very small numbers.

sources.title: Permanent exclusions

points.datasetTitle: Young lives: NEET, BEET and CHEET
points.heading: Latest year (2024/25)
points.text: Overall rates in 2024/25 (suspensions 10.88, permanent exclusions 0.12) were higher than in 2022/23 but lower than in 2023/24 (11.31 and 0.13). The release names Gypsy, Roma and Irish Traveller pupils as having the highest rates; 2024/25 rates for Black groups are not shown here.
points.note: Ethnicity breakdown for 2024/25 not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Suspensions and permanent exclusions in England, 2024/25 (DfE, Explore education statistics)

points.datasetTitle: Young lives: NEET, BEET and CHEET
points.heading: Timpson review (2019)
points.text: The government response to the Timpson review accepted that some groups, including Black Caribbean and Mixed White and Black Caribbean pupils, are more likely to be permanently excluded, even when other factors are taken into account.
points.note: The often-cited '1.7 times' figure for Black Caribbean pupils is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Timpson review of school exclusion: government response (May 2019)

points.datasetTitle: Young lives: NEET, BEET and CHEET
points.heading: Adultification
points.text: Adultification is when children are not given the presumption of innocence and vulnerability that childhood should bring. Inspectorate and charity sources link it to racialised discrimination against Black children.
points.note: Definition originates with Davis and Marsh (2020), as cited by Missing People.

points.datasetTitle: Young lives: NEET, BEET and CHEET
points.heading: Child Q (City and Hackney, 2022)
points.text: The safeguarding practice review into the strip search of a Black schoolgirl at school found racism and adultification bias were likely influencing factors. A 2023 update was positive about progress but found concerns extend to all statutory services.
points.note: Findings are as reported in Hackney Council's summary; the full review text is not cited here.

points.datasetTitle: Young lives: NEET, BEET and CHEET
points.heading: Strip searches of children (2026)
points.text: The Children's Commissioner found that between July 2023 and June 2024 Black children in England and Wales were almost eight times more likely than White children to be strip searched by police: 35% of the children strip searched were Black, although Black children were 6% of 10–17-year-olds in the 2021 census (report published April 2026). Earlier reports measured against population figures: Black children were up to six times more likely to be strip searched than population figures would suggest in 2018–mid-2022 (March 2023 report) and over four times more likely in July 2022–June 2023 (August 2024 report).
points.year: Jan 2018 to Jun 2024 data; published April 2026
points.note: Police searches, not school; included because Child Q prompted the series.

points.text: At 16 and 17, Black young people in England are less likely than average to be NEET; at 16 to 24, Milburn finds the highest rate. These are different measures (council tracking v survey) and both can be true.

points.heading: Disparity is not cause
