points.heading: Face analysis was least accurate for darker-skinned women
points.text: The Gender Shades study tested three commercial gender-classification systems. Error rates reached 34.7% for darker-skinned women, compared with no more than 0.8% for lighter-skinned men. The training and benchmark datasets were mostly lighter-skinned faces.
points.figure: Up to 34.7% error (darker-skinned women) vs at most 0.8% (lighter-skinned men)
points.note: This study tested gender classification, not identity matching. It shows bias in commercial systems at that time, not in today's products.

sources.title: Gender Shades: Intersectional Accuracy Disparities in Commercial Gender Classification (PMLR 81, 2018)
MIT News: Study finds gender and skin-type bias in commercial artificial-intelligence systems (11 Feb 2018)

points.heading: A US government test found large demographic differences across face recognition algorithms
points.text: In 2019 the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) tested 189 algorithms from 99 developers. Many produced more false positives for Asian and African American faces than for white faces, often by 10 to 100 times. Results varied widely between algorithms.
points.figure: False-positive differences often 10 to 100 times; 189 algorithms tested
points.note: The source is a US study using US image sets. The news release also says the most accurate algorithms showed much smaller differences.

sources.title: NIST: NIST Study Evaluates Effects of Race, Age, Sex on Face Recognition Software (19 Dec 2019)

points.heading: The Court of Appeal found South Wales Police had not met the equality duty on facial recognition
points.text: In R (Bridges) v Chief Constable of South Wales Police, judgment handed down on 11 August 2020, the Court of Appeal found the force had not complied with the Public Sector Equality Duty. It had not checked whether the software was biased by race or sex. The court did not find that the software was in fact biased.
points.note: Only the judgment's cover page was readable on judiciary.uk, so the paragraph [199] wording is quoted from a barrister's case note. It should be checked against the full judgment before publication.

sources.title: Judiciary UK: R (Bridges) v CC South Wales
Inforrm case note: R (Bridges) v Chief Constable of South Wales Police (17 Aug 2020)
Law Gazette: Court of Appeal warns of race bias in facial recognition technology
R (Bridges) v Chief Constable of South Wales Police, Court of Appeal judgment (2020)

points.heading: Police live facial recognition: fairness depends on the setting used
points.text: Testing by the National Physical Laboratory for the Metropolitan Police and South Wales Police (2023) found that the algorithm can be run at settings where there is no statistically significant difference in performance between demographic groups. At lower settings, differences between groups appear.
points.note: Disputed. Civil liberties group Big Brother Watch said the report confirms live facial recognition has significant race and sex biases (as reported by The Register). The full report is not cited here, so the exact thresholds are not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: College of Policing: Operational testing of facial recognition technology
The Register: UK police facial recognition (6 Apr 2023)

points.heading: The rules on police facial recognition are being rewritten
points.text: On 4 December 2025 the Home Office launched a 10-week consultation on a new legal framework for law enforcement use of biometrics and facial recognition.
points.note: The ministerial statement does not mention bias or fairness.

sources.title: UK Parliament written statement HLWS1128 (4 Dec 2025)

points.heading: A visa-streaming algorithm that used nationality was withdrawn under legal challenge
points.text: A Home Office tool risk-scored visa applications partly by nationality. After a legal challenge by the Joint Council for the Welfare of Immigrants (JCWI), supported by Foxglove, the Home Office agreed to stop using it from 7 August 2020 and to redesign it.
points.note: The source is a specialist immigration law publisher; no GOV.UK or Parliament source is cited. Which nationalities were affected, and any racial effect, are not confirmed by the sources cited. Campaigners called the tool racist; the Home Office did not accept that.

sources.title: Free Movement: Government to redesign controversial visa algorithm (4 Aug 2020)

points.heading: The 2020 A-level algorithm: no sourced ethnicity effect
points.text: In August 2020 Ofqual reported that its equalities analysis, which included ethnicity, found no evidence that the grade-awarding process had introduced systemic bias. No source found shows an ethnicity-specific effect from the algorithm.
points.note: Any ethnicity effect is not confirmed by the sources cited. The concern at the time was mainly about disadvantage by school and socio-economic background. The later reversal of the algorithm's grades is not covered by the sources cited here.

sources.title: Ofqual / GOV.UK: Guide to AS and A level results for England, 2020 (13 Aug 2020)

points.heading: Algorithms learn yesterday's decisions, and the data to check for bias is often missing
points.text: The CDEI review (November 2020) covered recruitment, financial services, policing and local government. It found that algorithms trained on past decisions can encode existing bias, and that data on protected characteristics is often not available to monitor outcomes. It recommended a mandatory transparency obligation for the public sector.
points.note: The CDEI is now the Responsible Technology Adoption Unit.

sources.title: CDEI review into bias in algorithmic decision-making (27 Nov 2020)

points.heading: Pulse oximeters overestimate oxygen levels for people with darker skin
points.text: The independent review on equity in medical devices, chaired by Professor Dame Margaret Whitehead and published on 11 March 2024, found that pulse oximeters overestimate true oxygen levels in people with darker skin. This can delay treatment. The review also warned of bias in AI-enabled medical devices.
points.note: Pulse oximeters are not AI. They are included because they show how biased data and design harm people physically. The summary page's AI warning names women; it describes the risks to ethnic minority groups only in general terms.

sources.title: DHSC: Equity in medical devices: independent review, summary report (11 Mar 2024)

points.heading: The equality duty applies from the moment a public body considers using AI
points.text: The Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) says the Public Sector Equality Duty applies from the start, when a public body is deciding whether to use AI. It also applies to AI already in use and to systems that others develop. Northern Ireland has its own duty under section 75, and Scotland and Wales have specific duties that cover AI procurement.

sources.title: EHRC: Artificial intelligence: meeting the Public Sector Equality Duty (1 Sep 2022)

points.heading: Communities can look up the algorithmic tools government uses
points.text: The Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (ATRS) is mandatory for central government. It applies to algorithmic tools that significantly influence decisions with public effect, or that interact directly with the public. Few records had been published by January 2025, according to the Committee of Public Accounts (Public Accounts Committee).
points.figure: 33 ATRS records published as at January 2025 (Committee of Public Accounts)
points.note: The record count changes over time. Read the live count on the ATRS hub at the point of use.

sources.title: ATRS mandatory scope and exemptions policy (17 Dec 2024)
Public Accounts Committee report HC 356

points.heading: Black people are slightly under-represented among IT specialists
points.text: BCS analysis of the ONS Labour Force Survey for 2023 shows people of Black, African, Caribbean or Black British ethnicity making up 3% of IT specialists, compared with 4% of all occupations. Ethnic minority people overall made up 21% of IT specialists.
points.figure: 3% of IT specialists vs 4% of all occupations (2023)
points.note: This is not an official statistics release. It is a professional body's analysis of ONS survey data. No official figure for Black people in AI-specific roles was found, so that is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: BCS Diversity Report 2024: Ethnicity and IT employment

points.heading: Africa's own AI strategy puts development, languages and heritage first
points.text: The African Union Executive Council endorsed a Continental AI Strategy in Accra in July 2024. It describes an Africa-centric, development-focused approach and says AI must reflect Africa's languages and cultural heritage. The Ethics Atlas sets out a 'Global South reading' of shared AI ethics words. In that reading, wellbeing means development, inclusion and closing the AI divide, and control means sovereign control of one's own data and infrastructure.
points.note: The Ethics Atlas labels its African Union row S (found in search, primary not opened). Its reference to Ubuntu ethics is labelled K (unsourced background) and is not used here.

sources.title: African Union: committed to developing AI capabilities in Africa (Continental AI Strategy)

points.heading: Who ethics frameworks protect: colonial exemptions and missing frameworks
points.text: The Ethics Atlas notes that every AI ethics framework it found limits 'whose wellbeing' to the state that wrote it. Its history of war ethics records that Grotius's law of war between states left colonial wars outside it. It also records an Algerian statement at the UN Security Council that the AI divide is about sovereignty itself. It flags that public ethics frameworks are absent in Sudan and the Sahel, which it describes as where most deaths occur.
points.note: These are low-confidence research labels. The colonial-exemption row is K (standard history, unsourced). The Algeria quote is S (UN). The Sudan and Sahel line is marked 'to verify'. These points should not be presented as established facts until they are sourced.

points.heading: Government's Standards for Ethnicity Data (2023)
points.text: Following a public consultation, the government published Standards for Ethnicity Data on 17 April 2023. This was Inclusive Britain action 6. They set out best practice for collecting, analysing and reporting ethnicity data in government and public bodies. Data collected for the whole UK should use the GSS harmonised standard. The standards also point to RDU style guidance, which avoids terms such as 'BAME'.
points.note: Following the standards is good practice, not a legal requirement.

sources.title: Standards for ethnicity data (GOV.UK)
Inclusive Britain action plan: updates (GOV.UK)

points.heading: Census 2021: African, Caribbean and Mixed options, with write-ins
points.text: The 2021 Census in England and Wales offered 19 tick-box responses. Under 'Black, Black British, Caribbean or African' these were Caribbean, African and a write-in 'Any other' option. Under Mixed they included White and Black Caribbean and White and Black African. In Wales the heading also included 'Black Welsh'. The Black African group grew from 1.8% (990,000) in 2011 to 2.5% (1.5 million) in 2021.
points.figure: Black African: 2.5% (1.5 million) in 2021, up from 1.8% (990,000) in 2011
points.note: Detailed write-in results (for example, single countries or peoples of origin) are not confirmed by the sources cited here. The Ethnicity facts and figures page lists 19 categories, but its page description says 18. Scotland and Northern Ireland use different questions.

sources.title: ONS: Ethnic group, England and Wales, Census 2021
List of ethnic groups (Ethnicity facts and figures)

points.heading: Government stopped using 'BAME'
points.text: The Commission on Race and Ethnic Disparities recommended dropping the term 'BAME', and the Inclusive Britain plan (March 2022, 74 actions) committed government to stop using it. The Equality Hub explained that grouping all ethnic minorities together can hide large differences in outcomes. It also said many ethnic minority people dislike the term. Government now uses specific Census groups where it can.
points.note: Some staff networks and organisations outside government still use the term, and preferences differ. The hub should explain why it uses the terms it does, rather than enforce one.

sources.title: Why we no longer use the term 'BAME' in government (Race Disparity Unit, 7 April 2022)
Inclusive Britain action plan: updates (GOV.UK)

points.heading: The Commission on Race and Ethnic Disparities (2021) and the dispute about it
points.text: The Commission reported in March 2021. Its foreword said it no longer saw a Britain where the system is deliberately rigged against ethnic minorities. UN human rights experts rejected the report, saying it distorted historic facts and misused data. The government's Inclusive Britain response followed in 2022.
points.note: Both the Commission's findings and the criticism of it are cited. The hub should present both and should not adopt either side's conclusion.

sources.title: Commission on Race and Ethnic Disparities: foreword, introduction and full recommendations (GOV.UK)
UN OHCHR blog: UN experts condemn 'reprehensible' racism report

points.heading: The Inclusive Data Taskforce: everyone counts and is counted
points.text: The Inclusive Data Taskforce reported in September 2021, with 46 recommendations under 8 Inclusive Data Principles. The National Statistician's response and the January 2022 implementation plan aim for everyone to count and be counted in UK data. This includes work to build trust with the people who supply data.
points.note: How far the recommendations have been delivered by 2026 is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Inclusive Data Taskforce implementation plan (UK Statistics Authority)

points.heading: Ethnicity in NHS records often differs from the Census
points.text: In May 2024 the ONS compared ethnicity in four health data sources with what people told the 2021 Census. Black African was among the groups with the highest agreement. Mixed groups and 'Other' groups had the lowest. In hospital and talking-therapy records, the 'Other Black' category agreed less than 20% of the time.
points.figure: 'Other Black' agreement under 20% (Hospital Episode Statistics and Talking Therapies)
points.note: Covers England only. The ONS gives agreement for each data source and group, not a single overall rate.

sources.title: Understanding consistency of ethnicity data recorded in health-related administrative datasets in England: 2011 to 2021 (ONS)

points.heading: NHS Race and Health Observatory: poor ethnicity monitoring data
points.text: In February 2022 a rapid evidence review of ethnic inequalities in healthcare, funded by the NHS Race and Health Observatory, found large inequalities across health services. One of its authors pointed to years of poor-quality ethnic monitoring data in NHS systems.
points.note: The source is a university news release about the review, not the review itself. When the Observatory was founded is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Review highlights stark ethnic healthcare inequalities in the UK (University of Manchester)

points.heading: Black people are under-represented among survey respondents
points.text: The ONS says ethnic minority groups tend to be less likely to take part in government surveys. On its Opinions and Lifestyle Survey, Asian, Black and Mixed groups were under-represented compared with population estimates (as of April 2025). The ONS tested a targeted £10 incentive to improve response and representativeness.
points.note: The ONS page was last revised on 27 July 2026. Under-coverage in other named surveys, such as the Labour Force Survey, is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Targeted incentives on the Opinions and Lifestyle Survey (ONS)

points.heading: Trust, willingness and fear of discrimination in sharing health data
points.text: Research for Understanding Patient Data found that many Black and South Asian people have low trust in the NHS and worry about how their data is protected. Respondents from all ethnic groups were willing to share most types of personal data with the NHS. Black and South Asian respondents were more concerned that sharing data could lead to discrimination. Suggested reasons for gaps in ethnicity data include structural racism, lack of training and mistrust.
points.note: The findings are mixed: low trust in the NHS sits alongside willingness to share. The Ada Lovelace Institute is not covered here. Any finding attributed to it is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Bringing together our work on equitable data collection with Black and South Asian communities (Understanding Patient Data)
Insights from Black & South Asian people on patient data (Understanding Patient Data)

points.heading: Ethnicity facts and figures: government's public evidence base
points.text: The Race Disparity Audit was published in October 2017. Its data is kept up to date on the GOV.UK Ethnicity facts and figures service, built by the Race Disparity Unit. The service brings together government data on how different ethnic groups experience public services.
points.note: The page does not give a launch date for the website itself.

sources.title: Background (Ethnicity facts and figures)

points.heading: Start from a fixed point, with no hierarchy of blame or suffering
points.text: The ledger rests on numbered principles. Its fixed point is that human beings were made property and nothing excuses it. Every actor (European, African, Arab, Ottoman and others) is held to one standard of evidence; complicity explains scale but never moves responsibility. The gravity of enslavement is not ranked against other atrocities, and harm and achievement are held together, so the record does not define a continent or a people.

points.heading: Language with dignity: ‘enslaved people’, not ‘slaves’
points.text: The ledger names people as people: 'enslaved people', not 'slaves'; 'enslavers', not 'owners'. Euphemisms are replaced with what happened, slurs survive only inside titles and quotations, and ancestors are named before their remains. Government's own style guide does not use 'BAME' or 'BME', because the terms hide differences between groups. The hub can adopt both rules and enforce them with a language check.
points.note: The ledger records that its language was revised after four independent sensitivity reads and a second editor.

sources.title: Ethnicity facts and figures: Writing about ethnicity

points.heading: Abolition paid £20 million to enslavers, not to the enslaved
points.text: The Slavery Abolition Act 1833 funded £20 million of compensation to enslavers. The enslaved received nothing and were forced into unpaid 'apprenticeship'. The UCL Legacies of British Slavery database records the compensation claims, with enslavers, estates and later investments, and is the authoritative public source.
points.note: The ledger says 'about 46,000 claims' and 'about 40% of 1833 government spending'. Neither figure is confirmed by the sources cited here; the UCL page gives 'more than forty thousand slave-owners' (a later phase added another twenty thousand).

sources.title: Legacies of British Slave-ownership — UCL Centre for the Study of the Legacies of British Slavery
HM Treasury: FOI2018/00186, Slavery Abolition Act 1833

points.heading: The abolition loan was finally repaid in 2015, but the sum is unknown
points.text: Money borrowed in 1835 to fund the compensation was rolled into other government debt and the last of it was redeemed in 2015. The Treasury has no record of how much of the original loan was still outstanding when it was consolidated in 1927, so the amount repaid in 2015 cannot be stated. Avoid claims that taxpayers 'paid off' a specific sum.
points.note: The fact of 2015 repayment is confirmed; the amount repaid is unknown, and popular claims often overstate it.

sources.title: HM Treasury: FOI2018/00186, Slavery Abolition Act 1833
Full Fact: the government loan to pay slave owners compensation after 1833

points.heading: CARICOM's Ten Point Plan for Reparatory Justice
points.text: The CARICOM Reparations Commission's plan has ten points: full formal apology, repatriation, an Indigenous peoples development programme, cultural institutions, the public health crisis, illiteracy eradication, an African knowledge programme, psychological rehabilitation, technology transfer and debt cancellation. The ledger books it as a claim with no monetary amount and nothing paid, and records that heads of government have approved a revised plan.
points.note: The ten headings are confirmed on caricom.org. The 2014 approval date is from the ledger (it cites a Leigh Day press release of 11 March 2014). The revised plan and the September 2026 Barbados conference are from the ledger only and are not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: CARICOM Ten Point Plan for Reparatory Justice (caricom.org)

points.heading: Where the UK state stands, and what is live in 2026
points.text: The ledger records the UK government's position as no reparations: it says the Prime Minister in October 2024 preferred to work on 'future-facing challenges'. It also tracks live moves, including Jamaica's petition of 7 September 2026 asking the King to refer three questions on slavery to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, without a money claim, and the African Union's Decade of Justice through Reparations, 2026–2035.
points.note: From the ledger only (it cites Al Jazeera and Jamaica's Ministry of Culture); not confirmed by the sources cited. A politically live area: present it as reported positions, not as government policy statements.

points.heading: Return of ancestors and looted heritage
points.text: UK law lets nine named national museums transfer human remains out of their collections (Human Tissue Act 2004, section 47). The British Museum Act 1963 bars most other disposals and is the main legal barrier to restitution. The ledger tracks 28 returns and requests of ancestral remains, and cases such as the sack of Benin City in 1897, when thousands of brass and ivory works were taken.
points.note: From the ledger only (it links legislation.gov.uk for s.47); the statute wording was not rechecked. The ledger's rule: ancestors are named before their remains, and burial sites are never mapped precisely.

points.heading: Windrush: the empire's legacy inside the UK state
points.text: Commonwealth-born residents, many of whom arrived as children before 1973, were denied work, housing and healthcare, and some were detained or removed. The Windrush Lessons Learned Review (2020) identified 164 people who had been in the country before 1973 and had been detained or removed, or both, since 2002.
points.figure: 164 detained or removed, or both, since 2002
points.note: The ledger also records the 2018 apology and the Windrush Compensation Scheme; see the hub's inequalities page for the scheme's figures.

sources.title: Home Office: Windrush Lessons Learned Review (Wendy Williams)

points.heading: Black civil servants: present across the service, scarcer at the top
points.text: At 31 March 2026, 19.2% of civil servants with a known ethnicity were from an ethnic minority background, a record high (11.2% in 2016). Representation falls with seniority: the Senior Civil Service is lowest at 10.6%. Black civil servants are the second-largest ethnic minority group, at 26,655 people. The bulletin gives no separate Black share by grade.
points.figure: SCS ethnic minority representation 10.6% (all ethnic minorities); Black headcount 26,655
points.note: The percentages exclude unknown and undeclared ethnicity. A Black-only SCS percentage is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Statistical bulletin: Civil Service Statistics 2026 (Cabinet Office)

points.heading: Civil service pay by ethnicity: a 4.5% gap nationally, 27.8% in London
points.text: The Civil Service Ethnicity Pay Gap Statistics 2025 give a median hourly pay gap of 4.5% for Black civil servants against White civil servants across the UK, and 27.8% in London. Annual medians at 31 March 2024 were £33,980 for Black and £34,300 for White civil servants; at junior grades Black civil servants had among the highest median pay of any group, but in London the lowest. A service-wide median says more about where people sit in the grades than about equal pay for equal work.
points.note: Unadjusted gaps partly reflect grade mix and London location. The grade-mix argument comes from the hub's pay work.

sources.title: Civil Service pay — Ethnicity facts and figures
Statistical bulletin - Civil Service Ethnicity Pay Gap Statistics: 2025

points.heading: Ethnicity pay gaps across the economy: where people were born matters
points.text: In 2022, Black, African, Caribbean or Black British employees earned a median £13.53 an hour against £14.35 for White employees, a gap that has held since 2012. UK-born Black employees earned more (£15.18) than UK-born White employees (£14.26), while non-UK-born Black employees earned less (£12.95). UK-born Black African and Black Caribbean employees earned less than UK-born White British employees.
points.note: The ONS article (released 29 November 2023) does not give a separate median for Black African employees against White British, so that exact comparison is not confirmed by the sources cited. The latest ONS release covers 2012 to 2022.

sources.title: Ethnicity pay gaps, UK: 2012 to 2022

points.heading: Honours: Black recipients slightly below their population share
points.text: In the 2025 New Year Honours list, 3.7% of recipients were Black, against a Black population share of 4.0% in England and Wales (Census 2021). Since June 2015 the share of recipients from Asian, Black, Mixed and Other backgrounds has risen from 7.0% to 12.5%.
points.figure: 3.7% Black recipients (2025 New Year Honours) vs 4.0% Black population (E&W 2021)
points.note: The geographies differ: UK honours compared with an England and Wales population, so treat the comparison as indicative. Ethnicity facts and figures makes no direct population comparison.

sources.title: Honours recipients — Ethnicity facts and figures
Ethnicity facts and figures: Population of England and Wales (Census 2021)

points.heading: The handover from children's to adult services is where people fall out of view
points.text: The hub's social care work names the transition between children's and adult social care as the point where records and support most often break. Young Black people in care and care leavers face that handover too. The hub can name the seam rather than treat childhood and adulthood as separate topics.
points.note: The hub's work frames this as interpretation, not a measured rate. No figure for how many people are lost at the seam has been checked.

points.heading: Children looked after in England by ethnicity, 2025
points.text: At 31 March 2025, 8% of children looked after were Black, African, Caribbean or Black British, and 11% were Mixed or Multiple ethnic groups. DfE says children from Mixed groups were over-represented. Among unaccompanied asylum-seeking children, 33% were Black or Black British.
points.note: The DfE text that was checked names Mixed groups as over-represented. It does not say that Black children are over-represented, so that claim is not confirmed by the sources cited. Comparing with the share in the child population needs ONS population figures, which are not covered here here.

sources.title: Children looked after in England including adoptions, reporting year 2025

points.heading: Ethnic minority and internationally recruited workers in adult social care
points.text: Skills for Care reported that about a third of the adult social care workforce come from ethnic minority backgrounds. In 2023/24, 105,000 international recruits started direct care roles in the independent sector, while the number of British workers fell.
points.note: This is a secondary source quoting the Skills for Care 2024 report. The 2026 report (2025/26 data) exists, but its ethnicity tables sit in an Excel appendix that was not read. The share of Black workers specifically, and Nigeria or Zimbabwe as leading source countries, are not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Learning Disability Today, reporting Skills for Care, State of the adult social care sector and workforce in England 2024

points.heading: A race equality standard already exists for the social care workforce
points.text: The Social Care Workforce Race Equality Standard (SC-WRES) collects workforce data across nine metrics so that organisations can plan action. Social Work England publishes SC-WRES data, including on fitness-to-practise referrals.
points.note: No finding or figure on referral disparities was confirmed on the page checked (data labelled as at December 2025).

sources.title: Social Work England: Social Care Workforce Race Equality Standard (SC-WRES) data and insights

points.heading: Windrush: a records and data failure, not only a policy failure
points.text: The Windrush Lessons Learned Review (March 2020) found that the state gave people no documents and kept no records, and then demanded an unreasonable level of proof. It described institutional ignorance and thoughtlessness towards the issue of race. For a data-governance audience, this is the clearest case of harm done by missing records.
points.note: The GOV.UK page shows 'first published 19 July 2018' (when the review was commissioned). The report itself was ordered to be printed on 19 March 2020 and makes 30 recommendations.

sources.title: Home Office: Windrush Lessons Learned Review (Wendy Williams)

points.heading: Windrush landing card slips destroyed in 2010
points.text: In 2018 it was reported that landing card slips recording arrival dates were destroyed when a Home Office office in Croydon closed in October 2010. The Home Office said the decision was operational and that the slips were not reliable evidence of residence.
points.note: The claim comes from a former employee, reported by The Guardian and Civil Service World. The Home Office disputed the slips' value as evidence. The review's text, as checked by automated extraction, did not mention landing cards, so their role in the review's findings is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Civil Service World, 18 April 2018: Fury over revelation that Home Office destroyed thousands of Windrush landing cards

points.heading: How government should record ethnicity: ask people, and avoid 'BAME'
points.text: The 2023 Standards for ethnicity data say the best way to collect ethnicity is to ask people, and the Race Disparity Unit avoids the term 'BAME'. The hub's own forms, analytics and statistics should follow these standards, and use aggregated groups only when reliable detailed data is not available.
points.note: Published 17 April 2023. The page refers to the GSS harmonised standards. The ONS review of the harmonised standard is ongoing and is not covered here.

sources.title: Standards for ethnicity data (GOV.UK)

points.heading: Ethnic minority representation in the civil service is at a record high, and lowest in the SCS
points.text: The Civil Service statistics bulletin for 31 March 2026 shows ethnic minority representation at a record high overall and lowest in the Senior Civil Service. Its figures, including the Black headcount, are set out under the history lens.
points.figure: 19.2% ethnic minority; 10.6% at SCS; 26,655 Black civil servants
points.note: The 2026 bulletin does not give official Senior Civil Service headline figures or a Black share as a percentage. Ethnicity pay gaps are published separately, in the Civil Service Ethnicity Pay Gap Statistics 2025 (4.5% UK-wide and 27.8% in London, Black against White).

sources.title: Statistical bulletin: Civil Service Statistics 2026 (Cabinet Office)
Statistical bulletin - Civil Service Ethnicity Pay Gap Statistics: 2025

points.heading: Housing costs more than double persistent low income in Black households
points.text: Over 2019 to 2023, 9% of people in Black households were in persistent low income before housing costs, against 22% after housing costs. This was the biggest gap of any ethnic group.
points.note: Data from DWP Understanding Society analysis, page last updated 17 September 2025. These are Black households in aggregate, and the data does not separate Black African from Black Caribbean.

sources.title: Persistent low income, Ethnicity facts and figures (GOV.UK)

points.heading: An average can describe nobody
points.text: The hub's household-costs work found two gradients running in opposite directions: the Brexit output loss falls mostly on richer regions, while the price shock falls mostly on poorer households, who spend more on food and energy. A national average hides both. The hub should apply the same rule to ethnicity: show the distribution and the group, not one headline figure.
points.note: The hub's Brexit work did not break costs down by ethnicity. The link to Black households is drawn here by inference and needs its own sourced data.

points.heading: Black people are detained under the Mental Health Act at nearly four times the White rate
points.text: In 2024-25 the detention rate for the Black or Black British group was 262.4 per 100,000 people, nearly four times the White rate of 65.8. Detentions involve health services, police and local authority social care, so the issue crosses the same service boundaries as the hub's interoperability work.
points.note: Rates are crude per-population rates. The role of Approved Mental Health Professionals in local authorities is general knowledge and is not covered here against a source here.

sources.title: Mental Health Act Statistics, Annual Figures 2024-25: detentions, differences between groups (NHS England)

points.heading: Ethnicity data that doesn't match across systems is a semantic interoperability problem
points.text: The hub's interoperability work has four layers: technical, syntactic, semantic, and organisational and legal. Ethnicity recorded with different categories in schools, care, the NHS and HR is the semantic layer failing. A disparity cannot be traced across a person's journey if 'Black African' means different things in different systems. The hub's data dictionary should use the GSS harmonised categories and give crosswalks to them.
points.note: The four layers come from the hub's work. Applying them to ethnicity coding is the hub's inference, and no cross-system mismatch rate has been checked.

points.heading: Equality analysis of the life events where systems fail people
points.text: The hub's pay and reward analysis found that its recommendations were about life events the system fails, such as an allowance reassessment window falling during parental leave. It called for equality analysis of outcomes for people returning from leave. For careers and leadership, the hub can apply the same test by ethnicity: look at progression, assessment and reward at each transition, not just headcount.
points.note: The hub's analysis was not broken down by ethnicity. The civil service does publish ethnicity pay gaps: 4.5% UK-wide and 27.8% in London for Black against White civil servants (2025).

sources.title: Statistical bulletin - Civil Service Ethnicity Pay Gap Statistics: 2025

points.heading: Birth: Maternal deaths
points.text: Black women's maternal mortality rate was nearly three times that of White women in the MBRRACE-UK report covering 2022–24. The overall rate was 12.80 per 100,000 maternities, and women in the most deprived areas had around twice the rate of those in the least deprived.
points.figure: Nearly 3 times the White women's rate (2022–24)

sources.title: UK maternal death rate 20% higher than in 2009-11, new MBRRACE-UK report finds

points.heading: Work: Pay across the economy
points.text: Black employees' median hourly pay was £13.53 against £14.35 for White employees in 2022. UK-born Black employees earned more than UK-born White employees; non-UK-born Black employees earned less.

sources.title: Ethnicity pay gaps, UK: 2012 to 2022

points.heading: Work: Leadership in the civil service
points.text: Ethnic minority representation is lowest in the Senior Civil Service, at 10.6% in 2026, against 19.2% across the whole service.

sources.title: Statistical bulletin: Civil Service Statistics 2026 (Cabinet Office)

points.heading: Health: Detention under the Mental Health Act
points.text: In the year to March 2023, Black people were 3.5 times as likely as White people to be detained: 228 detentions per 100,000 Black people against 64 per 100,000 White people.

sources.title: Detentions under the Mental Health Act — Ethnicity facts and figures

points.heading: Justice: Stop and search
points.text: In the year ending 31 March 2023 there were 24.5 stop and searches for every 1,000 Black people and 5.9 for every 1,000 White people in England and Wales. That is about 4 times the rate, but the ratio is our own arithmetic: the service no longer publishes relative likelihoods.

sources.title: Ethnicity facts and figures: Stop and search

points.heading: Housing: Home ownership
points.text: In the two years to March 2023, 70% of White British households in England owned their home. Mixed White and Black African households had the lowest rate, at 14%. The data table gives 22% for Black African, 31% for Black Caribbean and 24% for all Black households.
points.figure: 70% White British vs 22% Black African (table value), 2021–23

sources.title: Home ownership

points.heading: Recognition (later career): Honours
points.text: 3.7% of recipients in the 2025 New Year Honours list were Black, against 4.0% of the population of England and Wales.

sources.title: Honours recipients — Ethnicity facts and figures
Ethnicity facts and figures: Population of England and Wales (Census 2021)

points.heading: Equality means fair treatment and equal opportunity
points.text: Acas defines workplace equality as equal job opportunities and fairness, and links it to not treating people unfairly because of a protected characteristic.

sources.title: What they are - Equality, diversity and inclusion (Acas)

points.heading: Diversity describes the mix of people
points.text: Acas defines diversity as the range of people in a workforce, and as valuing those differences.

sources.title: What they are - Equality, diversity and inclusion (Acas)

points.heading: Inclusion is about being valued and safe to speak up
points.text: Acas says an inclusive workplace lets everyone feel valued and safe to raise ideas and issues.

sources.title: What they are - Equality, diversity and inclusion (Acas)

points.heading: Equity is not the same as equality
points.text: A university glossary separates equality (the same opportunities) from equity (giving people what they need because starting points differ). It also says equity aims at equal outcomes.
points.note: Contested. Defining equity as "equality of outcomes" is the point critics object to. UK statutory duties are framed as "equality of opportunity" (s149), not equity.

sources.title: Glossary of terms - Equality, diversity and inclusion (University of Bath)

points.heading: Blombos Cave engraved ochre
points.text: Pieces of ochre deliberately engraved with cross-hatched designs were found in Middle Stone Age layers at Blombos Cave, South Africa. They are among the oldest known abstract designs made by humans. When first reported in 2002, the closest comparable European evidence was much younger. Later work dated other engraved pieces as far back as about 100,000 years.
points.note: Well evidenced as deliberate engraving. What the designs meant is unknown, so calling them "art" or "writing" goes beyond the evidence. The 2002 comparison with Europe is from that date; newer finds elsewhere are not covered by the sources cited.

sources.title: Henshilwood, d'Errico and Watts (2009) Engraved ochres from the Middle Stone Age levels at Blombos Cave, South Africa. Journal of Human Evolution 57(1) - abstract
ScienceDaily (2002), National Science Foundation release: Abstract engravings show modern behavior emerged earlier than previously thought

points.heading: Blombos ochre-processing workshop
points.text: A toolkit for making and storing ochre paint in shells, about 100,000 years old, was found at the same cave.
points.note: Shows planning and simple chemistry (mixing pigments). It does not by itself show "science" in the modern sense.

sources.title: AAAS (2011) Science: Early ochre workshop represents critical point in human evolution

points.heading: Lebombo bone and Border Cave notched bones
points.text: A notched baboon fibula from Border Cave, on the South Africa-Eswatini border, is about 42,000 to 43,000 years old. A peer-reviewed reanalysis of Border Cave finds concluded that people there used notched bones for notational (record-keeping) purposes.
points.note: Cautious reading: a tally or record of some kind. Bolder readings (a lunar calendar, for example) are not confirmed by the sources cited. The Lebombo bone is often confused with the younger Ishango bone.

sources.title: d'Errico et al. (2012) Early evidence of San material culture represented by organic artifacts from Border Cave, South Africa. PNAS - abstract
Lebombo bone (Wikipedia, used for the dating disagreement only)

points.heading: Ishango bone: the cautious reading
points.text: A baboon fibula with groups of notches in three columns, found in 1950 on the shore of Lake Edward (Democratic Republic of the Congo). An ICOMOS-IAU study dates it to about 25,000 to 16,000 years ago and describes it as possible evidence of early number knowledge beyond simple counting. It is held in Brussels.
points.note: The age range is wide because the dating has been revised. Older engraved bones also exist in Europe, so it is not unique as a counting object.

sources.title: ICOMOS-IAU Thematic Study on Astronomical Heritage, Case Study 1.3: The Ishango Bone
Wikipedia: Ishango bone

points.heading: Ishango bone: the bolder readings
points.text: Some researchers read the columns as a number system (bases 10 and 12), a list of prime numbers or a lunar calendar of about six months. A 2025 preprint found further patterns. These readings are hypotheses.
points.note: Disputed. A small number of notches can produce patterns by chance; see the myths section. The 2025 study is a preprint, not peer reviewed.

sources.title: ICOMOS-IAU Thematic Study on Astronomical Heritage, Case Study 1.3: The Ishango Bone

points.heading: Nabta Playa stone circle and megaliths
points.text: In the Egyptian Sahara, a small stone circle and lines of standing stones were built by Neolithic communities who used the area seasonally. A 1998 Nature paper reported alignments to north-south and to the summer solstice horizon. The university press release said it predates Stonehenge by about 1,000 years.
points.figure: c. 4500 to 4000 BC (6,500 to 6,000 years ago)
points.note: The stones and the dates of the settlement are well evidenced. Whether the alignments were intended as astronomy is an interpretation. The press release language ("oldest") is stronger than the paper. Comparison: the Stonehenge stone circle went up about 2500 BC; its first earthwork about 3000 BC.

sources.title: Malville, Wendorf, Mazar and Schild (1998) Megaliths and Neolithic astronomy in southern Egypt. Nature 392 - abstract
University of Colorado Boulder (1998) Oldest astronomical megalith alignment discovered in southern Egypt by science team
English Heritage: History of Stonehenge

points.heading: Early pottery in the Sahara (Ounjougou, Mali)
points.text: Pottery and small arrowheads at Ounjougou in Mali date to before 9400 BC, during a wetter phase of the Sahara. This is one of the earliest pottery traditions in Africa, linked to cooking wild grasses.
points.note: Well evidenced and likely an independent invention. It is not the oldest pottery in the world: the same paper notes very early ceramics in East Asia. Comparison: pottery reached Europe much later, but the exact date is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Huysecom et al. (2009) The emergence of pottery in Africa during the tenth millennium cal BC: new evidence from Ounjougou (Mali). Antiquity 83 - abstract, University of Geneva

points.heading: Sorghum domestication
points.text: Sorghum, a staple grain today, was domesticated from wild sorghum in eastern Sudan. A UCL-led team found evidence at a site near Kassala dated 3500 to 3000 BC.
points.note: Well evidenced as an African domestication. Dates for full domestication vary between studies.

sources.title: Earliest Evidence of Domesticated Sorghum Discovered (Sci.News, 28 September 2017)

points.heading: African rice
points.text: African rice (Oryza glaberrima) was domesticated in Africa, separately from Asian rice. Older work placed its origin in the inner Niger delta; genetic studies now suggest several origins across West and Central Africa.
points.note: The African origin is secure. Where and when it happened is debated, and a date is not confirmed by the sources cited.

points.heading: Cattle
points.text: Early cattle remains at Nabta Playa were once taken as evidence that Africans domesticated cattle independently. Later studies argue these were wild aurochs, with domestic cattle arriving from south-west Asia; this is still debated.
points.note: Contested: some researchers still argue for local domestication. Do not present either view as settled. Part of this rests on one independent source.

points.heading: Egyptian writing
points.text: Writing was invented independently in only a few places, usually counted as four: Mesopotamia, Egypt, China and Mesoamerica. Egypt's earliest writing, labels from the tombs of its first kings, dates to about 3300 BC (dates given range from about 3320 to 3250 BC), close in date to Mesopotamia (Iraq).
points.note: Well evidenced. Comparison: Europe's earliest deciphered script, Linear B in Greece, dates from about 1450 BC; it was adapted from the earlier, undeciphered Linear A, whose date is not confirmed by the sources cited.

ISAC Museum, University of Chicago (Google Arts & Culture): The Invention of Writing in Egypt
British Museum: Egyptian hieroglyphs decipherment timeline
The Past / Ancient Egypt magazine (Andrew Fulton)
Wikipedia: History of writing (secondary source)

points.heading: Rhind Mathematical Papyrus
points.text: A scroll of mathematical tables and problems, copied by the scribe Ahmes about 1650 BC. It includes a table for working with unit fractions (fractions with 1 on top) and a method of multiplication by doubling.
points.note: Well evidenced. Britannica also gives an earlier date for the original text (c. 2000 BC); the dating of the original is uncertain. This is practical mathematics for administration and building, not abstract proof.

sources.title: Britannica: Rhind papyrus
MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews: Mathematics in Egyptian papyri

points.heading: Moscow Mathematical Papyrus: volume of a frustum
points.text: Problem 14 calculates the volume of a truncated pyramid (a frustum) correctly for a worked example. Historians often call this the high point of Egyptian mathematics.
points.note: The calculation is correct, but it is a worked example, not a general proof. The papyrus date (Middle Kingdom, about 1850 BC) is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews: Mathematics in Egyptian papyri
Wikipedia: Moscow Mathematical Papyrus (secondary source)

points.heading: Egyptian number writing and the state
points.text: By about 3000 BC Egypt was a single state with hieroglyphic writing and numerals, needed for tax, grain and building records.
points.note: Shows the link between writing, number and administration.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews: An overview of Egyptian mathematics
UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Memphis and its Necropolis - the Pyramid Fields from Giza to Dahshur

points.heading: Edwin Smith Surgical Papyrus
points.text: The oldest known surgical text. It sets out 48 injury cases, each with examination, diagnosis, prognosis and treatment, with almost no magic.
points.note: Well evidenced. The copy dates from about the 17th century BC; the content may be about 1,000 years older, which is an estimate.

sources.title: US National Library of Medicine Technical Bulletin (2010): An ancient medical treasure at your fingertips (Edwin Smith Surgical Papyrus)

points.heading: Ebers Papyrus
points.text: A long Egyptian medical papyrus of remedies and medical texts from about 1550 BC (the end of the 16th century BC), now held by Leipzig University Library.
points.note: It mixes remedies with spells; how much of it worked is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Ebers papyrus
Leipzig University Library: Ebers Papyrus
Wikipedia: Ebers Papyrus (secondary source)

points.heading: Astronomy and the 365-day civil calendar
points.text: Egypt used a 365-day civil calendar: 12 months of 30 days plus five extra days. It ran alongside a lunar calendar throughout the pharaonic period.
points.note: The calendar is well evidenced. How it was set up is debated: some link it to the star Sirius, others to averaging Nile flood records. Part of this rests on one independent source.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Egyptian calendar (print version; same publisher as original)
Metropolitan Museum of Art: Telling Time in Ancient Egypt
UCL Digital Egypt: Calendar
Alexandra V. Mironova, 'Ancient Egyptian calendar', Calendars and Festivals of the Ancient Near East, St Petersburg State University
Wikipedia: Egyptian calendar (secondary source)

points.heading: Pyramid engineering at Giza
points.text: The Great Pyramid of Khufu is the only one of the ancient Seven Wonders still standing. Excavations found a purpose-built town for the workforce.
points.note: Well evidenced. Comparison: Giza (4th Dynasty, about 2575 to 2467 BC) is roughly contemporary with the Stonehenge stone circle (about 2500 BC).

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Memphis and its Necropolis - the Pyramid Fields from Giza to Dahshur
Ancient Egypt Research Associates (AERA): The Lost City of the Pyramids (Heit el-Ghurab)
NBC News / Associated Press (2010): Egypt discovers workers' tombs near pyramids

points.heading: Kerma
points.text: The Kingdom of Kerma in Upper Nubia (Sudan) flourished from about 2500 BC. It was the most powerful Nubian state of the early 2nd millennium BC, until Egypt took control by about 1500 BC.
points.note: Well evidenced archaeologically.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Kerma tentative list entry
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Karmah
British Museum, Room 65: Sudan, Egypt and Nubia (gallery page)
Wikipedia: Kerma culture (secondary source)

points.heading: Kush rules Egypt
points.text: Kings from Kush (Sudan) ruled Egypt as the 25th Dynasty in the 8th and 7th centuries BC. UNESCO describes their power reaching the Egyptian Delta and Palestine.
points.note: Well evidenced. A reminder that influence ran south to north as well as north to south.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Gebel Barkal and the Sites of the Napatan Region
Wikipedia: Twenty-fifth Dynasty of Egypt (secondary source)

points.heading: Meroë: pyramids and iron-working
points.text: Meroë was the heartland of Kush. Its pyramids and iron-working remains show wealth and production.
points.note: Iron-working at Meroë is well evidenced. Popular phrases like "the Birmingham of Africa" and claims about the exact scale and start date are not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Archaeological Sites of the Island of Meroe, UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Nok and Taruga (Nigeria)
points.text: The Nok culture of central Nigeria, known for its terracotta sculptures, gives some of the earliest evidence of iron smelting in West Africa, about 500 BC, from excavations at Taruga.
points.note: Dates of about 500 BC are well supported; claims of much earlier dates are less secure. Comparison: Britain's Iron Age began about 800 BC, central Europe's about 800 BC, the Aegean's about 1200 BC.

sources.title: Rupp, Breunig and Kahlheber, Exploring the Nok enigma. Antiquity Project Gallery (Goethe University Frankfurt project)
Nok culture, Encyclopaedia Britannica
Wikipedia: Iron Age Europe (secondary source)

points.heading: Invented in Africa or brought in?
points.text: Scholars still debate whether iron-working south of the Sahara came from the Mediterranean or was invented there. Very early dates from the Termit Massif in Niger have been used to argue for independent invention, but remain disputed.
points.note: Open question. Very early claims (some as far back as 3600 BC) are outliers and are not accepted as established. Part of this rests on one independent source.

sources.title: Alpern (2005), 'Did They or Didn't They Invent It? Iron in Sub-Saharan Africa', History in Africa 32
Chemistry World (Royal Society of Chemistry), 'The archaeologists saving Africa's ironworking heritage'
Killick, van der Merwe, Gordon and Grébénart (1988) 'Reassessment of the Evidence for Early Metallurgy in Niger, West Africa', Journal of Archaeological Science 15: 367–394 (PDF reprint)
Wikipedia: Iron metallurgy in Africa (secondary source)

points.heading: Great Lakes: Haya iron and the carbon steel claim
points.text: Peter Schmidt's fieldwork in the 1970s, including work with Donald Avery published in 1978, studied Haya smelting in north-west Tanzania and argued that furnaces reached high temperatures by preheating the air blast. Popular accounts go further and say the Haya made carbon steel for 2,000 years, hotter than anything in Europe.
points.figure: Early Iron Age (dates not confirmed by the sources cited)
points.note: Contested. The preheating idea is reported as a suggestion. The "hotter than Europe" claim comes from a popular radio script citing a 1983 anthology, not a technical study. The 1978 paper and any published scientific critique of it are not confirmed by the sources cited, so treat the bold claim as unproven.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Kemondo Iron Age Sites (secondary source)
University of Houston, The Engines of Our Ingenuity No. 385: African Steel Making (John H. Lienhard, radio script c.1990)

points.heading: Spread to the east and south
points.text: Iron-working spread through eastern Africa and reached South Africa by about AD 200, with the ancestors of today's Bantu-speaking peoples. Djenné-Djenno in Mali worked iron from its first settlement, about 250 BC.
points.note: Broad dates from a secondary source.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: Inland Niger Delta
Encyclopaedia Britannica: South Africa, The Iron Age
South African History Online
McIntosh and McIntosh (1981) 'The Inland Niger Delta before the Empire of Mali: Evidence from Jenne-Jeno', Journal of African History 22(1) – abstract
Wikipedia: Iron metallurgy in Africa (secondary source)

points.heading: Europe for comparison
points.text: In Europe iron came into use first in the south-east, from about 1200 BC; in Greece the Iron Age is usually dated from about 1050 BC, and in Britain from about 800 BC.
points.note: West African iron (about 500 BC) is later than the Aegean and similar to northern Europe. It does not support a claim that Africa had iron "before Europe" in general.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Iron Age
British Museum: Room 50, Britain and Europe 800 BC–AD 43
Ashmolean Museum, University of Oxford: Iron Age
Wikipedia: Iron Age Europe (secondary source)

points.heading: A great power
points.text: UNESCO calls Aksum the most powerful state between the Eastern Roman Empire and Persia.
points.note: UNESCO summary of the historical record.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Aksum

points.heading: Monumental stelae
points.text: Aksum's carved granite stelae date from the 3rd and 4th centuries AD. The largest may be the biggest single-stone stele anyone ever tried to raise.
points.note: Well evidenced.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Aksum

points.heading: Coinage
points.text: Aksum issued its own coins, mainly in gold and silver, from the reign of King Endubis (about AD 270 to 300).
points.note: Well evidenced. Which metals were used and how unusual this was in Africa at the time are not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: British Museum (via Smarthistory): Aksumite coins
British Museum collection: Endubis (ruler)
American Numismatic Society collection 1966.22.1
Fitzwilliam Museum, Cambridge: CM.2-2000
Wikipedia: Aksumite currency (secondary source)

points.heading: Christianity in the 4th century
points.text: Aksum adopted Christianity in the 4th century AD and built churches.
points.note: Well evidenced. Popular accounts link the conversion to King Ezana and compare it with Rome's adoption in the same century; those details are not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Aksum

points.heading: Djenné-Djenno: a city before Islam
points.text: Djenné-Djenno in Mali was settled from about 250 BC and became a large town. Archaeologists found no city walls, temples or signs of a state bureaucracy in the pre-Islamic period. UNESCO calls it evidence of pre-Islamic urban life.
points.note: The early town is well evidenced. Population figures (up to about 42,000 for the whole complex around AD 900) are estimates.

sources.title: Old Towns of Djenné, UNESCO World Heritage Centre
ORIAS, University of California Berkeley: From Djenné to Mali - state and empire (lecture notes)

points.heading: Ghana (Wagadu)
points.text: The Ghana Empire, or Wagadu, was based in what is now south-east Mauritania and western Mali.
points.figure: c. AD 300 to mid-13th century (start uncertain)
points.note: Its start date is uncertain, and the identification of its capital (Koumbi Saleh) is debated. Its role in the gold trade is widely reported but not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Ghana, historical West African empire
Metropolitan Museum of Art: Western Sudan, 500–1000 A.D.
Wikipedia: Ghana Empire (secondary source)

points.heading: Mali and Mansa Musa's hajj (1324)
points.text: Mansa Musa ruled Mali from 1307 or 1312. His pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 was so lavish that his gold gifts are said to have affected the value of gold in Egypt.
points.note: The hajj is well documented by Arabic writers. "Wealthiest person in history" cannot be measured and should be avoided. The same sources note that his reign also involved warfare and slave raiding.

sources.title: Britannica: Musa I of Mali
Wikipedia: Mansa Musa (secondary source)

points.heading: Songhai
points.text: Songhai, ruled from Gao, was at its peak one of the largest empires in West African history, until its defeat at the Battle of Tondibi in 1591.
points.note: Well evidenced. Part of this rests on one independent source.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Tomb of Askia
History Today: Fall of Africa's Greatest Empire
Issihak II – Encyclopaedia Britannica
Songhai empire summary – Encyclopaedia Britannica
Julianna Tesfu, 'Songhai Empire (ca. 1375-1591)', BlackPast.org
Western and Central Sudan, 1400–1600 A.D. – Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, The Metropolitan Museum of Art
Wikipedia: Songhai Empire (secondary source)

points.heading: Timbuktu as a centre of learning
points.text: UNESCO describes Timbuktu as an intellectual and spiritual capital, with Sankore and other schools, and a market where manuscripts were traded.
points.note: Well evidenced.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Timbuktu

points.heading: Sankore: a "university"?
points.text: Sankore is often called a university, but some scholars say the term is misleading. Timbuktu's scholars learned through informal teaching, often within families, not in universities like those of medieval Europe. Many of the city's manuscripts are still held in private libraries.
points.note: The learning was real; the word "university" overstates its structure. Part of this rests on one independent source.

sources.title: Cleaveland, 'Timbuktu and Walata: lineages and higher education', in The Meanings of Timbuktu (CODESRIA/HSRC Press)
Stewart (2021), 'What's in the Manuscripts of Timbuktu? A Survey of the Contents of 31 Private Libraries', History in Africa 48
Library of Congress: Timbuktu, an Islamic cultural center
Wikipedia: Sankore Madrasah (secondary source)

points.heading: Subjects of the Timbuktu manuscripts
points.text: Library of Congress exhibits from Timbuktu family libraries include an astronomy text, an arithmetic primer, a medical compilation and many works of Islamic law.
points.note: Well evidenced. Most surviving copies date from the 16th to 19th centuries (for example an astronomy text copied 1733); much of the science follows the wider Islamic tradition rather than being unique to Timbuktu.

sources.title: Library of Congress exhibition: Ancient Manuscripts from the Desert Libraries of Timbuktu - Exhibition items

points.heading: How many manuscripts?
points.text: Figures vary. Librarians said almost 400,000 manuscripts were moved to Bamako in 2012 to 2013; another account says about 350,000. About 4,203 were lost from the Ahmed Baba Institute. An early report that 25,000 were burned was false.
points.note: Numbers vary by source and are estimates; private family collections were never fully catalogued.

sources.title: Mail & Guardian (2014): Scroll smugglers - how Timbuktu's secret treasures were saved
Wikipedia: Timbuktu Manuscripts (secondary source)
MPR News / Associated Press (2013): Timbuktu manuscripts mostly safe, university says

points.heading: Ife sculpture
points.text: Between about 1200 and 1500, Ife (Nigeria) produced naturalistic heads in bronze, terracotta and stone. Their discovery challenged European assumptions about African art.
points.note: Well evidenced. The Met calls them "bronzes"; the exact alloys are not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: The Met, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History: Ife (from ca. 6th century)

points.heading: Benin Bronzes and brass casting
points.text: The Benin Bronzes, made of brass and bronze by royal guilds for the Oba of Benin, date from at least the 16th century. British forces looted them in 1897.
points.note: Well evidenced. The British Museum is one of several museums holding looted pieces; their return is a live public debate.

sources.title: British Museum: Benin Bronzes

points.heading: Benin City walls and earthworks
points.text: Benin City and its region are crossed by earthen walls and ditches built between about AD 700 and 1400. Patrick Darling estimated in 1977 a total length of about 16,000 km, the longest earthworks of the pre-mechanical era.
points.note: The earthworks are real. The 16,000 km length is one researcher's estimate, mostly of low banks, and has not been fully re-measured. Comparisons such as "four times the Great Wall of China" rest on this estimate.

sources.title: Guinness World Records: Longest earthworks of the pre-mechanical era
NASA Earth Observatory (2025): A glimpse of history in Benin City

points.heading: Kilwa's own coins
points.text: Kilwa Kisiwani (Tanzania) minted its own currency from the 11th to the 14th century. Kilwa coins have even been found in northern Australia.
points.note: The coins are well evidenced. How they reached Australia is unknown.

sources.title: Ruins of Kilwa Kisiwani and Ruins of Songo Mnara, UNESCO World Heritage Centre
Australian Geographic (2014): Unravelling the mystery of Arnhem Land's ancient African coins

points.heading: Husuni Kubwa palace and the Great Mosque
points.text: The Husuni Kubwa palace was built about 1310 to 1333 with a large octagonal bathing pool. Kilwa's Great Mosque is the oldest standing mosque on the East African coast.
points.note: Well evidenced.

sources.title: Ruins of Kilwa Kisiwani and Ruins of Songo Mnara, UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Trade with China
points.text: Gold and ivory were traded for Chinese porcelain and other goods. A Ming coin of the Yongle emperor (1403 to 1425) was excavated on Manda island, Kenya.
points.note: The porcelain trade is well evidenced. A visit by Admiral Zheng He to this coast is possible but not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Ruins of Kilwa Kisiwani and Ruins of Songo Mnara, UNESCO World Heritage Centre
Field Museum press release (2013): Ancient Chinese coin found on Kenyan island by Field Museum expedition

points.heading: Slave trading on the coast
points.text: Kilwa's medieval wealth came mainly from trading gold and ivory from the interior. By the late 18th century it had become a key port in the Indian Ocean slave trade.
points.note: Included for balance: African states were sophisticated, and some also traded in enslaved people.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art: Historic Towns of Kilwa Kisiwani and Songo Mnara
Ruins of Kilwa Kisiwani and Ruins of Songo Mnara (UNESCO WHC)
Encyclopaedia Britannica: eastern Africa
Wikipedia: Kilwa Sultanate (secondary source)

points.heading: Mapungubwe
points.text: Mapungubwe (South Africa), which rose and fell between about 900 and 1300, grew into the largest kingdom in the subcontinent, trading through East African ports to India and China, before it was abandoned.
points.note: UNESCO's own page gives two end dates (end of 13th century and 14th century). Dates are approximate.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Mapungubwe Cultural Landscape

points.heading: Great Zimbabwe
points.text: Great Zimbabwe was built by the Shona between about 1100 and 1450. Its granite walls were fitted without mortar. Its population may have topped 10,000.
points.note: Builders and dates are well evidenced. The population figure is an estimate.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Great Zimbabwe National Monument
The Met, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History: Great Zimbabwe (11th-15th century)

points.heading: Trade
points.text: Finds at Great Zimbabwe show long-distance trade with the outside world.
points.note: Well evidenced.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Great Zimbabwe National Monument

points.heading: Egyptian hieroglyphs
points.text: One of the world's few independent inventions of writing. Egypt's earliest writing dates to about 3300 BC (dates given range from about 3320 to 3250 BC).
points.note: See the Nile Valley section.

sources.title: University of Chicago News: Oriental Institute 'Visible Language' exhibition
ISAC Museum, University of Chicago (Google Arts & Culture): The Invention of Writing in Egypt
British Museum: Egyptian hieroglyphs decipherment timeline
The Past / Ancient Egypt magazine (Andrew Fulton)
Wikipedia: History of writing (secondary source)

points.heading: Meroitic
points.text: Kush developed its own script, Meroitic: a cursive form appeared in the 3rd century BC and a hieroglyphic form in the 2nd century BC. It was deciphered (can be sounded out) in 1911 by F. Ll. Griffith, but the language is still only partly understood.
points.note: Well evidenced.

sources.title: UCL Petrie Museum, Digital Egypt: Meroitic script
Rilly, 'Meroitic Writing', UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology
Wikipedia: Meroitic script (secondary source)

points.heading: Ge'ez
points.text: Aksum's inscriptions use Greek, Sabaean and Ge'ez. Ge'ez added vowel marks in the 4th century AD and is still used in Ethiopia and Eritrea.
points.note: Ge'ez grew out of the South Arabian script; it was not invented from nothing.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Aksum
Wikipedia: Ge'ez script (secondary source)

points.heading: Libyco-Berber and Tifinagh
points.text: Peoples of ancient North Africa wrote inscriptions in the Libyco-Berber script; Tuareg Tifinagh is related to it and a modern form (Neo-Tifinagh) is used today.
points.note: Its origin (possibly linked to the Phoenician alphabet) is uncertain.

sources.title: British Museum African Rock Art: Written in stone, the Libyco-Berber scripts
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Tifinagh
Wikipedia: Tifinagh (secondary source)

points.heading: Nsibidi
points.text: Nsibidi is a system of symbols of the Ejagham and neighbouring peoples of the Cross River region of Nigeria and Cameroon. Designs on pottery from Calabar dated to the 5th to 15th centuries AD may foreshadow it.
points.note: It is usually classed as proto-writing (symbols), not a full script for writing a language. Early dates are debated.

sources.title: Slogar (2005), PhD dissertation, University of Maryland: Calabar terracottas
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Ekoi
Adekunle Temilade Adeniji, 'The Akwanshi Stone Monoliths of the Cross River Region in Nigeria and Cameroon', Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, The Metropolitan Museum of Art (25 Sept 2025)
Wikipedia: Proto-writing (secondary source)

points.heading: Vai
points.text: The Vai script of Liberia was created in the early 1830s by a small group of Vai speakers. Momolu Duwalu Bukele was one of its main inventors.
points.note: Well evidenced. It is a 19th-century invention, not an ancient one.

sources.title: Tykhostup and Kelly (2018), 'A Diachronic Comparison of the Vai Script of Liberia (1834-2005)', Journal of Open Humanities Data
Tuchscherer & Hair 2002, History in Africa 29 (Cambridge)
Unicode Technical Committee document L2/05-053 (2005), Vai code chart proposal
Max Planck Institute for the Science of Human History press release, 'Rare African Script Offers Clues to the Evolution of Writing' (13 Jan 2022)
Wikipedia: Vai syllabary (secondary source)

points.heading: Ron Eglash, African Fractals (1999)
points.text: Eglash argued that many African settlement plans and designs use repeating patterns at different scales (fractals), sometimes on purpose.
points.note: Critique: a reviewer notes that all complex settlements may look fractal for natural reasons, and Eglash himself says the patterns do not prove knowledge of fractal geometry.

sources.title: Bangura (2000) review of Eglash, African Fractals. Nexus Network Journal 2(4)

points.heading: Yoruba counting in twenties
points.text: Yoruba counts in base 20 and builds numbers by adding, subtracting and multiplying, for example 60 as "three twenties".
points.note: Well known, but the source page is flagged as needing more citations. Base-20 counting is also found elsewhere; the source compares one feature with Danish.

sources.title: University at Buffalo, Mathematicians of the African Diaspora: early Nigeria
Akinadé and Ọdẹjọbí (2014) 'Computational modelling of Yorùbá numerals in a number-to-text conversion system', Journal of Language Modelling 2(1): 167–211 (repository copy, BazTech)
Agbeyangi, Eludiora and Popoola (2016) 'Web-Based Yorùbá Numeral Translation System', IAES International Journal of Artificial Intelligence 5(4)
Wikipedia: Yoruba numerals (secondary source; flagged by Wikipedia as needing more citations)

points.heading: Sona sand drawings
points.text: Chokwe sona are continuous one-line drawings made in sand around a grid of dots. Mathematicians, notably Paulus Gerdes, have analysed the rules used to make them.
points.note: The drawings are real; describing them as "algorithms" is a modern mathematical reading. How old the tradition is is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Chavey (2010) Strip symmetry groups of African sona designs. Bridges 2010 Proceedings (Beloit College)
Wikipedia: Lusona (secondary source)

points.heading: Al-Kishnawi on magic squares
points.text: Muhammad ibn Muhammad al-Kishnawi, a Fulani scholar from northern Nigeria, wrote on how to construct magic squares. He died in Cairo in 1741.
points.note: His magic squares sat within numerology and esoteric study, not only pure mathematics. The often-quoted treatise date of 1732 is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: University at Buffalo, Mathematicians of the African Diaspora: Muhammad ibn Muhammad
Muslim Heritage (FSTC), Natty Mark Samuels 2015 (non-academic)
Wikipedia: Muhammad ibn Muhammad al-Kishnawi (secondary source)

points.heading: Arithmetic teaching in Timbuktu
points.text: A Timbuktu arithmetic primer explained the four operations and the history of mathematics, and was used by students in Timbuktu and North Africa.
points.note: Well evidenced as a teaching text, in the wider Islamic scholarly tradition.

sources.title: Library of Congress exhibition: Ancient Manuscripts from the Desert Libraries of Timbuktu - Exhibition items

points.heading: Onesimus and smallpox inoculation in Boston
points.text: Onesimus, an enslaved African man, told Cotton Mather about inoculation against smallpox practised in his homeland. Mather reported it to the Royal Society in 1716 and promoted inoculation in the Boston epidemic of 1721.
points.note: Well evidenced. Balance: Mather also learned the practice was used in Turkey and China, so it was not uniquely African. The account first reached Mather by 1716, not in 1721.

sources.title: HISTORY (A&E): How an enslaved African man in Boston helped save generations from smallpox
Wikipedia: Onesimus (Bostonian)

points.heading: Medicine in the Timbuktu manuscripts
points.text: A Timbuktu compilation explains how to diagnose and treat the sick using animal, plant and mineral substances, alongside prayers.
points.note: Mixes practical remedies with religious practice, as most medicine of the period did.

sources.title: Library of Congress exhibition: Ancient Manuscripts from the Desert Libraries of Timbuktu - Exhibition items

points.heading: Kano and Zaria manuscripts
points.text: Northern Nigeria has an Arabic manuscript tradition. The Kano Chronicle, an Arabic history of Kano's kings written in the 1890s, is the best-known local history of the Hausa.
points.note: The surviving Kano Chronicle was written in the late 1880s, so it is a late source for early history. Details of Zaria manuscript collections are not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Kano, historical kingdom
Hiskett (1957), 'The Kano Chronicle', Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society
British Library Endangered Archives: Arabic manuscripts held by the Kano State History and Culture Bureau
Hunwick 1994, History in Africa 21 (Cambridge), quoting Palmer
Wikipedia: Kano Chronicle (secondary source)

points.heading: "The Dogon knew about Sirius B" - unproven, probably false
points.text: The French anthropologist Marcel Griaule reported that the Dogon of Mali knew of an invisible companion star of Sirius. In 1991 Walter van Beek restudied the Dogon and found no shared knowledge of this; his informants said they learned about the star from Griaule. Britannica describes a Dogon ceremony as resting on a belief that beings from Sirius visited the Dogon, but does not discuss this dispute.
points.note: Verdict: unproven and probably the result of contact with the researcher. Griaule's daughter disputed van Beek's method, so the debate is not fully closed.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Dogon people (secondary source quoting van Beek 1991, Current Anthropology 32(2))
Dogon and Bangime Linguistics bibliography: van Beek (1991) Dogon Restudied: A Field Evaluation of the Work of Marcel Griaule
Dogon, Encyclopaedia Britannica
The Skeptic's Dictionary: Dogon

points.heading: "Ishango proves prime numbers" - unproven
points.text: One column of the Ishango bone has groups of 11, 13, 17 and 19 notches, the primes between 10 and 20. Some scholars doubt this shows knowledge of primes, as there is no evidence of the idea before classical Greece.
points.note: Verdict: unproven. The bone is evidence of counting or recording; "proves primes" goes beyond the evidence.

sources.title: ICOMOS-IAU Thematic Study on Astronomical Heritage, Case Study 1.3: The Ishango Bone
Pletser, 'Does the Ishango Bone Indicate Knowledge of the Base 12?' (arXiv)
Parkinson-Coombs et al. (2026), Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society 48
Wikipedia: Ishango bone

points.heading: "Africans invented algebra" - false as stated
points.text: Algebra as a named subject comes from al-Khwarizmi's book, written in Baghdad, where he worked until about 850. North Africans contributed later: Abu Kamil in Egypt (about 850 to 930) and Ibn al-Banna and al-Qalasadi, who used symbols in the 15th century. Egyptian papyri solved some equation-like problems much earlier.
points.note: Verdict: false as a blanket claim; Africa's real contributions are Egyptian problem-solving and later North African work in the Islamic tradition.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews: Al-Khwarizmi biography
Britannica: al-Khwarizmi
Wikipedia: History of algebra (secondary source)
MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews: Arabic mathematics - forgotten brilliance?

points.heading: "The pyramids were built by slaves" - not supported
points.text: Excavations at Giza found a town for workers and tombs for builders beside the pyramids, with regular meat supplies and three-month work rotations. Egypt's antiquities chief concluded they were paid labourers.
points.note: Verdict: the slave story is not supported. But "free volunteers" also overstates it: rotated labour may have been compulsory service for the state. The "paid" reading is the excavators' interpretation.

sources.title: NBC News / Associated Press (2010): Egypt discovers workers' tombs near pyramids
Ancient Egypt Research Associates (AERA): The Lost City of the Pyramids (Heit el-Ghurab)

points.heading: "Egypt was not African" and the race debate - frame by ancestry and geography
points.text: Egypt is in Africa, at its junction with Asia. Ancient DNA is still scarce: one Old Kingdom genome is mostly North African Neolithic ancestry with about 20% from the eastern Fertile Crescent. Later mummies from Middle Egypt share more ancestry with Near Eastern peoples than today's Egyptians, who have more recent sub-Saharan ancestry. Mainstream scholars say modern "black" and "white" labels do not fit ancient Egypt.
points.note: Verdict: "Egypt was not African" is false on geography and misleading on ancestry. Equally, claims that Egypt was a single "race" are not supported. Limits: very few genomes, mostly from northern and middle Egypt, none from Upper Egypt or Nubia in these studies.

sources.title: Schuenemann et al. (2017) Ancient Egyptian mummy genomes suggest an increase of Sub-Saharan African ancestry in post-Roman periods. Nature Communications - abstract
Morez Jacobs et al. (2025) Whole-genome ancestry of an Old Kingdom Egyptian. Nature - abstract
Wikipedia: Ancient Egyptian race controversy (secondary source)

points.heading: "Africa was more advanced than Europe" - partly true for some fields and dates, false as a blanket claim
points.text: In some fields Africa was earlier: Egyptian writing (about 3250 BC) came about 1,800 years before Europe's earliest deciphered script (Linear B, about 1450 BC), and Giza's pyramids match Stonehenge in date. In others Europe was level or earlier: farming in Britain began about 4100 BC, the Aegean used iron before West Africa, and Europe has engraved bones as old as Ishango. Egypt itself drew on contacts with south-west Asia, including farming and writing ideas.
