points.note: Verdict: compare like with like, by date and by region. "Africa" and "Europe" were never single societies, so league tables mislead.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Linear B (secondary source)
Wikipedia: Ishango bone
Wikipedia: Neolithic British Isles (secondary source)
English Heritage: History of Stonehenge
Morez Jacobs et al. (2025) Whole-genome ancestry of an Old Kingdom Egyptian. Nature - abstract

points.heading: "Europeans brought civilisation to Africa" - false
points.text: Every section of this page records cities, states, writing, metalwork, coinage, scholarship and trade in Africa long before European colonial rule. The idea that Africa had no history before Europeans arrived was voiced in the 20th century by the Oxford historian Hugh Trevor-Roper. Colonial authorities in Rhodesia pressed archaeologists to deny that Africans built Great Zimbabwe. UNESCO's General History of Africa (from 1964) was created to correct this.
points.note: Verdict: false. Balance: African states were not ideal societies; several (Mali, Kilwa) also took part in slavery, as did European states.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Hugh Trevor-Roper (secondary source)
Wikipedia: Great Zimbabwe (secondary source)
The Met, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History: Great Zimbabwe (11th-15th century)
UNESCO: General History of Africa

points.heading: "Mansa Musa was the richest person ever" - unmeasurable
points.text: Britannica repeats that he is widely considered the wealthiest man in history. There is no way to compare medieval wealth with modern fortunes reliably.
points.note: Verdict: exaggerated. Say instead that his 1324 hajj displayed enormous wealth in gold.

sources.title: Britannica: Musa I of Mali

points.heading: "Benin's walls were four times longer than the Great Wall" - exaggerated precision
points.text: The total length rests on a single 1977 estimate of about 16,000 km, mostly of low banks and ditches, not a measured wall.
points.note: Verdict: impressive and real, but the comparison treats an estimate of low earthworks as if it were a measured stone wall.

sources.title: Guinness World Records: Longest earthworks of the pre-mechanical era
NASA Earth Observatory (2025): A glimpse of history in Benin City

points.heading: "Nabta Playa is the world's first observatory, older than Stonehenge" - partly true
points.text: Nabta's stones are older than Stonehenge's stone circle, and some alignments to the solstice are reported in Nature. "First observatory" goes beyond what the paper claims.
points.note: Verdict: older, yes; an astronomical observatory, unproven.

sources.title: Malville, Wendorf, Mazar and Schild (1998) Megaliths and Neolithic astronomy in southern Egypt. Nature 392 - abstract

points.heading: "The Haya made steel hotter than anything in Europe" - unproven
points.text: This comes from popular sources based on 1970s fieldwork and recreated smelts in the 20th century, not on dated ancient steel analysed in a lab.
points.note: Verdict: unproven. Present Haya smelting as skilled and inventive, without the superlative.

sources.title: University of Houston, The Engines of Our Ingenuity No. 385: African Steel Making (John H. Lienhard, radio script c.1990)

points.heading: Herodotus on Egypt and the Greek gods
points.text: Herodotus (5th century BC) wrote that the names of most Greek gods came from Egypt, while making clear he was repeating what Egyptians told him.
points.note: This is Herodotus's own claim, reported neutrally. Modern scholars treat his Egyptian derivations with caution; the passage shows what Greeks believed, not a proven borrowing.

sources.title: Herodotus, Histories 2.50 (trans. A. D. Godley) - Perseids / Perseus Digital Library text

points.heading: Plato's Egyptian priest
points.text: In Plato's Timaeus, an elderly priest at Sais in Egypt tells the Athenian lawmaker Solon that Greeks are "always children" compared with Egypt's long records.
points.note: A literary dialogue, not a historical record. It shows Greek respect for Egyptian antiquity, not a documented transfer of specific knowledge.

sources.title: Plato, Timaeus 22b - Perseus Digital Library, Tufts University

points.heading: Thales and Egyptian geometry
points.text: Later Greek writers said Thales learned geometry in Egypt and brought it to Greece. MacTutor adds that Egyptian geometry was largely practical rules, not deductive proof.
points.note: The tradition is late ("is said to"). Both sides are shown: Egyptian practice influenced Greeks; formal proof is credited to later Greeks.

sources.title: Thales of Miletus - MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Euclid of Alexandria
points.text: Euclid, author of the Elements, worked in Alexandria, Egypt, a Greek-speaking city on African soil founded by Alexander the Great.
points.note: Alexandria was an African city, but its scholarship was written in Greek and drew on the whole eastern Mediterranean. Euclid's own ethnicity is unknown.

sources.title: Euclid of Alexandria - MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Ptolemy in Alexandria
points.text: Ptolemy made astronomical observations from Alexandria. His great work reached medieval Europe through Arabic as the "Almagest".
points.note: A clear example of a two-step route: Greek text written in Egypt, translated into Arabic, then from Arabic into Latin (see Gerard of Cremona).

sources.title: Claudius Ptolemy - MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Hypatia of Alexandria
points.text: Hypatia, a mathematician and philosopher taught by her father Theon, worked in Alexandria and was killed in 415.
points.note: MacTutor calls her the first woman (to make a substantial contribution to mathematics, in its fuller sentence).

sources.title: Hypatia of Alexandria - MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Carthage
points.text: Carthage, founded by Phoenician colonists in present-day Tunisia, built a Mediterranean trading empire until Rome destroyed it in 146 BC; it was later rebuilt as capital of Roman Africa.
points.note: Carthage was founded by settlers from the Levant (Phoenicians) and mixed with local Berber/Libyan populations; it is African in place, Levantine in origin. UNESCO page also gives "146 AD" in one section, an evident typo.

sources.title: Archaeological Site of Carthage (UNESCO WHC)
Western North Africa, 1000 B.C.-1 A.D. - Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, The Met

points.heading: Septimius Severus, emperor from Africa (193-211)
points.text: Septimius Severus was born at Lepcis (Leptis) Magna in present-day Libya, ruled Rome from 193 and died at York in 211.
points.note: English Heritage says his father's family was Punic (of Phoenician descent) and his mother's Italian. He is sometimes called "Rome's Black Emperor"; Historic Environment Scotland says his skin colour cannot be verified. Present him as the first emperor from Africa, not as Black.

sources.title: Septimius Severus - English Heritage
Scotland's African Emperor - Historic Environment Scotland Blog

points.heading: Augustine of Hippo
points.text: Augustine, among the most influential Christian thinkers, was born in Thagaste in Roman Africa (modern Souk Ahras, Algeria) and was bishop of Hippo.
points.note: Born to a Roman-African family; often described as of Berber descent, but that is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Saint Augustine - Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy

points.heading: Africans in Roman Britain
points.text: North Africans served and lived in Roman Britain; English Heritage notes a tombstone of Victor, a former slave from North Africa, at South Shields.
points.note: Covered in the hub already (Black Romans in Britain); link there rather than repeat.

sources.title: Septimius Severus - English Heritage

points.heading: Tariq ibn Ziyad and 711
points.text: In 711 North African Muslim forces led by the Berber general Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed into the Iberian Peninsula.
points.note: Conquest under the Umayyad caliphate of Damascus; the rank and file were largely Berber, leadership mixed Arab and Berber.

sources.title: Who were the Moors? It's complicated - National Geographic

points.heading: Cordoba as a caliphal capital
points.text: UNESCO records that in 929 Abd al-Rahman III made Cordoba the seat of an independent caliphate, and that the Great Mosque was begun in the 8th century.
points.note: The Umayyads of Cordoba were a Syrian Arab dynasty; the mosque's style draws on Syrian, Visigothic and local traditions.

sources.title: Historic Centre of Cordoba (UNESCO WHC)

points.heading: The Cordoba library: how big?
points.text: Medieval sources credit Caliph al-Hakam II (r. 961-976) with a palace library of over 400,000 books. A peer-reviewed study calls the figure likely hyperbole, while agreeing the library was a major centre.
points.note: Report the figure only as a claim in later sources. The library drew scholars from Baghdad and Constantinople, per the same article.

sources.title: U. Bongianino, The page architecture of a deluxe Arabic dictionary from Islamic Spain - Manuscript and Text Cultures (peer-reviewed)

points.heading: New crops and irrigation
points.text: Andrew Watson (1974, book 1983) argued for an "Arab Agricultural Revolution": new crops spread, especially from India, across the Middle East, North Africa and al-Andalus.
points.note: Crops such as sugar cane, rice, citrus and cotton are often cited; a crop-by-crop list is not confirmed by the sources cited here. Many came from India or South-East Asia, with North Africa as route.

sources.title: D. Varisco and D. Fuks, Andrew Watson's contribution to the history of agriculture - Journal of Economic History, In Memoriam (Cambridge Core)

points.heading: Critics of the "revolution"
points.text: Later scholars accept that Watson's survey is valuable but argue several crops were already present before Islam and that "revolution" overstates change. Michael Decker (2009) and others have challenged the thesis.
points.note: Decker, "Plants and Progress: Rethinking the Arab Agricultural Revolution", Journal of World History 20(2), 2009, is cited in the Squatriti reference list; its argument is summarised here from the Varisco and Fuks piece, not from Decker directly.

sources.title: D. Varisco and D. Fuks, Andrew Watson's contribution to the history of agriculture - Journal of Economic History, In Memoriam (Cambridge Core)
P. Squatriti, Of Seeds, Seasons, and Seas: Andrew Watson's Medieval Agrarian Revolution Forty Years Later - Journal of Economic History (2014)

points.heading: The Alhambra
points.text: UNESCO describes the Alhambra and Generalife as exceptional testimony to Muslim Spain, built mainly under the Nasrid emirs of Granada.
points.note: Nasrid art is Andalusi: Iberian, with roots in North African and eastern Islamic traditions. Quote reproduced as the page gives it (missing "of").

sources.title: Alhambra, Generalife and Albayzin, Granada - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Toledo translations
points.text: In the second half of the 12th century, Toledo became a centre for translating Arabic works, and Greek works preserved in Arabic, into Latin. Gerard of Cremona and Dominicus Gundisalvi were the most prolific translators.
points.note: Other named translators include the Jewish scholar Avendauth and, later, Michael Scot (SEP). The texts were mostly by Persian, Iraqi and Greek authors (Avicenna, al-Farabi, Ptolemy).

sources.title: Influence of Arabic and Islamic Philosophy on the Latin West - Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy

points.heading: Gerard of Cremona and the Almagest
points.text: Gerard went to Toledo to learn Arabic so he could read and translate Ptolemy's Almagest, and made Arabic science available in Latin.

sources.title: Gherard of Cremona - MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Ibn Rushd (Averroes)
points.text: Ibn Rushd was born in Cordoba in 1126, served the Almohad court in Marrakesh as judge and physician, and became the Latin West's great commentator on Aristotle.
points.note: Andalusi-born; career split between Iberia and Morocco. Death in Marrakesh (1198) is given by one account (SEP); IEP says he returned to Cordoba and died the following year without naming the place.

sources.title: Ibn Rushd [Averroes] - Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy

points.heading: Maimonides
points.text: Moses Maimonides was born in Cordoba in 1138; his family later left, and he settled in Fustat (old Cairo), Egypt, where he worked as a physician and scholar.
points.note: A Jewish Andalusi scholar who wrote mainly in Arabic: Iberian-born, career in Morocco and Egypt.

sources.title: Maimonides - Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy

points.heading: Al-Zarqali and the Toledan Tables
points.text: Al-Zarqali (Arzachel), an instrument maker and astronomer in 11th-century Toledo, is best known for the Toledan Tables, which circulated in Latin.
points.note: Andalusi, working in Islamic Toledo before its conquest by Castile in 1085.

sources.title: Al-Zarqali - MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Abbas ibn Firnas and flight
points.text: Ibn Firnas, a 9th-century Cordoban scholar, is said to have attempted a glide with feathered wings about 875. The accounts survive through al-Maqqari, a 17th-century Moroccan scholar.
points.note: The sources are late and brief; "first aviator" claims go beyond the evidence. Often described as of Berber descent, but that is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Flights of Fancy on Manmade Wings - AramcoWorld, Nov/Dec 2008

points.heading: Ziryab
points.text: Ziryab, a musician from Baghdad, reached the Cordoban court in the 9th century. Later writers credit him with changes to the lute and to music, dress and dining customs.
points.note: Came from Baghdad via North Africa. Much of his reputation rests on Ibn Hayyan (11th century) and later sources; specific "innovations" are often embellished. His ethnic origin is debated; the dark-complexion report is from Ibn Hayyan.

sources.title: R. W. Lebling Jr, Flight of the Blackbird - AramcoWorld, July/August 2003

points.heading: Almoravids
points.text: The Almoravids were a confederation of Berber (Sanhaja) peoples from the western Sahara who founded Marrakesh and ruled both Morocco and al-Andalus.
points.note: Marrakesh founding date (c.1070) and conquest of al-Andalus (from 1086) are not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Almoravids - Encyclopedia.com (Europe, 1450 to 1789 / Encyclopedia of Islam and the Muslim World entry)
Ibn Rushd (Averroes) - Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy

points.heading: Almohads
points.text: The Almohads, a rival Berber movement from the Moroccan High Atlas, replaced the Almoravids and patronised scholars such as Ibn Rushd and Ibn Tufayl.

sources.title: Almoravids - Encyclopedia.com (Europe, 1450 to 1789 / Encyclopedia of Islam and the Muslim World entry)
Ibn Rushd (Averroes) - Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy

points.heading: Indian origin of the numerals
points.text: The numerals originated in India; the scholar al-Biruni (11th century) said Arabs used a selection of Indian figures.

sources.title: Indian numerals - MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: The western route: North Africa and Spain
points.text: MacTutor states the numerals reached Europe through the western Arabic world, mainly North Africa and Spain.

sources.title: The Arabic numeral system - MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Ghubar ("dust") numerals
points.text: In the Maghreb and al-Andalus, the western forms were called ghubar ("dust") numerals, after the dust board used for calculating.
points.note: European numeral shapes descend from these western forms.

sources.title: The Arabic numeral system - MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Codex Vigilanus, 976
points.text: The earliest known appearance of these numerals in a European manuscript is in the Codex Vigilanus, copied by a monk in Spain in 976.

sources.title: The Arabic numeral system - MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Gerbert of Aurillac (Pope Sylvester II)
points.text: Gerbert studied in Catalonia in the 960s, learned the Hindu-Arabic numerals there and promoted them, with the abacus, in Europe.
points.note: He studied in Christian Catalonia, which was in contact with al-Andalus; he did not study in Muslim Cordoba, despite popular claims.

sources.title: Gerbert of Aurillac - MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Fibonacci in Bejaia (Bugia), Algeria
points.text: Leonardo of Pisa (Fibonacci) learned the "nine Indian figures" as a boy in Bugia (now Bejaia, Algeria), where his father represented Pisan merchants. He said so in the Liber Abaci (1202).
points.note: The clearest single example of North Africa as the route: Indian numerals, learned from North African teachers, published in Italy.

sources.title: Leonardo Pisano Fibonacci - MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Al-Khwarizmi's algebra
points.text: Al-Khwarizmi, working at the House of Wisdom in Baghdad around 820, wrote the book that gave us the word "algebra"; his name gave us "algorithm".
points.note: Baghdad and Central Asia (Khwarazm), not Africa. The route to Europe ran through Spain.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews: Al-Khwarizmi biography

points.heading: Robert of Chester, 1145, Segovia
points.text: The English scholar Robert of Chester translated al-Khwarizmi's algebra into Latin in 1145, working in Segovia.

sources.title: Robert of Chester - Muslim Heritage

points.heading: Ibn al-Banna of Marrakesh
points.text: Ibn al-Banna (born Marrakesh) taught mathematics and astronomy in Fez and used some symbolic notation.
points.note: MacTutor argues that neither al-Banna nor al-Qalasadi invented algebraic notation; earlier attempts existed.

sources.title: Ibn al-Banna - MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Al-Qalasadi and algebraic symbols
points.text: Al-Qalasadi (1412-1486), born at Baza in al-Andalus and died at Beja in Tunisia, used short Arabic words or letters as algebraic symbols.
points.note: Andalusi-born, career ended in Tunisia (Ifriqiya). "First" claims are qualified by MacTutor itself.

sources.title: Al-Qalasadi - MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Al-Qarawiyyin, Fez (859)
points.text: Guinness World Records lists the University of al-Qarawiyyin, founded in 859 in Fez, as the oldest existing, continually operating educational institution. Its founder is traditionally named as Fatima al-Fihri.
points.note: UNESCO's own wording is not confirmed by the sources cited. "First degree-granting" is a contested claim; it began as a mosque with teaching and became a state university in 1963 (not confirmed by the sources cited). Fatima al-Fihri as founder is reported by the NYU page.

sources.title: Guinness World Records: Oldest higher-learning institution
Islam and Knowledge - The Muslim Experience at NYU Tandon, Poly Archives (New York University)

points.heading: Al-Azhar, Cairo (970)
points.text: Al-Azhar was founded in 970 by the Fatimids, a dynasty that came from North Africa, and became a leading seat of Sunni learning.
points.note: Fatimids rose in Ifriqiya (Tunisia) before conquering Egypt. Teaching began 972 per Muslim Heritage.

sources.title: Al-Azhar - Encyclopedia.com
Al-Azhar University - Muslim Heritage

points.heading: Bologna (1088)
points.text: The University of Bologna dates itself to 1088, which it describes as a conventional date.

sources.title: Our history - University of Bologna

points.heading: Oxford (c.1096-1167)
points.text: Oxford has no founding date; teaching existed by 1096 and grew rapidly from 1167.
points.note: Not confirmed by the sources cited; this is the range commonly stated.

points.heading: Conquest from Ifriqiya
points.text: The Aghlabid emir Ziyadat Allah, governing Ifriqiya (Tunisia) for the Baghdad caliph, intervened in Sicily; Palermo fell in 831.
points.note: French-language source; quotes in French.

sources.title: N. Hautemaniere, La Sicile islamique - Les cles du Moyen-Orient

points.heading: End of Muslim rule
points.text: Norman leaders Robert Guiscard and Roger de Hauteville took Sicily in stages from 1061; this source dates the end of the conquest to 1071.
points.note: The commonly cited end date of 1091 (fall of Noto) is not confirmed by the sources cited; this source gives 1071 (Palermo fell 1072).

sources.title: N. Hautemaniere, La Sicile islamique - Les cles du Moyen-Orient

points.heading: Al-Idrisi and the Tabula Rogeriana
points.text: Al-Idrisi, probably born in Ceuta (North Africa) in 1100, joined the court of the Norman king Roger II around 1138 and produced a world geography and map, completed in 1153/1154.
points.note: Date is given as 1154 in many sources and 1153 by Factum; Les clés du Moyen-Orient gives 1154. Al-Idrisi was a Moroccan-Andalusi Arab of Idrisid descent.

sources.title: al-Idrisi and Roger II: Mapping the World in the 12th Century - Factum Foundation

points.heading: Constantine the African
points.text: Constantine left his North African homeland, reached Salerno, then joined Monte Cassino (about 1077), translating more than two dozen medical texts from Arabic into Latin.
points.note: Usually said to come from Ifriqiya (Kairouan/Carthage area); exact birthplace is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Medicine at Monte Cassino: Constantine the African and the oldest manuscript of his Pantegni (Kwakkel and Newton, Brepols 2019) - Garrison-Morton-Norman

points.heading: The Pantegni: Persian source, African translator
points.text: His main work, the Pantegni, adapted the Complete Book of the Medical Art by the Persian physician Ali ibn al-Abbas al-Majusi.
points.note: A model case for this hub: the translator was African, the source text Persian.

sources.title: Medicine at Monte Cassino: Constantine the African and the oldest manuscript of his Pantegni (Kwakkel and Newton, Brepols 2019) - Garrison-Morton-Norman

points.heading: Hiding the Arabic origin
points.text: Constantine tried to disguise the Arabic origin of his texts.
points.note: One reason the African and Islamic route was later under-recognised in Europe.

sources.title: Influence of Arabic and Islamic Philosophy on the Latin West - Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy

points.heading: Salerno school
points.text: Salerno was the leading medical school of medieval Europe, and Constantine's translations fed its teaching.
points.note: The direct link between Constantine's translations and the Salerno curriculum is widely stated but not confirmed in detail by the sources cited.

sources.title: Medicine at Monte Cassino: Constantine the African and the oldest manuscript of his Pantegni (Kwakkel and Newton, Brepols 2019) - Garrison-Morton-Norman

points.heading: The Catalan Atlas (1375) and Mansa Musa
points.text: The Catalan Atlas, made in Majorca about 1375 and now in the Bibliotheque nationale de France, shows Mansa Musa of Mali holding gold.
points.note: BnF holding: the BnF attribution is not confirmed by the sources cited. Attributed to Abraham Cresques.

sources.title: New Exhibition Highlights Story of the Richest Man Who Ever Lived - Smithsonian Magazine
The Catalan Atlas - Carleton College Library

points.heading: Ethiopian monks at Florence (1441)
points.text: Ethiopian monks from the Jerusalem community attended the Council of Florence in 1441 at the pope's invitation.
points.note: Other Ethiopian embassies to Europe (e.g. to Aragon, Venice, Lisbon) are not confirmed by the sources cited here.

sources.title: Ethiopia - Contact with European Christendom (Library of Congress Country Studies)

points.heading: Black St Maurice, Magdeburg (c.1240)
points.text: The statue of St Maurice in Magdeburg Cathedral, about 1240, is the earliest known depiction of the saint as a Black African, shown as a dignified knight.
points.note: Maurice was said to be an Egyptian (Theban) soldier; depicting him as Black was a 13th-century European choice, not evidence of his appearance.

sources.title: J. Bowersox, St. Maurice in Magdeburg (ca. 1240) - Black Central Europe
Statue of St. Maurice - Art and Architecture of the Middle Ages (Caskey, Cohen, Safran)

points.heading: Juan Latino in Granada
points.text: Juan Latino (c.1517-c.1594), born to parents from Guinea and once enslaved, became a Latin professor at Granada and published Latin poetry in 1573 and 1576.
points.note: Often called "African-born"; Cambridge University Library says he was most likely born in Spain. Use "of African descent".

sources.title: Juan Latino, 16th-century Afro-Spaniard freed slave, poet and Latin professor - Cambridge University Library, Languages across Borders

points.heading: Abba Gregorius and Hiob Ludolf
points.text: The Ethiopian monk Abba Gregorius (Gorgoryos) worked with the German scholar Hiob Ludolf; in 1652 he was invited to Gotha. Ludolf's Ge'ez-Latin dictionary owed much to him.
points.note: Founding of Ethiopian Studies in Europe was a collaboration with an Ethiopian scholar. German quote: "At his request the prince invited Gregorius to Gotha in 1652."

sources.title: Ethiopia and Ethiopian Studies - Thomas Fisher Rare Book Library, University of Toronto
Ludolf, Hiob - Deutsche Biographie (NDB/ADB)

points.heading: Africans in Renaissance Europe
points.text: The Walters Art Museum's 2012-13 exhibition used European art to reveal the presence of Africans in Renaissance society.
points.note: Exhibition ran 14 October 2012 to 21 January 2013 (Walters page).

sources.title: Revealing the African Presence in Renaissance Europe - The Walters Art Museum

points.heading: Aksum and the Rome-India trade
points.text: Aksum (Ethiopia/Eritrea) sought to control sea trade between the Roman Empire and India, and minted its own coins for about 300 years.
points.note: The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea names King Zoskales as promoting commerce with Rome, Arabia and India.

sources.title: Ethiopia - The Aksumite State (Library of Congress Country Studies)

points.heading: Malindi's giraffe for the Ming court (1414)
points.text: In 1414 Zheng He's fleet met envoys from Malindi (Kenya) in Bengal, who gave a giraffe that was taken to China; Malindi sent another the next year.
points.note: The first giraffe came via Bengal, not directly from Africa.

sources.title: The giraffes that sailed to medieval China - Science News

points.heading: Zheng He on the East African coast (1417-19)
points.text: On the fifth voyage (1417-19) the fleet reached the east coast of Africa, returning ambassadors from Mogadishu, Brawa and Malindi.
points.note: The brief's "1418" falls within this voyage.

sources.title: History 104, Lecture 02: Zheng He's Treasure Ship Expeditions - University of Delaware

points.heading: West African gold
points.text: West African gold made the region indispensable to the medieval world; Mansa Musa of Mali is remembered as one of the wealthiest people in history.
points.note: "Richest person ever" rankings are not measurable; present as reputation. Exhibition: Caravans of Gold, Fragments in Time, Block Museum 2019.

sources.title: New Exhibition Highlights Story of the Richest Man Who Ever Lived - Smithsonian Magazine
Medieval Africa as a cultural force is subject of major exhibition at Block Museum - Block Museum, Northwestern University

points.heading: Habshi and Sidi in India; Malik Ambar
points.text: Africans, many from Ethiopia, reached South Asia from as early as the 7th century as merchants, sailors and enslaved people. Malik Ambar (1548-1626), born in Ethiopia, rose to rule in the Deccan.
points.note: Siddi communities in India today descend from these and later East African arrivals.

sources.title: C. A. Stewart, Habshi and Sidi: Africans in the Deccan - The Met

points.heading: "The Moors were all Black Africans"
points.text: "Moor" was never a single ethnicity. It first meant people of Roman Mauretania (North-west Africa), later Muslims in Europe, and from the Renaissance any dark-skinned person. Al-Andalus's Muslims were mainly Berbers, Arabs and Iberian converts, with some sub-Saharan Africans.
points.note: Both erasure (treating Moors as non-African) and overclaim (treating them all as Black) are wrong. The proportion of sub-Saharan Africans in al-Andalus is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Who were the Moors? It's complicated - National Geographic

points.heading: Library sizes
points.text: Figures like 400,000 books for Cordoba are repeated in popular writing as fact, sometimes with comparisons to small Christian libraries. Specialist scholarship calls the number likely hyperbole.
points.note: Say "sources claim" and give the scholarly caveat.

sources.title: The ornament of the world - The Peninsula (Qatar), 2013
U. Bongianino, The page architecture of a deluxe Arabic dictionary from Islamic Spain - Manuscript and Text Cultures (peer-reviewed)

points.heading: "The Arabs invented zero"
points.text: Rules for calculating with zero were set out by the Indian mathematician Brahmagupta in the 7th century. The word "zero" comes, through Arabic sifr, from the transmitting culture, not the inventing one.

sources.title: A history of Zero - MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Crediting Africa with Persian or Indian knowledge
points.text: Much "African" learning in medieval Europe was African in route, not in origin: Indian numerals, Baghdad algebra, Persian medicine. Credit North Africa for transmitting, teaching and extending it (Fibonacci's teachers, Ibn al-Banna, Constantine), not for inventing all of it.

sources.title: Medicine at Monte Cassino: Constantine the African and the oldest manuscript of his Pantegni (Kwakkel and Newton, Brepols 2019) - Garrison-Morton-Norman
A history of Zero - MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Calling famous figures "Black" without evidence
points.text: Septimius Severus's skin colour cannot be verified; Juan Latino was probably born in Spain; Ziryab's origin is debated. Use place of birth and documented ancestry rather than assumed appearance.

sources.title: Scotland's African Emperor - Historic Environment Scotland Blog

points.heading: Single heroic "firsts"
points.text: Claims such as "first aviator" (Ibn Firnas), "first algebraic notation" (al-Qalasadi) or "first university" (al-Qarawiyyin) rest on thin, late or definition-dependent evidence.

sources.title: Ibn al-Banna - MacTutor, University of St Andrews
Flights of Fancy on Manmade Wings - AramcoWorld, Nov/Dec 2008

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Transatlantic trade: about 12.5 million embarked
points.text: Research based on the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database (SlaveVoyages) estimates that about 12.5 million Africans were forced aboard slave ships over some 350 years.
points.note: These figures are taken from the National Endowment for the Humanities (a funder of the database) and from PBS, both citing the database.

sources.title: Gross Injustice (HUMANITIES, NEH, Sept/Oct 2010)
How Many Slaves Landed in the U.S.? (PBS, The African Americans: Many Rivers to Cross)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: About 10.7 million survived the crossing
points.text: About 10.7 million people survived the Middle Passage and were landed in the Americas.

sources.title: Gross Injustice (HUMANITIES, NEH, Sept/Oct 2010)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Deaths at sea
points.text: The same source says that nearly 1.5 million Africans died because of conditions on the Middle Passage.
points.note: 12.5 million embarked minus 10.7 million landed gives about 1.8 million. The difference from 1.5 million is not explained by the source cited; treat both as estimates.

sources.title: Gross Injustice (HUMANITIES, NEH, Sept/Oct 2010)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Older totals have been revised
points.text: Very different totals were once quoted. Decades of research have narrowed the range, so modern figures are more reliable than older claims of 20 or 100 million.

sources.title: Gross Injustice (HUMANITIES, NEH, Sept/Oct 2010)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Four trades together: about 18 million
points.text: Nathan Nunn’s 2008 paper counts about 12 million people exported in the transatlantic trade and about 6 million in the trans-Saharan, Red Sea and Indian Ocean trades.
points.note: Nunn’s figures are for people exported. They do not include people killed in raids or who died before reaching the coast or the desert routes.

sources.title: Nathan Nunn, The Long-Term Effects of Africa’s Slave Trades, Quarterly Journal of Economics 123(1), 2008 (author copy)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Deaths before embarkation
points.text: Many people died before reaching the coast. Estimates of deaths during the march to the coast vary widely, from 10% to 50%.
points.note: The wide range shows how uncertain this figure is.

sources.title: Nathan Nunn, The Long-Term Effects of Africa’s Slave Trades, Quarterly Journal of Economics 123(1), 2008 (author copy)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Deaths at sea by period
points.text: Nunn also reports that deaths during the Atlantic crossing ranged from 7% to 20%, depending on the period and the length of the voyage.

sources.title: Nathan Nunn, The Long-Term Effects of Africa’s Slave Trades, Quarterly Journal of Economics 123(1), 2008 (author copy)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Africa’s “missing” population (Manning)
points.text: Patrick Manning modelled what Africa’s population might have been without the slave trades. Nunn reports Manning’s finding that, by 1850, Africa’s population was only half of what it would otherwise have been.
points.figure: about 50% of the counterfactual population by 1850
points.note: This is a modelled counterfactual estimate (Manning, Slavery and African Life, 1990, p. 171, as cited by Nunn), not a count. Manning’s other estimates and his method in detail are not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Nathan Nunn, The Long-Term Effects of Africa’s Slave Trades, Quarterly Journal of Economics 123(1), 2008 (author copy)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: How reliable are Manning’s models?
points.text: A 2019 review by the economic historian Ewout Frankema finds that Manning’s models capture the likely negative effect of the transatlantic trade on Africa’s population well, but notes how hard it is to project African population back in time.
points.note: Frankema also points to the difficulty of projecting African population series back into earlier centuries.

sources.title: Ewout Frankema, Africa and the Demographic Consequences of the Columbian Exchange, Asian Review of World Histories 7 (2019)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: The areas that exported most people are poorest today
points.text: Nunn built country-by-country estimates of the number of people exported and found that the countries that lost the most people are poorer today.

sources.title: Nunn, The Long-Term Effects of Africa's Slave Trades (NBER Working Paper 13367, abstract)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Testing for cause, not just correlation
points.text: Critics asked whether poorer areas were simply more likely to be raided (selection), or whether poverty caused the trade (reverse causality). Nunn tested this with historical evidence and with instrumental variables, such as sailing distances to slave markets.

sources.title: Nunn, The Long-Term Effects of Africa's Slave Trades (NBER Working Paper 13367, abstract)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: More developed areas were hit hardest
points.text: Nunn's evidence suggests that it was the more developed and more densely populated parts of Africa that were drawn most into the slave trades. Nunn reads this as support for the idea that the trades held back places that were advancing; it does not show what those places would otherwise have become.
points.note: This is Nunn’s interpretation of historical population density data. It is relevant to the counterfactual but does not show what those areas would have achieved.

sources.title: Nathan Nunn, The Long-Term Effects of Africa’s Slave Trades, Quarterly Journal of Economics 123(1), 2008 (author copy)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: State building interrupted
points.text: Nunn cites historians who found that state systems in Senegambia were developing before the slave trades, and that this development stalled after the Portuguese arrived in the 15th century.

sources.title: Nathan Nunn, The Long-Term Effects of Africa’s Slave Trades, Quarterly Journal of Economics 123(1), 2008 (author copy)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Lower trust today
points.text: Nunn and Wantchekon (2011) linked survey data to records of slave shipments by ethnic group. People whose ancestors were heavily raided are less trusting today.

sources.title: Nunn and Wantchekon, The Slave Trade and the Origins of Mistrust in Africa, AER 101(7), 2011 (abstract)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Effects passed on through culture
points.text: The same study finds that most of the effect works through norms, beliefs and values passed down within communities.

sources.title: Nunn and Wantchekon, The Slave Trade and the Origins of Mistrust in Africa, AER 101(7), 2011 (abstract)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: More ethnic division
points.text: Whatley and Gillezeau (2011) find that areas that exported more people are more ethnically divided today.

sources.title: Whatley and Gillezeau, The Impact of the Transatlantic Slave Trade on Ethnic Stratification in Africa, AER 101(3), 2011 (abstract)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Critique: “compression of history”
points.text: The economic historian Gareth Austin argues that these long-run studies squash different periods and paths of history together and so oversimplify the causes.

sources.title: Gareth Austin, The ‘reversal of fortune’ thesis and the compression of history, Journal of International Development 20(8), 2008 (abstract, RePEc)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Critique: poverty came first, then was made worse
points.text: Austin argues that low labour productivity in Africa was a starting condition for the external slave trades, while also accepting that the trades greatly reinforced African poverty.
points.note: Austin’s view supports harm from the slave trades but challenges the idea that Africa started from a position of overall economic advantage.

sources.title: Gareth Austin, The ‘reversal of fortune’ thesis and the compression of history, Journal of International Development 20(8), 2008 (abstract, RePEc)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: What the economics can and cannot show
points.text: These studies explain differences within Africa today. They do not measure what Africa as a whole would have achieved without the trades.
points.note: The research question is about part of present-day underdevelopment, not a full counterfactual history.

sources.title: Nunn, The Long-Term Effects of Africa's Slave Trades (NBER Working Paper 13367, abstract)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Rodney: Europe underdeveloped Africa
points.text: Walter Rodney’s 1972 book argues that European exploitation actively underdeveloped Africa while enriching Europe.

sources.title: Gerald L. Caplan, 'The Use of African History: How Europe Underdeveloped Africa by Walter Rodney' (review article, African Review, University of Dar es Salaam), quoting Rodney
Rodney, Walter (International Encyclopedia of the Social Sciences, via Encyclopedia.com)
Walter Rodney papers – finding aid, Robert W. Woodruff Library of the Atlanta University Center
How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (Wikipedia)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Criticism of Rodney
points.text: Some scholars have criticised Rodney for relying too heavily on the dependency theory of the 1960s, and for not looking enough at factors inside Africa that drove the slave trade.
points.note: The source page flags parts of this criticism as poorly referenced. It is reported here as a position held by some historians. Part of this rests on one independent source.

sources.title: Rodney, Walter (International Encyclopedia of the Social Sciences, via Encyclopedia.com)
Ana Lucia Araujo (2022) 'Did Rodney Get It Wrong? Europe Underdeveloped Africa but Enslaved People Were Not Always Purchased with Rubbish', African Economic History 50(2): 22–32 (author's PDF)
How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (Wikipedia)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Williams: slavery helped pay for industrialisation
points.text: Eric Williams's Capitalism and Slavery (1944) argued that wealth from slavery helped finance Britain's Industrial Revolution, and that economic self-interest, not humanitarianism, drove abolition.

sources.title: Slavery and the British Industrial Revolution (UBS Center, University of Zurich)
David Richardson, review of Kenneth Morgan, Slavery, Atlantic Trade and the British Economy (Institute of Historical Research, Reviews in History)
Brandon 2017, International Review of Social History 62 (Cambridge), quoting Williams
Capitalism and Slavery (Wikipedia)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Reply: the profits were small
points.text: The economic historian Stanley Engerman (1972) estimated that profits from the slave trade and West Indian plantations were less than 5% of the British economy in any year of the Industrial Revolution. This figure is reported here from a secondary source.

sources.title: Slavery and the British Industrial Revolution (UBS Center, University of Zurich)
Heblich, Redding and Voth, Slavery and the British Industrial Revolution (CEPR VoxEU), citing Engerman (1972)
Eltis & Engerman 2000, Journal of Economic History 60(1)
Capitalism and Slavery (Wikipedia)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Reply: the decline thesis
points.text: Many later historians have rejected Williams's claim that the Caribbean colonies were in economic decline before abolition, though the wider debate about Capitalism and Slavery continues.

sources.title: Seymour Drescher, Econocide: British Slavery in the Era of Abolition (University of North Carolina Press)
Brandon 2017, International Review of Social History 62 (Cambridge), quoting Williams
Capitalism and Slavery (Wikipedia)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Inikori: Africans and England’s industrialisation
points.text: Joseph Inikori (2002) argues that Africans, on the continent and in the diaspora, made a major contribution to England’s industrialisation through Atlantic trade.
points.note: “disaporic” is spelled as on the source page.

sources.title: Africans and the Industrial Revolution in England (Business History Explorer, Business Archives Council)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Thornton: African agency
points.text: John Thornton argues that African states resisted early European raids and were not forced into the Atlantic trade by economic pressure. This complicates a story in which Africa was only acted upon.

sources.title: John Thornton, Africa and Africans in the Making of the Atlantic World, 1400-1800, ch. 4 summary (Cambridge University Press)
John Thornton, Africa and Africans in the Making of the Atlantic World, 1400-1800, ch. 2 summary (Cambridge University Press)
J.C. Sharman (2023) 'Something New out of Africa: States Made Slaves, Slaves Made States', International Organization 77(3) (quoting Thornton)
John Thornton (historian) (Wikipedia)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Reversal of fortune
points.text: Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson found that, among colonised countries, those that were relatively rich in 1500 are relatively poor today. They link this to the institutions that colonisers set up.

sources.title: Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson, Reversal of Fortune (NBER Working Paper 8460, abstract; published QJE 2002)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Institutions, not geography
points.text: The same authors argue that colonial powers set up extractive institutions in places that were already prosperous, and that this caused the reversal.

sources.title: Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson, Reversal of Fortune (NBER Working Paper 8460, abstract; published QJE 2002)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Diamond: geography
points.text: Jared Diamond argues that differences in power and technology between societies come mainly from geography and environment. On this view, Africa's long north–south layout made it harder for crops and animals to spread.
points.note: Diamond explicitly rejects any idea of inherent superiority. His explanation is a counter-argument to the claim mainly because it places the causes much earlier than the slave trades.

sources.title: Guns, Germs, and Steel (Encyclopaedia Britannica)
PBS: Guns, Germs and Steel, episode 3 transcript
Laitin, Moortgat and Robinson (2012) 'Geographic axes and the persistence of cultural diversity', PNAS 109(26): 10263 – abstract as reproduced by National Taiwan University
Guns, Germs, and Steel (Wikipedia)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Critics of the geographic explanation
points.text: Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson argue that their reversal-of-fortune evidence is hard to square with a purely geographic explanation, because places that were rich in 1500 did not stay rich. This is their argument, aimed at geographic explanations in general.
points.note: This criticism is directed at geographic explanations in general, not only at Diamond.

sources.title: Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson, Reversal of Fortune (NBER Working Paper 8460, abstract; published QJE 2002)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: The Great Divergence: Europe’s lead came late
points.text: Kenneth Pomeranz (2000) argues that living standards in the most advanced parts of Europe and East Asia were comparable as late as 1750. If he is right, Europe's global lead was recent. Whether it was inevitable is a counterfactual that this evidence cannot settle.
points.note: Pomeranz compares Europe with East Asia, not with Africa. His work is used here as a frame, not as evidence about Africa.

sources.title: The Great Divergence (Princeton University Press)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: The Great Divergence is debated
points.text: Pomeranz’s argument is influential but contested. Some economic historians date the divergence earlier.

sources.title: Martin Daunton, 'Why Did Europe's Economies Diverge from Asia?' (Gresham College lecture, 2022)
Stephen Broadberry, 'Historical national accounting and dating the Great Divergence' (University of Oxford, Department of Economics)
The Great Divergence (book) (Wikipedia)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Historians rarely use the term
points.text: Britannica notes that historians now rarely use the term “Dark Ages” because of the value judgement it carries.

sources.title: Dark Ages (Encyclopaedia Britannica)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Where the idea came from
points.text: The idea of a European “Dark Age” came from Italian Renaissance humanists, who saw a thousand years of darkness between ancient Rome and their own time. Historians now rarely use the term.

sources.title: Middle Ages (Encyclopaedia Britannica)
Dark Ages (Encyclopaedia Britannica)
Europeana: The not-so-dark Middle Ages (blog)
Naoíse Mac Sweeney, 'The Myth of the "Dark Ages" Ignores How Classical Traditions Flourished Around the World', Smithsonian Magazine (18 May 2023)
Dark Ages (historiography) (Wikipedia)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Western Europe, about 500 to 1000
points.text: In its narrower meaning, the term describes Western Europe from about 500 to 1000, a period of frequent warfare and much reduced town life.
points.note: This describes Western Europe only. Other parts of Europe, such as the Byzantine Empire, are not covered by it.

sources.title: Dark Ages (Encyclopaedia Britannica)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: The House of Wisdom, Baghdad
points.text: Under the Abbasid caliphs, Baghdad’s House of Wisdom was a royal library. The caliph al-Ma’mun (813–833) made it a centre for translating and studying classical works. The Mongols largely destroyed Baghdad in 1258.

sources.title: Bayt al-Hikmah (Encyclopaedia Britannica)
Hülegü (Encyclopaedia Britannica)
Berggren, Biographical Encyclopedia of Astronomers (Springer 2007): Ma'mun
Smithsonian Magazine, 'How an Artist Is Rebuilding a Baghdad Library Destroyed During the Iraq War'
Linda Komaroff, 'The Art of the Ilkhanid Period (1256–1353)', Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, The Metropolitan Museum of Art (2001)
House of Wisdom (Wikipedia)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Aksum
points.text: Aksum, in present-day Ethiopia and Eritrea, sat at the crossroads of Africa, Arabia and the Greco-Roman world. Its evidence is set out in full on the journeys page.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Aksum

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Ghana Empire: the “Land of Gold”
points.text: From the 8th century, trade caravans crossed the Sahara on routes later described by Arabic-language writers. The Ghana Empire in West Africa grew wealthy from gold and became known as the “Land of Gold”.

sources.title: The Trans-Saharan Gold Trade (7th–14th Century), Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History (Metropolitan Museum of Art)
Wikipedia: Ghana Empire (secondary source)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Mali Empire and Mansa Musa
points.text: The Mali Empire (about 1235 to 1610) became the largest empire in West Africa. The Arab writer al-Umari, writing about twelve years later, recorded that the gold Mansa Musa's party spent in Egypt during his 1324 pilgrimage lowered the value of gold there, and that it had stayed low since.
points.note: Part of this rests on one independent source.

sources.title: Mali (historical empire) | Britannica
The Trans-Saharan Gold Trade (7th–14th Century), Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History (Metropolitan Museum of Art)

Boston University African Studies Center: Kingdom of Mali (primary source extract, al-Umari)
Mali Empire (Wikipedia)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Kilwa and Indian Ocean trade
points.text: From the 13th to the 16th century, the Swahili city of Kilwa Kisiwani traded gold and ivory for Persian pottery and Chinese porcelain. The traveller Ibn Battuta called it one of the most beautiful cities in the world.

sources.title: Ruins of Kilwa Kisiwani and Ruins of Songo Mnara, UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Metalworking: Igbo-Ukwu
points.text: Excavations at Igbo-Ukwu in present-day Nigeria found hundreds of highly skilled bronze castings, which may date from as early as the 9th century AD.

sources.title: Igbo-Ukwu (ca. 9th century), Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History (Metropolitan Museum of Art)
Smarthistory: Igbo-Ukwu
Igbo-Ukwu (Wikipedia)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Great Zimbabwe
points.text: UNESCO describes Great Zimbabwe as a unique testimony to the Shona civilisation between the 11th and 15th centuries, and an important trading centre.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Great Zimbabwe National Monument

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: City sizes: Cairo
points.text: In Tertius Chandler's historical estimates, as tabulated on Wikipedia, Cairo was the largest city in the world in 1325, with about 500,000 people. These are rough estimates and are not confirmed by an institutional source.
points.note: Colin McEvedy’s estimates, as reproduced by Fordham University’s Internet History Sourcebooks. Pre-modern city populations are rough estimates and other scholars give different figures.

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: City sizes: Paris, London and Córdoba
points.text: Estimates vary widely. Britannica puts Córdoba, under Muslim rule, at about 100,000 people in 1000, making it the largest city in Europe. Colin McEvedy put Paris at 50,000 to 125,000 people in 1346.
points.note: Córdoba from Britannica; Paris from Colin McEvedy’s estimates as reproduced by Fordham University. Figures are rough estimates. Part of this rests on one independent source.

sources.title: Córdoba, Spain (Encyclopaedia Britannica)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Benin City, 1897
points.text: In February 1897 British forces captured Benin City in a punitive expedition. Houses, shrines and palaces were looted and many buildings were burned.

sources.title: Horniman to return ownership of Benin bronzes to Nigeria (Horniman Museum, 7 August 2022)
Benin Expedition of 1897 (Wikipedia)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: How many objects were taken
points.text: The British Museum says that thousands of objects of ceremonial and ritual value were taken to the UK in 1897, as official spoils of war or shared among members of the expedition. They include over a thousand metal plaques and sculptures known as the Benin Bronzes. One secondary source says about 40% went to the British Museum.
points.note: Totals vary by source and by how objects are counted.

sources.title: British Museum: Benin Bronzes

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: British Museum holdings
points.text: The British Museum says it holds over 900 objects from the historic Kingdom of Benin.

sources.title: British Museum: Benin Bronzes

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Horniman Museum returns ownership
points.text: In 2022 the Horniman Museum in London agreed to transfer ownership of 72 objects taken from Benin City to Nigeria, and formally did so in November 2022.

sources.title: Horniman to return ownership of Benin bronzes to Nigeria (Horniman Museum, 7 August 2022)
Six objects to return to Nigeria as Horniman formally transfers ownership of ‘Benin Bronzes’ (Horniman Museum, 28 November 2022)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Jesus College, Cambridge
points.text: Jesus College, Cambridge, handed a bronze cockerel (okukor) to Nigerian representatives on 27 October 2021, the first return of a Benin Bronze by a UK institution. The University of Aberdeen handed over a Benin Bronze head of an Oba the next day.
points.note: This return took place in 2021, before the Horniman transfer of 2022.

sources.title: Benin Bronze October return date agreed (Jesus College, Cambridge)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: The British Museum’s position
points.text: The British Museum Act 1963 allows the Trustees to dispose of objects only in limited cases, such as duplicates. The Museum says it is committed to working with Nigerian institutions and lends Benin objects around the world.
points.note: Section 5 lists the limited conditions (duplicates, certain objects made after 1850, objects unfit to keep). UK Parliament petitions have asked for the Act to be changed.

sources.title: British Museum Act 1963, section 5 (legislation.gov.uk)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Calls to change the law
points.text: Petitions to the UK Parliament have asked for the British Museum Act 1963 to be amended so that the Trustees can accept requests to return objects.
points.note: This petition opened in November 2021 and closed without a government response or debate.

sources.title: Petition: Amend the British Museum Act 1963 (UK Parliament petitions)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: A contested counterpoint on Benin
points.text: Some US campaigners, led by the Restitution Study Group, link the Bronzes to the Kingdom of Benin’s role in selling enslaved people and have tried to stop them being returned to Nigeria. The British Museum notes that Benin played a role in the trade, though its extent is debated.
