points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Maqdala, 1868
points.text: After defeating Emperor Tewodros II at Maqdala, British troops looted the fortress, its church and its treasury, taking hundreds of manuscripts and religious objects.

sources.title: The Legacy of Maqdala 1868 at the Bodleian Library (School of Anthropology and Museum Ethnography, University of Oxford)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Manuscripts now in British libraries
points.text: Over 300 manuscripts were acquired on the spot for the British Museum. Many are now in the British Library, with others in Oxford and Cambridge.

sources.title: The Legacy of Maqdala 1868 at the Bodleian Library (School of Anthropology and Museum Ethnography, University of Oxford)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: The British Museum’s Maqdala holdings
points.text: The British Museum cares for more than 90 objects from Maqdala, including 11 tabots (consecrated altar tablets). It says it remains open to dialogue.

sources.title: Maqdala collection (British Museum)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Kumasi, 1874: Asante gold
points.text: In 1874 British troops raided the Asante capital Kumasi. Several hundred items of gold regalia were looted from the royal palace and later sold in London.

sources.title: Homecoming – Exhibition of Asante Gold Regalia at Manhyia Palace Museum, Kumasi (V&A, 2 May 2024)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Asante gold goes on show in Kumasi
points.text: In 2024 items from the V&A and the British Museum went on show in Kumasi on loan for three years, with an option to extend. This is a loan, not a return of ownership.

sources.title: Homecoming – Exhibition of Asante Gold Regalia at Manhyia Palace Museum, Kumasi (V&A, 2 May 2024)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Great Zimbabwe: denial of African builders
points.text: When the German explorer Karl Mauch reached Great Zimbabwe in 1871, he credited it to outsiders, linking it to the Queen of Sheba and to Phoenicians.

sources.title: Mysteries of Great Zimbabwe (NOVA, PBS)
Preben Kaarsholm, 'The past as battlefield in Rhodesia and Zimbabwe' (SAS-Space, School of Advanced Study, University of London)
Webber Ndoro, 'Great Zimbabwe', Scientific American (special edition, Vol. 15 No. 1s)
Wikipedia: Great Zimbabwe (secondary source)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Great Zimbabwe: damage to the evidence
points.text: In the early colonial period, diggers such as Richard Hall stripped away up to 12 feet of layered deposits while looking for non-African builders, destroying evidence archaeologists use to date the site.

sources.title: Mysteries of Great Zimbabwe (NOVA, PBS)
Roderick J. McIntosh, 'Riddle of Great Zimbabwe', Archaeology (Archaeological Institute of America), 1998
Shadreck Chirikure and Innocent Pikirayi (2008) 'Inside and outside the dry stone walls: revisiting the material culture of Great Zimbabwe', Antiquity 82: 976–993
Wikipedia: Great Zimbabwe (secondary source)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Rhodesia: censorship
points.text: Under white minority rule, the Rhodesian government suppressed archaeologists’ findings that Africans built Great Zimbabwe. Official publications were barred from stating plainly that it was an African creation.

sources.title: Mysteries of Great Zimbabwe (NOVA, PBS)
Preben Kaarsholm, 'The past as battlefield in Rhodesia and Zimbabwe' (SAS-Space, School of Advanced Study, University of London)
Webber Ndoro, 'Great Zimbabwe', Scientific American (special edition, Vol. 15 No. 1s)
Shadreck Chirikure and Innocent Pikirayi (2008) 'Inside and outside the dry stone walls: revisiting the material culture of Great Zimbabwe', Antiquity 82: 976–993
Wikipedia: Great Zimbabwe (secondary source)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Peter Garlake forced out
points.text: The archaeologist Peter Garlake, a senior inspector with Rhodesia’s Historical Monuments Commission, condemned government interference over Great Zimbabwe. He was forced out of the country and had left by early 1971.

sources.title: Editorial, Antiquity 45 (177), March 1971
Mysteries of Great Zimbabwe (NOVA, PBS)
Shadreck Chirikure and Innocent Pikirayi (2008) 'Inside and outside the dry stone walls: revisiting the material culture of Great Zimbabwe', Antiquity 82: 976–993
Peter Garlake (Wikipedia)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Science corrected the record
points.text: Professional archaeologists, starting with David Randall-MacIver and Gertrude Caton-Thompson in the early 20th century, confirmed that Great Zimbabwe was of African origin.
points.note: This shows that the erasure was challenged, though official denial in Rhodesia continued afterwards.

sources.title: Roderick J. McIntosh, 'Riddle of Great Zimbabwe', Archaeology (Archaeological Institute of America), 1998
UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Great Zimbabwe National Monument
Wikipedia: Great Zimbabwe (secondary source)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Most heritage is outside Africa
points.text: The Sarr–Savoy report (2018) relies on an expert estimate that over 90% of the material cultural heritage of sub-Saharan Africa is held outside the continent.
points.note: The report presents this as a figure “often reiterated by experts” rather than its own count.

sources.title: Felwine Sarr and Bénédicte Savoy, The Restitution of African Cultural Heritage (2018), English translation (PDF mirror)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Size of European collections
points.text: The same report gives examples: about 69,000 objects from sub-Saharan Africa in the British Museum and about 70,000 in the Musée du quai Branly in Paris.

sources.title: Felwine Sarr and Bénédicte Savoy, The Restitution of African Cultural Heritage (2018), English translation (PDF mirror)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Timbuktu, 2012–2013: a different kind of loss
points.text: During the occupation of northern Mali by armed jihadist groups, a UNESCO specialist reported that 4,203 manuscripts held by the Ahmed Baba Institute were burned or stolen. This loss was not caused by Europeans. Local people moved many more manuscripts to safety; a widely repeated estimate is about 350,000.

sources.title: Damage to Timbuktu's cultural heritage worse than first estimated (UNESCO)
Endangered Libraries in Timbuktu (British Library Endangered Archives Programme)
PRI The World (3 July 2013): Islamists have destroyed one-tenth of Timbuktu's ancient manuscripts, UN finds
Timbuktu manuscripts (Wikipedia)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: A war crimes conviction
points.text: The International Criminal Court convicted Ahmad Al Faqi Al Mahdi in 2016 of the war crime of attacking religious and historic buildings in Timbuktu.

sources.title: The Prosecutor v. Ahmad Al Faqi Al Mahdi (International Criminal Court)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Oral tradition as an archive
points.text: In West Africa, griots (jeli) have traditionally preserved genealogies, historical narratives and oral traditions. Historians writing UNESCO’s General History of Africa used oral traditions as a source.
points.note: Where the written record was lost or never made, oral tradition is a source of evidence in its own right.

sources.title: Griot, Encyclopaedia Britannica
UNESCO's work on General History of Africa helps restore forgotten history (Africa Renewal, United Nations)
Hakimah Abdul-Fattah, 'How Griots Tell Legendary Epics Through Stories and Songs in West Africa', The Metropolitan Museum of Art (20 April 2020)
UNESCO, 'A new page in the General History of Africa' (29 March 2019, updated 20 April 2023)
Griot (Wikipedia)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Losses elsewhere: Baghdad and Alexandria
points.text: Great libraries were lost in other places too. The Mongols largely destroyed Baghdad, home of the House of Wisdom, in 1258. Later writers say a fire in 48 BC destroyed the Library of Alexandria, but how much was lost is unclear.
points.note: This is included for balance: the loss of archives is not unique to Africa.

sources.title: Hülegü (Encyclopaedia Britannica)
The fate of the Library of Alexandria (Encyclopaedia Britannica)
Linda Komaroff, 'The Art of the Ilkhanid Period (1256–1353)', Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, The Metropolitan Museum of Art (2001)
Smithsonian Magazine, 'How an Artist Is Rebuilding a Baghdad Library Destroyed During the Iraq War'
Erin Blakemore, 'What really happened to the Library of Alexandria? These are the theories.', National Geographic (16 Oct 2025)
House of Wisdom (Wikipedia)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: The “civilising mission”
points.text: European powers presented colonisation as a duty to “civilise” other peoples. Historians treat this as a political justification for conquest.

sources.title: Carey A. Watt, Introduction, Civilizing Missions in Colonial and Postcolonial South Asia (Anthem/Cambridge Core)
Margaret Kohn and Kavita Reddy, 'Colonialism', Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (substantive revision 17 Jan 2023)
Civilizing mission (Wikipedia)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Hegel: Africa outside history
points.text: The German philosopher G.W.F. Hegel, in lectures given in the 1820s, dismissed Africa from world history. Many scholars have strongly criticised him for this.
points.note: The exact wording “no historical part of the world” is widely quoted from an English translation, but is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Tom C. McCaskie, Exiled from History: Africa in Hegel’s Academic Practice, History in Africa 46 (2019) (abstract)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Hegel used and misused his sources
points.text: A historian of Africa has shown that Hegel read, misread and misused the texts about Africa that were available to him.

sources.title: Tom C. McCaskie, Exiled from History: Africa in Hegel’s Academic Practice, History in Africa 46 (2019) (abstract)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Trevor-Roper’s remark
points.text: The Oxford historian Hugh Trevor-Roper said in 1963 that there was “only the history of Europeans in Africa” and that the rest was “the unrewarding gyrations of barbarous tribes in picturesque but irrelevant corners of the globe”.
points.note: The 1963 date (a lecture series later published as The Rise of Christian Europe) is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Enocent Msindo (Rhodes University), keynote to the Zimbabwe Historical Association, 2019, quoting Trevor-Roper
Fuglestad 1992, History in Africa 19 (Cambridge)
The Spectator, Michela Wrong, 23 Jan 2025 (magazine)
Stephen Ellis, review of Finn Fuglestad, The Ambiguities of History (2005), African Affairs (2006) – Leiden University Scholarly Publications

Tunde Adeleke (2000) 'Guerilla Intellectualism: Walter A. Rodney and the Weapon of Knowledge in the Struggle for Black Liberation', Journal of Thought 35(1): 37–59 (PDF hosted by Princeton University)
Wikipedia: Hugh Trevor-Roper (secondary source)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: The response to Trevor-Roper
points.text: The remark was strongly challenged by Africanist historians such as J.D. Fage, who argued that Africa’s past showed complex societies and change, so Africa did have a history.

sources.title: Enocent Msindo (Rhodes University), keynote to the Zimbabwe Historical Association, 2019, quoting Trevor-Roper
Stephen Ellis, review of Finn Fuglestad, The Ambiguities of History (2005), African Affairs (2006) – Leiden University Scholarly Publications
Wikipedia: Hugh Trevor-Roper (secondary source)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: UNESCO’s General History of Africa
points.text: In 1964 UNESCO began work on the General History of Africa, reflecting its growing number of African member states. Its writers used oral traditions and archaeology as well as written archives.

sources.title: UNESCO's work on General History of Africa helps restore forgotten history (Africa Renewal, United Nations)
General History of Africa (UNESCO Library guide)
UNESCO: General History of Africa
UNESCO press release, 'General History of Africa: UNESCO completes pioneering historical oeuvre …' (17 Oct 2025)
UNESCO, 'A new page in the General History of Africa' (29 March 2019, updated 20 April 2023)
General History of Africa (UNESCO project) (Wikipedia)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: The Hamitic hypothesis
points.text: The “Hamitic hypothesis” claimed that progress in Africa was the work of “Hamitic” migrants from the north and north-east. C.G. Seligman set it out in Races of Africa (1930). It has since been discredited.

sources.title: Charles Seligman (LSE Department of Anthropology)
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Hamitic hypothesis
Hamites / Hamitic hypothesis (Wikipedia)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: The Scramble for Africa
points.text: By the early 20th century European powers controlled most of Africa. Only Ethiopia and Liberia remained outside European rule.
points.note: See also the hub’s peoples page for the Scramble and its effects on communities.

sources.title: Scramble for Africa | Britannica
EBSCO Research Starters: Scramble for Africa
Scramble for Africa (Wikipedia)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: The harm is well evidenced
points.text: The scale of the trades, the population loss and the long-term economic effects are supported by several independent kinds of evidence.

sources.title: Nunn, The Long-Term Effects of Africa's Slave Trades (NBER Working Paper 13367, abstract)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: The counterfactual is not testable
points.text: Estimates of the “missing” population are modelled, and projecting African population back in time is hard. No method can measure what Africa would have achieved.
points.note: Frankema discusses the difficulty of extending African population series into earlier centuries.

sources.title: Ewout Frankema, Africa and the Demographic Consequences of the Columbian Exchange, Asian Review of World Histories 7 (2019)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: “More advanced” depends on the measure
points.text: On some measures, such as city size around the year 1000, the Islamic world led: Córdoba, under Muslim rule, was then the largest city in Europe. Population figures are rough estimates, and no single measure supports an overall ranking.
points.note: Part of this rests on one independent source.

sources.title: Córdoba, Spain (Encyclopaedia Britannica)
Medieval urban population estimates from Colin McEvedy, New Penguin Atlas of Medieval History (Internet Medieval Sourcebook, Fordham University) – 1346, 50,000–125,000 band
Historic Centre of Cordoba – UNESCO World Heritage Centre
Egypt: A Country Study, U.S. Library of Congress (Federal Research Division), 'Major Cities' (countrystudies.us reproduction)
List of largest cities throughout history (Wikipedia; Chandler 1987 column)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Africa’s economic position before the trades
points.text: Some economic historians argue that low labour productivity already existed before the external slave trades. This challenges the idea that Africa was on course to overtake Europe.

sources.title: Gareth Austin, The ‘reversal of fortune’ thesis and the compression of history, Journal of International Development 20(8), 2008 (abstract, RePEc)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Europe’s lead was late and not inevitable
points.text: Great Divergence research led by Kenneth Pomeranz argues that Europe's lead over other advanced regions came only after about 1750; some economic historians date it earlier. If the lead came late, other paths of development were possible, but the evidence does not show that Africa would have taken one.

sources.title: The Great Divergence (Princeton University Press)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: African states were also involved
points.text: The trades involved African rulers and merchants as well as Europeans and others. This does not lessen the harm, but it complicates a simple Europe-versus-Africa account.
points.note: “that” is as written on the source page.

sources.title: Bristol Museums (Bristol City Council)
British Museum: Benin Bronzes
John Thornton, Africa and Africans in the Making of the Atlantic World, 1400-1800, ch. 4 summary (Cambridge University Press)
John Thornton (historian) (Wikipedia)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Not all losses were caused by Europeans
points.text: The trans-Saharan, Red Sea and Indian Ocean trades were not European. The destruction in Timbuktu in 2012–2013 was carried out by jihadist occupiers.

sources.title: Nathan Nunn, The Long-Term Effects of Africa’s Slave Trades, Quarterly Journal of Economics 123(1), 2008 (author copy)
The Prosecutor v. Ahmad Al Faqi Al Mahdi (International Criminal Court)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Much evidence survives
points.text: Despite looting and loss, substantial evidence survives: World Heritage sites, hundreds of thousands of manuscripts, museum collections and oral traditions.

sources.title: Endangered Libraries in Timbuktu (British Library Endangered Archives Programme)
UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Great Zimbabwe National Monument
British Museum: Benin Bronzes
Griot, Encyclopaedia Britannica
Timbuktu manuscripts (Wikipedia)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: The Black Death in Egypt
points.text: Plague reached Egypt in the mid-14th century. The historian Michael Dols concluded that between a third and a half of Egypt's people died in this first outbreak. His work is still the standard reference.
points.figure: One-third to one-half of Egypt's population (Dols's estimate)
points.note: The exact dates 1346-1353 are commonly given for the pandemic but are not confirmed by the sources cited here.

sources.title: Stuart Borsch, The Black Death in the Middle East and Central Asia (Islamic Law Blog, Harvard Law School Program in Islamic Law, 29 May 2020)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: The Black Death in the Maghreb
points.text: Eyewitnesses and historians agree plague devastated North-West Africa, but it is much less studied than Europe or Egypt.
points.note: Death rates for the Maghreb are not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Rachel Singer, The Black Death in the Maghreb: A Call to Action (University of Chicago Lexicon Project PDF)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Sleeping sickness was known in Africa long before colonial rule
points.text: Sleeping sickness is old in Africa. A 14th-century Arab historian recorded a ruler of Mali dying of it. Historians argue that African societies had learned to live alongside the tsetse fly before colonial upheaval broke that balance.

sources.title: Headrick (2014) Sleeping Sickness Epidemics and Colonial Responses in East and Central Africa, 1900-1940, PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases (PMC)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Malaria and sickle-cell trait
points.text: Malaria shaped human populations in Africa long before European contact. Sickle-cell trait gives some protection against it. The hub's genome page covers this in depth.
points.note: See the hub genome page; not repeated here.

sources.title: David S. Jones (2003) Virgin Soils Revisited, William and Mary Quarterly 60(4) (PDF via MITx course)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Yellow fever began in Africa
points.text: Yellow fever virus came from Africa and reached the Americas with the slave ships, as did the mosquito that carries it. Today yellow fever is still a risk in both regions.
points.figure: 27 African and 13 Latin American countries classified high-risk today (WHO)
points.note: The African origin is stated by a history blog (We're History); WHO gives the present-day distribution only.

sources.title: Zika Virus, Yellow Fever, and the Mosquito Behind Them (We're History, 2 February 2016)
Yellow fever fact sheet (World Health Organization, 20 October 2025)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: The Columbian Exchange as an idea
points.text: In 1972 the historian Alfred Crosby named the "Columbian Exchange": the movement of crops, animals, people and germs across the Atlantic after 1492. His thesis is still debated.
points.note: Historians of medicine have challenged parts of Crosby's later argument (see "Conditions").

sources.title: European Exploration, Perception of the Other, and the Columbian Exchange (Oxford University Press, Backman, Cultures of the West, student resources)
The Columbian Exchange - seminar page (Department of History, University of Warwick)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Portugal, the Canaries and the West African coast
points.text: Portuguese voyages along the African Atlantic coast in the 15th century were driven by gold and then by trade in enslaved people. Canary Islanders were among the first taken.
points.note: Disease at the early trading forts (for example Elmina) is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Brookbanks & Mbambo (2025) Reimaging, from a decolonised perspective, the Grade 10 intended curriculum..., Yesterday & Today No 33 (SciELO South Africa)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Syphilis: did it travel from the Americas to Europe?
points.text: A 2011 review found no reliable skeletal proof of syphilis in Europe before 1492, which supports an American origin. A later study claimed earlier European cases. The question stays open.
points.note: Debated. Neither side is settled by the sources cited.

sources.title: Skeletons point to Columbus voyage for syphilis origins (ScienceDaily, source: Emory University, 20 December 2011)
Did Columbus Bring Syphilis To Europe? Study Raises Doubts (Scripps News)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Smallpox on Hispaniola, 1518
points.text: In December 1518 smallpox broke out among enslaved Africans in the mines of Hispaniola. It then killed many of the remaining Taíno and spread to other islands and the mainland.
points.figure: About one-third of the remaining Indigenous people of Hispaniola by May 1519 (as reported)
points.note: Secondary website; figure is an estimate.

sources.title: Smallpox Comes to the Americas (1507-1524) (Indigenous Mexico, secondary website citing Jonathan B. Tucker)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Smallpox moved through the slave trade
points.text: The historian Jonathan B. Tucker argues that ships carrying enslaved Africans from places where smallpox was common brought the disease to the Americas again and again.
points.note: Quoted from Tucker via a secondary website.

sources.title: Smallpox Comes to the Americas (1507-1524) (Indigenous Mexico, secondary website citing Jonathan B. Tucker)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Yellow fever reaches the Caribbean, 1647
points.text: The first clear yellow fever epidemic in the Americas struck Barbados and Yucatán in 1647. The mosquito had crossed in water casks on slave ships.
points.note: Malaria also crossed with the slave trade; its timing is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Zika Virus, Yellow Fever, and the Mosquito Behind Them (We're History, 2 February 2016)
The Columbian Exchange - seminar page (Department of History, University of Warwick)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: The scale of the collapse
points.text: A 2019 UCL study pooled 119 regional estimates. It put the population before 1492 at about 60.5 million and found that about 90% died within a century.
points.figure: About 60.5 million before 1492 (range 44.8-78.2 million); about 90% died
points.note: Estimates of the pre-1492 population vary widely between scholars.

sources.title: Koch, Brierley, Maslin & Lewis (2019) Earth system impacts of the European arrival and Great Dying in the Americas after 1492, Quaternary Science Reviews (White Rose Research Online record)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: "The Great Dying" and a cooler climate
points.text: The same study estimates that European epidemics removed about 90% of an estimated 60.5 million people within a century of 1492. UCL puts the deaths at about 55 million; press coverage rounded this to 56 million. The study links the loss to a dip in atmospheric carbon dioxide: abandoned farmland returned to forest and drew down carbon, which contributed to the cooling known as the "Little Ice Age".
points.figure: About 56 million deaths by 1600; CO2 fell 7-10 ppm
points.note: The authors attribute 47-67% of the carbon dioxide fall to the Americas; natural causes also played a part. The 56 million figure is from press coverage of the study.

sources.title: UCL Geography news (8 February 2019): The 'Great Dying' of 1492 led to lower CO2 and a cooler planet
European colonization of Americas killed so many it cooled Earth's climate (eceee news summary of The Guardian, 31 January 2019)
Koch, Brierley, Maslin & Lewis (2019) Earth system impacts of the European arrival and Great Dying in the Americas after 1492, Quaternary Science Reviews (White Rose Research Online record)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Smallpox in Tenochtitlan, 1520
points.text: Smallpox arrived in Mexico in 1520 with a Spanish expedition. It killed perhaps a third to a half of the population, including Moctezuma's successor, weakening the Mexica just as they resisted the Spanish.
points.figure: One-third to one-half of the population
points.note: Some accounts name the carrier as Francisco de Eguía and describe him as an enslaved African; that description is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Aztec Empire smallpox epidemic (EBSCO Research Starters)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Cocoliztli: the great epidemics of 1545 and 1576
points.text: Two waves of a disease called cocoliztli ("pest" in Nahuatl) swept Mexico. The 1545-1548 wave alone may have killed 5 to 15 million people.
points.figure: 5-15 million deaths; up to 80% of the Indigenous population (1545-1548)
points.note: The cause is debated; see next point.

sources.title: Acuna-Soto et al. (2002) Megadrought and Megadeath in 16th Century Mexico, Emerging Infectious Diseases 8(4), CDC

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Cocoliztli: Salmonella or an Indigenous fever?
points.text: In 2002 researchers argued cocoliztli was a native haemorrhagic fever made worse by severe drought. In 2018 ancient DNA from victims in Oaxaca found Salmonella Paratyphi C. The researchers themselves called it a possible cause.
points.note: The DNA came from one burial site; it does not rule out other pathogens.

sources.title: Acuna-Soto et al. (2002) Megadrought and Megadeath in 16th Century Mexico, Emerging Infectious Diseases 8(4), CDC
Possible cause of early colonial-era Mexican epidemic identified (University of Tübingen, 2018)
Possible cause of early colonial-era Mexican epidemic identified (Max Planck Society, 19 January 2018)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: The Taíno: collapse on Hispaniola
points.text: The Taíno population of the Caribbean fell sharply within a generation of 1492. Forced labour, hunger, disease and violence all played a part.
points.figure: Some 85% lost by the early 1500s (contested extrapolation)
points.note: Pre-contact numbers are uncertain; some scholars estimate over three million on Hispaniola.

sources.title: What Became of the Taíno? (Smithsonian Magazine article by Robert M. Poole, 2011, as reproduced by the CARICOM Reparations Commission)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: The encomienda system
points.text: Under the encomienda, Spanish settlers were granted the labour of Indigenous people. In practice it was a system of forced labour and exploitation on Hispaniola.

sources.title: Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies (Magdalen College, University of Oxford, Old Library blog, 28 October 2020)
What Became of the Taíno? (Smithsonian Magazine article by Robert M. Poole, 2011, as reproduced by the CARICOM Reparations Commission)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Las Casas's testimony
points.text: Bartolomé de las Casas, a Spanish friar who reached Hispaniola in 1502, became a fierce critic of Spanish cruelty. His figures are polemical and not precise counts.
points.note: Historians treat Las Casas's numbers as testimony, not census data.

sources.title: Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies (Magdalen College, University of Oxford, Old Library blog, 28 October 2020)
Bartolomé de las Casas, Brief Account of the Destruction of the Indies (1542; excerpts, National Humanities Center primary source set)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Were the Taíno "extinct"?
points.text: No. A 2018 ancient-genome study found Taíno-related ancestry in present-day Puerto Ricans. Many Caribbean people have long claimed Taíno heritage.
points.figure: 10-15% Native American ancestry in a sample of 104 Puerto Ricans
points.note: Genetic ancestry is not the same as cultural or community identity.

sources.title: Traces of indigenous Taíno found in present-day Caribbean populations (University of Cambridge press release on Schroeder et al., PNAS 2018, republished by Brewminate)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: The Beothuk of Newfoundland
points.text: European settlement cut the Beothuk off from food. Tuberculosis, other diseases and violence reduced their numbers. Shanawdithit, often called the last Beothuk, died in 1829.
points.note: Mi'kmaq oral histories say Beothuk people married into other Indigenous nations.

sources.title: Shawnadithit (The Canadian Encyclopedia)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Enslaved Africans brought in as Indigenous people died
points.text: As the Indigenous labour force collapsed, Spanish colonists imported enslaved Africans to work the mines and plantations.
points.note: Quoted from Tucker via a secondary website.

sources.title: Smallpox Comes to the Americas (1507-1524) (Indigenous Mexico, secondary website citing Jonathan B. Tucker)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Smallpox at the Cape, 1713
points.text: Smallpox reached the Cape on a Dutch ship's laundry in 1713. The Khoikhoi and San suffered terrible losses.
points.note: Precise death tolls are not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Smallpox Epidemic Strikes at the Cape, 13 February 1713 (South African History Online)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Sleeping sickness in Uganda, 1901-1905
points.text: A severe epidemic broke out around Lake Victoria in 1901. Historians link the wider epidemics to the trade and movement that colonial rule set in motion.
points.figure: Over 200,000 deaths, one-third of the regional population, by 1905
points.note: The parasite responsible for the Uganda epidemic has been questioned by later researchers.

sources.title: Headrick (2014) Sleeping Sickness Epidemics and Colonial Responses in East and Central Africa, 1900-1940, PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases (PMC)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Sleeping sickness in the Congo basin
points.text: Cases grew along the Sangha and Ubangi rivers in the 1890s and spread through the Congo region. Roger Casement saw it as one cause of population loss.

sources.title: Headrick (2014) Sleeping Sickness Epidemics and Colonial Responses in East and Central Africa, 1900-1940, PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases (PMC)
Report of the British Consul, Roger Casement, on the Administration of the Congo Free State (1904; excerpts, Vancouver Island University course page)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Rinderpest, 1887-1897
points.text: Rinderpest arrived in 1887 with cattle shipped from India for Italian troops at Massawa. It swept the continent, killed most cattle and brought famine. There is no evidence it was spread on purpose.
points.figure: About 90% of Africa's cattle in a decade; perhaps a third of Ethiopians dead by 1892
points.note: The one-third figure for Ethiopia is described by the source as an estimate from "some sources".

sources.title: How was rinderpest eradicated? (Gavi VaccinesWork, Maya Prabhu, 24 September 2026)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: The Congo Free State and the Casement Report
points.text: Under King Leopold II's rule, people were forced to gather rubber under threat of violence. Roger Casement's 1904 report described villages emptied since his previous visit in 1887.
points.note: Overall population-loss estimates for the Congo Free State vary widely between historians; no figure is confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Report of the British Consul, Roger Casement, on the Administration of the Congo Free State (1904; excerpts, Vancouver Island University course page)
Casement in the Congo Free State, exhibition panel 4 (National Museum of Ireland)
Roger Casement - voice of the voiceless (History Ireland)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Herero and Nama, 1904–1908: recognised by Germany as genocide in 2021
points.text: German forces in what is now Namibia drove Herero people into the desert and cut them off from water. Survivors were held in camps. According to the Kupferberg Holocaust Center (CUNY), up to 80,000 Herero (about 80%) and 10,000 Nama (about 50%) died. The German government has officially called these events a genocide since 28 May 2021.
points.note: Figures from the Kupferberg Holocaust Center (CUNY), which calls it the first genocide of the 20th century.

sources.title: Namibia (1904-1908) (Kupferberg Holocaust Center, Queensborough Community College, CUNY)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Shark Island camp
points.text: The camp on Shark Island, off the Namibian coast, held Herero and Nama prisoners from 1905 to 1907. Beatings, hunger and disease killed many.
points.note: Death-rate estimates for Shark Island vary between sources; higher figures are not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Shark Island Concentration Camp (The Holocaust Explained, The Wiener Holocaust Library)
Namibia (1904-1908) (Kupferberg Holocaust Center, Queensborough Community College, CUNY)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Germany's recognition, 2021
points.text: On 28 May 2021 Germany's Foreign Minister, Heiko Maas, said Germany would officially call these events a genocide and ask forgiveness. Germany pledged 1.1 billion euro but said no legal claim for compensation follows from it.
points.note: The term "genocide" here is the German government's own, from 28 May 2021.

sources.title: Foreign Minister Maas on the conclusion of negotiations with Namibia (German Federal Foreign Office, 28 May 2021)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: "The white man's grave" and quinine
points.text: Disease, above all malaria, killed so many Europeans in West Africa that the coast became known as "the white man's grave", a phrase examined by the historian Philip Curtin. From the mid-19th century, regular quinine doses changed this. In 1854 Baikie's Niger expedition returned without a single death.
points.note: This disease barrier slowed European settlement; it did not protect Africans from the slave trade.

sources.title: Philip D. Curtin, "The White Man's Grave": Image and Reality, 1780-1850, Journal of British Studies 1(1) (Cambridge Core)
"The forgotten man of Africa" (British Society for the History of Medicine, Lee Coppack, 14 May 2024)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Deaths on the Middle Passage fell over time
points.text: Most historians find that death rates on slave ships fell between the 17th and early 19th centuries, though data are patchy and one study of the Dutch trade found no trend.
points.note: SlaveVoyages percentages by period are not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Deaths of Slaves in the Middle Passage, Journal of Economic History 45(3), 1985 (abstract, Cambridge Core)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Death rates by period
points.text: One large study measured deaths per month at sea, per 1,000 captives. The average fell from about 98 (1676-1700) to about 46 (1776-1800). It rose again in the illegal trade after 1850 (about 197, from only 20 voyages).
points.note: These are monthly rates, not the share of captives who died on a whole voyage.

sources.title: Klein, Engerman, Haines & Shlomowitz (2001) Transoceanic Mortality: The Slave Trade in Comparative Perspective, William and Mary Quarterly, supplement Table A.1

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Caribbean plantations: populations shrank
points.text: Richard Dunn compared a Jamaican sugar estate with a Virginia plantation. Mesopotamia in Jamaica lost population while Mount Airy in Virginia grew.

sources.title: A Tale of Two Plantations: a comparative approach to Caribbean and US slavery, Richard S. Dunn (Case Western Reserve University, Baker-Nord Center event page)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Smallpox around Sydney, 1789
points.text: Smallpox broke out among Aboriginal people around Sydney in April 1789, the year after the British arrived. Where it came from is debated.
points.note: One theory says Macassan traders in the north brought it earlier. Most researchers think First Nations people had no earlier exposure; whether the British fleet brought it is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: Huang & Bashford (2024) Smallpox Geographies: vaccination, borders and Indigenous peoples in Australia's coastal north (open access, Europe PMC)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Tasmania and Truganini
points.text: Truganini (Trukanini), a Nuennone woman who died in 1876, lost her mother, sister and intended husband to colonial violence. She was wrongly called "the last Tasmanian".
points.note: Wider frontier violence across Australia is not quantified by the sources cited.

sources.title: Aborigines, the last of the race, Tasmania, c. 1866 (National Portrait Gallery of Australia)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Tasmanian Aboriginal people today
points.text: Tasmanian Aboriginal people did not die out. Descendants of Truganini's contemporaries live in Tasmania today.
points.note: AIATSIS was not reachable to check; the National Portrait Gallery is cited.

sources.title: Aborigines, the last of the race, Tasmania, c. 1866 (National Portrait Gallery of Australia)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Hawaii after 1778
points.text: One estimate puts the Native Hawaiian population at 683,000 when Cook arrived in 1778. Other estimates range from 200,000 to 1 million. Introduced diseases caused steep falls over the next 60 years.
points.note: The pre-contact estimate is highly disputed.

sources.title: After 200 years, Native Hawaiians make a comeback (Pew Research Center, 6 April 2015)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Māori population decline
points.text: The Māori population fell from about 100,000 in 1769 to about 42,000 in 1896. Introduced diseases were the main cause, more than warfare. The fall sped up after 1840 as settlers arrived.

sources.title: Epidemics and Pandemics: Impact on Māori (National Library of New Zealand Services to Schools, DigitalNZ; quotes Te Ara)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: The Pacific labour trade ("blackbirding")
points.text: Pacific islanders, such as Solomon Islanders, were recruited or taken to work in the sugar fields of Fiji and Queensland. Many died.

sources.title: Shanks, Pacific Island Societies Destabilised by Infectious Diseases, Journal of Military and Veterans' Health (PDF)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Measles in Fiji, 1875
points.text: Measles arrived in January 1875 on HMS Dido, carrying the chief Cakobau back from Sydney. It killed a fifth to a quarter of Fijians in five months, and almost all the chiefs.
points.figure: One-fifth to one-quarter of the population

sources.title: Shanks, Pacific Island Societies Destabilised by Infectious Diseases, Journal of Military and Veterans' Health (PDF)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Pacific islands exposed from the 18th century
points.text: Many isolated Pacific islands lost large parts of their populations when new infections first reached them.

sources.title: Shanks, Pacific Island Societies Destabilised by Infectious Diseases, Journal of Military and Veterans' Health

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Asia: the Black Death in the Middle East and Central Asia
points.text: Plague also struck Central Asia and Iraq in the 14th century. Research on mortality there is still being developed.
points.note: Colonial-era epidemics in South and South-East Asia are not covered by the sources cited.

sources.title: Stuart Borsch, The Black Death in the Middle East and Central Asia (Islamic Law Blog, Harvard Law School Program in Islamic Law, 29 May 2020)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Virgin Soils Revisited
points.text: The historian David S. Jones argued in 2003 that what happened to each Indigenous population depended on its circumstances, not only on a lack of immunity.
points.note: Jones challenges the "virgin soil" explanation; others still stress immunity.

sources.title: David S. Jones (2003) Virgin Soils Revisited, William and Mary Quarterly 60(4) (PDF via MITx course)
Virgin Soils Revisited - excerpt (Gladue Rights Research Database, University of Saskatchewan)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Poverty and stress drive epidemics
points.text: Jones suggests Indigenous epidemics were driven by the same forces that drive epidemics everywhere.

sources.title: David S. Jones (2003) Virgin Soils Revisited, William and Mary Quarterly 60(4) (PDF via MITx course)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Hunger and disease feed each other
points.text: Epidemics stopped people working their land, which caused famine, which left survivors weaker against the next disease.
points.note: Colin Calloway, quoted by Jones.

sources.title: David S. Jones (2003) Virgin Soils Revisited, William and Mary Quarterly 60(4) (PDF via MITx course)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: "No immunity" hides too much
points.text: Jones warns that saying Indigenous people had "no immunity" blurs very different causes.

sources.title: David S. Jones (2003) Virgin Soils Revisited, William and Mary Quarterly 60(4) (PDF via MITx course)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Drought and disease in Mexico
points.text: The cocoliztli epidemics coincided with the worst drought in 500 years, which magnified their effect.

sources.title: Acuna-Soto et al. (2002) Megadrought and Megadeath in 16th Century Mexico, Emerging Infectious Diseases 8(4), CDC

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Famine used to force labour
points.text: After rinderpest and famine, some mine owners in Southern Africa saw hunger as a way to push down wages.
points.note: Quote attributed by the source to a mine managers' association president.

sources.title: How was rinderpest eradicated? (Gavi VaccinesWork, Maya Prabhu, 24 September 2026)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Camps as a system
points.text: In Namibia, the camps combined beatings, hunger, disease and sexual violence.

sources.title: Namibia (1904-1908) (Kupferberg Holocaust Center, Queensborough Community College, CUNY)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Loss of leaders
points.text: When epidemics killed chiefs and elders, communities lost their leaders at the moment they were most needed.

sources.title: Shanks, Pacific Island Societies Destabilised by Infectious Diseases, Journal of Military and Veterans' Health (PDF)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: "Extinct" is often wrong
points.text: Peoples described as extinct, including the Taíno, Beothuk and Tasmanian Aboriginal people, have living descendants or living communities with oral histories of survival.
points.note: See the Taíno, Beothuk and Tasmania points.

sources.title: Traces of indigenous Taíno found in present-day Caribbean populations (University of Cambridge press release on Schroeder et al., PNAS 2018, republished by Brewminate)
Aborigines, the last of the race, Tasmania, c. 1866 (National Portrait Gallery of Australia)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Recovery as well as loss
points.text: Native Hawaiians, for example, have grown in number again since their low point.

sources.title: After 200 years, Native Hawaiians make a comeback (Pew Research Center, 6 April 2015)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Numbers come with wide ranges
points.text: Estimates for the Americas, Hawaii and Mexico span wide ranges. We give ranges and name who gives them.

sources.title: After 200 years, Native Hawaiians make a comeback (Pew Research Center, 6 April 2015)
Koch, Brierley, Maslin & Lewis (2019) Earth system impacts of the European arrival and Great Dying in the Americas after 1492, Quaternary Science Reviews (White Rose Research Online record)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: "Age of Discovery" is a Eurocentric label
points.text: Lands "discovered" by Europeans were already home to millions of people. Two South African history teachers, drawing on the journalist-historian Howard French (2021), argue that a Eurocentric narrative has sidelined Africa's role in this era.
points.note: We keep the phrase in quotation marks.

sources.title: Brookbanks & Mbambo (2025) Reimaging, from a decolonised perspective, the Grade 10 intended curriculum..., Yesterday & Today No 33 (SciELO South Africa)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Who says "genocide", and when
points.text: Germany's government formally used "genocide" for the Herero and Nama killings on 28 May 2021. The Kupferberg Holocaust Center and the Wiener Holocaust Library also use the term. The 2019 UCL study uses "Great Dying" for the Americas, not "genocide".
points.note: We attribute the word to the speaker rather than applying it ourselves.

sources.title: Foreign Minister Maas on the conclusion of negotiations with Namibia (German Federal Foreign Office, 28 May 2021)
Namibia (1904-1908) (Kupferberg Holocaust Center, Queensborough Community College, CUNY)
Koch, Brierley, Maslin & Lewis (2019) Earth system impacts of the European arrival and Great Dying in the Americas after 1492, Quaternary Science Reviews (White Rose Research Online record)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Disease moved in more than one direction
points.text: Germs travelled from Europe and Africa to the Americas and the Pacific, and possibly from the Americas to Europe (syphilis, debated).

sources.title: European Exploration, Perception of the Other, and the Columbian Exchange (Oxford University Press, Backman, Cultures of the West, student resources)
Did Columbus Bring Syphilis To Europe? Study Raises Doubts (Scripps News)

points.datasetTitle: What was taken, lost and might have been
points.heading: Disease is not the same as intent
points.text: Some introductions were accidental, as the rinderpest source notes. That does not lessen the harm, or the responsibility for the conditions that made it worse.

sources.title: How was rinderpest eradicated? (Gavi VaccinesWork, Maya Prabhu, 24 September 2026)

points.heading: Linnaeus ranks human 'varieties' by continent
points.text: In his classification of nature, Linnaeus divided humans into 'varieties' linked to the continents. In the 1758 edition of Systema Naturae he added the four temperaments, or 'humours', to each variety. The African variety was always placed last, and the descriptions as a whole favoured Europeans.

sources.title: Linnaeus and Race (Linnean Society of London)
Linnaeus, Carolus (1707–1778) – Understanding RACE glossary (American Anthropological Association)

points.heading: Blumenbach names five varieties, including 'Caucasian'
points.text: In 1795 Blumenbach set out a five-part naming system for human varieties, including 'Caucasian'. He held that all humans were one species and did not propose a hierarchy, but he treated the white 'Caucasian' form as the most beautiful. Later writers misused his labels to support racist ideas.

sources.title: Blumenbach and the concept of race (University of Göttingen)
Race (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)

points.heading: Hume's footnote on 'national characters'
points.text: In a footnote to his essay 'Of National Characters', added in the 1753–54 edition of his essays, Hume wrote that he was 'apt to suspect' Black people to be 'naturally inferior' to white people. He claimed there were no arts or sciences among them, and dismissed an educated Black man in Jamaica as admired only for 'slender accomplishments'.
points.note: Sources differ on the edition date: the University of Edinburgh appendix refers to 'the 1753 version' and the Stanford Encyclopedia to 'the 1754 edition'; the collected essays were dated 1753 and issued 1753–54.

sources.title: James Beattie (1735—1803) (Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
Appendix 2: The University of Edinburgh, Theories of Race and Civilisation, and British Imperialism, by Ian Stewart (University of Edinburgh)
Race (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)

points.heading: Beattie answers Hume in 1770
points.text: The Scottish philosopher James Beattie replied to Hume's footnote in his Essay on Truth (1770). He argued that Africans and Americans had many ingenious arts and manufactures, and that the condition of slavery was not favourable to genius. Beattie was a committed abolitionist who called slavery 'a barbarous piece of policy'.

sources.title: James Beattie (1735—1803) (Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
James Beattie (1735-1803), by Dr Julie Watt (Brycchan Carey, Abolition website)

points.heading: Kant defines 'race' and ranks humanity
points.text: Kant wrote a series of essays defining 'race' as a scientific concept from the 1770s onward. In his lectures he said humanity reached its 'highest degree of perfection in the white race' and placed Africans much lower. How central this was to his philosophy, and whether he changed his mind, is disputed.
points.note: Robert Bernasconi (with Tommy Lott) presents Kant as 'the first to propose a rigorous scientific concept of race', and treats race as part of Kant's system. Pauline Kleingeld (2007) argues that Kant ranked white people above others in the 1780s but gave up the racial hierarchy in the 1790s for a more egalitarian, cosmopolitan view. Inder Marwah (2022) notes that Kleingeld and others see Kant as having 'ultimately' retracted his predictions, but argues racial ideas still shaped his account of human progress.

sources.title: Inder S. Marwah, 'White Progress: Kant, Race and Teleology', Kantian Review 27 (2022), 615–634 (Cambridge University Press)
'Kant, Race, and Natural History' (Kingston University research repository), citing Bernasconi 2001
Pauline Kleingeld, 'Kant's Second Thoughts on Race', Philosophical Quarterly 57 (2007) (abstract on PhilArchive)

points.heading: Edinburgh removes Hume's name from a building
points.text: In September 2020 the University of Edinburgh renamed its David Hume Tower as 40 George Square, as an interim decision. It cited Hume's 'comments on matters of race', which it said, 'though not uncommon at the time, rightly cause distress today'. The decision drew international scrutiny and debate.

sources.title: Making sense of silenced archives: Hume, Scotland and the 'debate' about the humanity of Black people (University of Edinburgh, Race and Decoloniality blog, 2021)
Edinburgh Uni renames David Hume tower over 'racist views' (STV News, 13 September 2020)

points.heading: Edward Long's History of Jamaica
points.text: Edward Long, a Jamaican planter and enslaver, published The History of Jamaica in 1774. He was a polygenist, believing that human races did not share a common origin. Historian Catherine Hall shows that the book tried to define Black and white people as 'essentially different and unequal', using natural history to build a fixed racial hierarchy.

sources.title: Enlightenment Race Science in the Colonies: Edward Long and the… (University of Michigan, Science, Technology and Society Program)
Catherine Hall, Lucky Valley: Edward Long and the History of Racial Capitalism (Cambridge University Press, 2024)

points.heading: Banneker challenges Jefferson's doubts
points.text: In Notes on the State of Virginia (1785), Thomas Jefferson set out his doubts about the intellect of Black people. In August 1791 Benjamin Banneker sent Jefferson, then Secretary of State, a manuscript copy of his almanac with a letter challenging those views. Jefferson replied that 'no body wishes more than I do to see such proofs as you exhibit'.

sources.title: Letter to Thomas Jefferson from Benjamin Banneker, August 19, 1791 (Britannica)
Thomas Jefferson to Benjamin Banneker, 30 August 1791 (Library of Congress exhibition)

points.heading: Equiano's Interesting Narrative
points.text: Olaudah Equiano's autobiography, published in London in 1789, described his life as an enslaved person. It was timed to coincide with the May 1789 parliamentary debate on the slave trade, and Equiano toured the country promoting it. By writing his own life, he directly contradicted the claim that Black minds were inferior.

sources.title: Olaudah Equiano (Britannica)
The Interesting Narrative by Olaudah Equiano – Ten-Minute Book Club (Faculty of English, University of Oxford)

points.heading: Cugoano demands immediate abolition
points.text: In 1787 Ottobah Cugoano published Thoughts and Sentiments on the Evil and Wicked Traffic of the Slavery and Commerce of the Human Species. It is one of the first anti-slavery books by a Black author published in Britain, and the most radical of its time, calling for immediate abolition and the emancipation of enslaved people. He was a leading member of the Sons of Africa and a friend of Equiano.

sources.title: Ottobah Cugoano – blue plaque (English Heritage)
Learning about Britain's Black abolitionists (University of Wolverhampton blog, October 2022)

points.heading: Carlyle's 'Occasional Discourse'
points.text: In December 1849 Carlyle published an essay in Fraser's Magazine arguing that emancipation had left Black Jamaicans in idleness and that freed workers should be compelled to work. He reissued it in 1853 as a pamphlet with an even more offensive title.

sources.title: Speech beyond Toleration: On Carlyle and Moral Controversialism Now (Oxford University Research Archive)
The War on Woke is 200 years old (Snapshots of Empire blog, University of Sussex, 2022)

points.heading: Mill's reply: 'The Negro Question'
points.text: In January 1850 John Stuart Mill replied in the same magazine. He said Carlyle's picture of Jamaican labour was 'copied from the wildest prophecies of the slavery party before emancipation'. Their different views on race and slavery helped to end their friendship.

sources.title: Speech beyond Toleration: On Carlyle and Moral Controversialism Now (Oxford University Research Archive)
Sheila McIntosh, 'Carlyle and the Caribbean', Carlyle Society Occasional Papers 21 (Edinburgh, 2008)

points.heading: Morant Bay and the Governor Eyre controversy
points.text: After the Morant Bay rising in Jamaica in 1865, Governor Edward John Eyre declared martial law and hanged Paul Bogle and the assembly member George William Gordon. In Britain, the Jamaica Committee, led by Mill, sought to have Eyre prosecuted, while Carlyle joined the Eyre Defence Committee in 1866.

sources.title: Jamaica – British rule (Britannica)
Sheila McIntosh, 'Carlyle and the Caribbean', Carlyle Society Occasional Papers 21 (Edinburgh, 2008)
When Intellectuals Split: The Eyre Case (JSTOR Daily)

points.heading: Robert Knox and The Races of Men
points.text: Knox, an Edinburgh surgeon and anatomist, became a popular lecturer on race. In The Races of Men (1850) he classified all known human races and argued that race was the greatest single factor shaping behaviour and character. He also played on fears that Europeans could be driven out of their colonies.
points.note: Birkbeck notes that, despite his racism, some scholars have recently argued Knox used his theories to criticise colonialism.

sources.title: Colonialism and science (University of Glasgow)

points.heading: James Hunt and the Anthropological Society
points.text: In 1863 James Hunt led about a dozen members out of the Ethnological Society to found the Anthropological Society of London. His paper 'On the Negro's Place in Nature' (1863) defended the subjection and even the enslavement of Black people and argued that humans were several species.

sources.title: Paul Turnbull, 'British Anthropological Thought in Colonial Practice' (ANU Press)
On the Negro's place in nature – catalogue record (Conway Hall Library and Archives)

points.heading: Samuel Morton's skull collection
points.text: Morton, who trained in medicine at Edinburgh, built the largest skull collection in North America. In Crania Americana (1839) he used skull capacity to rank races, with Caucasians at the top. He believed different races had separate origins.
points.note: Stephen Jay Gould (1981) argued that Morton skewed his data to fit his preconceptions. Lewis et al. (PLoS Biology, 2011) remeasured the skulls and concluded that Morton 'did not manipulate data to support his preconceptions, contra Gould'. Weisberg (2014) argues most of Gould's arguments are sound and that Morton did mismeasure in ways that matched 19th-century racial bias; Kaplan and Pigliucci (2015) argue the data cannot properly answer the question. All sides agree Morton's racial views were racist.

sources.title: Appendix 2: The University of Edinburgh, Theories of Race and Civilisation, and British Imperialism, by Ian Stewart (University of Edinburgh)
Lewis et al., 'The Mismeasure of Science: Stephen Jay Gould versus Samuel George Morton on Skulls and Bias', PLoS Biology (2011)
Race – Gobineau's Essay on the Inequality of Human Races (Britannica)
Michael Weisberg, 'Remeasuring man', Evolution and Development (2014) (ANU research portal abstract)
Kaplan and Pigliucci, 'Gould on Morton, Redux', Studies in History and Philosophy of Biological and Biomedical Sciences 52 (2015) (PhilArchive abstract)

points.heading: Nott and Gliddon's Types of Mankind
points.text: Physician Josiah Nott and George Gliddon published Types of Mankind in 1854. It promoted the idea that human races were separate species, included a contribution by Louis Agassiz and ran through ten editions.

sources.title: Polygenism – 'This Abominable Traffic': Physicians on Slavery (Center for the History of Medicine, Countway Library, Harvard)
The Claims of the Negro Ethnologically Considered, 12 July 1854 (Frederick Douglass Papers Project, Digital Edition)

points.heading: Douglass answers the ethnologists
points.text: On 12 July 1854 Frederick Douglass gave a commencement address at Western Reserve College in Ohio, 'The Claims of the Negro Ethnologically Considered'. He named Morton and Nott and Gliddon, argued that the evidence favoured the unity of the human species, and said that the pull to 'read the negro out of the human family' came from pride and self-interest.

sources.title: Frederick Douglass – Our Stories (Case Western Reserve University)
The Claims of the Negro Ethnologically Considered, 12 July 1854 (Frederick Douglass Papers Project, Digital Edition)
Frederick Douglass (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Summer 2021 edition)

points.heading: Gobineau's Essay on the Inequality of Human Races
points.text: Gobineau's Essay (1853–55) claimed that all civilisations were the work of white races, that 'Aryans' were the purest, and that mixing with other races caused civilisations to decline. It was widely read and publicised, with admirers in the United States and Germany, including the composer Richard Wagner.

sources.title: Race – Gobineau's Essay on the Inequality of Human Races (Britannica)
Race (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)

points.heading: Firmin's The Equality of the Human Races
points.text: The Haitian scholar Anténor Firmin wrote De l'égalité des races humaines (1885) as a response to Gobineau. He used the scientific methods of his day to argue that the human races were equal. The book was sidelined for its 'radical' position and was out of print even in Haiti until 1968.

sources.title: The Equality of the Human Races (University of Illinois Press)
Russell, 'Positivism and Progress in Firmin's Equality of the Human Races', Journal of Pan African Studies 7:2 (2014)
Anténor Firmin (1850-1911) (BlackPast.org)

points.heading: Galton and the founding of eugenics
points.text: In Hereditary Genius (1869) Galton argued that mental ability is inherited, and proposed arranged marriages between 'men of distinction' and wealthy women to produce a 'gifted race'. He coined the term 'eugenics' in 1883.

sources.title: Hereditary Genius (Britannica)
Eugenic Thinking and the Cognitive Sciences (Open Encyclopedia of Cognitive Science, MIT)
Bricks + Mortals: a history of eugenics told through buildings (UCL Culture)

points.heading: Karl Pearson framed race as a struggle won by the 'fitter race'
points.text: In National Life from the Standpoint of Science (1900), the statistician Karl Pearson argued that a nation is kept efficient by competition, including war with what he called 'inferior races'. UCL's eugenics inquiry found earlier correspondence in which he ranked peoples on a scale he linked to 'civilisation'.

sources.title: Modern History Sourcebook: Karl Pearson, National Life from the Standpoint of Science, 1900 (Fordham University)
Inquiry into the History of Eugenics at UCL: final report, February 2020 (University College London)

points.heading: Galton's money created a eugenics laboratory and chair at UCL
points.text: Francis Galton funded a eugenics laboratory in the University of London, which Pearson directed from 1907, and left money in his will for a professorship of eugenics. Pearson became the first Galton Professor of Eugenics at University College in 1911; the chair was renamed Human Genetics only in 1963.

sources.title: Oxford DNB article: Pearson, Karl, by Joanne Woiak (Oxford University Press, reproduced by University of St Andrews MacTutor)
Inquiry into the History of Eugenics at UCL: final report, February 2020 (University College London)

points.heading: A eugenics journal set out to study 'racial problems'
points.text: Pearson founded the Annals of Eugenics in 1925, published for the Galton Laboratory by Cambridge University Press. Its original subtitle described it as a journal for the scientific study of racial problems. It was renamed the Annals of Human Genetics in 1954.

sources.title: Catalogue record: Annals of eugenics (Wellcome Collection)
Inquiry into the History of Eugenics at UCL: final report, February 2020 (University College London)

points.heading: The 1930 Fletcher Report stigmatised mixed-heritage children
points.text: A 1930 report on mixed-heritage children in Liverpool, written for the a Liverpool association for the welfare of mixed-heritage children (its name used a term now considered offensive) with the backing of a eugenicist, described the children of Black men and white women as having inherited defects. It was criticised at the time for its biased methods.

sources.title: Mark Christian, 'The Fletcher Report 1930: A Historical Case Study of Contested Black Mixed Heritage Britishness', Journal of Historical Sociology 21(2–3), 2008 (Wiley; abstract and extracts reproduced by Mixed Race Studies)
The Fletcher report, timeline entry (Mix-d: Museum)

points.heading: Indirect rule governed Africans through fixed 'customary' units
points.text: Lord Lugard's The Dual Mandate in British Tropical Africa (1922) set out indirect rule: governing through chiefs and 'native' courts. Later scholars argue that this system defined people by ethnic group and let state-appointed authorities decide what counted as 'custom'.
points.note: Assessments differ. Britannica describes indirect rule as 'cooperative in spirit and economical in staff and expense' and says it 'helped bridge the gap between tribal systems' and modern government, though it was 'sometimes misapplied or overprolonged'. Mamdani (Princeton University Press) argues it was a form of 'decentralized despotism' that hardened ethnic divisions.

sources.title: Frederick Lugard (Encyclopaedia Britannica)
Mahmood Mamdani, Citizen and Subject: Contemporary Africa and the Legacy of Late Colonialism, book description (Princeton University Press)

points.heading: Africans were put on show at the 1924 British Empire Exhibition
points.text: At Wembley in 1924, about sixty West African craftspeople and workers lived and worked in a mock walled city and 'native village' for visitors to watch. Press coverage leaned on stereotypes of African 'backwardness'.

sources.title: Marc Matera, Afro-Metropolis: Black Life and Political Activism in Interwar London, chapter 1 (University of California Press)
Philip Grant, When Nigeria came to Wembley, 1924 (Brent Museum and Archives, London Borough of Brent, 2014)

points.heading: Arthur Jensen claimed group IQ gaps were largely inherited
points.text: In 1969 the Harvard Educational Review published Arthur Jensen's article 'How Much Can We Boost IQ and Scholastic Achievement?'. It argued that compensatory education had apparently failed and that differences in intelligence between groups had a substantial genetic basis.

sources.title: In Memoriam: Arthur R. Jensen (University of California Academic Senate)
Jensen, Arthur Robert, Scribner Encyclopedia of American Lives: The 1960s (Charles Scribner's Sons, via Encyclopedia.com)

points.heading: A Nobel physicist campaigned on race and heredity
points.text: From the late 1960s, William Shockley, who shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics, argued that Black Americans scored lower on IQ tests because of genetics, and advocated eugenics while a professor at Stanford.

sources.title: Guide to the William Shockley papers (Stanford University Libraries, via Online Archive of California)
William B. Shockley (Britannica Student Encyclopedia)

points.heading: The Pioneer Fund and Mankind Quarterly sustained race science
points.text: The Pioneer Fund, a US foundation set up in 1937 with Wickliffe Draper's money, financed opponents of racial integration. Mankind Quarterly, founded in Edinburgh in 1960 with Robert Gayre as editor, described itself as a journal of 'race and inheritance'.

sources.title: Francesco Cassata, 'Against UNESCO: Gedda, Gini and American Scientific Racism', Medicina nei Secoli 20(3), 2008 (Sapienza University of Rome)
Catalogue record: The mankind quarterly, Edinburgh, 1960– (Wellcome Collection)
Charles Lane, 'The Tainted Sources of The Bell Curve', New York Review of Books, 1 December 1994

points.heading: A journal retracted a Rushton paper as unsound in 2020
points.text: In 2020 the Elsevier journal Personality and Individual Differences retracted a 2012 paper by J. Philippe Rushton and a co-author linking skin pigmentation to aggression and sexuality. The notice said the paper misrepresented the literature and ignored social and educational explanations. That year his former department at Western University in Canada said much of his research was racist.

sources.title: Retraction notice for Rushton & Templer (2012), Personality and Individual Differences (Elsevier), as reproduced in Retraction Watch, 29 June 2020
Department statement on Dr. Philippe Rushton (Department of Psychology, Western University, June 2020)

points.heading: Richard Lynn's 'national IQ' data led to a Royal Society retraction
points.text: In 2024 Proceedings of the Royal Society B retracted a 2010 paper because it relied on between-country IQ data published in 2004 by Tatu Vanhanen and the British psychologist Richard Lynn. Critics had shown that the data contained substantial inaccuracies and biases. In 2018 Ulster University withdrew Lynn's emeritus title after a student campaign.

sources.title: Retraction: 'Parasite prevalence and the worldwide distribution of cognitive ability' (2010), Proceedings of the Royal Society B 291, 2024 (The Royal Society)
Do some IQ data need a 'public health warning?' (Retraction Watch, 18 March 2024)
UU students call for removal of former professor's title (Irish News, 14 February 2018)

points.heading: Caribbean children were over-placed in 'ESN' schools
points.text: In the 1960s and 1970s, schools for the 'educationally subnormal' (ESN) took a disproportionate share of Caribbean children. The Inner London Education Authority noted in 1967 that 28% of children in its ESN schools were 'immigrant', and a 1973 Department of Education and Science letter found West Indian children four times over-represented.

sources.title: Sally Tomlinson, 'Disgraceful Labelling: Race, Special Education and Exclusion' (Excluded Lives project, Department of Education, University of Oxford, 14 July 2021)
A history of education campaigning (Black Cultural Archives, via Google Arts & Culture)

points.heading: A 1971 pamphlet exposed the labelling and mobilised parents
points.text: How the West Indian Child is Made Educationally Subnormal in the British School System (1971) argued that schools and teachers, not children, were the source of the problem, through low expectations and biased assessment. It recommended Black supplementary schools.

sources.title: A history of education campaigning (Black Cultural Archives, via Google Arts & Culture)
Sally Tomlinson, 'Disgraceful Labelling: Race, Special Education and Exclusion' (Excluded Lives project, Department of Education, University of Oxford, 14 July 2021)
West Indian Children in Our Schools (Rampton interim report), HMSO 1981, full text hosted by education-uk.org

points.heading: A government inquiry named low teacher expectations and prejudice
points.text: The government's Rampton inquiry reported in 1981 (West Indian Children in Our Schools). It found West Indian children as a group were underachieving and said teachers' low expectations could become a self-fulfilling prophecy. It recommended ethnic monitoring of special-needs assessments.

sources.title: West Indian Children in Our Schools (Rampton interim report), HMSO 1981, full text hosted by education-uk.org
Multi-cultural Education, catalogue description (BFI Replay, British Film Institute)

points.heading: Policing the Crisis showed how a 'mugging' panic was built
points.text: Policing the Crisis: Mugging, the State and Law and Order (1978), by Stuart Hall and colleagues at Birmingham's Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies, analysed the 1972–73 wave of press and police attention to 'mugging'. It traced how race, immigration and crime were linked in 1970s public debate.

sources.title: Kieran Connell, 'Policing the Crisis 35 Years On', Contemporary British History 29(2), 2015 (Queen's University Belfast research portal)
