Policing the Crisis: Mugging, the State and Law and Order, 2nd edition (Open Research Online, The Open University)

points.heading: 1950s Home Office reports repeated stereotypes of Caribbean workers
points.text: By December 1953 the Home Office had produced five internal reports on colonial migration that linked Black and Asian workers with supposed laziness, poor discipline and low intellect. A 1953 Ministry of Labour note listed employers' objections such as 'low output' and 'irresponsibility' without testing them.

sources.title: The historical roots of the Windrush scandal: independent research report (Home Office, published 26 September 2024)
Race relations in industry 1953, HO 344/105 (The National Archives)

points.heading: 1960s–70s immigration laws aimed to reduce migration of people who were not white
points.text: A history written for Home Office staff after the Windrush scandal concluded that major immigration laws in 1962, 1968 and 1971 were designed to reduce the proportion of people in the UK who did not have white skin. The Home Office published it only in September 2024, after a tribunal ordered its release.

sources.title: The historical roots of the Windrush scandal: independent research report (Home Office, published 26 September 2024)
Home Office internal 'roots of Windrush' report published after FoI battle (Civil Service World, 2024)

points.heading: Windrush review: 'institutional ignorance' about race and history
points.text: The independent Windrush Lessons Learned Review (2020) found that the Home Office had shown institutional ignorance and thoughtlessness about race and about the history of the Windrush generation. It recommended that staff learn about Britain's colonial history and the history of Black Britons.

sources.title: Home Office: Windrush Lessons Learned Review (Wendy Williams)
Statement on Windrush lessons learned review (UK Parliament, March 2020)

points.heading: Swann Report: stereotyped views affected West Indian pupils
points.text: The Swann Report, 'Education for All' (1985), and its 1981 interim report concluded that racism, intentional and unintentional, had an important bearing on the performance of West Indian children, partly through teachers' stereotyped or patronising views. When the report was published the Education Secretary, Sir Keith Joseph, told Parliament he did not accept that racism explained underachievement.
points.note: The committee concluded that racism had a direct and important bearing on West Indian pupils' performance (Swann Report, chapter 2). The Education Secretary said in the Commons on 14 March 1985 that he had seen 'precious little evidence of any racist prejudice' among teachers.

sources.title: Education for All: report of the Committee of Inquiry into the Education of Children from Ethnic Minority Groups (HMSO, 1985), Annex A para 9 and chapter 2
Ethnic Minority Children (Education), Hansard HC Deb 14 March 1985 (UK Parliament)

points.heading: False beliefs about biology linked to under-rating Black pain
points.text: A 2016 study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences found that half of a sample of white US medical students and residents endorsed at least one false belief about biological differences, such as that Black people have thicker skin. Those who held such beliefs rated a Black patient's pain lower and made less accurate treatment recommendations.

sources.title: Racial bias in pain assessment and treatment recommendations, and false beliefs about biological differences between blacks and whites, PNAS 2016;113(16):4296–301 (PubMed)
University of Virginia news release on the study (University of Virginia, 2016)

points.heading: Black women's pain dismissed in UK maternity care
points.text: A 2022 inquiry by the charity Birthrights heard that health professionals described Black women and babies as having 'thick, tough skin', and that women's pain was often dismissed. A 2023 House of Commons committee report on Black maternal health recorded that staff sometimes repeated stereotypes about Black women's pain.

sources.title: Systemic racism, not broken bodies: executive summary (Birthrights, May 2022)
Black maternal health – Third Report of Session 2022–23, Women and Equalities Committee (18 April 2023)

points.heading: Lung tests carried a 'race correction' rooted in slavery-era claims
points.text: Lung-function tests long applied lower 'normal' values for Black patients. Historians trace this to Thomas Jefferson's speculation about the lungs of enslaved people and to Samuel Cartwright, a pro-slavery physician who used a spirometer to claim a 20 per cent 'deficiency'. In 2023 the American Thoracic Society recommended race-neutral equations, and in 2025 the UK's Association for Respiratory Technology and Physiology backed the race-neutral GLI Global equations.

sources.title: Race and Ethnicity in Pulmonary Function Test Interpretation: An Official American Thoracic Society Statement, Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2023;207(8):978–995
Race, ethnicity and lung function: A brief history, Canadian Journal of Respiratory Therapy 2015;51(4):99–101
ARTP race neutral position statement (Respiratory Futures, August 2025)

points.heading: Child Q: 'adultification' named as a likely factor
points.text: A 2022 safeguarding practice review into the strip-search of a Black 15-year-old girl at a Hackney school found that racism was likely an influencing factor and named 'adultification', where Black children are treated as older and less in need of protection than their white peers.

sources.title: Child Q: powerful set of actions undertaken by Council (Hackney Council, 2022)
Local Child Safeguarding Practice Review: comment by BASW (British Association of Social Workers, 21 March 2022)

points.heading: Black children far more likely to be strip-searched by police
points.text: After Child Q, the Children's Commissioner for England analysed police strip-searches of children. Black children were about six times more likely to be strip-searched than their share of the population suggested between 2018 and 2022, and about four times more likely in 2022–23.

sources.title: Child strip searched every 14 hours by police in England and Wales (Children's Commissioner for England, 19 August 2024)
Black children six times likelier to be strip-searched: UK report (Al Jazeera, 27 March 2023)

points.heading: A quarter or more of Britons admit racial prejudice
points.text: The British Social Attitudes survey has asked people since the 1980s whether they are prejudiced against people of other races. The share saying 'very' or 'a little' prejudiced was 38% in 1987, 30% in 2013 and 26% in 2017.

sources.title: Would you describe yourself as very or a little prejudiced? (LSE Equity, Diversity and Inclusion blog, June 2014)
NatCen report: Racial Prejudice in Britain Today (Equally Ours, summarising NatCen, September 2017)
Racial prejudice in Britain today (Runnymede Trust, 2017)

points.heading: Survey of 14,000 people finds widespread racism against Black groups
points.text: The Evidence for Equality National Survey (2023), run by university researchers, found that almost one in six minority ethnic respondents had suffered a racially motivated physical assault. Around half of Black Caribbean and other Black respondents reported racial discrimination in education, and over a third reported discrimination by the police.

sources.title: More than a third of people from minority groups in the UK have experienced racist assaults, survey finds (King's College London, April 2023)
Over a third of people from minority groups have experienced racist assaults, survey finds (University of Manchester, April 2023)

points.heading: Du Bois in London, 1900: 'the problem of the colour line'
points.text: At the 1900 Pan-African Conference in London, W.E.B. Du Bois's address 'To the Nations of the World' declared that the problem of the twentieth century is the problem of the colour line. He went on to organise four Pan-African Congresses between 1919 and 1927.

sources.title: 'To the Nations of the World (1900)', in A. Getachew and J. Pitts (eds), W. E. B. Du Bois: International Thought (Cambridge University Press, 2022)
W.E.B. Du Bois (Encyclopaedia Britannica)

points.heading: Black Reconstruction overturned a racist school of history
points.text: In Black Reconstruction (1935), Du Bois challenged the dominant 'Dunning School', which held that Black Americans had been unfit for the rights granted after the US Civil War. His chapter on 'the propaganda of history' criticised how textbooks portrayed the period.

sources.title: Eric Gardner, 'Black Reconstructions: Introduction', African American Literature in Transition, 1865–1880 (Cambridge University Press), excerpt
The Dunning School: The Biased Study of Reconstruction that Shaped 'Gone With the Wind' (Atlanta History Center)

points.heading: Cheikh Anta Diop placed Africa at the origin of civilisations
points.text: In Nations nègres et culture (1954) and later work, the Senegalese scholar Cheikh Anta Diop argued that Africa was the source of many forms of human civilisation, including that of ancient Egypt. He proposed the 1974 UNESCO symposium in Cairo on the peopling of ancient Egypt.
points.note: Diop's thesis that ancient Egyptian civilisation was Black African remains contested among Egyptologists and historians; Encyclopaedia Universalis notes 'Des jugements contradictoires, souvent passionnels, ont été portés sur ses travaux' (contradictory, often passionate judgements). His challenge to the idea that Africa had no history is widely recognised.

sources.title: Jean Devisse, 'Diop Cheikh Anta (1923–1986)' (Encyclopaedia Universalis)
Cheikh Anta Diop's short biography (Musée des Civilisations noires, Dakar)

points.heading: Psychologists found no direct evidence for a genetic race gap
points.text: After a decade of controversy, the American Psychological Association set up a task force whose 1996 report, 'Intelligence: Knowns and Unknowns', reviewed group differences in test scores. It found no direct evidence for a genetic explanation of the Black–White average score gap.

sources.title: Neisser et al., 'Intelligence: Knowns and Unknowns', American Psychologist 51(2), 1996 (University of North Florida research portal record)
Ulric Neisser, 'Never a Dull Moment', American Psychologist, January 1997 (reply to commentaries on the task force report)

points.heading: Gould's Mismeasure of Man and the skull dispute
points.text: In The Mismeasure of Man (1981), Stephen Jay Gould argued that racial science, from 19th-century skull measurement to IQ testing, was shaped by its authors' prejudices. His case against Samuel Morton's skull data has been re-examined since 2011.
points.note: Lewis et al. (PLOS Biology, 2011) re-measured Morton's skulls and concluded that Morton did not manipulate his data and that Gould's own analysis was biased. Weisberg (2014) and Kaplan, Pigliucci and Banta (2015) argue that most of Gould's criticisms stand and that Morton's analysis was inappropriate and misleading, though Kaplan et al. also say Gould was wrong to think a better analysis was available.

sources.title: J. E. Lewis et al., 'The Mismeasure of Science: Stephen Jay Gould versus Samuel George Morton on Skulls and Bias', PLOS Biology, 2011
Michael Weisberg, 'Remeasuring man', Evolution and Development (2014) (ANU research portal abstract)
Kaplan and Pigliucci, 'Gould on Morton, Redux', Studies in History and Philosophy of Biological and Biomedical Sciences 52 (2015) (PhilArchive abstract)

points.heading: UCL inquiry into eugenics and removal of Galton and Pearson names
points.text: University College London commissioned an independent inquiry into its history of eugenics, which reported in February 2020. In June 2020 UCL removed the names of Francis Galton, who coined the word 'eugenics', and Karl Pearson, the first holder of the eugenics chair Galton funded, from a lecture theatre and a building. In January 2021 UCL issued a formal public apology. UCL formally apologised for its history and legacy of eugenics on 7 January 2021.

sources.title: UCL denames buildings named after eugenicists (UCL News, 19 June 2020)
UCL to begin process of renaming buildings named after eugenicists (Times Higher Education)
UCL makes formal public apology for its history and legacy of eugenics (UCL News, 7 January 2021)
Bricks + Mortals: a history of eugenics told through buildings (UCL Culture)
UCL makes formal apology for its history and legacy of eugenics (The Boar, January 2021)

points.heading: The Galton Institute renames itself the Adelphi Genetics Forum
points.text: The learned society founded as the Eugenics Education Society, later the Galton Institute, changed its name to the Adelphi Genetics Forum in 2021. Its trustees said Galton's name had become a barrier because of his racism and eugenics, and the society now explicitly rejects those ideas.

sources.title: Adelphi Genetics Forum: an evolving organisation (The Biologist, Royal Society of Biology)
Why the Galton Institute is now called the Adelphi Genetics Forum (Adelphi Genetics Forum)

points.heading: Glasgow: first UK university to count its gains from slavery
points.text: In 2018 the University of Glasgow published 'Slavery, Abolition and the University of Glasgow', which estimated that gifts and bequests linked to slavery were worth up to almost £200 million in today's money. It began a programme of 'reparative justice', including a partnership with the University of the West Indies and a centre for the study of slavery.

sources.title: Slavery in Britain: making reparation (University of Glasgow)
Universities urged to follow Glasgow's lead on slave trade past (Times Higher Education, 2018)

points.heading: Cambridge finds its scholars helped justify racism and slavery
points.text: The University of Cambridge's Advisory Group on Legacies of Enslavement reported in September 2022. Besides money from slavery, it found that Cambridge writers had produced ideas used to justify enslavement, including an early claim that differences between white and Black people were biological, and that 20th-century Cambridge thought connected to rigid ideas of race within eugenics.

sources.title: Advisory Group on Legacies of Enslavement: Final Report, section 4.2.6 (University of Cambridge, 2022)
Cambridge University received 'significant benefits' from slavery, inquiry finds (ITV News, 22 September 2022)

points.heading: UNESCO 1950: race 'less a biological fact than a social myth'
points.text: In July 1950 UNESCO published 'The Race Question', drafted mainly by the anthropologist Ashley Montagu with a panel of experts. It said that all humans belong to one species and put group differences in measured intelligence down mainly to environment. A revised 1951 statement by geneticists and physical anthropologists partly stepped back, while still rejecting the use of mental traits to classify races.
points.note: The 1950 text was criticised at the time for its statements on intelligence and its sociological approach; UNESCO's 1951 revision accepted a division of humanity into major groups on physical traits only (Duedahl; Alberta Eugenics Archive).

sources.title: From Racial Strangers to Ethnic Minorities: on the socio-political impact of UNESCO, 1945–60 (Aalborg University repository)
UNESCO 'The Race Question', 18 July 1950 (Eugenics Archives, Canada)
M. C. Maio and R. V. Santos, 'Antiracism and the uses of science in the post-World War II: An analysis of UNESCO's first statements on race (1950 and 1951)', Vibrant 12(2), 2015

points.heading: US human genetics society apologises for its eugenic past
points.text: In January 2023 the American Society of Human Genetics apologised for the part some of its founders, past presidents and other leaders played in eugenics, and for staying silent when genetics was used to support racism. Its report found that nine early leaders held posts in the American Eugenics Society.

sources.title: ASHG documents and apologizes for past harms of human genetics research (American Society of Human Genetics, 24 January 2023)
Genetics society issues apology for ties to eugenics and racism (Smithsonian Magazine, 2023)

points.heading: Pitt Rivers Museum removes human remains that fed racist thinking
points.text: Over the summer of 2020, Oxford's Pitt Rivers Museum removed 120 human remains, including shrunken heads, from open display after a three-year ethical review. The museum said audience research showed visitors read the displays as showing other cultures as 'savage' or 'primitive'.

sources.title: Critical Changes (Pitt Rivers Museum, University of Oxford)
Pitt Rivers Museum removes shrunken heads from display after ethical review (Museums Association, 18 September 2020)

points.heading: Wellcome Collection closes its 'Medicine Man' gallery
points.text: In November 2022 the Wellcome Collection in London closed its long-running 'Medicine Man' display. It said the gallery still presented a version of medical history based on racist, sexist and ableist theories, in which Black people, Indigenous peoples and disabled people were exoticised and exploited.

sources.title: Wellcome Collection speaks out on Medicine Man closure (Museums Association, November 2022)
London museum Wellcome Collection closes 'racist, sexist and ableist' exhibit (Euronews, 28 November 2022)

points.heading: Du Bois proposes an 'Encyclopaedia Africana' (1909)
points.text: The idea of a reference work on the history and culture of people of African descent goes back to W.E.B. Du Bois, who first announced it in a 1909 letter to the Sierra Leone-based Pan-Africanist Edward Wilmot Blyden. Later efforts, including an 'Encyclopedia of the Negro' begun in 1931, were never completed for lack of funding.
points.note: Date of the first idea: the article title and the Emory and BlackPast texts give 1909; the indexed abstract of the same author's 2000 journal article says 1901. 1909 is the date supported by two independent sources; 1901 may be an abstract error but is not ruled out.

sources.title: Emory Report, October 1999 (Emory University)

points.heading: Ghana launches the Encyclopaedia Africana (1962)
points.text: At the invitation of Kwame Nkrumah, Du Bois moved to Ghana and in March 1962 set up an Encyclopaedia Africana secretariat under the Ghana Academy of Sciences. In December 1962 he told a conference at the University of Ghana that the work should be based in Africa and compiled by Africans.

sources.title: L.H. Ofosu-Appiah, 'The Encyclopaedia Africana', Journal of Modern African Studies 5:4 (1967) (Cambridge University Press)
W.E.B. Du Bois Address at the Conference on the Encyclopaedia Africana, 1962 - collection record (University of Virginia Library)
'Let's tell our story through Encyclopaedia Africana' (Graphic Online, 12 June 2026)

points.heading: Three volumes published, then a long pause
points.text: The project's published output is a Dictionary of African Biography in three volumes: Ethiopia–Ghana (1977), Sierra Leone–Zaire (1979) and South Africa–Botswana–Lesotho–Swaziland (1995). It was planned as a 20-volume series. In 2016 the African Union said progress had slowed for decades and sought to revive it under Agenda 2063.

points.heading: Volume IV under way (2026)
points.text: In June 2026 scholars from Africa and the diaspora met at Peduase, Ghana, for a three-day workshop to develop the conceptual framework, thematic structure, editorial standards and contributor database for Encyclopaedia Africana Volume IV. The African Union had earlier made the project one of its Agenda 2063 objectives.
points.note: The June 2026 workshop itself is reported only by Graphic Online - not confirmed by a second source cited. The African Union source confirms the revival context, not the 2026 workshop.

sources.title: 'Let's tell our story through Encyclopaedia Africana' (Graphic Online, 12 June 2026)

points.text: In January 1999 Microsoft launched Encarta Africana, a multimedia encyclopedia of African and African-descended history edited by Henry Louis Gates Jr and Kwame Anthony Appiah, with over 3,000 articles. A print version, Africana, followed in 1999; Oxford University Press published an expanded second edition in 2005 with more than 4,000 articles.
points.note: Publishers Weekly gives conflicting page counts (2,144 and 1,200) for the 1999 print edition, so no page count is stated.

points.text: Oxford University Press published the six-volume Dictionary of African Biography in November 2011, with about 2,100 entries of 750–2,000 words, each reviewed by an editorial board. Its editors aimed to grow it to 10,000 biographies online, through the subscription Oxford African American Studies Center.
points.note: Sources differ on the exact count (nearly 2,100 vs 2,129) and year (November 2011 vs 2012 imprint); the page uses 'about 2,100' and 2011. The two Harvard pages count as one publisher; The Root is the independent second source.

points.heading: Dictionary of Caribbean and Afro-Latin American Biography (2016)
points.text: In 2016 Oxford University Press published a companion Dictionary of Caribbean and Afro-Latin American Biography, covering historically significant people across the whole Caribbean and Afro-descended populations throughout Latin America.

sources.title: Dictionary of Caribbean and Afro-Latin American Biography (Hutchins Center, Harvard University)
Dictionary of Caribbean and Afro-Latin American biography - catalogue record (WorldCat/OCLC)

points.heading: UNESCO General History of Africa
points.text: UNESCO began the General History of Africa in 1964 with newly independent African states. Eight volumes appeared up to 1993. In October 2025 UNESCO announced the completion of three further volumes (IX, X and XI), written with more than 200 experts.

points.heading: Oxford Companion to Black British History (2007)
points.text: The main single-volume reference on Black British history is The Oxford Companion to Black British History, edited by David Dabydeen, John Gilmore and Cecily Jones and published by Oxford University Press in March 2007. It covers Black people in Britain from classical times to the present.

points.heading: Oxford DNB adds Black British lives
points.text: The Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, the national record of people who shaped British history, has published updates focused on people of Black and African descent, including an 'Early Black Lives' release marked with a University of Oxford seminar in October 2019.
points.note: Number of entries added and the date of the University College item are not stated in the sources opened. University College is a separate legal body from the University, but both are Oxford; OUP is the publisher of the ODNB itself.

points.heading: Open online references: BlackPast
points.text: BlackPast.org, created by University of Washington historian Quintard Taylor, is a free online reference on African American and global Black history; by 2016 it held about 4,000 encyclopedia entries. It is US-based and US-focused.
points.note: Founding date: a University of Washington library guide says founded in 2004; UW News (2016) says Taylor started it in 2007 with fewer than 100 entries. Both are University of Washington pages. Year left open.

points.heading: What is missing: a current, open, UK-focused reference
points.text: Hub reading: the major references are either US-centred (BlackPast, Africana), continental (Encyclopaedia Africana, UNESCO), behind subscriptions (the Dictionary of African Biography online sits in a restricted Oxford database), or now nearly 20 years old (the 2007 Oxford Companion). There is no current, openly licensed reference focused on African, Caribbean and Black British history in the UK.
points.note: This is the hub's own assessment, not a finding of any source. The claim that no such reference exists is an absence claim: it reflects the sources searched, not an exhaustive survey.

points.heading: England: the Curriculum and Assessment Review (Nov 2025)
points.text: The independent Curriculum and Assessment Review's final report (November 2025) recommended that curriculum reforms reflect the diversity of society and the contributions that shaped it. It reported that young people said not seeing themselves in the curriculum could be disempowering.

sources.title: Curriculum and Assessment Review final report (deposited paper DEP2025-0723)
The school curriculum in England, Research Briefing CBP06798 (House of Commons Library, 21 Nov 2025)

points.heading: England: the government's response and timetable
points.text: The government accepted the direction of the review. It will publish a revised national curriculum in 2027 for first teaching in 2028, and update GCSEs for first teaching from 2029. For history it committed that teachers can 'reflect the innate diversity of British history, including British Black and Asian history'.
points.note: The government response quote was returned by the fetcher in two parts across a line break; it is reproduced here as one sentence.

sources.title: GOV.UK: Government response to the Curriculum and Assessment Review
The school curriculum in England, Research Briefing CBP06798 (House of Commons Library, 21 Nov 2025)
What has the government committed to for history? (Historical Association)

points.heading: Historical Association: welcome, with a warning on time
points.text: The Historical Association, the subject association for history, supported the recommendation for a curriculum reflecting British Black and Asian history, and welcomed that it reaches beyond Key Stage 3. It warned that wider changes and more testing could leave less time for history.
points.note: The HA's view is its own statement; the government response confirms the commitment it responds to.

sources.title: Curriculum and Assessment Review Final Report - response (Historical Association, 6 Nov 2025)
GOV.UK: Government response to the Curriculum and Assessment Review

points.heading: The Black Curriculum: 'sidesteps the most pressing issues'
points.text: The Black Curriculum, a social enterprise campaigning for Black British history in schools, called the review cautious and said it contained no explicit mention of race, migration or colonialism. It welcomed the emphasis on local stories but said teachers need protected time and training to teach contested histories.
points.note: Views differ: the Historical Association welcomed the diversity recommendation; The Black Curriculum judged the review too cautious. TBC's statement that the review never names race or colonialism was not independently checked against the full report (the history annex was not extractable); the Commons Library briefing likewise mentions diversity but not Black or Asian history.

sources.title: The Black Curriculum: response to the Curriculum and Assessment Review
The school curriculum in England, Research Briefing CBP06798 (House of Commons Library, 21 Nov 2025)

points.heading: England before the review: 'flexibility' (2020–21)
points.text: In July 2020 the then Schools Minister, Nick Gibb, said the flexibility of the history curriculum meant Black British history could already be included. The government gave the same answer to a 2020 e-petition asking for a more inclusive curriculum, and did not change the statutory curriculum.

sources.title: House of Commons Library Debate Pack CDP 2021/0102, Black history and cultural diversity of the curriculum (24 June 2021)
E-petition 323961 and Government response, 30 Jul 2020 (UK Parliament Petitions)

points.heading: Wales: mandatory since 2022
points.text: Wales became the first UK nation to make teaching Black, Asian and Minority Ethnic histories and experiences mandatory, through the Curriculum for Wales rolled out from September 2022. Schools design their own curriculum within that requirement.

sources.title: Learning Black, Asian and Minority Ethnic histories included in new Welsh curriculum (Welsh Government, 1 Oct 2021)
Written Question WQ95452 and answer, 21 Jan 2025 (Senedd Cymru)

points.heading: Scotland: open curriculum, new slavery lessons (Oct 2025)
points.text: Scotland has an open curriculum, so teachers choose topics. Research found fewer than two-thirds of secondary schools taught even one lesson on the transatlantic slave trade. In October 2025 the universities of Stirling, Edinburgh and Glasgow launched Teaching Slavery in Scotland lesson plans, funded by the Scottish Government and mapped to BGE, National 5 and Higher.

sources.title: Lesson plans launched to teach slavery in Scottish schools (University of Stirling, 24 Oct 2025)
New resources for teaching slavery (Royal Historical Society blog, 17 Feb 2026)

points.heading: Northern Ireland: no named Black history requirement
points.text: Northern Ireland's statutory minimum content for history requires study of Irish, British, European and global contexts and the ability to challenge stereotypical, biased or distorted viewpoints. No source opened showed a specific statutory requirement to teach Black history; slavery appears only in non-statutory guidance examples.
points.note: Absence of a requirement is stated as 'not found in the sources cited', not as proven. CCEA notes bold type marks statutory items and that formatting was lost in extraction.

points.heading: Royal Historical Society (2018): history's diversity gap
points.text: The Royal Historical Society's 2018 report on race, ethnicity and equality found that Black historians made up less than 1% of UK university history staff, and that only 11% of undergraduate history students were from ethnic minority backgrounds (2.4% Black, 3.8% Asian).

sources.title: 10 key findings from the RHS Race, Ethnicity & Equality report (Institute of Historical Research blog, Oct 2018)

points.heading: Only about 4% of GCSE history pupils took 'Migration to Britain'
points.text: A 2019 Runnymede Trust and University of Liverpool report found that about 4% of GCSE History pupils took the AQA or OCR migration units launched in 2016 (2018 entries). It also found 78% of teachers surveyed wanted training on teaching migration and 71% on empire.
points.note: The figure is from 2018 Ofqual entries; no more recent uptake figure was found. The Runnymede report (with a university partner) is the authoritative source; Al Jazeera and Schools Week report it independently.

points.heading: Schools are changing, but often only by a lesson or two
points.text: A 2021 Historical Association survey of history teachers in England found most schools had made substantial curriculum changes to address diversity, with switching to a GCSE migration unit the most commonly mentioned change. But only 23% devoted a series of lessons to Black or Asian British history; 57% gave it one or two lessons.
points.note: The two sources describe the same Historical Association survey (316 responses). The HA report gives 83% for Key Stage 3 changes; the Oxford/Reading summary gives 87% - the scope differs, so the page says 'most schools'. The 23% and 57% figures come from the HA report only.

sources.title: HA Survey of History in Schools in England 2021 (Historical Association)

points.heading: GCSE options that cover Black British history
points.text: All three main English exam boards now offer an optional migration unit: OCR's 'Migrants to Britain, c.1250 to present', AQA's 'Britain: Migration, empires and the people, c790 to the present day' (including Windrush and Caribbean migrants), and Pearson Edexcel's 'Migrants in Britain, c800–present and Notting Hill, c1948–c1970', first assessed in June 2022.
points.note: Impact sentence source: Pearson page - 'Teaching guide produced in partnership with The Black Curriculum on the new Notting Hill historic environment'. In 2019 Runnymede noted Pearson had then made no such offer; its unit came later. All are optional, not compulsory.

points.heading: Proposal: past, present and future themes
points.text: Hub proposal: a UK framework could run from African civilisations and knowledge, through enslavement, abolition and empire, early Black Britons, Windrush and post-war migration, to present-day representation, enterprise, health and young people, and future-facing themes such as reparative history and data. Each theme links to hub pages that already hold verified points. Existing GCSE content already covers parts of this arc.
points.note: Hub proposal, not a finding of any source. Suggested links: African civilisations; Knowledge transfer; What was lost; Who built the stereotypes; Peoples of our places; Settlers, borders, births; Slavery and the gremio; Representation; Enterprise; Youth; Blackness and identity.

points.heading: Proposal: cross-cutting skills
points.text: Hub proposal: every theme should build the same skills - reading and questioning sources, using archives, oral history, local history and comparing the four UK nations. The government has already committed to strengthen source criticism in history, and both curriculum campaigners and the review stress local case studies.
points.note: Hub proposal. Four-nations comparison links to this page's curriculum section; archives links to the hub's archives page.

points.heading: Proposal: seed an open encyclopaedia from verified hub content
points.text: Hub proposal: the hub's sourced, triangulated points could seed an openly licensed UK reference, using the governance that existing works rely on - named editors, editorial standards, signed entries with bibliographies and board review. Encyclopaedia Africana Volume IV and the Dictionary of African Biography show the model.
points.note: Hub proposal; the sources describe how other reference works are governed, not this proposal.

sources.title: Dictionary of African Biography (Hutchins Center, Harvard University)

points.heading: Proposal: partners and funders
points.text: Hub proposal: possible partners include Black Cultural Archives (founded 1981, the national heritage centre for African and Caribbean histories in Britain), the George Padmore Institute (an archive and research centre set up in 1991), the Institute of Historical Research, the Historical Association, The Black Curriculum and the University of the West Indies. Possible funders include the National Lottery Heritage Fund, whose Heritage 2033 programme offers grants from £10,000 to £10 million, and the AHRC, which has co-funded work on legacies of race.
points.note: Hub proposal; naming an organisation does not imply it has agreed to anything. The 1991 founding date of the George Padmore Institute comes from New Beacon Books only (the University of London page gives no date). Funding programmes change - check the NLHF and UKRI pages for current status before citing; an NLHF page showed the smaller grants band temporarily closed in Nov 2023 before Heritage 2033 opened. No sourced factual claims are made about the IHR, HA, The Black Curriculum or UWI beyond those elsewhere on this page.

points.heading: About 1 in 5 to 1 in 4 Latin Americans is of African descent
points.text: The World Bank estimates that around 133 million people in Latin America identify as Afro-descendant, most of them in Brazil. The UN regional commission ECLAC (CEPAL) gives a similar figure of 134 million, or 21% of the population. Estimates differ because countries ask different census questions and some do not ask at all.
points.note: World Bank says 'one in four'; CEPAL says 21%. Both are estimates built from national censuses that use different categories.

sources.title: World Bank: Eliminating Afro-descendant exclusion in Latin America is vital for development (2018)
CEPAL: Afrodescendientes y la matriz de la desigualdad social en América Latina

points.heading: Afro-descendants are more likely to live in chronic poverty
points.text: The World Bank found Afro-descendants are 2.5 times more likely to be chronically poor than white or mestizo people. In 6 countries they make up 38% of the population but about half of people in extreme poverty.
points.note: The 2.5 times figure rests on the World Bank alone; CEPAL supports the wider point that race is a structural axis of inequality.

sources.title: World Bank: Eliminating Afro-descendant exclusion in Latin America is vital for development (2018)
CEPAL: Afrodescendientes y la matriz de la desigualdad social en América Latina

points.heading: The UN has declared a second Decade for People of African Descent
points.text: The first International Decade for People of African Descent was proclaimed by UN General Assembly resolution 68/237 in 2013. In 2024 the Assembly proclaimed a second decade from 1 January 2025 to 31 December 2034, keeping the theme 'recognition, justice and development'.

sources.title: UN General Assembly resolution A/RES/79/193
UN: International Decade for People of African Descent

points.heading: A UN Permanent Forum now advises on people of African descent
points.text: The UN General Assembly set up the Permanent Forum on People of African Descent in August 2021 (resolution 75/314). It is a consultative body that also advises the Human Rights Council. Its first session met in Geneva on 5 to 8 December 2022.

sources.title: UN: Permanent Forum on People of African Descent
Quaker UN Office: first session of the Permanent Forum

points.heading: More than half of Brazilians identify as Black or brown
points.text: In the 2022 census, 45.3% of Brazilians identified as pardo (brown, of mixed heritage) and 10.2% as preto (Black), about 20.7 million people. The Brazilian state and the Black movement usually count both groups together as negro (Black), making them a majority.
points.note: Figures are from the IBGE 2022 census; the IBGE news page could not be read directly, so these rest on two press reports of the IBGE release. Not every pardo person identifies as Afro-Brazilian.

sources.title: Jornal do Brasil: Censo 2022 – população parda supera a branca
O Povo (Agência Brasil report of IBGE results)

points.heading: 1.3 million quilombolas were counted for the first time
points.text: Quilombolas are people living in communities descended from settlements founded by people who escaped slavery (quilombos). The 2022 census counted 1,327,802 quilombolas for the first time, 0.65% of the population; nearly a third live in Bahia.
points.note: Census count rests on IBGE as reported by CNN Brasil; IBGE's own page could not be read. The ISA source supports the definition, not the count.

sources.title: CNN Brasil: Brasil tem mais de 1,3 milhão de quilombolas (IBGE)
Instituto Socioambiental teaching kit on quilombos (quoting Decree 4.887/2003)

points.heading: Quilombos were promised land in 1988, but few hold titles
points.text: Article 68 of the transitional provisions of Brazil's 1988 Constitution recognises quilombo communities' permanent ownership of their land and requires the state to issue titles. In practice only 12.6% of quilombolas live in officially delimited territories, and 4.3% in fully titled ones.

sources.title: Instituto Socioambiental teaching kit on quilombos (quoting Decree 4.887/2003)
CNN Brasil: Brasil tem mais de 1,3 milhão de quilombolas (IBGE)

points.heading: Zumbi dos Palmares Day became a national holiday in 2024
points.text: Zumbi led Palmares, the largest quilombo, and was killed when Portuguese forces destroyed it on 20 November 1695. Law 14.759 of December 2023 made 20 November, the National Day of Zumbi and Black Consciousness, a national holiday, first observed nationwide in 2024.

sources.title: Câmara dos Deputados: Lei nº 14.759, de 21 de dezembro de 2023

points.heading: Capoeira and samba de roda are world heritage
points.text: UNESCO lists 2 Afro-Brazilian traditions as intangible cultural heritage of humanity. Samba de roda of the Recôncavo of Bahia grew from the dances of enslaved Africans and influenced urban samba in Rio (proclaimed 2005, inscribed 2008). The capoeira circle, both fight and dance, was inscribed in 2014.

points.heading: Afro-Brazilian history must be taught in every school
points.text: Since Law 10.639 of 2003, all primary and secondary schools in Brazil, public and private, must teach Afro-Brazilian history and culture. The same law puts 20 November in the school calendar as Black Consciousness Day.

sources.title: Lei nº 10.639, de 9 de janeiro de 2003 (text published by Santos city council)

points.heading: Black Brazilians still earn less and are more likely to be poor
points.text: IBGE data show white workers earned 61.4% more per hour than Black or brown workers in 2022. In 2021 the poverty rate was 34.5% for Black people against 18.6% for white people, and Black and brown people held only 29.5% of management jobs.
points.note: Both sources are IBGE, so this rests on one (authoritative) publisher. The same IBGE report gives a 2020 homicide rate of 34.1 per 100,000 for pardo people against 11.5 for white people.

points.heading: Colombia's census count of Black people is disputed
points.text: Colombia's 2018 census recorded 2,982,224 Black, Afro-Colombian, Raizal and Palenquero people (6.8%), well below 2005. Statistics office DANE admitted an omission and adopted an official figure of 4,671,160 (9.34%) from a survey.
points.note: Census count 2,982,224 (6.8%) versus DANE's adjusted official figure 4,671,160 (9.34%).

points.heading: Law 70 of 1993 gave Black communities collective land
points.text: Law 70 recognises Black communities' right to collective ownership of the lands they have occupied, mainly in the Pacific basin. Over 168 community councils have received collective titles totalling almost 6 million hectares, from the Panama border to Ecuador.

sources.title: Ley 70 de 1993 (text published by Agencia Nacional de Minería)
Universidad de los Andes, School of Government: Nota de política 26

points.heading: San Basilio de Palenque kept a unique African-rooted language
points.text: Palenqueros are people of San Basilio de Palenque, founded by people who escaped slavery in the 17th century. Their language is the only creole in Latin America with Spanish vocabulary and Bantu grammar. UNESCO proclaimed the cultural space in 2005.

sources.title: UNESCO: Cultural space of Palenque de San Basilio
Colombian Ministry of Foreign Affairs: intangible heritage

points.heading: The Raizal are a distinct Afro-Caribbean people of San Andrés
points.text: The Raizal are the native people of the San Andrés, Providencia and Santa Catalina islands. They speak an English-based Creole and are mainly Protestant. Colombia's Constitutional Court recognises them as a clearly defined ethnic group.

points.heading: Pacific marimba music links Afro-Colombians and Afro-Ecuadorians
points.text: Marimba music, chants and dances of people of African descent in Colombia's South Pacific and Ecuador's Esmeraldas province are on UNESCO's list, jointly since 2015. The whole community is seen as the bearer of the tradition.
points.note: First inscribed for Colombia alone in 2010, extended to Ecuador in 2015.

points.heading: Ecuador's Afro-Ecuadorian count fell sharply in 2022
points.text: Afro-Ecuadorians live mainly in Esmeraldas, Guayas and the Andean Chota Valley. The 2022 census counted 814,495 (4.8%), down from 1,041,559 (7.2%) in 2010. Ecuador's 2008 Constitution recognises their collective rights.

points.heading: The Chota Valley's bomba is national heritage
points.text: In the Chota Valley, between Imbabura and Carchi, people descended from Africans enslaved in mines and plantations from the 17th century created the bomba, a drum and music. Ecuador's heritage institute and culture ministry certified it as national intangible heritage in 2020.
points.note: Two press sources reporting a government (INPC and Ministry of Culture) decision; no official page was read.

points.text: In Peru's 2017 census, about 828,000 people aged 12 and over (3.6%) identified as Afro-Peruvian. Since 2006 Law 28761 has marked 4 June as Afro-Peruvian Culture Day, the birthday of poet and musician Nicomedes Santa Cruz (born 1925).

points.heading: Venezuela counted Afro-Venezuelans for the first time in 2011
points.text: In the 2011 census, the first to let people self-identify this way, 2.9% of Venezuelans identified as Black (negra/negro) and 0.7% as Afro-descendant. Afro-Venezuelan drumming, dance and spirituality remain central to the culture.

points.heading: Garifuna language, dance and music are world heritage
points.text: The Garifuna descend from African and Indigenous Caribbean people on Saint Vincent, deported by the British from 1797. They now live mainly in Honduras, Guatemala, Nicaragua and Belize and speak an Arawakan language. UNESCO proclaimed their language, dance and music in 2001.

points.heading: Honduras has not yet returned Garifuna land as the court ordered
points.text: In October 2015 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights ruled that Honduras violated the collective property rights of the Garifuna communities of Triunfo de la Cruz and Punta Piedra and ordered land restored within 2 years. Court monitoring in 2019 and 2021 found no substantial progress.

points.heading: Limón is the heart of Afro-Costa Rican life
points.text: In Costa Rica's 2011 census 7.75% identified as Afro-descendant, up from 1.9% in 2000. Limón province on the Caribbean coast has the highest share at 15.75%, and many people there speak Limonese Creole.

points.heading: Mexico recognised Afro-Mexicans in 2019 and counted them in 2020
points.text: A 2019 amendment to Article 2 of Mexico's Constitution recognised Afro-Mexican peoples and communities as part of the nation's pluricultural make-up. The 2020 census counted 2,576,213 Afro-Mexicans, about 2% of the population, many on the Costa Chica of Guerrero and Oaxaca.

points.heading: Argentina's Afro-descendant count nearly doubled
points.text: Argentina's 2022 census counted 302,936 people who identified as Afro-descendant or of African ancestry, 0.7% of the population, up from 0.4% in 2010. The University of Buenos Aires notes these groups are often invisible in official statistics.

points.heading: Candombe drumming is Uruguay's Afro-descendant heritage
points.text: Candombe's drum calls belong to the Sur, Palermo and Cordón districts of Montevideo, home to people of African descent, and are passed down in families. Uruguay made 3 December the national day of candombe, Afro-Uruguayan culture and racial equity in 2006, and UNESCO inscribed candombe in 2009.

points.heading: France does not collect ethnic statistics
points.text: France's statistics office says ethnic-based statistics are strictly controlled in law: a Constitutional Council decision of 15 November 2007 forbade processing data revealing racial or ethnic origin. Surveys can record country of birth and parents' country of birth, so there is no official count of Black people in France.
points.note: Any figure for France's Black population is an estimate, not an official statistic. Sabbagh notes the 2007 ruling struck the provision on procedural grounds; the Representative Council of Black Associations (CRAN) has argued for collecting such data.

points.heading: The 2001 Taubira law: slavery a crime against humanity
points.text: The law of 21 May 2001, named after Christiane Taubira, deputy for French Guiana, recognises the transatlantic slave trade and slavery as a crime against humanity. The Foundation for the Remembrance of Slavery says it made France the first country to do so.

sources.title: Fondation pour la mémoire de l'esclavage – Kit mairies 2022
Public Sénat – 20 ans après la loi Taubira

points.heading: 10 May remembrance and local abolition days overseas
points.text: 10 May is the national day for the memories of the slave trade, slavery and their abolition, set in 2006 to mark the Senate's vote on the Taubira law. Each overseas territory also marks its own abolition day: Mayotte 27 April, Martinique 22 May, Guadeloupe 27 May, French Guiana 10 June and Réunion 20 December.
points.note: A separate national date, 23 May, commemorates the victims of slavery; Public Sénat reports the choice of dates is still debated.

sources.title: Fondation pour la mémoire de l'esclavage – Kit mairies 2022
Public Sénat – 20 ans après la loi Taubira

points.heading: Négritude: a movement born of Caribbean and African writers
points.text: In 1930s Paris, Aimé Césaire of Martinique, Léon-Gontran Damas of French Guiana and Léopold Sédar Senghor of Senegal shaped Négritude, a literary and political movement that reassessed African culture and challenged colonial values.
