points.heading: The Dutch government apologised for slavery in 2022
points.text: On 19 December 2022 Prime Minister Mark Rutte apologised on behalf of the Dutch government for the state's past actions, speaking at the National Archives. He said that by 1814 more than 600,000 enslaved African people had been shipped to the Americas.

sources.title: Government of the Netherlands – Speech by Prime Minister Mark Rutte
Al Jazeera – Netherlands apologises for Dutch government's role in slavery

points.heading: The King's own apology on Keti Koti 2023
points.text: On 1 July 2023, at the National Slavery Monument in Amsterdam's Oosterpark, King Willem-Alexander made his own apology and asked forgiveness for the failure to act against 'this crime against humanity'.

sources.title: Royal House of the Netherlands – Speech by King Willem-Alexander
Open Research Amsterdam – King Willem-Alexander apologizes

points.heading: Keti Koti: 'broken chains', 1 July
points.text: Keti Koti means 'broken chains' in Sranantongo. It marks 1 July 1863, when slavery was formally abolished in Suriname and the Dutch Antilles; enslaved people in Suriname were only fully freed in 1873 after a compulsory 10-year transition. It is a national holiday in Suriname and is marked across Dutch cities, with a national ceremony in Oosterpark.
points.note: The government source confirms the significance of 1 July; the meaning of the name and the 1873 date come from the two non-government sources. Campaigners have sought to make 1 July a public holiday in the Netherlands.

sources.title: DutchNews – Keti Koti: what you need to know
Leiden International Centre – Celebrating Keti Koti
Government of the Netherlands – Speech by Prime Minister Mark Rutte

points.heading: Surinamese Dutch: a community shaped by 50 years since independence
points.text: Between 1975 and 2024, 256,000 people migrated from Suriname to the Netherlands. Today about 181,000 people born in Suriname live there, alongside 189,000 Dutch-born people with at least one Surinamese-born parent.
points.note: Rests on one source (CBS, authoritative). The combined total is our sum, not a CBS figure. Surinamese origin is not the same as Black: Suriname's population includes people of African, Indian, Javanese and other heritage.

sources.title: CBS (Statistics Netherlands) – Over 250,000 Surinamese have settled in the Netherlands

points.heading: Belgium's King expressed 'deepest regrets' to Congo in 2020
points.text: On the 60th anniversary of Congolese independence in June 2020, King Philippe wrote to President Félix Tshisekedi expressing his 'deepest regrets' for acts of violence and cruelty under colonial rule – a first for the Belgian monarchy. The letter did not name Leopold II and was not framed as an apology.
points.note: Neither source is in the authoritative category; we could not reach the Royal Palace's text. Treat wording as reported.

sources.title: NPR – Belgian King conveys 'deepest regrets'
Al Jazeera – Belgium's Congolese mark 60 years since DRC's independence

points.heading: Matonge: a Brussels quarter named after Kinshasa
points.text: Matonge in Ixelles takes its name from a lively district of Kinshasa. Congolese students and elites began gathering there in the early 1960s near the Free University of Brussels; it became a hub for shops, bars and music. In 2018 Ixelles named a square after Patrice Lumumba.

sources.title: University of Liège (Reflexions) – Matonge, a story of Congolese immigration
Al Jazeera – Belgium's Congolese mark 60 years since DRC's independence
Brussels Times – Hidden Belgium: Place Lumumba

points.heading: The AfricaMuseum reopened with a 'decolonised' aim
points.text: Belgium's AfricaMuseum at Tervuren reopened on 8 December 2018 after a five-year renovation, aiming to present 'a contemporary and decolonised vision of Africa' and working with artists from Africa or with African roots. Reviewers have said parts of the museum still fall short.
points.note: The museum's own aims are contested; the peer-reviewed review criticises the Rotunda and the lack of Black staff and visitors.

sources.title: AfricaMuseum – History and renovation
Science Museum Group Journal – 'Everything passes, except the past'

points.heading: Afro-German self-organisation since the 1980s
points.text: Black Germans founded the Initiative of Black People in Germany (ISD), one of the first Black German organisations, in the 1980s, with ADEFRA as a feminist sister organisation. The 1986 volume Farbe bekennen (Showing Our Colors), with the poet May Ayim (died 1996), was a landmark.

sources.title: University of Waterloo Centre for German Studies – interview with Tiffany Florvil
African American Intellectual History Society – Seeing May Ayim through Her Friends' Eyes

points.heading: Afrozensus: over a million people of African origin in Germany
points.text: The 2020 Afrozensus, a community-led survey, estimates there are over one million people of African origin in Germany, noting there was hardly any other statistical data on the group. Respondents were born in 144 countries, and large majorities reported discrimination in housing and dealings with authorities.
points.note: Germany collects no official data on Black people; the figure is a community-survey estimate. Rests on one source (the Afrozensus report itself, not in the authoritative category) — treat as indicative.

sources.title: Afrozensus 2020 report

points.heading: Africans made up about a tenth of 16th-century Lisbon
points.text: By 1551 Africans – mostly enslaved – made up about 10% of Lisbon's population. In 1593 the Mocambo neighbourhood was created, named after an Angolan word for a place of refuge, and Black confraternities such as Nossa Senhora do Rosário dos Homens Pretos supported the community.
points.note: Sixteenth-century counts are estimates.

sources.title: Project MANIFEST – Aurora Almada e Santos (NOVA University Lisbon)
Lapham's Quarterly – Africans in Renaissance Lisbon

points.heading: Portugal still has no official ethnic data
points.text: Portugal's statistics office left an ethnic-origin question out of the 2021 census, despite most of a government working group favouring it, and is testing a separate survey instead. UN experts who visited in 2021 noted the lack of data disaggregated by race, and that citizens of Cape Verde, Angola and other Portuguese-speaking African countries form most of the population of African descent.
points.note: The UN report also cites a 'Historical Road Map of an African Lisbon' and urges recognition of the contributions of people of African descent.

sources.title: UN Working Group of Experts on People of African Descent – Visit to Portugal (A/HRC/51/54/Add.1)
The Portugal News – Government backs omission of ethnic data in census

points.heading: Cécile Kyenge: Italy's first Black cabinet minister
points.text: Cécile Kyenge, who came to Italy from Congo in 1983, became Minister for Integration in April 2013 – Italy's first Black cabinet minister. She prepared a bill to give citizenship to children born in Italy, and faced sustained racist abuse from political opponents.
points.note: Named in her public role as a former minister. Children born in Italy to foreign parents still cannot apply for citizenship until 18 (Al Jazeera, 2025).

sources.title: NPR – Italy's first Black minister
TIME – Italy's First Black Minister Suffers Even More Racial Abuse

points.heading: Spain's first study of its African and Afro-descendant people
points.text: In 2021 Spain's Ministry of Equality published its first study of the African and Afro-descendant population in Spain, covering identity and access to rights, by Mª Ángeles Cea D'Ancona and Miguel S. Valles.
points.note: Rests on one source: both pages are Spanish government. We did not verify the study's findings, so none are quoted.

sources.title: La Moncloa – Igualdad celebra la Semana Antirracista
Spanish Government Publications Catalogue – Examination of the African and afro-descendant population in Spain

points.heading: Afro-Swedes face the most hate crimes in Sweden
points.text: Sweden's National Council for Crime Prevention found people of African descent are the group subjected to the most hate crimes. UN experts who visited in 2014 said authorities had failed to effectively investigate and prosecute Afrophobic hate crimes, while commending the government for prioritising Afrophobia.
points.note: Sweden does not count people by ethnicity, so there is no official figure for Afro-Swedes. Afro-Swede is the community's own term.

sources.title: UN News – UN experts urge Sweden to intensify fight against discrimination
Sveriges Radio – Afro-Swedes subjected to the most hate crimes in Sweden

points.heading: Black Irish: over 76,000 in the 2022 census
points.text: In Ireland's 2022 census, 67,546 people identified as Black or Black Irish – African, up 17% since 2016, and a further 8,699 as Black or Black Irish – any other Black background, up 28%.
points.note: Rests on one source (Central Statistics Office, authoritative). Total is our sum of the two categories.

sources.title: CSO – Census 2022 Profile 5: Ethnic Group/Background

points.heading: EU survey: nearly half face racial discrimination
points.text: The EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 'Being Black in the EU' (2023, latest edition, fieldwork 2022) surveyed almost 6,800 people of African descent in 13 EU countries. Al Jazeera reports 46% had experienced racial discrimination; FRA says 12-month prevalence rose from 24% to 34% since 2016. Rates were highest in Germany and Austria, at over three-quarters.
points.note: The 46% five-year figure is as reported by Al Jazeera; FRA's page gives the 12-month rise and a peak of 77% in one country. The 13 countries were Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, Poland, Portugal, Spain and Sweden. The survey did not cover the Netherlands.

sources.title: Being Black in the EU – Experiences of people of African descent
Al Jazeera – 'Wake-up call' for EU as report reveals spike in anti-Black racism

points.heading: EU survey: housing discrimination rose sharply
points.text: FRA found discrimination in the housing market rose from 6% in 2016 to 28% in 2022. Police stopped 26% of respondents in the previous five years, and 30% experienced racist harassment. FRA concluded the findings 'do not show any progress'.
points.note: The second source confirms the overall survey, not the housing figure, which rests on FRA alone.

sources.title: Being Black in the EU – Experiences of people of African descent
Al Jazeera – 'Wake-up call' for EU as report reveals spike in anti-Black racism

points.heading: 1.5 million Black Canadians in the 2021 census
points.text: The 2021 census counted 1,547,870 Black people in Canada, 4.3% of the population. Over 4 in 10 (41%) were born in Canada, and the Canadian-born Black population grew by 165.8% from 1996 to 2021.
points.note: Justice Canada projects the Black population could exceed 3 million by 2041.

sources.title: Statistics Canada – Black History Month 2025… By the numbers
Department of Justice Canada – Demographics and Diversity of Black Populations

points.heading: Black Loyalists founded Birchtown in 1783
points.text: About 3,000 Black Loyalists left New York for Nova Scotia in 1783, many recorded in the 'Book of Negroes'. Birchtown became the largest community of free Black people outside Africa. In 1792 about 1,200 left Nova Scotia to help found Freetown in Sierra Leone.
points.figure: About 3,000 arrived; about 1,200 left for Sierra Leone

sources.title: Canada's Historic Places – Birchtown
Royal Canadian Mint – A legacy of courage
Black Loyalist Heritage Centre – Exhibits

points.heading: Africville: a community razed, then an apology
points.text: Africville, a Black community on Halifax's edge settled by the 1840s, was denied running water and sewers and sited near a dump. Halifax razed and relocated it between 1964 and 1970. The city apologised on 24 February 2010, and a replica of its church opened in 2011.
points.note: CBC dates the founding to after the War of 1812, and oral history links some families to the 1700s.

sources.title: Halifax Regional Municipality – Recognizing the past, present, and future
CBC – Africville: A Community Destroyed

points.heading: Viola Desmond: from wrongful conviction to the $10 note
points.text: In 1946 the Halifax businesswoman Viola Desmond, who ran a beauty school drawing students from three provinces, was forcibly removed from a segregated New Glasgow cinema and convicted. Nova Scotia granted her a free pardon in 2010, and in 2018 she became the first Canadian woman on the face of a banknote.
points.note: Both sources are government bodies but different publishers.

sources.title: Bank of Canada – Backgrounder
Government of Nova Scotia – Viola Desmond, First Canadian Woman to Appear on a Banknote

points.heading: Emancipation Day became national in 2021
points.text: In March 2021 the House of Commons voted unanimously (335 to 0) to make 1 August Emancipation Day, marking the Slavery Abolition Act taking effect in 1834. Many Black Canadian communities had marked the day for decades; 2021 was the first national observance.

sources.title: Canadian Heritage – Statement on first national Emancipation Day
CBC – MPs vote to designate Aug. 1 as Emancipation Day

points.heading: Siddi communities live in four Indian states and in Sindh
points.text: The Siddi (also spelled Sidi) descend from East Africans who came to India mainly through the Indian Ocean slave trade. Communities live in Gujarat, Karnataka, Maharashtra and Telangana, and in Sindh in Pakistan; one estimate puts their number in India at about 65,000.
points.note: Population figure from one source (the Met); other sources give no count, so treat it as an estimate. 'Siddi' and 'Sidi' are both used; 'Sidi' derives from an Arabic honorific meaning 'my lord'.

sources.title: Habshi and Sidi – The Metropolitan Museum of Art
Sidi – Encyclopedia of World Cultures (Helene Basu), via Encyclopedia.com
Sahapedia: Who are the Siddis?

points.heading: Siddi music and faith blend East African and Sufi traditions
points.text: The central Siddi ritual is a drum-and-dance performance called goma or dhamal (dhamaal), honouring saints such as Bava Gor. In Karnataka Siddis are Hindu, Muslim and Christian; in Gujarat most are Muslim.

sources.title: Sidi – Encyclopedia of World Cultures (Helene Basu), via Encyclopedia.com
The incredible story of how East African culture shaped the music of a state in India – The Conversation

points.heading: Malik Ambar: from enslaved boy to ruler of Ahmadnagar
points.text: Malik Ambar was born Chapu in Ethiopia in 1548, enslaved and taken to India. He became the de facto ruler of the Ahmadnagar sultanate in the Deccan, resisted the Mughals for years with guerrilla tactics, and founded Khadki, later Aurangabad, around 1619.
points.note: Year of death differs: the Met gives 1626, BlackPast gives 1627.

sources.title: Habshi and Sidi – The Metropolitan Museum of Art
Habshi – Encyclopaedia Britannica
Malik Ambar (1548–1627) – BlackPast.org (Omar H. Ali)

points.heading: Habshi sultans ruled Bengal and Siddi nawabs held Janjira
points.text: 'Habshi' comes from the Arabic for Abyssinian. Habshi rulers held the throne of Bengal from 1487 to the early 1490s, and the Sidis of Janjira on India's west coast commanded a fleet and kept their own state until 1948.
points.note: End date of Habshi rule in Bengal differs: Banglapedia dates Shamsuddin Muzaffar Shah to 1491–1493; the Daily Star gives 1491–94.

sources.title: Eunuch – Banglapedia (Asiatic Society of Bangladesh)
Habshi rule in Bengal (1487-94) – The Daily Star (Muhammad Ahmedullah)
Habshi – Encyclopaedia Britannica

points.heading: Pakistan's Sheedi community and the Mangho Pir festival
points.text: Pakistan has the largest Sheedi (Siddi) population in South Asia, mostly in southern Sindh. The Sheedi Mela at the Mangho Pir shrine near Karachi, with its dhamal dance procession, is the community's central celebration.
points.note: Population estimate rests on one press source (Dawn/AFP); the encyclopedia confirms Sindh but gives no number. Sheedis also faced discrimination under British rule and after 1947, per Dawn.

sources.title: Crocodiles guard secrets of Pakistan's lost African past – Dawn (AFP)
Sidi – Encyclopedia of World Cultures (Helene Basu), via Encyclopedia.com

points.heading: Afro-Sri Lankans: a Portuguese-era community and its own name
points.text: Sri Lanka has a small community of African descent, brought from Mozambique by the Portuguese about 500 years ago and later by the Dutch and British. They are known locally and in official records as 'Kaffirs' (Lanka Kapiri), but the word comes from Arabic for 'unbeliever' and is a grave racial slur in South Africa, so this hub uses 'Afro-Sri Lankans'. Their manja/kaffringha songs in Sri Lanka Portuguese creole are endangered.
points.note: Population figure (around 3,000) rests on one press source. Community members use the local name themselves; 'Afro-Sri Lankan' is the term used in this hub to avoid repeating a slur. The Cambridge project reports a 90-year-old last mother-tongue speaker of Sri Lanka Portuguese at the time of the project.

sources.title: Tracing the African roots of Sri Lanka Portuguese – UKRI Gateway to Research (University of Cambridge)
Sunday Times (Sri Lanka), 24 April 2011
SARS v CCMA and Others [2016] ZACC 38 – Constitutional Court of South Africa (via SARS)
Kaffir – Dictionary.com

points.heading: Chagossians: descendants of enslaved Africans, removed by Britain
points.text: Chagossians are mostly descended from enslaved people from Madagascar and Mozambique and later indentured labourers. Britain removed the entire population, about 1,500 people, between 1967 and 1973 for a US military base; in 2019 the International Court of Justice found continued UK control unlawful.
points.note: Many Chagossians now live in the UK. In October 2024 the UK announced it would cede sovereignty to Mauritius; the agreement's current status is not confirmed by the sources cited.

sources.title: UN News, February 2019
Newcastle University Press Office (Sue Farran)
Chagos 2025 – Minority Rights Group

points.heading: The Zanj rebellion in Basra, 869–883
points.text: East Africans (Zanj) were brought to southern Iraq to drain the salt marshes east of Basra. Their revolt against the Abbasid caliphate lasted from 869 to 883, one of the largest uprisings of enslaved people in history.
points.note: MRG reports that the rebellion 'reportedly involved half a million slaves'; Britannica describes 'several thousand' brought in. Numbers are uncertain.

sources.title: Zanj rebellion – Encyclopaedia Britannica
World Directory of Minorities and Indigenous Peoples – Iraq: Black Iraqis (Minority Rights Group, via UNHCR Refworld)

points.heading: Black Iraqis today: centred on Basra, without recognition
points.text: Black Iraqis (Afro-Iraqis) live mostly in southern Iraq, with the largest community in Basra. Estimates range from 250,000 to 2 million. They are mainly Shi'a Muslims, keep African musical and spiritual traditions, and are sought-after wedding musicians, but face systematic discrimination and have no political representation.
points.note: No official count exists; the range is informal. MRG is an NGO hosted on UNHCR's Refworld, not a statistics office. MRG reports that Jalal Thiyab, founder of the Free Iraqi Movement, was assassinated in Basra.

sources.title: World Directory of Minorities and Indigenous Peoples – Iraq: Black Iraqis (Minority Rights Group, via UNHCR Refworld)
Centuries-old black community still on the margins in Iraq – Africanews (AFP), 2022

points.heading: Afro-Iranians along the Persian Gulf coast
points.text: Descendants of enslaved Africans live in rural and urban communities along Iran's Gulf coast, especially in Sistan and Baluchistan, Hormozgan and Khuzestan. They have blended African heritage with local religious traditions. Slavery in Iran is studied in the first full history of the subject, covering 1800 to emancipation in 1929.
points.note: The 1929 date comes from the book's title; the publisher's description says emancipation came 'in the mid-twentieth century'.

sources.title: Afro-Iranian Lives – Middle East Center, University of Pennsylvania
A History of Slavery and Emancipation in Iran, 1800–1929 – UBC Press (Behnaz A. Mirzai)

points.heading: Afro-Turks and the revival of Izmir's Calf Festival
points.text: After the Ottoman Empire abolished the trade in enslaved Africans in 1857, Izmir had possibly the largest share of freed Africans of any Ottoman city. Their descendants now celebrate an Afro-Turkish identity, including the revived Dana Bayramı (Calf Festival), now supported by Izmir's municipality.
points.note: The late Mustafa Olpak, who founded the Afro-Turk Association, led much of the revival (Al-Monitor). No reliable count of Afro-Turks exists.

sources.title: The Making and Unmaking of the African Community of Ottoman Izmir, 1870-1922 (University of Arizona)
Afro-Turks seek visibility in Turkey's cultural mosaic – Al-Monitor, September 2025

points.heading: Slavery was abolished late on the Arabian Peninsula
points.text: Enslaved Africans were carried across the Red Sea and sold throughout Arabia. Saudi Arabia was the last country in Arabia to abolish the legal status of slavery, by royal decree in November 1962, offering compensation to those who freed enslaved people.
points.note: The Antislavery in Domestic Legislation database is a university-led project (Rights Lab, University of Nottingham), though the page fetched did not name the university. The King Saud Library is a foundation linked to the royal family. Handled factually; dates for Yemen and Oman were not verified in this run.

sources.title: Saudi Arabia – Antislavery in Domestic Legislation database
Slavery During the Reign of King Saud – King Saud Library

points.heading: Liwa: East African music in the Gulf
points.text: Gulf genres such as liwa (lēwa) and tanbura have roots in East Africa and keep Swahili phrases and African rhythms. They are performed by African-descended communities in Oman and the United Arab Emirates, and many well-known Gulf singers of the 20th century were of African descent.
points.note: The second source is a University of Georgia undergraduate journal and Fanack is an independent media site; the evidence is weaker than for other points.

sources.title: Khaliji music: a unique blend of Indian and African influences – Fanack
Lēwa and the Misguided Perception of Cultural Appropriation – The Classic Journal, University of Georgia

points.heading: Yemen's Muhamasheen: discrimination clear, African origin contested
points.text: The Muhamasheen ('the marginalised', replacing the slur 'akhdam') face descent-based discrimination in Yemen, including being barred from owning land and from schools. Some say they descend from African enslaved people or Ethiopian soldiers; others say they have Yemeni roots.
points.note: Include as an example where African descent is claimed but not settled; do not describe the Muhamasheen as Afro-Yemeni without this caveat. Population estimates vary enormously (2004 census vs UN-cited 3.5 million).

sources.title: Summary of stakeholders' information, UPR of Yemen (A/HRC/WG.6/18/YEM/3) – UN Human Rights Council
Climate worsens the distress of Yemen's Muhammasheen – Carnegie Endowment, May 2026

points.heading: Haiti: the first country founded by formerly enslaved people
points.text: A general uprising of enslaved people in Saint-Domingue began in 1791. Led by figures including Toussaint Louverture and Jean-Jacques Dessalines, it defeated French and British forces, and on 1 January 1804 the country declared independence as Haiti.

sources.title: Haitian Revolution – Encyclopaedia Britannica
Haiti's independence debt – Bibliothèque nationale de France

points.heading: France made Haiti pay 150 million francs for recognition
points.text: In 1825 Charles X of France demanded 150 million francs from Haiti, to compensate former colonists, in exchange for recognising its independence. The sum was later cut to 90 million francs, and Haiti took decades to pay, borrowing to do so: the 'double debt'.
points.note: Sources differ on the reduced total and end date: BnF says 90 million francs, paid off in 1878 via an 1875 loan; LSU says 112 million francs paid over five decades after 1838. Present as disputed accounting, not a single figure.

sources.title: Haiti's independence debt – Bibliothèque nationale de France
1825–2025: France, Haiti, & the Question of Indebtedness – Louisiana State University

points.heading: Barbados became a republic in 2021
points.text: Barbados, independent since 1966, became a parliamentary republic on 30 November 2021, when Dame Sandra Mason took office as its first President and the Queen ceased to be head of state. It chose to stay in the Commonwealth.
points.note: The republic date and details rest on one authoritative source (House of Commons Library); the Commonwealth Secretariat source confirms only 1966 independence.

sources.title: Barbados becomes a republic – House of Commons Library
Barbados – Commonwealth Secretariat

points.heading: Suriname: Maroons are a fifth of the population
points.text: Maroons, descendants of Africans who escaped slavery and built free societies in the interior, make up about one-fifth of Suriname's population; Creoles of mainly African descent are another tenth to a fifth. Slavery was abolished on 1 July 1863, and in 2022 the Dutch government apologised for the Netherlands' role.
points.note: 1 July is marked as Keti Koti ('the chains are broken'), but neither source fetched uses that name. Freed people were kept under 10 years of state supervision after 1863 (Britannica). UNESCO's listed Maroon heritage (Moore Town, 2008) is in Jamaica, not Suriname.

sources.title: Suriname: People – Encyclopaedia Britannica
Suriname: History – Encyclopaedia Britannica
Government apologises for the Netherlands' role in the history of slavery – Government of the Netherlands

points.heading: Guyana: freed people bought land and built villages
points.text: The Dutch and then the British brought enslaved West Africans to grow sugar in Berbice, Demerara and Essequibo; about 100,000 people were enslaved there in 1807. After full emancipation in 1838, Black freedmen left the plantations to set up their own settlements.
points.note: Rests on one source (authoritative). The 1763 Berbice uprising and the 1823 Demerara rebellion could not be verified in this run.

sources.title: Guyana: History – Encyclopaedia Britannica

points.heading: St Kitts and Antigua: World Heritage built by enslaved Africans
points.text: Two UNESCO World Heritage Sites were built by enslaved Africans: Brimstone Hill Fortress on St Kitts (inscribed 1999) and the Antigua Naval Dockyard (inscribed 2016). UNESCO credits their 'labour and skills'.
points.note: Both entries come from one publisher (UNESCO), so this counts as one authoritative source.

sources.title: Brimstone Hill Fortress National Park – UNESCO World Heritage Centre
Antigua Naval Dockyard and Related Archaeological Sites – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Bermuda: enslaved Africans in a British Overseas Territory
points.text: Africans transported in the slave trade were brought to Bermuda from the early colonial period. Slavery was outlawed there along with the rest of the British Empire under the 1833 Act; Bermuda remains a British Overseas Territory.
points.note: Rests on one source (authoritative). The Abolition Act was passed in 1833 and took effect on 1 August 1834. Mary Prince, born in Bermuda, could not be verified in this run (see rejected).

sources.title: Bermuda: History – Encyclopaedia Britannica

points.heading: Trinidad and Tobago: calypso, Carnival and the steelpan
points.text: Calypso grew from the early 19th century, when enslaved people in Trinidad sang veiled, improvised lyrics in the streets at Carnival. The steelpan, made from oil barrels, grew from early 20th-century Carnival percussion groups; the UN now marks 11 August as World Steelpan Day.
points.note: Britannica's text uses the word 'slaves'; this hub uses 'enslaved people'. Canboulay and the colonial bans on drumming were not verified in this run.

sources.title: Calypso – Encyclopaedia Britannica
Steel band – Encyclopaedia Britannica
World Steelpan Day – United Nations

points.heading: Saint Lucia: two Nobel laureates from one small island
points.text: Saint Lucia has produced two Nobel laureates, both born in Castries on 23 January: the economist Sir Arthur Lewis (1915–1991, Economic Sciences 1979), for research on economic development, and the poet Derek Walcott (1930–2017, Literature 1992). Lewis was also Vice Chancellor of the University of the West Indies.
points.note: Both laureates have died. The two NobelPrize.org pages are from one publisher; UWI is the independent second source.

sources.title: Derek Walcott – Facts – NobelPrize.org
Arthur Lewis – Facts – NobelPrize.org
Nobel Laureates – University of the West Indies

points.heading: Garifuna: an Afro-Indigenous people from St Vincent
points.text: The Garifuna formed on St Vincent from Africans, many of whom had escaped slavery, and Indigenous Caribs (Kalinago). After they resisted British colonisation in the Carib Wars, Britain deported them in 1797 to Roatán off Honduras. Their language, dance and music are UNESCO-listed.
points.note: Accounts of African origins differ: some describe escapees from Barbados plantations (Britannica), others a shipwrecked slave ship (International Encyclopedia of the Social Sciences). Garifuna communities today live mainly in Honduras, Guatemala, Nicaragua and Belize, with descendants still on St Vincent. UNESCO inscribed the element in 2008. The plural self-name is Garinagu.

sources.title: UNESCO: Language, dance and music of the Garifuna
Saint Vincent and the Grenadines: History – Encyclopaedia Britannica
Garifuna – Worldmark Encyclopedia of Cultures and Daily Life, via Encyclopedia.com

points.heading: Cuba: Afro-Cuban rumba and Santería
points.text: Rumba, mainly associated with African culture and popular where enslaved African communities lived, was inscribed by UNESCO in 2016. Santería, also called Regla de Ocha or the Lukumí religion, was brought by Yoruba people enslaved in great numbers in the early 19th century, who linked their orishas with Catholic saints.
points.note: The Santería sentence rests on one source (Britannica, authoritative).

sources.title: Rumba in Cuba – UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage
Rumba – Encyclopaedia Britannica
Santería – Encyclopaedia Britannica (Joseph M. Murphy)

points.heading: Mbanza Kongo: capital of a great central African state
points.text: The Kingdom of Kongo was one of the largest states in the region from the 14th to the 19th century. Its capital, Mbanza Kongo in northern Angola, was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2017.
points.note: Both sources are UNESCO pages and count as one publisher; the inscription is a UNESCO decision, so it rests on the authoritative record itself.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: three cultural sites inscribed (8 July 2017)
Mbanza Kongo, Vestiges of the Capital of the former Kingdom of Kongo (UNESCO WHC)

points.heading: Kongo's Christianisation from 1491
points.text: Kongo envoys returned from Portugal in 1491 with Catholic missionaries, and Kongo's royal family was baptised. Kongo became a Catholic kingdom on its own terms, holding a distinctive place among African states.
points.note: Britannica confirms the baptisms but not the year; the 1491 date comes from the Bloomsbury textbook and an independent teaching site.

sources.title: Bloomsbury, Panorama: A World History vol. 2 (Dunn and Willoughby), Source 3.1
Britannica: João I (Nzinga a Nkuwu), king of Kongo
Religion and Slavery: Afonso I to Portugal (independent teaching site)

points.heading: Afonso I's 1526 letters against the slave trade
points.text: In 1526 King Afonso I of Kongo (Nzinga Mbemba) began a series of letters to King João III of Portugal protesting that Portuguese merchants were seizing his people, and stating that there should be no trade in enslaved people in his kingdoms. They are among the earliest African-written protests against the Atlantic slave trade.
points.note: Historians differ on emphasis: the Bloomsbury text frames the letters as seeking to limit and control the trade rather than end slavery outright. The quoted letter wording uses the historical term 'slaves'.

sources.title: World History Commons (Roy Rosenzweig Center, George Mason University): Afonso I letters
Bloomsbury, Panorama: A World History vol. 2 (Dunn and Willoughby), Source 3.1
Religion and Slavery: Afonso I to Portugal (independent teaching site)

points.heading: Njinga, queen of Ndongo and Matamba
points.text: Njinga (about 1582–1663) took power in Ndongo after her brother's death in 1624, later conquered Matamba, and fought the Portuguese and their allies for decades. At her height in the 1640s she ruled about a quarter of today's northern Angola, and she is revered in Angola as a national heroine.
points.note: Spellings vary (Njinga, Nzinga). The UNC page also records that she took part in slave trading after 1626; her legacy is complex. Birth year given as 1582 (UNC) or 1583 (other sources).

sources.title: Britannica: Njinga
University of North Carolina: Njinga of Angola: Africa's Warrior Queen
Thornton, 'Legitimacy and Political Power: Queen Njinga, 1624–1663', Journal of African History

points.heading: The Loango coast and the Vili kingdom
points.text: North of the Congo River, the Vili kingdom of Loango dominated a coast shared with Kakongo and Ngoyo from the 16th century. Its trade with Europeans shifted from cloth and other goods to the trade in enslaved people, which reshaped its politics until the old kingdom's demise in the 19th century.
points.note: Rests on one source (a university repository record of Martin's doctoral study, later published by Clarendon Press).

sources.title: SOAS Research Online: Phyllis M. Martin, The External Trade of the Loango Coast and its Effects on the Vili, 1576–1870

points.heading: Kuba cloth: raffia textiles of the Kuba kingdom
points.text: In the Kuba kingdom of today's Democratic Republic of the Congo, men weave raffia-palm cloth and women decorate it, including the velvety cut-pile technique. Prestige panels served as currency, tribute and markers of status and were worn at ceremonies including funerals.

sources.title: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Double Prestige Panel (Kuba)
McClung Museum, University of Tennessee: Raffia cloth
University of Michigan Museum of Art: Raffia textile panel

points.heading: The Luba and Lunda states
points.text: The Luba and Lunda states flourished from the late 15th to the late 19th century in the south of today's DRC and neighbouring areas. The Lunda empire reached its height by the 1850s, trading ivory and enslaved people for cloth and guns, before being eroded by Chokwe incursions and partitioned by colonial powers.
points.note: Rests on one source (two Britannica pages count as one publisher). Britannica's wording uses 'slaves'.

sources.title: Britannica: Luba-Lunda states
Britannica: Lunda empire

points.heading: King Njoya and the Bamum script of Cameroon
points.text: From about 1896 King Ibrahim Njoya of the Bamum kingdom (western Cameroon) created an original writing system, revising it several times until around 1910. Njoya used it for records including a map of his kingdom; French colonial rule later removed him and suppressed its use.
points.note: Sources differ on the final character count (70 in Riley; 80 in Endangered Alphabets). The suppression detail rests on the non-authoritative Endangered Alphabets page.

sources.title: Unicode Consortium document L2/07-023: Bamum script report (Charles Riley, Bamum Scripts and Archives Project)
British Library Endangered Archives Programme EAP051: Bamum script and archives project
Endangered Alphabets Project: Bamum

points.heading: Fang reliquary guardians of Gabon
points.text: Fang communities of Gabon and Cameroon carved byeri guardian figures to watch over containers holding the relics of lineage ancestors and founders. Collected by European modernist artists such as André Derain and Jacob Epstein, they are now held by major museums.

sources.title: Smarthistory: Female Figure from a Reliquary Ensemble (Fang peoples)
National Museums Scotland: bieri
The Menil Collection: Reliquary Guardian Figure (Eyima Byeri)

points.heading: Kanem-Bornu: a thousand-year state around Lake Chad
points.text: Kanem-Bornu, founded around the 9th century, controlled the Lake Chad region until the 19th century, making it one of Africa's longest-lasting states. It became an Islamic state, and Idris Alawma (reigned about 1571–1603) is remembered as one of its great rulers.
points.note: Britannica gives the Sef dynasty's end as 1846; World History Encyclopedia says the empire lasted until French takeover in the late 19th century.

sources.title: Britannica: Kanem-Bornu
World History Encyclopedia: Kingdom of Kanem (Mark Cartwright, 2019)

points.heading: Barthélemy Boganda and the Central African Republic
points.text: Barthélemy Boganda (1910–1959), a former priest, founded the Social Evolution Movement of Black Africa (MESAN) in 1949 and led Ubangi-Shari towards independence. He died in a plane crash in 1959, before independence on 13 August 1960, and is revered as a national martyr.
points.note: The cause of the 1959 crash is unresolved; the AfricaMuseum says it 'remains unknown to this day'.

sources.title: Britannica: Barthélemy Boganda
AfricaMuseum (Royal Museum for Central Africa, Belgium): République centrafricaine

points.heading: Congolese rumba: UNESCO heritage of the two Congos
points.text: Congolese rumba, the music and dance of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Republic of the Congo, was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in December 2021 after a joint bid. Its roots run back to the old Kongo kingdom, across the Atlantic to Cuba and back again, carried by artists such as Franco and TPOK Jazz and Tabu Ley Rochereau.

sources.title: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: Congolese rumba
Al Jazeera: Rumba added to UNESCO heritage list (15 December 2021)
Africanews: Congolese rumba wins UNESCO heritage status

points.heading: The Congo Free State: forced labour and mass death
points.text: From 1885 to 1908 the Congo Free State was under King Leopold II of Belgium's personal control. Forced labour was used to gather wild rubber and ivory, people who failed to collect rubber were punished or killed and their wives taken hostage, and the population is said to have fallen sharply.
points.note: Population estimates are contested; Britannica itself hedges ('is said to have'). No reliable census existed.

sources.title: Britannica: Congo Free State
Casement in the Congo Free State, exhibition panel 4 (National Museum of Ireland)

points.heading: Exposure by Casement and British campaigners
points.text: Roger Casement's report, based on observation and interviews, was published in February 1904, and a campaign group founded by British citizens spread the truth about the regime. In 1908 Leopold was forced to hand the territory to the Belgian state, which ran it as the Belgian Congo.
points.note: Congolese testimony was central to the evidence; the reform campaign is often told through European figures alone.

sources.title: Casement in the Congo Free State, exhibition panel 4 (National Museum of Ireland)
Britannica: Congo Free State

points.heading: Congolese, Angolan and Cameroonian communities in England and Wales
points.text: The 2021 Census recorded 29,439 people in England and Wales born in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, 19,717 born in Angola and 14,614 born in Cameroon. Birmingham alone had 3,848 residents born in Central African countries.
points.note: Rests on one source (a council profile quoting ONS Census 2021 country-of-birth data; the ONS dataset page could not be read as text). Country of birth counts first-generation migrants only, so UK-born Congolese, Angolan and Cameroonian people are not included.

sources.title: Birmingham City Council: Central African community health profile (Census 2021 data)

points.heading: Mary Prince: the first Black woman's narrative published in Britain
points.text: Mary Prince, born to enslaved parents in Bermuda in 1788 and enslaved in Bermuda, Turks Island and Antigua, published The History of Mary Prince in London in 1831. It was the first narrative of a Black woman published in Britain and fed the campaign to end slavery.
points.note: The London Museum says only 'the West Indies' for her birthplace; Bermuda comes from the Women's History Network. That page also calls her petition the first anti-slavery petition by a Black woman to Parliament.

sources.title: London Museum: The life story of Mary Prince
University of Michigan Press: The History of Mary Prince
Women's History Network: Witness against slavery, the story of Mary Prince

points.heading: Grenada's Fédon rebellion, 1795–96
points.text: On 2 March 1795 Julien Fédon, a free man of colour, led a rising backed by the French Republic that aimed to end slavery and British rule in Grenada; some 7,000 enslaved people joined. It was put down in 1796 after more than a year of fighting and followed by mass executions.
points.note: UWI gives the official end as 19 June 1796; The National Archives cites the stronghold's capture reported by 4 July 1796. At least 77 men were sentenced to death.

sources.title: The National Archives (UK) blog: 'Excessive severity': Treason and the Grenadian Rebellion of 1795
University of the West Indies: Curtis Jacobs, The Fédons of Grenada, 1763–1814

points.heading: The Grenada Revolution, 1979–83
points.text: In March 1979 the New Jewel Movement under Maurice Bishop took power in a bloodless coup and formed the People's Revolutionary Government. The University of the West Indies credits it with gains in education, housing and employment.
points.note: Its record is contested; see the counter-argument on detentions and the 1983 collapse.

sources.title: UWI Today (University of the West Indies), September 2014
Global Voices: Grenada officially remembers the murders of Maurice Bishop and others (2023)

points.heading: Detentions, Bishop's killing and the 1983 invasion
points.text: The revolutionary government held people without trial; estimates range from 1,000 to 3,000. On 19 October 1983 Bishop and others were executed on orders from his deputy, and a United States-led invasion followed on 25 October. Grenada held its first public holiday to remember the killings in 2023.
points.note: Detention figures are estimates. The deputy prime minister who gave the order is not named here. UWI Today gives 25 October for the landing.

sources.title: UWI Today (University of the West Indies), September 2014
Global Voices: Grenada officially remembers the murders of Maurice Bishop and others (2023)

points.heading: The Bahamas: an African-descended majority and Junkanoo
points.text: About 85% of Bahamians are estimated to be of African descent; Loyalists arriving after the American Revolution brought enslaved people, and slavery ended in 1834. Junkanoo, begun by enslaved people as a New Year celebration, has been promoted since majority rule in 1967 as an expression of Black Bahamian culture.
points.note: An estimate: the Bahamian government does not record ethnicity. The Junkanoo detail rests on one source (CultureGrams). Haitians are estimated at 10–25% of the population (MRG), a wide range.

sources.title: CultureGrams 2014: Bahamas (ProQuest and Brigham Young University)
Minority Rights Group International: Bahamas

points.heading: Dominica: an African-descended nation alongside the Kalinago
points.text: The great majority of Dominicans are of African descent, the island also being home to about 4,000 Indigenous Kalinago people. Slavery was abolished in 1833–34, and Dominica became independent from Britain on 3 November 1978.
points.note: The African-descent share rests on MRG (non-government); the High Commission page confirms the Kalinago and independence only.

sources.title: Minority Rights Group International: Dominica
High Commission for the Commonwealth of Dominica in the UK: History
Discover Dominica: History and culture

points.heading: Trinidad and Tobago: first national Emancipation Day, 1985
points.text: On 1 August 1985 Trinidad and Tobago became the first country to declare a national holiday marking the abolition of slavery. The date recalls 1 August 1838, when full freedom came into effect; the holiday replaced Discovery Day, which marked Columbus's arrival.
points.note: The replacement of Discovery Day rests on the non-government guide only.

sources.title: Tobago House of Assembly: Free to Celebrate
Discover Trinidad & Tobago (Media & Editorial Projects): Emancipation Day

points.heading: Canboulay: from burnt cane to the start of Carnival
points.text: Canboulay, from the French cannes brûlées ('burnt cane'), began as a plantation work practice of the enslaved and became a procession celebrating the end of slavery. After the 1881 Canboulay Riots, when people defended it against colonial suppression, it survived as Carnival's opening procession before dawn on Carnival Monday.

sources.title: Patrick Murphy, 'Canboulay and the Nègre Jardin', Journal of Festive Studies 6 (2024), University of Chicago Knowledge repository
Trinidad Express: Canboulay, the origins of Carnival

points.heading: Berbice 1763 and Guyana's 23 February
points.text: On 23 February 1763 enslaved people in the Dutch colony of Berbice rose up, led by Cuffy (Kofi), an Akan man; the rising was crushed in 1764. Guyana chose 23 February for Republic Day in 1970 to mark it, and Cuffy, now a national hero, stands on the 1763 Monument in Georgetown, unveiled in 1976.
points.figure: more than 2,500 people rose up (DPI Guyana)
points.note: The Republic Day link rests on a newspaper editorial; the Guyana government page confirms the rising and Cuffy's status. Spellings vary: Cuffy, Coffy, Kofi.

points.heading: Brazil – pardo (and preto)
points.text: In Brazil's 2022 census 45.3% (about 92.1 million) declared themselves pardo (brown, of mixed ancestry), the largest group for the first time since 1991; a further 10.2% declared preto (black). Pretos and pardos together are 55.5%. Pardo has historically denoted people of mixed ancestry, including African descent, but it can also include people of Indigenous–European descent.
points.note: IBGE pages count as one publisher; Jornal do Brasil (with Agência Brasil) is the independent second source.

points.heading: Cuba – mestizo / mulato
points.text: Cuba's 2012 census recorded 26.6% of people as mestizo/mulato by skin colour (color de la piel), 9.3% negro and about 64% blanco.
points.note: White share given as 64%, 64.1% and 64.3% by different secondary sources; 26.6% agrees across all. ONEI primary tables not cited here.

points.heading: Dominican Republic – indio, mulato, moreno
points.text: The national census has not published a race result since 1960. A 2021 UNFPA national survey found 45% describing themselves with 'indio'-type terms, 16% moreno, 9% mulato, 8% negro, 18% blanco. 'Indio' here is a skin-colour term (e.g. indio claro, indio canela) for people of mixed African–European appearance, not a claim of Indigenous ancestry; the island's Taíno peoples were largely destroyed in the 16th century and the label was promoted in the Trujillo era.
points.note: Survey, not census. ENHOGAR 2021 (per Acento) gives different figures: 48% indio/mestizo, 27% mulato. 2022 census race results not located.

points.heading: Venezuela – moreno
points.text: In the 2011 census 51.6% identified as moreno/a (brown), 2.9% negro/a and 0.7% afrodescendiente; 43.6% blanco/a. 'Moreno' is a broad brown category that need not denote African ancestry.
points.note: MRG says the Afro-descendant shares are 'far lower than the likely actual proportion'.

points.heading: Colombia – mulato within the NARP group
points.text: Colombia's 2018 census asked one combined option 'Negro(a), mulato(a), afrodescendiente, afrocolombiano(a)' alongside raizal and palenquero; mulato cannot be separated out. The census counted 2,982,224 NARP people (DANE table; about 6.8% of those counted); the Ministry of Health cites 5.9%. DANE's official estimate after correcting census undercount is 9.34% (ECV 2018).
points.note: Census undercount acknowledged by DANE; mulato not separately published.

points.heading: Panama – afrodescendiente (no mixed category)
points.text: Panama's 2023 census asked about Afro-descendant self-recognition, with sub-groups including moreno(a), negro(a), afrocolonial and afroantillano(a). 31.7% (1,286,857) identified as Afro-descendant, up from 9.2% in 2010. There is no separate 'mixed' category.
points.note: A preliminary figure of 32.8% (swissinfo, March 2023) was superseded.

points.heading: Puerto Rico – two or more races
points.text: In the 2020 US census for Puerto Rico 49.8% chose two or more races (3.3% in 2010), while white alone fell to 17.1% and Black alone to 7.0%. The jump reflects changes to the question and coding, not a sudden change in ancestry.

points.heading: Cabo Verde – crioulo / mestiço
points.text: Cabo Verde's census does not publish a race or ethnicity count. Reference works describe more than two-thirds of the population as mestiço or crioulo (mixed African and European, mainly Portuguese); the 71% figure commonly quoted is a 2006 CIA World Factbook estimate, not a census figure.
points.note: Not a census figure.

sources.title: Britannica: Cabo Verde summary

points.heading: South Africa – Coloured
points.text: In Census 2022, 8.2% identified as Coloured (81.4% Black African, 7.3% White, 2.7% Indian/Asian). 'Coloured' was imposed as a legal category by the Population Registration Act 1950 but is today a self-identification with its own history and communities, rooted in Khoekhoe and San, enslaved people from Asia and East Africa, Bantu-speaking and European ancestors.

points.heading: Namibia – no race question
points.text: Namibia's censuses have not asked race since independence (it was not asked in 2001); the 2023 census recorded self-identified ethnic/language groups. Rehoboth Basters and Coloured communities exist but no census share is published here.
points.note: Census does not ask; no estimate given.

points.heading: Mauritius – no community question since 1972
points.text: Mauritius has not produced community-disaggregated census statistics since 1972 (questions dropped from the 1983 census). Creoles of African and Malagasy descent fall within the constitutional 'General Population'.
points.note: Census does not ask.

points.text: The French census does not ask about race or ethnicity, and public statistics generally do not collect ethnic affiliation; a 2007 Conseil constitutionnel decision (2007-557 DC) held that studies may use objective data but may not rest on ethnic origin or race. No share can be given.

points.text: Statistics Netherlands (CBS) classifies people by country of birth of the person and parents (e.g. Surinamese, Antillean origin), not by race or mixed heritage. No share of mixed heritage can be given.

points.heading: African Americans: average about three-quarters African ancestry
points.text: A 23andMe-based study of 5,269 self-described African Americans found average genome-wide ancestry of 73.2% African, 24.0% European and 0.8% Native American. A more representative 2016 study of 3,726 African Americans estimated 82.1% African, 16.7% European and 1.2% American ancestry.
points.note: Studies differ; the 2015 authors note their estimate is lower than earlier ones (77–93%).

points.heading: Brazil: colour is a poor guide to ancestry
points.text: Across four regions, European ancestry was predominant on average (60.6% in the Northeast to 77.7% in the South). Self-declared colour categories were unreliable indicators of genomic ancestry; the authors link this partly to European immigration intended to 'whiten' Brazil.

points.heading: Cabo Verde: highly admixed, sex-biased

points.heading: Caribbean: high and variable African ancestry
points.text: Caribbean island populations have higher African ancestry than mainland Latin American populations. Cubans ranged from 2% to 78% West African ancestry; Haitians averaged 84%; Dominicans cluster between African and European components.

points.heading: Ancestry is not race
points.text: Researchers stress that self-identity and genetic ancestry overlap but are not the same; the 2015 US study found self-identification as African American follows a probability curve with African ancestry rather than a 'one-drop' rule.

points.heading: Coined in a political hoax, 1863
points.text: 'Miscegenation' (Latin miscere, to mix, + genus, race) was coined in an anonymous 72-page pamphlet sold in New York shortly before Christmas 1863 (title page dated 1864). It was written by Democratic journalists on the New York World to make voters believe that Republicans and abolitionists favoured 'race mixing'.
points.note: Publication straddles December 1863 / early 1864; Merriam-Webster gives first use 1863.

sources.title: Museum of Hoaxes: The Miscegenation Hoax

points.heading: US anti-'miscegenation' laws ended in 1967
points.text: On 12 June 1967 the US Supreme Court in Loving v. Virginia unanimously held bans on interracial marriage unconstitutional, striking down laws still in force in 16 states. Alabama removed its unenforceable ban from its constitution only in 2000.

points.heading: Apartheid South Africa: Prohibition of Mixed Marriages Act 1949
points.text: One of the first apartheid laws, the 1949 Act banned marriages between White people and people of other groups; it was repealed by the Immorality and Prohibition of Mixed Marriages Amendment Act 1985.

points.heading: Why the hub does not use it
points.text: The word was invented to provoke fear of 'race mixing' and became the legal language of marriage bans in the US and South Africa; dictionaries associate it with those laws. It assumes separate biological races, which genetics does not support. The hub therefore says 'mixed heritage' or 'mixed ancestry', and quotes 'miscegenation' only in historical context.

sources.title: Merriam-Webster: miscegenation
Journal of the Civil War Era (Muster blog, 2021): Fake News, Dirty Tricks, and Civil War Politics
Britannica: miscegenation

points.heading: Self-identification is not ancestry
points.text: Census answers record how people see themselves (or how the question was asked), not genetic ancestry. STATIN says Jamaica's results reflect self-perception; Stats SA says population group is self-classified; Brazilian studies show colour categories poorly predict ancestry.

sources.title: STATIN: Population and Housing Census 2011 Jamaica, General Report Vol. 1
Human Molecular Genetics 19(3) (2010): Genetic structure of a unique admixed population: implications for medical research
Pesquisa FAPESP: Many colors, one people

points.heading: Categories differ, so shares are not comparable
points.text: Some censuses offer 'mixed' categories (UK, Trinidad, Guyana), some colour terms (Brazil, Cuba, Venezuela), some multi-tick race (USA, Canada), some Afro-descendant identity (Colombia, Panama), and some ask nothing (France, the Netherlands, Mauritius, Namibia). Question changes alone can transform results: Puerto Rico's 'two or more races' rose from 3.3% to 49.8% between 2010 and 2020.

sources.title: Center for Puerto Rican Studies (Hunter College, CUNY): Puerto Rico's 2020 Race/Ethnicity Decennial Analysis
US Census Bureau: Improved Race and Ethnicity Measures Reveal U.S. Population Is Much More Multiracial (2021)

points.heading: Whitening and colourism shape answers
points.text: Brazil's branqueamento ideology promoted subsidised European immigration and mixing to 'whiten' the population; research finds interviewers and respondents shifted lighter-skinned people towards 'white'. In the Dominican Republic 'indio' became a preferred label distancing people from Blackness.

sources.title: PLoS ONE 6(2) (2011): The genomic ancestry of individuals from different geographical regions of Brazil is more uniform than expected
Revista de Antropologia 67 (2024): Race and color in contemporary Brazil, political opportunism and historical trends
El Día: Solo el 8 % de los dominicanos se identifica como negro

points.heading: Counter-trend: more people now claim Black or mixed identity
points.text: Brazil's pardo and preto shares rose between 2010 and 2022 and Panama's Afro-descendant share rose from 9.2% to 31.7%, partly reflecting campaigns for self-recognition rather than demographic change.

sources.title: IBGE News Agency: 2022 Census: self-reported brown population is the majority in Brazil for the first time
TVN Noticias (Panamá): resultados del Censo

points.heading: English Heritage blue plaques: under 4% honour Black and Asian figures
points.text: In 2016 English Heritage said fewer than 4% of London's 900-plus blue plaques honoured Black and Asian figures. It set up a working group to propose Black and Asian nominees, held to the same criteria as public nominations. On the same day it unveiled a plaque to the footballer Laurie Cunningham at his childhood home in Stroud Green, north London.
points.note: Both pages come from English Heritage, so they count as one publisher. English Heritage is a national heritage body (authoritative). The point rests on one source. The share may have changed since 2016.

sources.title: Diversity and blue plaques – English Heritage
Blue plaque for Laurie Cunningham – English Heritage

points.heading: Anyone can nominate a London blue plaque
points.text: English Heritage's London scheme is driven mainly by public suggestions. The person must have died at least 20 years ago, and a building linked to them must survive in Greater London. You email the completed form to A shortlisted plaque usually takes two to three years to go up.
points.note: Both pages are English Heritage's (one publisher, authoritative), so the point rests on one source. How to apply: the Propose a plaque page gives the form and email address.

sources.title: Propose a plaque – English Heritage
London's Black history – Blue plaque stories, English Heritage

points.heading: Nubian Jak Community Trust: Black-led plaques across the UK
points.text: Since 2006 the Nubian Jak Community Trust has installed more than 100 blue and black plaques and three memorials across the UK. Its plaques include a bronze plaque to Mary Prince on Senate House, University of London, in Camden, and the first commemorative plaque in Whitehall, on the Foreign Office.
points.note: The Camden Council planning record (local government) is the authoritative source. The Trust's own page is the source for the count. Neither page sets out how to nominate.

sources.title: Plaques and memorials – Nubian Jak Community Trust
Camden Council planning document

points.heading: National Windrush Monument at Waterloo station (2022)
points.text: The National Windrush Monument by the Jamaican sculptor Basil Watson was unveiled at London Waterloo station on Windrush Day, 22 June 2022. It shows a man, woman and child in their Sunday best standing on suitcases. GOV.UK says it pays tribute to the dreams, ambition and resilience of the Windrush pioneers.
points.note: The GOV.UK page confirms the commission and purpose but not the date or location. The date, location and description come from ITV and Londonist, and the £1 million figure from Londonist alone.

sources.title: The National Windrush Monument – GOV.UK
Windrush generation makes our culture richer, says William as monument unveiled – ITV News
National Windrush Monument unveiled at Waterloo station – Londonist

points.heading: Mary Seacole statue at St Thomas' Hospital (2016)
points.text: On 30 June 2016 a statue of the Jamaican-born nurse Mary Seacole by Martin Jennings was unveiled in the gardens of St Thomas' Hospital, London. It is believed to be the first statue in the UK of a named Black woman. A public appeal raised over £500,000, and £240,000 of LIBOR fines paid for installation.
points.note: The NHS trust's own news release is a public-body source. The Mary Seacole Trust maintains the statue and runs education and diversity-in-leadership programmes.

sources.title: Mary Seacole statue unveiled – Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust
About – The Mary Seacole Trust

points.heading: Colston Hall renamed Bristol Beacon (2020)
points.text: On 23 September 2020 Bristol Music Trust renamed its concert hall Bristol Beacon. The old name, Colston Hall, had acted as a memorial to Edward Colston, a merchant in the trade in enslaved Africans Edward Colston. The new name followed a public consultation with over 4,000 people.
points.note: The venue's own statement is a primary source but is not on the brief's authoritative list. The Voice is an independent Black British newspaper. The consultation is a model others can copy.

sources.title: Our new name – Bristol Beacon
Bristol's Colston Hall renamed – The Voice

points.heading: Colston statue: from plinth to museum display
points.text: The statue of Edward Colston was pulled down during a Black Lives Matter protest in Bristol in June 2020, and the council recovered it from the harbour. The We Are Bristol History Commission then ran a public survey that drew almost 14,000 responses. Four in five respondents wanted the statue shown in a city museum. A temporary display at M Shed let people see the statue and learn its history.
points.note: The removal of the statue was contested and led to a criminal trial, which is not covered here because it was not sourced. The point is limited to the public consultation process.

sources.title: The Colston Statue: What Next? 'We are Bristol' History Commission – Full Report (UWE repository)
Colston statue should be displayed in a museum, say Bristol residents – Museums Association
Edward Colston statue on display at Bristol museum – Artnet News

points.heading: NHS trust plaques honour the Windrush generation
points.text: In October 2024 University Hospitals of Derby and Burton unveiled new plaques at all its sites honouring the Windrush generation and their descendants. It organised the unveilings with its EMBRACE Staff Network, starting at Florence Nightingale Community Hospitals on 1 October.
points.note: This point rests on one source, the NHS trust's own news release (a public body).

sources.title: UHDB honours the Windrush generation with commemorative plaques – UHDB NHS

points.heading: Black History Month began in London in 1987
points.text: Black History Month in the UK began with an event in London on 1 October 1987. It was coordinated by Akyaaba Addai-Sebo, a special projects officer at the Greater London Council. It is now marked every October.
points.note: The Senedd (Welsh Parliament) is the authoritative source. The two pages spell the name differently: the Senedd uses 'Sebbo' and UCU uses 'Addai-Sebo'.

sources.title: Senedd Cymru: Black History Month, a special anniversary
The History of Black History Month | UCU

points.heading: 2026 theme: Honouring Our Communities
points.text: The theme of Black History Month 2026 is 'Honouring Our Communities'. Black History Month UK says the theme is about people, and about recognising individuals whose everyday contributions too often go unseen. Organisations from town councils to the Royal College of Nursing have built their October programmes around it.
points.note: Lowestoft Town Council (local government) is the authoritative source. None of the sources says who chose the theme.

sources.title: Black History Month (UK) magazine and website
Black History Month 2026 – Inclusive Employers
Black History Month 2026 – Lowestoft Town Council

points.heading: Windrush Day, 22 June, and its government grant scheme
points.text: 22 June is National Windrush Day, marking the arrival of the MV Empire Windrush in 1948. For 2026 the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government offered £500,000 for events in England, with grants of £5,000 to £25,000. Councils, charities and community organisations could apply; individuals could not. Applications closed on 10 February 2026.
points.note: The GOV.UK guidance gives the arrival as both 21 June (at Tilbury) and 22 June 1948. Action Together also shows a £10,000 minimum in one panel. The first grant scheme ran in 2019 (GOV.UK National Windrush Monument page). How to take part: watch GOV.UK for the next round, which normally opens in January.

sources.title: Windrush Day Grant Scheme 2026: guidance for applicants – GOV.UK
Windrush Day Grant Scheme 2026 – Action Together

points.heading: 33 Windrush Day projects funded for 2026
points.text: GOV.UK lists 33 projects funded in 2026. They include a British Carnivals tapestry unveiled at Bath Abbey, talking benches in Pymmes Park in Enfield, a Windrush Festival in Coventry with an archive planned at the University of Warwick, and a Windrush Monument unveiling in Wolverhampton.
points.note: The second source is a separate National Lottery funding round (2023, Windrush 75). It shows the same kind of community activity, including carnivals, exhibitions and school workshops.

sources.title: Windrush Day Grant Scheme 2026: projects to be funded – GOV.UK

points.heading: Slavery Remembrance Day, 23 August, in Liverpool
points.text: Liverpool has marked Slavery Remembrance Day every 23 August since 1999. Liverpool City Council and National Museums Liverpool run it together, with a Walk of Remembrance and a libation ceremony. The date marks the 1791 uprising of enslaved Africans in Saint-Domingue (now Haiti).
points.note: Both sources are authoritative: a national museum and the city council's news service. How to take part: the walk is public and free, starting at noon on 23 August.

sources.title: 10 years of International Slavery Museum – National Museums Liverpool
Slavery Remembrance Day: 25 years of commemoration in Liverpool – Liverpool Express (Liverpool City Council)

points.heading: The international day behind 23 August
points.text: The UN marks 23 August as the International Day for the Remembrance of the Slave Trade and its Abolition. It recalls the uprising that began in Saint-Domingue on the night of 22 to 23 August 1791. It was first marked in Haiti in 1998 and on Gorée Island, Senegal, in 1999.
points.note: The UN source is authoritative.

sources.title: International Day for the Remembrance of the Slave Trade and its Abolition – United Nations
Slavery Remembrance Day: 25 years of commemoration in Liverpool – Liverpool Express (Liverpool City Council)

points.heading: Emancipation Day, 1 August
points.text: The Slavery Abolition Act 1833 took effect on 1 August 1834 across the British Empire. It did not bring immediate freedom: enslaved people over the age of six became 'apprentices' until 1838, and the compensation records cover estate owners and investors, not the people freed. Communities mark 1 August as Emancipation Day.
points.note: Both sources are authoritative: The National Archives and Parks Canada (a national government agency).

sources.title: The National Archives: 1833 Abolition of Slavery Act and compensation claims
Celebrations of Emancipation Day – Parks Canada

points.heading: Afrikan Emancipation Day march in Brixton
points.text: Every 1 August, campaigners hold the Afrikan Emancipation Day Reparations March from Windrush Square in Brixton. It ends in a rally calling for reparations and for wider recognition of Britain's role in the slave trade. Lambeth Council has publicly backed its aims.
points.note: Reparations are a contested political demand. The point records the event, not a position on reparations. Lambeth Council is the authoritative source.

sources.title: Brixton: March and rally set to go ahead – Lambeth Council
Emancipation Day Reparations March kicks off in London – CARICOM Reparations Commission

points.heading: International Slavery Museum, Liverpool
points.text: The International Slavery Museum opened on 23 August 2007 on the third floor of the Merseyside Maritime Museum at the Albert Dock. It had over four million visitors in its first ten years. It also hosts free events such as the Dorothy Kuya lecture.

sources.title: 10 years of International Slavery Museum – National Museums Liverpool
Slavery Remembrance Day: 25 years of commemoration in Liverpool – Liverpool Express (Liverpool City Council)

points.heading: London, Sugar & Slavery gallery, London Museum Docklands
points.text: The London, Sugar & Slavery gallery at London Museum Docklands opened in 2007 in a former sugar warehouse completed in 1802. The museum calls it one of the only permanent UK displays dedicated to the British trade in enslaved Africans. It is on the third floor, open 10am to 5pm daily, and listed among the free galleries.
points.note: The Museum of London Docklands is now called London Museum Docklands.

sources.title: London, Sugar & Slavery – London Museum
The Wake: London's docks and the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans – Greater London Authority

points.heading: Black Cultural Archives, Brixton, funded by National Lottery players
points.text: Black Cultural Archives on Windrush Square, Brixton, describes itself as the oldest national repository of Black history and culture in the UK. The National Lottery Heritage Fund awarded it £99,000 in 2020 for 'Securing the Future of Black British History'. A later £250,000 grant, 'Sankofa Resilience', is for clearing backlogs and widening access.
points.note: The two sources describe two different grants. How to take part: the reading room opens Wednesday to Friday, by appointment.

sources.title: Securing the Future of Black British History – National Lottery Heritage Fund
Sankofa Resilience: Strengthening Our Archive – Black Cultural Archives

points.heading: Heritage Fund grants: open to community groups year-round
points.text: The National Lottery Heritage Fund offers grants of £10,000 to £250,000 with no deadline and a decision target of eight weeks. Charities, community groups and councils can apply. The heritage it funds includes 'cultures, traditions and people's memories'. Larger grants of £250,000 to £10 million have set deadlines; the next is 6 August 2026.
points.note: Programme details checked in October 2026. Connected Voice is a community support body and covers the £250,000–£10 million strand. One of the fund's investment principles is 'inclusion, access and participation'.

sources.title: National Lottery Grants for Heritage £10,000 to £250,000 – National Lottery Heritage Fund
The National Lottery: Heritage Fund – Connected Voice

points.heading: Portsmouth records its African and Caribbean stories
points.text: The Portsmouth Black History Group received £68,645 from the National Lottery Heritage Fund. The money pays for recording the memories of African and Caribbean people who came to Portsmouth, mainly from after the Second World War to the early 1980s. The interviews will go to Portsmouth History Centre, with pop-up exhibitions and work with schools.
points.note: This point rests on one source, a university (authoritative).

sources.title: University supports project to share Portsmouth's post-WW2 Black stories – University of Portsmouth

points.heading: Wales: diverse histories mandatory in the curriculum
points.text: Wales has made the stories of Black, Asian and minority ethnic people a mandatory part of learning about Welsh history in the new curriculum. Teaching began in all primary schools and some secondary schools from September 2022. This followed a 2021 working group, chaired by Professor Charlotte Williams OBE, which made 51 recommendations; the minister accepted all of them.
points.note: Both pages are Welsh Government's (one publisher), so the point rests on one authoritative source. The official term 'Black, Asian and minority ethnic' is kept because it is in the quotation.

sources.title: Six things you may not know about the new curriculum (Welsh Government, 14 Jun 2022)
Black, Asian and Minority Ethnic education report welcomed by Minister – Welsh Government

points.heading: Stormzy Scholarship at Cambridge
points.text: The Stormzy Scholarship, launched in 2018, pays full tuition fees and a maintenance grant for Black UK students on any undergraduate course at the University of Cambridge. At least 10 awards were available for students starting in 2026. Applications open in August.
points.note: The University of Cambridge is the authoritative source. ITV (2021) says applicants must be a UK student of Black or mixed-race heritage.

sources.title: Stormzy Scholarship – University of Cambridge
Stormzy will fund 30 more scholarships for Black students at Cambridge – ITV News

points.heading: Anyone can nominate someone for a national honour
points.text: Anyone can nominate someone for an honour, such as an MBE, through GOV.UK. Honours go to people who have made life better for others or are outstanding at what they do, and nominees must still be active in that work. You need two supporting letters from people who know the nominee. It can take 12 to 18 months to hear back, and the lists are published at New Year and on the King's official birthday.
points.note: Both sources are authoritative: GOV.UK and The Gazette (the official public record). How to take part: use the nomination form on GOV.UK.

sources.title: Honours – GOV.UK

points.heading: NHS Windrush 70 Awards (2018)
points.text: To mark 70 years of both Windrush and the NHS in 2018, NHS England ran the Windrush 70 Awards to celebrate the contribution of Black and minority ethnic staff. More than 11,000 patients, members of the public and staff made nominations across 11 categories.
points.note: This was a one-off scheme. The Oxford Health page uses the abbreviation ‘BME’, which the hub style avoids; it is not used in our own text.

sources.title: Black and ethnic minority NHS staff honoured in NHS Windrush 70 awards – NHS England

points.heading: MOBO Awards: Music Of Black Origin since 1996
points.text: Kanya King founded the MOBO (Music Of Black Origin) Awards in 1996 to celebrate music rooted in Black British culture that mainstream awards had overlooked. MOBO now runs programmes for emerging artists, such as MOBO Unsung. Kanya King CBE died on 3 June 2026.
points.note: Neither source is on the brief's authoritative list. MOBO's own page is used as the official source for its own scheme, with an independent news source.

points.heading: The Powerlist: published annually since 2007
points.text: Powerful Media has published the Powerlist every year since 2007. It recognises the UK's most influential people of African, African Caribbean and African American heritage, chosen by an independent judging panel. It is sent to schools, sixth-form colleges, universities and corporate affinity groups.
points.note: Neither source is on the brief's authoritative list. The publisher's own page is used as the official source for its scheme.

Segun Osuntokun named in UK Black Powerlist – Bryan Cave Leighton Paisley

points.heading: Black British Business Awards: public nominations
points.text: Since 2014 the Black British Business Awards have celebrated Black British professionals and entrepreneurs. There are Rising Star and Senior Leader awards across six sectors, from Arts and Media to STEM. The public can nominate themselves or someone else.

points.heading: Town council small grants and youth competitions
points.text: For Black History Month 2026, Lowestoft Town Council offered grants of up to £200 to local groups holding an event. It also ran creative writing and visual arts competitions for children from nursery to sixth form, with entries closing on 23 October.
points.note: This point rests on one source, a local council (authoritative).

sources.title: Black History Month 2026 – Lowestoft Town Council

points.heading: Professional bodies honour communities in October
points.text: The Royal College of Nursing's Eastern region held a free Black History Month 2026 day, 'Honouring Our Communities', at Kneesworth House Hospital in Royston on 23 October 2026. It focused on 'all the people and everyday local networks that shape and sustain British life' and counted for 4 CPD hours.

points.heading: Individuals: nominate a plaque or an honour
points.text: Hub proposal: Individuals can nominate someone. For a person who died 20 or more years ago, propose a London blue plaque to English Heritage or a plaque to Nubian Jak. For a living person in your community, use the GOV.UK honours form. Gather the two supporting letters in October so the nomination is in by the end of Black History Month.

sources.title: Propose a plaque – English Heritage
Everything you need to know about nominating someone for a UK honour – The Gazette

points.heading: Workplaces and staff networks: plaques and named awards
points.text: Hub proposal: Staff networks can work with leadership to unveil plaques or name awards after the people who built their organisation. University Hospitals of Derby and Burton's EMBRACE network did this with Windrush plaques at every site in October 2024. NHS England's Windrush 70 Awards show that colleagues, patients and the public will nominate in large numbers.

sources.title: UHDB honours the Windrush generation with commemorative plaques – UHDB NHS
Black and ethnic minority NHS staff honoured in NHS Windrush 70 awards – NHS England

points.heading: Schools: record local stories and teach local history
points.text: Hub proposal: Schools can partner with local Black history groups to record grandparents' memories and teach local Black history all year. Portsmouth's project and the Curriculum for Wales are models. A good time to start is Windrush Day (22 June), so the work can be shown the following October.

sources.title: University supports project to share Portsmouth's post-WW2 Black stories – University of Portsmouth
Six things you may not know about the new curriculum (Welsh Government, 14 Jun 2022)

points.heading: Councils and public bodies: small grants, consultations and calendars
points.text: Hub proposal: Councils and public bodies can offer small Black History Month event grants, as Lowestoft does. They can apply each January for the Windrush Day grant, which is open to councils. Before renaming or reinterpreting a contested site, they can run an open consultation, as Bristol did. They can also put 22 June, 1 August, 23 August and October in the civic calendar.

sources.title: Black History Month 2026 – Lowestoft Town Council
Windrush Day Grant Scheme 2026: guidance for applicants – GOV.UK
The Colston Statue: What Next? 'We are Bristol' History Commission – Full Report (UWE repository)

points.heading: Faith and community groups: archives and remembrance
points.text: Hub proposal: Faith and community groups can apply to the Heritage Fund at any time for £10,000 to £250,000 to collect members' memories and records. They can deposit what they gather with a local archive or Black Cultural Archives. They can also hold a public act of remembrance on 23 August, following Liverpool's walk and libation.

sources.title: National Lottery Grants for Heritage £10,000 to £250,000 – National Lottery Heritage Fund
10 years of International Slavery Museum – National Museums Liverpool
