points.heading: Media and cultural institutions: permanent spaces and named honours
points.text: Hub proposal: Media and cultural institutions can give Black history permanent space, not just an October slot. London Museum Docklands and the International Slavery Museum have permanent galleries. Black-led awards such as MOBO and the Powerlist show how naming and ranking achievement builds visibility for young people.

sources.title: London, Sugar & Slavery – London Museum
Powerful Media

points.heading: Government: keep national monuments and grants, publish what is funded
points.text: Hub proposal: Central government can keep funding the Windrush Day grant and publish each year's funded projects, as GOV.UK did for 2026. That lets communities in every region find and copy local models. It can also look after the National Windrush Monument as a place to gather on 22 June.

sources.title: Windrush Day Grant Scheme 2026: projects to be funded – GOV.UK
The National Windrush Monument – GOV.UK

points.heading: Border Cave notched bones, possibly used for counting
points.text: Excavations at Border Cave in the Lebombo Mountains recovered notched bones alongside other early Later Stone Age tools linked to the ancestors of San culture. Researchers suggest the notches may have been used for counting.
points.note: Popular accounts single out one piece as the 'Lebombo bone' and call it a lunar calendar. The research team says only that the bones 'may have been used for counting'; the calendar reading is speculative. Dates refer to the onset of the Later Stone Age at the site (44,000–42,000 years ago) rather than to each object.

sources.title: Later Stone Age got earlier start in South Africa than was previously thought – University of Colorado Boulder
University of the Witwatersrand news, Aug 2012

points.heading: The Ishango bone: grouped notches on a tool handle
points.text: A bone tool handle found in 1950 at Ishango, on the Congolese shore of Lake Edward, carries 168 incisions arranged in groups across three columns. Its excavator thought the groupings might reflect a mathematical link, making it one of the most discussed early marked objects.
points.note: The meaning of the marks is unresolved. Readings as a tally, a lunar calendar or a record of prime numbers are interpretations, not established facts; the Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences, which holds the bone, says it is still not clear what the marks represent. Dating is given as roughly 25,000–20,000 years ago for the lower layers at the site.

sources.title: Ishango – Bones with notches (Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences)
Ishango – Archaeological material (Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences)

points.heading: Kuk: independent invention of farming in New Guinea
points.text: At Kuk swamp, people moved from gathering plants to farming them around 7,000–6,400 years ago, an independent invention of agriculture.
points.note: 'Years ago' converted to approximate calendar years. Begins before the timeline's 3500 BC start.

sources.title: Kuk Early Agricultural Site – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Gunditjmara build eel traps at Budj Bim
points.text: The Gunditjmara people shaped lava-flow waterways at Budj Bim into channels, weirs and ponds to trap and farm eels; a Gunditjmara guide dates the system to about 6,600 years ago.
points.note: Continuing practice; end year 1900 marks the timeline's end, not the end of the system.

sources.title: Indigenous aquaculture site Budj Bim (Council of Australasian Museum Directors)

points.heading: Old Copper complex: early North American metalworking
points.text: As early as c. 4000 BC, Great Lakes peoples mined native copper and hammered it into tools and ornaments.
points.note: Start dates vary; some studies place the earliest copper working thousands of years earlier. Mostly cold-worked, not smelted.

sources.title: Old Copper Complex in North America – EBSCO Research Starters

points.heading: First peoples cross to the Caribbean islands
points.text: The earliest known evidence of people migrating into the Caribbean islands dates to c. 3520–3020 BC.
points.note: The same source notes people reached Trinidad, then joined to South America, much earlier.

sources.title: Amerindian Migrations – Grenada National Museum teacher kit

points.heading: Botai people and early horse herding
points.text: At Botai, c. 3500 BC, people kept large numbers of horses. Pottery residues suggest they used horse milk, but whether the horses were truly domesticated is debated.
points.note: Strongly contested: ancient DNA studies suggest Botai horses were not ancestors of modern domestic horses.

sources.title: Humans domesticated horses – The Conversation

points.heading: Sarazm: Bronze Age metalworking and long-distance trade
points.text: Sarazm was settled from the 4th to the late 3rd millennium BC. Its people worked copper and tin and traded across Central Asia.

sources.title: Proto-urban Site of Sarazm – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Watson Brake earthworks built by hunter-gatherers
points.text: Watson Brake, c. 3500–2800 BC, is among the oldest earthwork mound complexes in North America.
points.note: Early dates for Watson Brake were resisted by some archaeologists when first published in the 1990s.

sources.title: Watson Brake Archaeological Site – 64 Parishes (Louisiana Endowment for the Humanities)

points.heading: Early Egyptian writing on royal tomb labels
points.text: Tags and labels from the tombs of the first Egyptian kings carry some of the earliest writing in the Nile Valley. Egyptians developed their script at about the same time as Mesopotamians.
points.note: The page gives "about 3320 BC"; dating of the earliest Egyptian writing is debated, and the source does not name the site.

sources.title: University of Chicago News: Oriental Institute 'Visible Language' exhibition

points.heading: Liangzhu: early rice-farming state with water works
points.text: Liangzhu, c. 3300–2300 BC, was an early regional state built on rice farming. It had urban planning and a large water conservation system.

sources.title: Archaeological Ruins of Liangzhu City – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Uruk becomes the first true city
points.text: Uruk was the largest settlement in southern Mesopotamia, and perhaps the world. It was a true city of monumental mud-brick buildings.

sources.title: Uruk: The First City - The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)

points.heading: Earliest cuneiform tablets: pictographs on clay
points.text: Pictographs drawn on clay tablets recorded goods and workers' rations. They developed into cuneiform, one of the first writing systems.

sources.title: University of Chicago News: Oriental Institute 'Visible Language' exhibition
Uruk: The First City - The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)

points.heading: Memphis becomes capital of a unified Egypt
points.text: Memphis is traditionally said to have been founded as the capital of a politically unified Egypt. It stayed the seat of royal power for over eight dynasties.
points.note: UNESCO gives this as a traditional date.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Memphis and its Necropolis - the Pyramid Fields from Giza to Dahshur

points.heading: Hieroglyphic numerals in use in Egypt
points.text: Egyptians wrote numbers with hieroglyphic signs for ones, tens, hundreds and higher powers of ten. This decimal way of counting underpinned later Egyptian mathematics.
points.note: Listed under the year -3000 in the MacTutor chronology.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Chronology 30000 BC - 500 BC

points.heading: First Stonehenge: a circular ditch and bank
points.text: The earliest known major event at Stonehenge was digging a circular ditch and bank. It was an early form of henge monument.

sources.title: English Heritage: History of Stonehenge

points.heading: Base-60 counting used for accounts
points.text: Mesopotamians began using a sexagesimal (base-60) place-value number system for financial records. We still use base 60 for hours, minutes and degrees.
points.note: Listed under the year -3000 in the MacTutor chronology; the system developed over time.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Chronology 30000 BC - 500 BC

points.heading: Dholavira's walled city and water management
points.text: Dholavira, a Harappan city in a dry region, was occupied c. 3000–1500 BC. Its people built a sophisticated system to collect and store scarce water.

sources.title: Dholavira: a Harappan City – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Caral: earliest known civilisation in the Americas
points.text: Caral, built c. 3000–1800 BC, has monumental earthen platforms and sunken circular plazas. UNESCO calls it the earliest known civilisation in the Americas.

sources.title: Sacred City of Caral-Supe – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Egyptian civil calendar in use
points.text: Egypt used a calendar to organise the year, linked to the seasons of the Nile. It is one of the earliest calendars on record.
points.note: Chronology date; the origin of the Egyptian calendar is debated by scholars.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Chronology 30000 BC - 500 BC

points.heading: Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, later hero of epics
points.text: Uruk was surrounded by a massive wall said to have been built by King Gilgamesh. He became the hero of many later stories and epics.
points.note: Whether Gilgamesh was a historical king is uncertain.

sources.title: Uruk: The First City - The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)

points.heading: Great Pyramid of Khufu built at Giza
points.text: The Great Pyramid was built for King Khufu during the Old Kingdom. It was the tallest human-made structure for thousands of years.

sources.title: Giza - Great Pyramid of Khufu - Institute of Egyptian Art & Archaeology (University of Memphis)

points.heading: Stonehenge stones raised, aligned on the solstice
points.text: Great stones were set up at the centre of Stonehenge in about 2500 BC. Monuments in the landscape keep their alignment on the solstice sunrise and sunset.

sources.title: English Heritage: History of Stonehenge
Stonehenge, Avebury and Associated Sites - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Mohenjo-daro: planned city with sanitation and drainage
points.text: Mohenjo-daro flourished c. 2500–1500 BC. Its baked-brick streets were laid out in an orderly plan with built-in sanitation and drainage.

sources.title: Archaeological Ruins at Moenjodaro – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Harappans adopt uniform decimal weights and measures
points.text: The Indus civilisation, c. 2500–1700 BC, used a standard system of weights based on decimal ratios. Shared standards helped trade between its many towns.

sources.title: An overview of Indian mathematics – MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Indus script used on seals and objects
points.text: Harappan people wrote with a script of around 500 signs, c. 2500–1700 BC. It has not been convincingly deciphered.
points.note: Britannica gives core dates of about 2600–1900 BCE for the civilisation; sources vary.

sources.title: An overview of Indian mathematics – MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Lothal serves as a Harappan port and trading post
points.text: Lothal, on the Gulf of Khambhat, worked as a coastal trading station for the Indus civilisation, c. 2500–1700 BC.
points.note: Date range is that of the Indus civilisation as a whole; the Lothal page itself gives no dates.

sources.title: Lothal – Britannica
An overview of Indian mathematics – MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Bronze Age towns of the Murghab oasis
points.text: The Merv oasis has supported towns since the 3rd millennium BC, with Bronze Age centres dating c. 2500–1200 BC.

sources.title: State Historical and Cultural Park 'Ancient Merv' – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Quipu: knotted-cord records
points.text: Andean peoples recorded numbers on knotted cords, called quipu, from c. 2500 BC. The Inca used them for taxes, census data and storehouse stocks.
points.note: Very early quipu dates are debated; the Caral find is cited by UNESCO.

sources.title: Quipu – Britannica
Sacred City of Caral-Supe – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Metalworking knowledge reaches Britain with Beaker culture
points.text: Knowledge of metalworking arrived in Britain from the Continent as Stonehenge was being built. Rich 'Beaker' graves such as the Amesbury Archer appear nearby.

sources.title: English Heritage: History of Stonehenge

points.heading: Sargon of Akkad founds the first empire
points.text: Sargon conquered southern Mesopotamia and founded the Akkadian empire. At its height it reached as far as Anatolia.
points.note: Reign dates are approximate; "first empire" is a common description, not in the quoted text.

sources.title: The Akkadian Period (ca. 2350-2150 B.C.) - The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)

points.heading: Dilmun trading port flourishes in the Gulf
points.text: Qal'at al-Bahrain was a trading port and capital of Dilmun, one of the region's most important ancient civilisations.

sources.title: Qal'at al-Bahrain - Ancient Harbour and Capital of Dilmun - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: San rock painting tradition in the Drakensberg
points.text: The San painted animals and people in the Drakensberg over some 4,000 years. The paintings show their spiritual life and beliefs, into the 19th century.
points.note: Start date estimated from "4,000 years"; individual paintings are hard to date.

sources.title: Maloti-Drakensberg Park - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Hattusha, capital of the Hittite Empire
points.text: Hattusha was the capital of the Hittite Empire, which was powerful in Anatolia and northern Syria.
points.note: End date approximates the end of the 2nd millennium BC.

sources.title: Hattusha: the Hittite Capital - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Kuk farmers drain wetlands with ditches
points.text: From about 4,000 years ago, Kuk farmers dug ditches with wooden tools to drain the wetland for cultivation.

sources.title: Kuk Early Agricultural Site – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Babylonians solve quadratic equations
points.text: Babylonian scribes solved quadratic equations on clay tablets. They also compiled tables of squares and cube roots.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Chronology 30000 BC - 500 BC

points.heading: Moscow Papyrus records Egyptian geometry
points.text: The Moscow papyrus is one of the oldest surviving mathematical texts. It includes geometry problems such as volumes.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Chronology 30000 BC - 500 BC

points.heading: Minoan palaces and Linear A writing
points.text: Major palaces were built at Knossos and Mallia, and with them came writing. Linear A was perhaps inspired by eastern Mediterranean cuneiform.
points.note: Linear A has not been deciphered.

sources.title: Minoan Crete - The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)

points.heading: First alphabet derived from Egyptian hieroglyphs
points.text: The earliest alphabetic texts, found in the Sinai, adapted Egyptian hieroglyphs to write sounds. This alphabet is an ancestor of many later alphabets.
points.note: Dating of Proto-Sinaitic inscriptions is debated; earlier views placed the first alphabet in Phoenicia about 1000 BC.

sources.title: University of Chicago News: Oriental Institute 'Visible Language' exhibition

points.heading: Code of Hammurabi carved on a stone stele
points.text: Hammurabi of Babylon had his laws and judgements carved on a stone stele. It is one of the best-known early law codes.
points.note: Source is in French; dates are the reign of Hammurabi. Earlier law codes (such as that of Ur-Nammu) existed.

sources.title: Code de Hammurabi - Collections du Louvre

points.heading: Rhind Papyrus sets out Egyptian arithmetic
points.text: The Rhind (Ahmes) papyrus is a teaching text of worked problems. It shows multiplication by doubling and division by halving.
points.note: MacTutor lists c. 1700 BC; it is dated by a reign year of the Hyksos king Apophis, usually placed in the mid-17th to 16th century BC. Place is the usual attribution, not stated in the sources.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Chronology 30000 BC - 500 BC
Papyrus Edwin Smith - Science in Ancient Egypt (Saxon Academy of Sciences in Leipzig)

points.heading: Poverty Point earthworks and trade network
points.text: Hunter-fisher-gatherers built the Poverty Point earthworks c. 3,700–3,100 years ago, supplied by trade in stone from far away.
points.note: 'Years ago' converted to approximate calendar years.

sources.title: Monumental Earthworks of Poverty Point – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Edwin Smith Papyrus: early surgical treatise copied
points.text: The Edwin Smith papyrus describes the examination and treatment of injuries in a careful, case-by-case way. The surviving copy may come from an older original.
points.note: Copy date estimates range from c. 1650 to c. 1550 BC; the original text may be centuries older.

sources.title: Papyrus Edwin Smith - Science in Ancient Egypt (Saxon Academy of Sciences in Leipzig)

points.heading: Lapita voyagers settle the western Pacific
points.text: Lapita seafarers spread from the Bismarck Archipelago to the Solomons from c. 1600 BC and reached Fiji, Tonga and Samoa by 1000 BC.
points.note: Many archaeologists now date Lapita's start to c. 1350–1300 BC, later than Britannica's 1600 BC.

sources.title: Lapita culture – Britannica

points.heading: Chavín de Huántar temple and galleries
points.text: Chavín de Huántar developed c. 1500–300 BC. Its temple has an internal network of galleries, vents and drains unmatched in South America.

sources.title: Chavin (Archaeological Site) – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Ban Chiang: early bronze-making and rice farming
points.text: Ban Chiang was occupied from 1495 BC to c. 900 BC. It holds early evidence of bronze-making and of rice farming in the region.
points.note: Ban Chiang's chronology has been revised several times since 1966; UNESCO notes the dating has been 'adjusted and refined'.

sources.title: Ban Chiang Archaeological Site – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Shang oracle-bone inscriptions: earliest mature Chinese writing
points.text: At the late Shang capital of Yin Xu (c. 1300–1046 BC), inscriptions on oracle bones are the earliest known mature writing in China.

sources.title: Yin Xu – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Shang bronze casting reaches a high level
points.text: The late Shang capital, c. 1300–1046 BC, shows advanced bronze casting alongside a calendar system.

sources.title: Yin Xu – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Elamite ziggurat of Choga Zanbil built
points.text: The Elamite king Untash-Napirisha founded Choga Zanbil with an enormous ziggurat. It is the largest ziggurat outside Mesopotamia.

sources.title: Tchogha Zanbil - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Olmec civilisation sets Mesoamerican patterns
points.text: The Olmec, c. 1200–400 BC, were the first elaborate civilisation of Mesoamerica, known for colossal basalt heads.

sources.title: Olmec – Britannica

points.heading: Phoenician alphabet spreads across the Mediterranean
points.text: The Phoenicians used an alphabetic script that became the root of Western alphabets. Byblos is linked with its spread.
points.note: Earlier alphabetic texts from Sinai (c. 1800 BC) mean the Phoenician script was a development, not the first alphabet.

sources.title: The Phoenicians (1500-300 B.C.) - The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)
University of Chicago News: Oriental Institute 'Visible Language' exhibition
Byblos - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Napatan Kush builds temples, palaces and pyramids
points.text: At Gebel Barkal the Napatan kingdom of Kush built temples, palaces and royal tombs, some with pyramids. Kush was a major Nile power in its own right.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Gebel Barkal and the Sites of the Napatan Region

points.heading: Carthage founded on the Gulf of Tunis
points.text: Phoenician settlers founded Carthage, which became a great trading empire across much of the Mediterranean. It lasted until Rome destroyed it in 146 BC.
points.note: 814 BC is the traditional date.

sources.title: The Phoenicians (1500-300 B.C.) - The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)
Archaeological Site of Carthage - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Baudhayana Sulbasutra: geometry for altar building
points.text: The Baudhayana Sulbasutra, written c. 800 BC, gave geometric rules for building altars, including Pythagorean triples.
points.note: Dates of the Sulbasutras are approximate; MacTutor gives the texts a span of about the 15th to 5th century BC.

sources.title: The Indian Sulbasutras – MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Polynesian ancestors settle Samoa
points.text: Polynesian ancestors had settled in Samoa by around 800 BC.

sources.title: East Polynesia colonized faster and more recently than previously thought – University of Hawaiʻi

points.heading: Kingdom of Kush rules the Middle Nile
points.text: Kush was a major power for over a thousand years and its rulers occupied Egypt for close to a century. Meroe was its heartland.

sources.title: Archaeological Sites of the Island of Meroe, UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Phoenician sea traders found trading posts
points.text: Phoenician sailors set up trading posts around the Mediterranean, alongside the Greeks. They were famous seafarers and traders.

sources.title: The Phoenicians (1500-300 B.C.) - The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)

points.heading: Samarkand founded as Afrasiab
points.text: Samarkand was founded as Afrasiab in the 7th century BC and grew into a great crossroads city of the Silk Roads.

sources.title: Samarkand – Crossroad of Cultures – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Ashurbanipal's library gathers over 30,000 tablets
points.text: King Ashurbanipal assembled a great library at Nineveh. Over 30,000 cuneiform tablets were found in its ruins.

sources.title: What was Ashurbanipal's Library? - British Museum

points.heading: Lydians invent coinage
points.text: Ancient writers credited the Lydians with inventing coins, first made of electrum, a natural gold-silver alloy. Coins were minted at Sardis for about 1,000 years.
points.note: Exact date of the first coins is debated (late 7th century BC is widely cited).

sources.title: The Coins of Sardis (J. H. Kroll), The Lydians and their World - The Archaeological Exploration of Sardis (Harvard)

points.heading: Babylon rebuilt as Neo-Babylonian capital
points.text: Babylon was the capital of the Neo-Babylonian Empire under rulers such as Nebuchadnezzar. It is linked with the Hanging Gardens, a wonder of the ancient world.
points.note: The existence and location of the Hanging Gardens are debated.

sources.title: Babylon - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Sushruta's treatise on surgery
points.text: The surgeon Sushruta, active c. 6th century BC, is known for the Sushruta-samhita and early operations such as rebuilding the nose.
points.note: Dating of Sushruta and the compilation of the Sushruta-samhita is debated; many scholars place the text later.

sources.title: Sushruta – Britannica

points.heading: First pure gold coins struck in Lydia
points.text: Lydia's king Croesus introduced coins of solid gold, called Croeseids. Making them needed ways to separate gold from silver.
points.note: Croesus reigned c. 560-546 BC (not stated in the quoted text); the start of refining is debated.

sources.title: The Coins of Sardis (J. H. Kroll), The Lydians and their World - The Archaeological Exploration of Sardis (Harvard)

points.heading: Confucius teaches ethics and statecraft
points.text: Confucius (551–479 BC) became China's most famous teacher and political thinker. The Analects record his teaching.

sources.title: Confucius – Britannica

points.heading: Achaemenid Persia builds roads and a governor system
points.text: The Achaemenid Empire formed from 550 BC. Darius I stabilised it with roads for communication and provincial governors (satraps).

sources.title: The Achaemenid Persian Empire (550-330 B.C.) - The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)

points.heading: Panini writes a scientific grammar of Sanskrit
points.text: Panini, c. 520–460 BC, set out a comprehensive theory of Sanskrit sound and word structure. His dates are uncertain.
points.note: MacTutor gives about 520–460 BC but notes experts date him anywhere from the 7th to the 4th century BC.

sources.title: Panini – Biography – MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Darius I founds Persepolis
points.text: Darius I founded Persepolis as a capital of the Achaemenid Empire. Its terrace palaces are among the great works of ancient architecture.

sources.title: Persepolis - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Nok culture: early ironworking and terracotta sculpture
points.text: The Nok culture made striking terracotta figures and was one of the earliest centres of ironworking in Africa. Many questions about it remain open.
points.note: Date range is the Met heading; ironworking dates in the region are debated.

sources.title: Nok Terracottas (500 B.C.-200 A.D.) | Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, The Met

points.heading: Shushtar hydraulic system for water and mills
points.text: The hydraulic system at Shushtar, traced back to Darius the Great, used tunnels and channels to supply water to the city and its mills.

sources.title: Shushtar Historical Hydraulic System - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Babylonians predict planetary positions mathematically
points.text: Babylonian astronomers used their base-60 numbers to record and predict the positions of the Sun, Moon and planets.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Chronology 500 BC - 1

points.heading: Taxila becomes a Buddhist centre of learning
points.text: From c. 5th century BC to the 2nd century AD, Taxila was an important Buddhist centre of learning on routes linking South and Central Asia.

sources.title: Taxila – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Grand Canal links China's great rivers
points.text: Built in sections from the 5th century BC, the Grand Canal became one unified waterway in the 7th century AD. By the 13th century it ran over 2,000 km.

sources.title: The Grand Canal – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Dong Son bronze culture
points.text: The Dong Son culture of northern Viet Nam, c. 5th–1st century BC, is known for its bronze work, including large decorated drums.
points.note: The quote is a section heading on the Britannica page; the drums are not described on that page.

sources.title: Southeast Asian arts – Vietnam – Britannica

points.heading: Pazyryk tombs preserve textiles and tattoos
points.text: Frozen tombs at Pazyryk, c. 5th–3rd century BC, preserved some of the oldest surviving textiles and a man covered in tattoos.

sources.title: Pazyryk – Britannica

points.heading: Monte Albán: Zapotec capital
points.text: Monte Albán was the great Zapotec capital for thirteen centuries, from 500 BC to AD 850. Its monuments carry hieroglyphic inscriptions.

sources.title: Historic Centre of Oaxaca and Archaeological Site of Monte Albán – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Nasca lines scratched into the desert
points.text: Between 500 BC and AD 500 people scratched huge lines and figures into the surface of the Nasca desert.

sources.title: Lines and Geoglyphs of Nasca and Palpa – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Saladoid farmers and potters settle the Caribbean
points.text: Around 500 BC Saladoid people from the Orinoco basin in Venezuela moved into the Caribbean islands, bringing farming and pottery.

sources.title: Amerindian Migrations – Grenada National Museum teacher kit

points.heading: Parthenon and Acropolis monuments built in Athens
points.text: Under the statesman Pericles, artists built the Parthenon and other monuments on the Acropolis. UNESCO links the site with the birth of democracy and philosophy.

sources.title: Acropolis, Athens - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: First compilation of the elements of geometry
points.text: Hippocrates of Chios wrote the first known collection of the basic results of geometry, before Euclid.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Chronology 500 BC - 1

points.heading: Babylonians use a placeholder sign like zero
points.text: Babylonian scribes used a sign to mark an empty place in numbers. It was an early step towards zero, though not yet a number.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Chronology 500 BC - 1

points.heading: Nabataean Petra becomes a caravan city
points.text: Petra, the rock-cut capital of the Nabataeans, was a major caravan centre for incense, silks and spices. A clever water system made life possible in the desert.

sources.title: Petra - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Moche copper and gold metalwork
points.text: Moche artisans made masks of copper–gold alloy. A mask from Huaca de la Luna is dated c. 400 BC–AD 600.
points.note: The date is from a Britannica image caption; the Moche culture is usually dated c. AD 100–800.

sources.title: Pre-Columbian civilizations – Early Intermediate period – Britannica

points.heading: Plato founds the Academy in Athens
points.text: Plato set up his Academy, a school of philosophy and mathematics that lasted for centuries.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Chronology 500 BC - 1

points.heading: Iron-working and trade at Meroe
points.text: Excavations at Meroe show production of ceramics and iron along a major trade corridor. This makes Meroe an important early ironworking centre on the Nile.
points.note: Dates are approximate ("later centuries BCE and the first few centuries CE").

sources.title: Archaeological Sites of the Island of Meroe, UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Library of Alexandria founded
points.text: The Ptolemies built a library and research institute at Alexandria. It became the most famous centre of scholarship in the ancient Mediterranean.
points.note: Founding dates are approximate; Britannica also says Alexander the Great initiated the collection in 334 BCE.

sources.title: Library of Alexandria | Britannica
Eratosthenes of Cyrene - Biography - MacTutor History of Mathematics

points.heading: Euclid's Elements written at Alexandria
points.text: Euclid, who taught at Alexandria, set out geometry as a system built from definitions and proofs. The Elements was used as a textbook for over 2,000 years.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Chronology 500 BC - 1
Euclid of Alexandria - MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Nalanda Mahavihara: monastic university
points.text: Nalanda was a monastic and scholarly institution from the 3rd century BC to the 13th century AD. It passed on knowledge without a break for some 800 years.
points.note: Many sources date Nalanda as a university to the 5th century AD; UNESCO dates the wider site's remains from the 3rd century BC.

sources.title: Archaeological Site of Nalanda Mahavihara at Nalanda, Bihar – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Huangdi neijing sets out Chinese medical theory
points.text: The Huangdi neijing, the theoretical base of traditional Chinese medicine, was composed around the 3rd century BC. It stresses prevention and balance.
points.note: Dating is approximate; the text was compiled over time.

sources.title: Huangdi neijing – Britannica

points.heading: Aristarchus proposes that the Earth orbits the Sun
points.text: Aristarchus of Samos used geometry to estimate the distances of the Sun and Moon. He also suggested that the Earth moves around the Sun.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Chronology 500 BC - 1

points.heading: Ashoka's edicts carved on rocks and pillars
points.text: The Maurya emperor Ashoka (reigned c. 265–238 BC) published his policies in rock and pillar edicts and appointed officers to promote dharma.
points.note: Britannica gives two reign ranges: c. 265–238 BC and c. 273–232 BC.

sources.title: Ashoka – Britannica

points.heading: Dujiangyan irrigation system begun
points.text: The Dujiangyan system, begun around 256 BC, diverts the Minjiang River to irrigate the Chengdu plain. It is still in use.
points.note: The UNESCO page also once gives '2nd century BCE'; the c. 256 BC date is the one most often cited.

sources.title: Mount Qingcheng and the Dujiangyan Irrigation System – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Djenne settled; later a trans-Saharan gold market
points.text: The Djenne area has been lived in since about 250 BC. Djenne grew into a market centre and an important link in the trans-Saharan gold trade.
points.note: UNESCO spells it Djenné; accents removed here.

sources.title: Old Towns of Djenné, UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Archimedes calculates volumes of spheres and cylinders
points.text: Archimedes found formulae for the volume of a sphere and cylinder and approximated pi. He also stated the principle of floating bodies.
points.note: Place is where Archimedes lived; not stated in the quoted entry.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Chronology 500 BC - 1

points.heading: Brahmi numerals: ancestors of today's digits
points.text: By around the mid-3rd century BC, Brahmi numerals were in use. After many changes they became the digits 1 to 9 used worldwide.

sources.title: An overview of Indian mathematics – MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Chankillo's thirteen towers track the Sun
points.text: Chankillo, used c. 250–200 BC, has a line of 13 towers that marked sunrise and sunset to fix dates through the year.

sources.title: Chankillo Archaeoastronomical Complex – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Eratosthenes measures the Earth's circumference
points.text: Eratosthenes, librarian at Alexandria, estimated the Earth's size using shadows and geometry. His result was close to the true value.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Chronology 500 BC - 1
Eratosthenes of Cyrene - Biography - MacTutor History of Mathematics

points.heading: Terracotta army guards the first emperor's tomb
points.text: Qin Shi Huang, first unifier of China, died in 210 BC. His tomb is guarded by thousands of life-size terracotta warriors.

sources.title: Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Competitive examinations to recruit officials
points.text: China's examination system, with roots in the Han imperial university (from 206 BC), selected officials by competitive tests until it was abolished in 1905.
points.note: Start date marks the Han roots; the full examination system developed later, especially under the Sui and Song.

sources.title: Chinese examination system – Britannica

points.heading: Sanchi stupas and Buddhist monuments
points.text: Most of Sanchi's Buddhist monuments date from the 2nd and 1st centuries BC. It is the oldest Buddhist sanctuary still in existence.

sources.title: Buddhist Monuments at Sanchi – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Ajanta cave paintings and sculpture
points.text: Buddhist caves at Ajanta were begun in the 2nd and 1st centuries BC. Many richly decorated caves were added in the 5th and 6th centuries AD.

sources.title: Ajanta Caves – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art
points.text: The Nine Chapters, a key Chinese mathematics text, probably took shape around 200 BC. It was later explained by Liu Hui.
points.note: Liu Hui believed parts were much older (around 1000 BC); MacTutor says most historians favour about 200 BC.

sources.title: Nine chapters on the Mathematical Art – MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Pyu city-states: South-East Asia's first large cities
points.text: From c. 2nd century BC to the 9th century AD, the Pyu built the region's earliest large walled cities, with skilled water management.

sources.title: Pyu Ancient Cities – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Silk Roads network takes shape
points.text: Between the 2nd century BC and 1st century AD a 5,000 km network of trade routes formed across Central Asia. It stayed in use until the 16th century.

sources.title: Silk Roads: the Routes Network of Chang'an-Tianshan Corridor – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Hipparchus discovers the precession of the equinoxes
points.text: Hipparchus found the slow shift of the equinoxes and measured the year very accurately. His work used an early form of trigonometry.
points.note: Place is where Hipparchus worked; not stated in the quoted entry.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Chronology 500 BC - 1

points.heading: Ifugao rice terraces climb the Cordillera
points.text: UNESCO describes the Ifugao rice terraces as about 2,000 years old, farmed by communities who pass the skills between generations.
points.note: UNESCO's '2,000 years' is a round figure; some recent archaeological studies argue many terraces are much younger. Year range here is a placeholder for 'about 2,000 years ago'.

sources.title: Rice Terraces of the Philippine Cordilleras – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Early Maya hieroglyphs at San Bartolo
points.text: Maya hieroglyphs found at San Bartolo date from as early as c. 100 BC.
points.note: Other studies date the earliest San Bartolo writing to c. 300–200 BC; Britannica gives c. 100 BC.

sources.title: Pre-Columbian civilizations – Late Formative Period – Britannica

points.heading: Stela C: early Long Count calendar date
points.text: Stela C at Tres Zapotes bears a Long Count date read as 31 BC, over a century before any dated Maya monument.
points.note: Other sources give 32 BC or cite an earlier Long Count date at Chiapa de Corzo (36 BC).

sources.title: Pre-Columbian civilizations – Late Formative Period – Britannica

points.heading: Aksum raises monolithic obelisks
points.text: Massive ruins at Aksum, dated from the 1st to the 13th century AD, include monolithic obelisks.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Aksum

points.heading: Teotihuacan's Pyramids of the Sun and Moon
points.text: Teotihuacan was built between the 1st and 7th centuries AD, laid out on geometric principles around the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon.

sources.title: Pre-Hispanic City of Teotihuacan – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Hopewell earthworks aligned to Sun and Moon
points.text: Between AD 1 and 400, Hopewell communities built huge geometric earthworks aligned with the cycles of the Sun and Moon.

sources.title: Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Cai Lun presents paper to the emperor
points.text: About AD 105 the court official Cai Lun made sheets of paper from tree bark and other fibres. It wrote better than silk cloth.
points.note: Britannica says Cai Lun is 'traditionally credited'; archaeology has found earlier paper in China.

sources.title: Cai Lun – Britannica

points.heading: Ptolemy's astronomy, dominant for over a thousand years
points.text: Ptolemy observed the sky from Alexandria and wrote a full mathematical model of the heavens. His system was accepted for well over 1,000 years.

sources.title: Claudius Ptolemy - MacTutor, University of St Andrews
MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Chronology 1 - 500

points.heading: Galen of Pergamum shapes medicine for centuries
points.text: Galen, born in Pergamum, wrote medical works that dominated medical theory in Europe and the Islamic world until the 17th century.

sources.title: Galen | Britannica

points.heading: Zhang Heng builds a seismoscope
points.text: In AD 132 Zhang Heng built an instrument to detect earthquakes. He also made an early equatorial armillary sphere.

sources.title: Zhang Heng – Biography – MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Bakhshali manuscript: oldest recorded zero symbol
points.text: Radiocarbon dating in 2017 suggested parts of the Bakhshali manuscript date from the 3rd or 4th century AD. It contains hundreds of zeros used as placeholders.
points.note: Highly contested. Before 2017, Hayashi dated it to the 8th–12th centuries; the Oxford radiocarbon dates differ between leaves, and some scholars question the interpretation.

sources.title: Carbon dating finds Bakhshali manuscript contains oldest recorded origins of the symbol 'zero' – Bodleian Libraries, University of Oxford
The Bakhshali manuscript – MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Diophantus writes Arithmetica on number problems
points.text: Diophantus of Alexandria wrote Arithmetica, a collection of number problems. It later influenced algebra in the Islamic world and Europe.
points.note: Listed under AD 250 in the MacTutor chronology; his dates are uncertain.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Chronology 1 - 500

points.heading: Tikal's dated stelae span 577 years
points.text: Tikal's earliest carved monument, Stela 29, is dated 292 AD; the last, Stela 11, is dated 869.

sources.title: Tikal National Park – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Aksum's coins carry Ge'ez and Greek inscriptions
points.text: Aksum minted its own coins. Gold coins were inscribed in Greek for export, and silver and copper coins in Ge'ez, the Aksumite script.
points.note: Aksumite coinage began earlier (under King Endubis); exact dates are debated. 'insribed' is the source's spelling.

sources.title: British Museum (via Smarthistory): Aksumite coins

points.heading: My Son tower temples of the Cham kingdom
points.text: The Cham people built tower temples at My Son from the 4th to the 13th centuries AD.

sources.title: My Son Sanctuary – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: King Ezana of Aksum converts to Christianity
points.text: King Ezana's conversion made Aksum one of the earliest Christian states. Its coins changed to carry Christian symbols.

sources.title: British Museum (via Smarthistory): Aksumite coins

points.heading: Ge Hong's fever remedy that later led to artemisinin
points.text: Around AD 340 the Chinese physician Ge Hong described a remedy made by taking juice from sweet wormwood (Artemisia annua, qinghao) leaves with cold water rather than boiling them. Centuries later Tu Youyou used this clue to extract artemisinin, a malaria drug that won her a share of the 2015 Nobel Prize.
points.note: Ge Hong wrote long before the modern understanding of malaria; the scientific link between his recipe and the malaria parasite was made by Tu Youyou's team from the late 1960s.

sources.title: The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2015 – Advanced information, NobelPrize.org
The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2015 – Press release, NobelPrize.org
Indian Pediatrics 2011;48:914 (news item)

points.heading: Hypatia heads the Neo-Platonist school at Alexandria
points.text: Hypatia wrote commentaries on mathematics and led a philosophical school in Alexandria. She is the first recorded woman mathematician.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Chronology 1 - 500

points.heading: Camel caravans begin crossing the Sahara
points.text: With camels, Berber-speaking peoples began crossing the Sahara. This opened the trade routes that later linked West Africa with the Mediterranean.
points.note: Approximate date.

sources.title: The Trans-Saharan Gold Trade (7th-14th Century) - The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)

points.heading: Zu Chongzhi calculates pi as 355/113
points.text: Zu Chongzhi (429–501) gave 355/113 as a value for pi, correct to six decimal places.

sources.title: Zu Chongzhi – Biography – MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Ancestral Pueblo farming and cliff dwellings
points.text: Ancestral Pueblo people lived at Mesa Verde c. 450–1300, farming with terraces and check dams and building some 600 cliff dwellings.

sources.title: Mesa Verde National Park – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Aryabhata completes the Aryabhatiya
points.text: Aryabhata finished the Aryabhatiya in 499 AD. He argued that the heavens appear to turn because the Earth rotates on its axis.

sources.title: Aryabhata I – Biography – MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Ife grows from hamlets into a sacred kingdom
points.text: Ife began as a cluster of about thirteen hamlets and became the seat of Yoruba sacred kingship. Yoruba monarchs still trace their lineage to its founding.

sources.title: The Met, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History: Ife (from ca. 6th century)

points.heading: Palenque at its height
points.text: Palenque, a Classic Maya city, was at its height between AD 500 and 700.

sources.title: Pre-Hispanic City and National Park of Palenque – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Tiwanaku raised fields feed an empire
points.text: Tiwanaku reached its height between AD 500 and 900, fed by almost 50,000 raised farm fields known as Sukakollos.

sources.title: Tiwanaku: Spiritual and Political Centre of the Tiwanaku Culture – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Hagia Sophia designed by mathematician Anthemius
points.text: The great domed church of Hagia Sophia was designed by Anthemius of Tralles, a mathematician. Its dome was an engineering landmark.
points.note: Completion date 537 is general knowledge, not in the quoted source.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Chronology 500 - 900

points.heading: Srivijaya controls sea trade through the Strait of Malacca
points.text: Srivijaya, a maritime kingdom from the 7th to 13th centuries, controlled the Strait of Malacca. It was also a Buddhist centre visited by Chinese pilgrims.

sources.title: Srivijaya empire – Britannica

points.heading: Dresden Codex astronomical tables
points.text: The Dresden Codex, an astronomy treatise, was probably copied in the 11th century AD from an original of the 7th or 8th century.
points.note: Dating of the Dresden Codex varies between sources (often 11th–13th century for the copy).

sources.title: Mayan mathematics – MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Brahmagupta defines zero and rules for negative numbers
points.text: In 628 AD Brahmagupta wrote the Brahmasphutasiddhanta. He defined zero as a number subtracted from itself and gave rules for arithmetic with zero.

sources.title: Brahmagupta – Biography – MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Cheomseongdae observatory built in Silla
points.text: Cheomseongdae in Gyeongju was built under Queen Seondeok of Silla, who ruled 632–647. It is described as Asia's oldest astronomical observatory.
points.note: Its exact use as an observatory is debated by scholars; source is the Korean government's official website.

sources.title: [World Heritage Festival ②] Silla heritage shines in Gyeongju – Korea.net

points.heading: Maya base-20 place value with a zero
points.text: By 665 the Maya used a place-value number system in base 20 with its own symbol for zero.
points.note: 665 is MacTutor's 'by' date; Maya zero signs in Long Count dates are found earlier.

sources.title: A history of Zero - MacTutor, University of St Andrews
Mayan mathematics – MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Kairouan founded, with the Great Mosque
points.text: Kairouan was founded in 670 and its Great Mosque became a model for mosques across the Maghreb. The city was capital of Ifriqiya for five centuries.

sources.title: Kairouan - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Horyu-ji: among the oldest surviving wooden buildings
points.text: After a fire in 670, Horyu-ji was rebuilt into the early 8th century. Several of its buildings are among the oldest surviving wooden buildings in the world.

sources.title: Buddhist Monuments in the Horyu-ji Area – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Early dated zeros in South-East Asian inscriptions
points.text: Stone inscriptions from Sumatra and Cambodia carry dates equal to AD 683–686 written with a zero placeholder. Some scholars see these as the earliest dated zeros.
points.note: The claim to the 'first' zero is contested between South Asian and South-East Asian evidence (see Bakhshali and Gwalior). Source is an opinion article by the researchers making the case.

sources.title: The Elusive Origin of Zero – Scientific American

points.heading: Kojiki: Japan's earliest surviving chronicle
points.text: The Kojiki, compiled in 712, records events reign by reign. It is the oldest surviving Japanese chronicle.
points.note: 'Oldest surviving' is widely stated but is not in the quoted source.

sources.title: Chronology – Japanese – Britannica

points.heading: Orkhon inscriptions: oldest surviving Turkic writings
points.text: Two large stone monuments, put up in 732 and 735 for the prince Kül and his brother, carry the oldest surviving Turkic texts.

sources.title: Orhon inscriptions – Britannica

points.heading: Kisalian culture works iron and copper
points.text: Graves of the Kisalian culture contain many iron tools and ornaments and copper jewellery. They show a skilled metalworking society with emerging elites.

sources.title: Upemba Depression (N. Nikis, 2021) - Royal Museum for Central Africa

points.heading: Borobudur built under the Sailendra dynasty
points.text: Borobudur, a vast Buddhist monument covered in carved reliefs, was built in the 8th and 9th centuries AD.

sources.title: Borobudur Temple Compounds – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Igbo-Ukwu bronzes cast with great skill
points.text: Bronze objects from Igbo-Ukwu show very fine casting. The materials were obtained partly through long-distance trade.
points.note: The Met notes the ninth-century date remains controversial.

sources.title: Igbo-Ukwu (ca. 9th Century) - The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)

points.heading: Swahili trading city of Kilwa occupied
points.text: Kilwa Kisiwani was a Swahili trading city occupied from the 9th to the 19th century. It shows the growth of Swahili culture and commerce on the coast.

sources.title: Ruins of Kilwa Kisiwani and Ruins of Songo Mnara, UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Copper cross ingots used across south-central Africa
points.text: Cross-shaped copper ingots made in the Copperbelt spread widely. In time small ingots acted as a general purpose currency.
points.note: The currency use is of the later, smaller ingots.

sources.title: Upemba Depression (N. Nikis, 2021) - Royal Museum for Central Africa

points.heading: Angkor: Khmer capitals and reservoirs
points.text: Angkor holds the capitals of the Khmer Empire from the 9th to the 15th century, with temples, canals and large water reservoirs.

sources.title: Angkor – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Bukhara becomes a great centre of Islamic learning
points.text: Bukhara became a major cultural centre in the 8th century. From the 9th to the 16th century it was the largest centre of Muslim theology.

sources.title: Historic Centre of Bukhara – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: House of Wisdom set up in Baghdad
points.text: Scholars at the House of Wisdom translated Greek and Indian mathematics and astronomy into Arabic. Its library was the largest since Alexandria.
points.note: Founding date is approximate.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Chronology 500 - 900
MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews: Al-Khwarizmi biography

points.heading: Al-Khwarizmi writes the book that gives us algebra
points.text: Al-Khwarizmi's book on 'completion and balancing' gave us the word algebra. The word algorithm comes from his name.
points.note: Listed under the year 810 in the MacTutor chronology.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Chronology 500 - 900

points.heading: Kanem empire founded near Lake Chad
points.text: Kanem-Bornu was probably founded in the mid-9th century, with its first capital at Njimi. It controlled the Lake Chad region until the 19th century.
points.note: Britannica says "probably".

sources.title: Britannica: Kanem-Bornu

points.heading: Chan Chan: largest earthen city in the Americas
points.text: Chan Chan, capital of the Chimú kingdom (9th–15th centuries), was the largest earthen-built city of pre-Columbian America, fed by a long irrigation canal.
points.note: End date c. 1470 (Inca conquest) is implied by 'not long before falling to the Incas'.

sources.title: Chan Chan Archaeological Zone – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Chaco: great houses linked by engineered roads
points.text: Chaco Canyon was a major Ancestral Pueblo centre from 850 to 1250. Its great houses were linked by carefully engineered roads.

sources.title: Chaco Culture – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Al-Razi tells smallpox and measles apart
points.text: The Persian physician al-Razi (Rhazes), who ran hospitals in Rayy and Baghdad, was the first to distinguish smallpox from measles in a written treatise. In 1970 the World Health Organization praised the originality and accuracy of his account.
points.note: The exact year of the treatise is not known; the dates span his working life.

sources.title: Circulating Now / NLM in Focus – US National Library of Medicine
Haddad 1986, Journal of the Islamic Medical Association 18(1)

points.heading: Al-Qarawiyyin founded in Fez
points.text: Al-Qarawiyyin in Fez is often described as the world's oldest existing, continually operating educational institution. It was founded by Fatima al-Fihri.
points.note: Founded as a mosque with teaching; its status as the 'oldest university' depends on how a university is defined. The founder's name comes from wider sources, not the quoted page.

sources.title: Oldest university | Guinness World Records (institutional source)

points.heading: Diamond Sutra: earliest dated printed book
points.text: A woodblock-printed copy of the Diamond Sutra, made in AD 868, is the world's earliest dated printed book. It is held by the British Library.

sources.title: The Diamond Sutra – International Dunhuang Programme, British Library

points.heading: Mosque of Ahmad ibn Tulun built
points.text: The mosque of Ahmad ibn Tulun is one of the oldest and largest mosques in Cairo. Its date is recorded precisely.

sources.title: Historic Cairo - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Gwalior inscription: agreed early dated Indian zero
points.text: A stone inscription at Gwalior dated 876 AD is the first Indian use of zero that all scholars accept as genuine and dated.

sources.title: A history of Zero - MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Harar: some of its 82 mosques date from 10th century
points.text: Harar is a sacred Muslim city with 82 mosques, three of them from the 10th century. It became an important centre of Islamic culture.

sources.title: Harar Jugol, the Fortified Historic Town - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Mapungubwe: first indigenous kingdom in southern Africa
points.text: Mapungubwe grew into the largest kingdom in the sub-continent, with a sacred king set apart from commoners. It was abandoned in the 14th century.
points.note: UNESCO gives 900-1300 for the wider landscape; the Met dates the city itself to 1220-1290/1300.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Mapungubwe Cultural Landscape

points.heading: El Caracol observatory at Chichén Itzá
points.text: Chichén Itzá, a major Maya–Toltec city of the 10th–15th centuries, includes El Caracol, a round building used to watch the sky.

sources.title: Pre-Hispanic City of Chichen-Itza – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Al-Battani's astronomical tables advance trigonometry
points.text: Al-Battani wrote a major astronomy work in 57 chapters with advances in trigonometry. It was later used by European astronomers.
points.note: Place is where al-Battani worked; not in the quoted entry.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Chronology 900 - 1100

points.heading: Fatimids found Cairo as their capital
points.text: Cairo was founded as the headquarters of the Fatimid Caliphate. It became a leading centre of the Islamic world, home to the Al-Azhar mosque and school.

sources.title: Historic Cairo - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Abu'l-Wafa invents the wall quadrant
points.text: Abu'l-Wafa built a wall quadrant to measure the positions of stars accurately. He also improved trigonometric tables.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Chronology 900 - 1100

points.heading: First evidence of decimal numerals in Europe
points.text: The Codex Vigilanus, copied in Spain, shows Indian-Arabic numerals. It is the first evidence of decimal numbers in Europe.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Chronology 900 - 1100

points.heading: Ibn Sina writes The Canon of Medicine
points.text: Ibn Sina (980–1037), born near Bukhara, wrote The Canon of Medicine and The Book of Healing, both hugely influential.
points.note: Range is Ibn Sina's lifetime; the sources checked do not give a completion date for the Canon.

sources.title: Avicenna – Biography – MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Ibn Yunus compiles the Hakimi astronomical tables
points.text: Ibn Yunus, working in Fatimid Egypt, compiled a large astronomical handbook of observations and tables. It included calendar tables for several calendars.
points.note: Exact date of the handbook not given; range runs to his death in 1009.

sources.title: Ibn Yunus (950 - 1009) - Biography - MacTutor History of Mathematics

points.heading: Ibn al-Haytham writes on optics in Cairo
points.text: Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen) developed theories of light and vision and wrote on mathematics and astronomy. He spent his later life in Cairo.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Chronology 900 - 1100
Ibn al-Haytham - Biography - MacTutor History of Mathematics

points.heading: Saharan caravan towns founded, later centres of learning
points.text: These towns were founded to serve caravans crossing the Sahara. They became trading and religious centres and focal points of Islamic culture.

sources.title: Ancient Ksour of Ouadane, Chinguetti, Tichitt and Oualata - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Kilwa mints its own coins
points.text: Kilwa issued its own currency, a sign of its wealth and independence as a trading state.

sources.title: Ruins of Kilwa Kisiwani and Ruins of Songo Mnara, UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Great Zimbabwe stone city built
points.text: Bantu-speaking ancestors of the Shona began Great Zimbabwe in the 11th century and enlarged it for more than 300 years. Its dry-stone walls are the largest ancient structures south of the Sahara.

sources.title: The Met, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History: Great Zimbabwe (11th-15th century)

points.heading: Great Zimbabwe becomes a major trading centre
points.text: Great Zimbabwe was an important trading centre, known from the Middle Ages onwards. It is a unique record of Shona civilisation.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Great Zimbabwe National Monument

points.heading: Ibn Sina writes The Canon of Medicine
points.text: Ibn Sina (Avicenna) wrote The Canon of Medicine, which was used as a medical textbook in the Islamic world and Europe for centuries.
points.note: The Canon is usually dated to the early 11th century; the source gives his lifetime.

sources.title: Avicenna – Biography – MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Murasaki Shikibu writes The Tale of Genji
points.text: Murasaki Shikibu, a lady at the Japanese court, probably completed The Tale of Genji about 1010. It is often called the world's first novel.

sources.title: The Tale of Genji – Britannica

points.heading: Bagan: royal temple-building as statecraft
points.text: At its peak in the 11th–13th centuries, Bagan was capital of a regional empire. Kings used Buddhist gift-giving and temple building to hold power.

sources.title: Bagan – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Rapa Nui people carve and raise the moai
points.text: From the 10th to the 16th century, the people of Rapa Nui built shrines and raised huge stone figures called moai.
points.note: UNESCO's settlement date (c. AD 300) conflicts with radiocarbon work placing settlement c. 1190–1290 (oc-07).

sources.title: Rapa Nui National Park – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Chola king builds the Brihadisvara temple
points.text: The Chola king Rajaraja I began the great Brihadisvara temple at Thanjavur c. 1003–04 and consecrated it in 1009–10.

sources.title: Great Living Chola Temples – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Al-Biruni's solar observations in Khwarazm
points.text: In 1016 al-Biruni, born in Khwarazm, built an instrument at Jurjaniyya and made 15 observations of the Sun crossing the meridian.

sources.title: Al-Biruni – Biography – MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Voyagers reach the central Society Islands
points.text: High-precision radiocarbon dating suggests people first settled the Society Islands between AD 1025 and 1120.
points.note: Earlier studies put East Polynesian settlement centuries earlier; dates remain debated.

sources.title: East Polynesia colonized faster and more recently than previously thought – University of Hawaiʻi

points.heading: Merv, capital of the Great Seljuk Empire
points.text: In the 11th and 12th centuries Merv was a capital of the Great Seljuk Empire; its walled city of Sultan Kala dates from this time.

sources.title: State Historical and Cultural Park 'Ancient Merv' – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Bi Sheng invents movable type
points.text: About 1041–48 Bi Sheng (Pi Sheng) made movable type from baked clay and glue.

sources.title: Printing – History of printing – Britannica

points.heading: Ghana Empire controls the gold trade
points.text: The Soninke empire of Ghana grew rich on the trans-Saharan gold trade. By 1050 it controlled the trading town of Audaghost.

sources.title: The Trans-Saharan Gold Trade (7th-14th Century) - The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)

points.heading: Cahokia: largest city north of Mexico
points.text: At its peak, c. 1050–1150, the Mississippian city of Cahokia may have had 10,000–20,000 people, as many as many European cities.

sources.title: Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Temple of Literature founded in Hanoi
points.text: The Temple of Literature was founded in 1070, dedicated to Confucius, and first served as a university for the royal family and scholars.

sources.title: Temple of Literature – Britannica

points.heading: Omar Khayyam classifies cubic equations
points.text: Omar Khayyam classified cubic equations and solved them with geometry. He also measured the length of the year very accurately.
points.note: Place is approximate; not in the quoted entry.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Chronology 900 - 1100

points.heading: Magnetic compass described, then used at sea
points.text: Shen Kuo's Brush Talks from Dream Brook, written in his last years (1086–95), refers to a magnetic compass. By the 12th century Chinese sailors used compasses.
points.note: Earlier Chinese lodestone 'south-pointers' existed; Britannica dates maritime use to the 12th century, in China and Europe apparently independently.

sources.title: Shen Kua – Biography – MacTutor, University of St Andrews
Compass – Britannica

points.heading: University of Bologna founded
points.text: Bologna is considered the oldest university in the Western world. 1088 is the year conventionally given for its founding.
points.note: 1088 is a conventional date.

sources.title: Our history - University of Bologna

points.heading: Rock-hewn churches of Lalibela carved
points.text: King Lalibela set out to build a 'New Jerusalem' of 11 churches cut from solid rock. They have drawn pilgrims since the 12th century.
points.note: UNESCO gives both 12th and 13th centuries.

sources.title: Rock-Hewn Churches, Lalibela, UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Bhaskara II extends Brahmagupta's number work
points.text: Bhaskara II (1114–1185) wrote the Lilavati on arithmetic and the Bijaganita on algebra, building on Brahmagupta.

sources.title: Bhaskara II – Biography – MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Lubeck leads the Hanseatic trading network
points.text: Lubeck, founded in the 12th century, became capital of the Hanseatic League and the main trading centre of northern Europe until the 16th century.
points.note: UNESCO spells it Lübeck.

sources.title: Hanseatic City of Lubeck - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Arabic science translated into Latin
points.text: Gherard of Cremona began translating Arabic works, and Arabic versions of Greek works, into Latin. This brought Islamic and Greek science into European learning.
points.note: Gherard worked in Toledo, Spain; the quoted entry does not name the city.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Chronology 1100 - 1300

points.heading: Rapid voyaging to Hawaiʻi, New Zealand and Rapa Nui
points.text: In one rapid burst between AD 1190 and 1290, voyagers reached the far corners of Polynesia, including Hawaiʻi, New Zealand and Rapa Nui.
points.note: Contested: UNESCO dates Rapa Nui settlement c. AD 300 (see oc-09).

sources.title: East Polynesia colonized faster and more recently than previously thought – University of Hawaiʻi

points.heading: Qutb Minar rises in Delhi
points.text: The Qutb Minar was built in the early 13th century south of Delhi. Work on the minaret continued between 1199 and 1503.

sources.title: Qutb Minar and its Monuments, Delhi – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Ife becomes a flourishing artistic centre
points.text: Between about 1200 and 1500 Ife produced celebrated naturalistic sculpture. Its works are among the masterpieces of African art.

sources.title: The Met, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History: Ife (from ca. 6th century)

points.heading: Manden Charter proclaimed for the Mali Empire
points.text: After a major victory, the founder of the Mali (Mandingo) Empire proclaimed the Manden Charter. It is one of the oldest constitutions in the world, passed down mainly orally.
points.note: Oral tradition; the year 1236 is often given but is not stated in the source used.

sources.title: Manden Charter, proclaimed in Kurukan Fuga, UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage

points.heading: Kilwa's Great Mosque gains East Africa's largest dome
points.text: Kilwa's Great Mosque is the oldest standing mosque on the East African coast. Its 13th-century dome was the largest in East Africa until the 19th century.

sources.title: Ruins of Kilwa Kisiwani and Ruins of Songo Mnara, UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Kilwa merchants control Indian Ocean gold trade
points.text: Kilwa merchants traded gold, silver, pearls and other goods, so much Indian Ocean trade passed through their hands. Gold and ivory from inland were exchanged for imports.

sources.title: Ruins of Kilwa Kisiwani and Ruins of Songo Mnara, UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Harar walls built around the sacred city
points.text: The walls of Harar were built between the 13th and 16th centuries. The fortified town became a major trading and religious centre.

sources.title: Harar Jugol, the Fortified Historic Town - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Pax Mongolica opens safer trade across Eurasia
points.text: In the 13th and 14th centuries, Mongol rule made travel and trade safer across much of Eurasia, linking East Asia, Central Asia and Europe.

sources.title: Pax Mongolica – Britannica

points.heading: Nan Madol: basalt city of the Saudeleur dynasty
points.text: Between 1200 and 1500 the Saudeleur dynasty built stone palaces, temples and tombs on artificial islets at Nan Madol.

sources.title: Nan Madol: Ceremonial Centre of Eastern Micronesia – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Fibonacci's Liber abaci brings Arab arithmetic to Europe
points.text: Fibonacci set out the arithmetic and algebra he had learnt in Arab lands, including Indian-Arabic numerals. It helped European merchants adopt them.
points.note: He learnt much of this in North Africa (Bejaia); place Pisa is his home city, not stated in the quoted entry.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Chronology 1100 - 1300

points.heading: King John accepts Magna Carta
points.text: King John agreed to Magna Carta to end a civil war with his barons. It became a symbol of limits on royal power.

sources.title: Magna Carta 1214-1225 - The National Archives

points.heading: Mapungubwe trades gold and ivory to the coast
points.text: Mapungubwe flourished as a city and trading centre. It sent gold and ivory to East African ports for trade with India and China, and received glass beads and cloth.

sources.title: Mapungubwe (ca. 1050-1270) - The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)
UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Mapungubwe Cultural Landscape

points.heading: Gold foil rhinoceros made at Mapungubwe
points.text: Gold objects found at Mapungubwe, including a famous gold foil rhinoceros, are early evidence of goldsmithing in southern Africa.
points.note: Date given as the period when the city flourished; the object itself is not precisely dated in the quoted text.

sources.title: Mapungubwe (ca. 1050-1270) - The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)

points.heading: Karakorum founded as Mongol imperial capital
points.text: Chinggis Khan established Karakorum in 1220 as the capital of the vast Mongol Empire.

sources.title: Orkhon Valley Cultural Landscape – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Mosque and hospital founded at Divrigi
points.text: Emir Ahmet Shah founded a mosque with an adjoining hospital at Divrigi in Anatolia. It is a masterpiece of Islamic architecture.

sources.title: Great Mosque and Hospital of Divrigi - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Tripitaka Koreana carved on 80,000 woodblocks
points.text: Between 1237 and 1248, Korean craftsmen carved the Buddhist scriptures onto about 80,000 printing woodblocks, kept at Haeinsa temple.

sources.title: Haeinsa Temple Janggyeong Panjeon – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Qin Jiushao's Mathematical Treatise in Nine Sections
points.text: Qin Jiushao's Mathematical Treatise in Nine Sections appeared in 1247.

sources.title: Qin Jiushao – Biography – MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Polynesian voyagers settle Aotearoa New Zealand
points.text: Current understanding is that the first people arrived from East Polynesia between 1250 and 1300, on deliberate voyages using winds, currents and stars.
points.note: Te Ara says 'The date of first settlement is a matter of debate'.

sources.title: History – Te Ara: The Encyclopedia of New Zealand

points.heading: Ibn al-Banna writes a key arithmetic textbook
points.text: Ibn al-Banna of Marrakesh wrote a summary of arithmetical operations that was widely studied in North Africa. He was one of the leading mathematicians of the Maghreb.

sources.title: Ibn al-Banna - MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Al-Tusi builds the Maragheh observatory
points.text: Nasir al-Din al-Tusi led the building of a great observatory at Maragheh, with help from Chinese astronomers. It was also a centre of learning.

sources.title: Nasir al-Din al-Tusi - Biography - MacTutor History of Mathematics

points.heading: Yang Hui records the 'Pascal' triangle
points.text: In 1261 Yang Hui wrote a commentary on the Nine Chapters. It shows the number triangle later named after Pascal, which he credited to Jia Xian.

sources.title: Yang Hui – Biography – MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Guo Shoujing's accurate calendar for Kublai Khan
points.text: Guo Shoujing built new instruments and by 1280 measured the year to within 26 seconds. The new calendar came into use the next year.

sources.title: Guo Shoujing – Biography – MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Climate change ends farming at Mapungubwe
points.text: Mapungubwe supported a large population through farming, but climate change made the land unable to sustain it. The site was abandoned.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Mapungubwe Cultural Landscape

points.heading: Cowrie shells introduced as local currency
points.text: Cowrie shells from the east coast came into use as currency in the western Sudan. Gold and salt stayed the main goods in long-distance trade.

sources.title: The Trans-Saharan Gold Trade (7th-14th Century) - The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)

points.heading: Mbanza Kongo becomes capital of the Kingdom of Kongo
points.text: Mbanza Kongo was the political and spiritual capital of the Kingdom of Kongo, one of the largest states in the region. The town grew around the royal residence and court.

sources.title: Mbanza Kongo, Vestiges of the Capital of the former Kingdom of Kongo - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Taputapuātea: hub of Polynesian voyaging
points.text: Marae at Taputapuātea were built from the 14th to the 18th century. Voyagers in outrigger canoes were formally welcomed there.

sources.title: Taputapuātea – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Husuni Kubwa palace built at Kilwa
points.text: The Husuni Kubwa palace, with its large octagonal bathing pool, was built for Kilwa's rulers. The traveller Ibn Battuta visited Kilwa in 1331-1332.

sources.title: Ruins of Kilwa Kisiwani and Ruins of Songo Mnara, UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage shows Mali's gold wealth
points.text: Mansa Musa of Mali travelled to Mecca with so much gold that its price fell in Cairo. A Spanish map of 1375 shows the king of Mali holding a gold nugget.

sources.title: The Empires of the Western Sudan: Mali Empire - The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)
The Trans-Saharan Gold Trade (7th-14th Century) - The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)

points.heading: Tenochtitlan founded on Lake Texcoco
points.text: The Aztec capital Tenochtitlan was founded c. 1325 on marshes in Lake Texcoco and linked to the shore by causeways. About 400,000 people lived there by 1519.
points.note: Population estimates for 1519 vary widely between scholars.

sources.title: Tenochtitlán – Britannica

points.heading: Ibn Khaldun's Muqaddimah: an early philosophy of history
points.text: Ibn Khaldun, born in Tunis, wrote the Muqaddimah, one of the earliest non-religious philosophies of history. It analyses how states rise and fall.
points.note: Dates shown are his lifetime; the source extract does not date the Muqaddimah itself.

sources.title: Ibn Khaldun | Britannica

points.heading: The Black Death sweeps through the Middle East
points.text: The Black Death reached Constantinople and Alexandria in 1347 and Cairo and Damascus in 1348, then spread north into Anatolia and south-east to Mosul and Baghdad by 1349. The traveller Ibn Battuta, passing through Damascus in July 1348, saw the governor order three days of fasting during the pestilence; he wrote that deaths there did not reach two thousand a day, while in Cairo they reached twenty-four thousand.
points.note: The route and dates follow modern historians. Ibn Battuta's daily death counts are a traveller's report, not a census, and are likely exaggerated; they show how the epidemic was experienced rather than its true toll. The plague kept returning to the region for centuries; it subsided in the Middle East by about 1351.

sources.title: Yaron Ayalon, 'The Black Death and the Rise of the Ottomans', ch. 1 of Natural Disasters in the Ottoman Empire: Plague, Famine, and Other Misfortunes (Cambridge University Press, 2015)
Ibn Battuta, Travels in Asia and Africa 1325–1354, trans. and ed. H. A. R. Gibb (London: Broadway House, 1929) – Internet Medieval Sourcebook, Fordham University

points.heading: Madhava's infinite series in the Kerala school
points.text: Around 1400, Madhava of Sangamagrama found series for sine, cosine and arctangent, over 200 years before they were rediscovered in Europe.
points.note: Madhava's own writings on these series do not survive; they are known from later Kerala-school authors such as Jyesthadeva.

sources.title: Madhava – Biography – MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Ayutthaya: Siamese capital and global trading city
points.text: Founded in 1350, Ayutthaya was the second Siamese capital and a centre of trade and diplomacy until it was destroyed in 1767.

sources.title: Historic City of Ayutthaya – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Jikji printed with movable metal type
points.text: Jikji was printed in 1377 at Heungdeok-sa temple using movable cast-metal type. It is the oldest known book made this way.

sources.title: 'Jikji', a treasure of the world of printing – Bibliothèque nationale de France

points.heading: Oba Ewuare strengthens the Kingdom of Benin
points.text: The Kingdom of Benin grew powerful under Oba Ewuare in the 15th century. Portuguese traders later sought commercial treaties with its rulers.

sources.title: Plaque with equestrian oba (king) and attendants, ca. 1540-70 - The Metropolitan Museum of Art

points.heading: Timbuktu and Sankore become a capital of learning
points.text: Timbuktu, home of the Sankore university and other madrasas, was an intellectual and spiritual capital. Its great mosques recall its golden age.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Timbuktu

points.heading: Melaka sultanate on the Straits trade route
points.text: Melaka's history begins with the 15th-century Malay sultanate, which grew rich on trade between the Indian Ocean and East Asia.
points.note: End date 1511 (Portuguese capture) is not stated on the UNESCO page, which says the Portuguese period began 'in the early 16th century'.

sources.title: Melaka and George Town, Historic Cities of the Straits of Malacca – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Qhapaq Ñan: the Inca road system
points.text: The Inca road network, over 30,000 km long, reached its peak in the 15th century. It carried goods, messages and armies across the empire.

sources.title: Qhapaq Ñan, Andean Road System – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Zheng He's seven voyages across the Indian Ocean
