points.text: Between 1405 and 1433 the admiral Zheng He led seven fleets to South-East Asia, India, Arabia and East Africa.

sources.title: Zheng He timeline – Britannica

points.heading: Ulugh Beg's madrasa opens on the Registan
points.text: Ulugh Beg's madrasa on Samarkand's Registan Square was completed in 1420. He appointed the best scientists he could find to teach there.

sources.title: Ulugh Beg – Biography – MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Al-Kashi calculates pi to 16 decimal places
points.text: Working in Samarkand, Jamshid al-Kashi calculated 2π to sixteen decimal places in July 1424, far beyond earlier results.

sources.title: al-Kashi – Biography – MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Ulugh Beg's observatory and star catalogue
points.text: Ulugh Beg began an observatory at Samarkand in the 1420s. His star catalogue of 1437 gave positions of 992 stars.
points.note: MacTutor's two biographies disagree on when construction began: 1424 (al-Kashi page) or 1428 (Ulugh Beg page).

sources.title: Ulugh Beg – Biography – MacTutor, University of St Andrews
al-Kashi – Biography – MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: King Sejong creates the Korean alphabet, Hangul
points.text: King Sejong completed a new Korean alphabet in 1443 and promulgated it in 1446 in the Hunminjeongum.

sources.title: Hunminjeongum Manuscript – UNESCO Memory of the World

points.heading: Khami becomes capital of the Torwa dynasty
points.text: After Great Zimbabwe declined, Khami became the capital of the Torwa dynasty. It continued the Zimbabwe stone-building tradition.

sources.title: Khami Ruins National Monument - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Khami imports goods from Europe and China
points.text: Objects from Europe and China found at Khami show it was a major long-distance trading centre over a long period.

sources.title: Khami Ruins National Monument - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Machu Picchu built with farming terraces
points.text: Machu Picchu was built in the 15th century with irrigation canals and farming terraces. It was abandoned after the Spanish conquest.

sources.title: Historic Sanctuary of Machu Picchu – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Gutenberg Bible printed with movable type
points.text: Johann Gutenberg completed printing the Bible with movable metal type at Mainz. Printing spread books quickly across Europe.

sources.title: The Gutenberg Bible - Library of Congress Bible Collection

points.heading: Askia Mohamed builds his tomb at Gao
points.text: Askia Mohamed, emperor of Songhai, built a monumental earthen tomb in his capital Gao. It reflects the power of an empire that flourished in the 15th and 16th centuries.

sources.title: Tomb of Askia - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Sukur: iron smelting and terraced hill farming
points.text: Sukur has a recorded history of iron smelting going back to the 16th century. Its terraced fields show intensive hill farming that still continues.

sources.title: Sukur Cultural Landscape - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Kongo court commissions ivory carvings
points.text: Carved ivories from the 16th century are among the earliest known royal commissions of the Kongo Kingdom. Kongo carvers worked ivory for centuries afterwards.

sources.title: Kongo Ivories - The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)

points.heading: Lisbon monastery commemorates Vasco da Gama's voyage
points.text: The Jeronimos Monastery was begun in 1502 to commemorate Vasco da Gama's sea voyage to India. Portuguese voyages opened direct European sea routes around Africa.
points.note: The voyage itself took place in 1497-1499 (not stated in the quoted source). These voyages were later tied to the Atlantic slave trade.

sources.title: Monastery of the Hieronymites and Tower of Belem in Lisbon - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Kongo king Afonso I writes letters to Portugal
points.text: Nzinga Mbemba (Afonso I) wrote a series of letters to the king of Portugal. He asked for an end to the slave trade that was damaging his kingdom.

sources.title: World History Commons (Roy Rosenzweig Center, George Mason University): Afonso I letters

points.heading: Benin brass plaques cast for the royal palace
points.text: A guild of brass casters made some 900 relief plaques to decorate the royal palace. They record court life and history.
points.note: Date is the Met dating of this plaque (ca. 1540-70); the series spans a longer period.

sources.title: Plaque with equestrian oba (king) and attendants, ca. 1540-70 - The Metropolitan Museum of Art

points.heading: Copernicus places the Sun at the centre
points.text: Copernicus published his full theory that the Sun, not the Earth, is at rest at the centre. It began a revolution in astronomy.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Chronology 1500 - 1600

points.heading: Vesalius publishes the Fabrica on human anatomy
points.text: Vesalius, professor of anatomy at Padua, published a detailed, illustrated study of the human body based on dissection.

sources.title: Historical Anatomies on the Web: Vesalius - US National Library of Medicine

points.heading: World's first botanical garden created in Padua
points.text: Padua created the first botanical garden, a place to grow and study plants scientifically.
points.note: UNESCO calls it the first; earlier gardens existed elsewhere depending on definition.

sources.title: Botanical Garden (Orto Botanico), Padua - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Martín de la Cruz's Aztec herbal
points.text: In 1552 the Nahua physician Martín de la Cruz wrote an illustrated book of Mexican medicinal plants, translated into Latin by Juan Badiano.
points.note: The 1552 date is in the catalogue record ('1552') beside the quoted passage; the record is for a 1940 Smithsonian study of the manuscript.

sources.title: Concerning the Badianus manuscript, an Aztec herbal – Wellcome Collection

points.heading: Chinese variolation: protection against smallpox by the nose
points.text: By the 1560s Chinese practitioners protected children against smallpox by deliberately infecting them with material from smallpox scabs, often blown into the nose as a dried powder. The Kangxi Emperor later had his own children inoculated this way.
points.note: Where variolation began is unresolved: Needham and Chinese historians argue for China, others for India; stories of a 10th-11th-century Chinese origin are not supported by contemporary records. The method carried real risks and could spark outbreaks, so it is not comparable with modern vaccination.

sources.title: Iwo Amelung, 'Successful smallpox prevention and inoculation in China in the 17th and 18th centuries', Forschung Frankfurt 1.2021, Goethe University Frankfurt
Indiana University Libraries exhibit: Qing Dynasty

points.heading: Konso stone-walled farming terraces
points.text: The Konso people built stone-walled terraces and fortified villages on dry hills. This living farming tradition goes back at least 21 generations.
points.note: Start date estimated from "more than 400 years" (UNESCO listing, 2011); the terracing may be older.

sources.title: Konso Cultural Landscape - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Luba model of statecraft spreads to the Lunda
points.text: A Luba figure brought the Luba model of statecraft to the Lunda by marriage. The Luba and Lunda became major savanna states.
points.note: Based on oral tradition; date is approximate.

sources.title: Kingdoms of the Savanna: The Luba and Lunda Empires - The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)

points.heading: Chief Roi Mata's domain
points.text: Three early 17th-century sites in Vanuatu are linked to Roi Mata, the last paramount chief of central Vanuatu. Taboos on them have been kept for 400 years.

sources.title: Chief Roi Mata’s Domain – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Kepler shows planets move in ellipses
points.text: Kepler published his first two laws of planetary motion, based on observations of Mars.
points.note: Place is where Kepler worked; not stated in the quoted entry.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Chronology 1600 - 1625

points.heading: Napier publishes logarithms
points.text: John Napier published logarithms, which made long calculations much faster for astronomers and navigators.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Chronology 1600 - 1625

points.heading: Kingdom of Dahomey rules from Abomey
points.text: Twelve kings ruled the Kingdom of Dahomey from Abomey, each building a palace in the same walled area. The palaces are known for their coloured bas-reliefs.
points.note: The same UNESCO page also gives 1620 to 1900.

sources.title: Royal Palaces of Abomey - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Shyaam unites the chiefdoms of the Kuba kingdom
points.text: Shyaam aMbul aNgoong united the local chiefdoms and shaped Kuba political, social and economic life.

sources.title: Kingdoms of the Savanna: The Kuba Kingdom - The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)

points.heading: Taj Mahal built for Mumtaz Mahal
points.text: The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan had the Taj Mahal built from 1632 to 1648; the outer courtyard was finished in 1653.

sources.title: Taj Mahal – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Fasil Ghebbi becomes the Ethiopian royal seat
points.text: The fortress-city of Fasil Ghebbi at Gondar was the residence of Emperor Fasilides and his successors. It mixes Ethiopian, Arab and European building styles.
points.note: UNESCO says 16th and 17th centuries; Fasilides himself reigned in the 17th century.

sources.title: Fasil Ghebbi, Gondar Region - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Lunda ruler opens trade routes to the Atlantic
points.text: By 1650 the Lunda ruler Mwaant Yaav Naweej had set up trade routes from his capital to the Atlantic coast. The Lunda also controlled the regional copper trade.

sources.title: Kingdoms of the Savanna: The Luba and Lunda Empires - The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)

points.heading: Buchu: Khoi and San plant medicine adopted at the Cape
points.text: The Khoi and San used buchu (Agathosma species), mixing the dried, powdered leaves with sheep fat as an ointment and chewing the leaves for stomach complaints. The name 'buchu' comes from Khoi-San languages, and the plant became a staple remedy of early Cape colonists.
points.year: Recorded from the Cape colonial era (Khoi and San use older)
points.note: Khoi and San use long predates written records; the start date marks Dutch settlement at the Cape (1652), after which European use was recorded. Traditional uses are documented; modern clinical evidence for specific benefits is limited and is not claimed here. Part of this rests on one independent source.

sources.title: Agathosma crenulata – PlantZAfrica, South African National Biodiversity Institute
Skosana, Aboua and Du Plessis, 'Buchu – The Multi-Purpose Ethnomedicinally Important Specie' (IntechOpen, 2014), Cape Peninsula University of Technology repository
'buchu, n.', Dictionary of South African English (Dictionary Unit for South African English, Rhodes University), 2025
'Medicinal Plants Used in the Western Cape', Western Cape Department of Cultural Affairs and Sport, Museum Service (Google Arts & Culture)

points.heading: Royal Society of London founded
points.text: The Royal Society was founded to promote experimental science. It became one of the oldest scientific academies in continuous existence.
points.note: The Society first met in 1660; it received its royal charter in 1662.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Chronology 1650 - 1675

points.heading: Seki Takakazu studies determinants
points.text: In 1683 the Japanese mathematician Seki Takakazu studied determinants, ten years before Leibniz did so independently.

sources.title: Takakazu Seki – Biography – MacTutor, University of St Andrews

points.heading: Newton's Principia sets out laws of motion and gravity
points.text: Newton explained motion, gravity, tides and planetary orbits with mathematics.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Chronology 1675 - 1700

points.heading: Asante Kingdom reaches its peak
points.text: The Asante Kingdom was influential, powerful and wealthy, with its own architectural style. Its traditional buildings near Kumasi survive today.

sources.title: Asante Traditional Buildings - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Kuba king introduces ndop royal portrait sculpture
points.text: King Mishe miShyaang aMbul introduced ndop, wooden portrait figures of Kuba kings. They became a key royal art form.

sources.title: Kingdoms of the Savanna: The Kuba Kingdom - The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)

points.heading: Jantar Mantar observatory built at Jaipur
points.text: The Jantar Mantar at Jaipur, built in the early 18th century, has about 20 large fixed instruments for naked-eye astronomy.
points.note: UNESCO says 'early 18th century'; the year range here simply represents that phrase.

sources.title: The Jantar Mantar, Jaipur – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Coke-fired blast furnace at Coalbrookdale
points.text: The Coalbrookdale blast furnace marks the use of coke to smelt iron. It helped start the Industrial Revolution.
points.note: Often dated 1709 for the first coke smelting; UNESCO gives the furnace as built in 1708.

sources.title: Ironbridge Gorge - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Jamaican Maroons win freedom by treaty
points.text: After years of resistance, Maroon leaders Cudjoe (March 1739) and Quao (December 1739) signed treaties with the British; Nanny's followed a year later.
points.note: The treaties granted freedom and land but also required Maroons to return future escapees, which is debated in Maroon history.

sources.title: The Jamaican Maroons – National Library of Jamaica

points.heading: Kew Gardens founded for plant science
points.text: Kew's gardens have contributed to the study of plant diversity and economic botany since 1759. Much of this work was tied to colonial plant transfers.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Harrison's H4 sea clock tested on voyage to Jamaica
points.text: John Harrison's H4 timekeeper was tested on a voyage to Jamaica. Accurate sea clocks let sailors find longitude.

sources.title: Longitude found - the story of Harrison's timekeepers | Royal Museums Greenwich

points.heading: Tupaia charts the islands of the Pacific
points.text: In 1769–70 the Raʻiātean navigator Tupaia drew a chart of Pacific islands with crew of Cook's Endeavour, drawing on Polynesian navigation knowledge.

sources.title: Tupaia's Map – University of Potsdam
On tour with Tupaia – Natural History Museum

points.heading: First iron bridge erected
points.text: Abraham Darby III built the Iron Bridge, a landmark in the use of cast iron in construction.
points.note: "First" iron bridge is general knowledge, not stated in the quoted text.

sources.title: Ironbridge Gorge - UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Haiti: first state born of a slave revolt
points.text: After fourteen years of struggle by enslaved people, Jean-Jacques Dessalines proclaimed the independent Republic of Haiti on 1 January 1804.
points.note: Start year derived from 'fourteen years'; the general uprising is usually dated to August 1791.

sources.title: National History Park – Citadel, Sans Souci, Ramiers – UNESCO World Heritage Centre

points.heading: Marshallese stick charts teach ocean swells
points.text: Known to outsiders from the 19th century, Marshallese stick charts map swells and islands. Navigators used them to teach, not to carry at sea.
points.note: The practice is older than the 19th-century European records; no earlier date is given by the source.

sources.title: Stick chart from the Marshall Islands – Royal Museums Greenwich

points.heading: Luba lukasa memory boards record history and medicinal practice
points.text: Members of the Luba mbudye association used lukasa, hand-held boards studded with beads and pins or carved, as memory devices. Trained readers drew on them to recall royal genealogies, places of importance and medicinal practices.
points.note: Lukasa are knowledge and memory devices rather than medical texts; medicine is one of several kinds of knowledge they encoded, and they could only be 'read' by initiated members. Dates are those of surviving museum examples; the practice may be older.

sources.title: Ways of Recording African History – The Met, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History
Memory Board (Lukasa) – The Metropolitan Museum of Art
Penn State / Palmer Museum of Art: African Brilliance, catalogue 55

points.heading: IsiLimela: the Pleiades as the 'digging stars'
points.text: In southern Africa the Pleiades, called isiLimela, were the 'digging stars': their appearance signalled that it was time to begin hoeing for the new growing season. Xhosa men also counted their years of manhood from the June rising of isiLimela.
points.note: The knowledge is oral and much older than its written record; the 19th-century dates reflect when it was written down (for example by the missionary Henry Callaway), not when it began.

sources.title: South African star myths – Royal Museums Greenwich

points.heading: Sotho and Tswana watch for Canopus (Naka) to time the year
points.text: Sotho and Tswana communities watched for the pre-dawn appearance of the bright star Canopus, called Naka, as a seasonal marker. Tswana herders took it as the signal to start breeding sheep, and Sotho chiefs rewarded whoever saw it first.
points.note: Based on ethnographic records compiled in P. G. Alcock's 'Venus Rising' (2014) as published by the Astronomical Society of Southern Africa; the practice is undatable oral tradition and the dates reflect when it was recorded.

sources.title: African Ethnoastronomy – Astronomical Society of Southern Africa
University of Pretoria Sci-Enza

points.heading: Britain abolishes its slave trade, then slavery
points.text: Britain ended its slave trade in 1807, after long campaigns by enslaved Africans, Black Britons and abolitionists. Slavery in British colonies continued until emancipation was passed in 1833.
points.note: The 1833 Act took effect in 1834 with an "apprenticeship" period; this detail is not in the quoted source.

sources.title: Parliament and the British Slave Trade: Overview - UK Parliament

points.heading: Kamehameha I unites the Hawaiian Islands
points.text: By 1810 Kamehameha I had united all the Hawaiian islands. His 'law of the splintered paddle' protected ordinary people from violent chiefs.

sources.title: Kamehameha I – Britannica

points.heading: Sequoyah creates the Cherokee syllabary
points.text: By 1821 Sequoyah had created 86 symbols for the syllables of Cherokee. It spread rapidly and was used in the Cherokee Phoenix newspaper.

sources.title: Sequoyah – Britannica

points.heading: Vai syllabary invented in Liberia
points.text: Momolu Duwalu Bukele created a syllabic writing system for the Vai language. It is one of the best-known writing systems invented in West Africa.
points.note: Sources give about 1833 or 1834.

sources.title: Vai syllabary - Omniglot (institutional source)

points.heading: Slavery Abolition Act takes effect
points.text: The UK Slavery Abolition Act received Royal Assent on 28 August 1833 and took effect in the Caribbean colonies on 1 August 1834.
points.note: Formerly enslaved people were forced into 'apprenticeship' until 1838; slave-owners, not the enslaved, received compensation.

sources.title: Slavery Abolition Act – Britannica

points.heading: Treaty of Waitangi signed
points.text: On 6 February 1840 many leading Māori chiefs and the British representative William Hobson made the Treaty of Waitangi.
points.note: The English and te reo Māori texts differ in meaning, especially on sovereignty; this remains contested.

sources.title: Treaty of Waitangi – Britannica

points.heading: The Kongo dikenga: a diagram of the sun's daily path
points.text: The dikenga, a cross within a circle, is a Kongo cosmological diagram that maps the sun's positions relative to the horizon and links them to the cycle of birth, death and rebirth. It appears on objects such as power figures made by ritual specialists (banganga).
points.note: The Metropolitan Museum calls the symbol ancient, but it cannot be dated precisely; the dates here are for the documented museum object, not the origin of the idea. It is best understood as cosmology rooted in watching the sun, not as a measured astronomical record. Part of this rests on one independent source.

sources.title: Female power figure (nkisi), Kongo – The Metropolitan Museum of Art

points.heading: Sona sand drawings: geometry traced around grids of dots
points.text: Cokwe (Chokwe) storytellers in eastern Angola mark a grid of points in sand and trace lines around them, often as one continuous closed curve. Mathematicians have studied sona as graphs and symmetry problems, and UNESCO added the tradition to its Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2023.
points.note: The tradition is older than its written records, but its origin cannot be dated; the start year here is a placeholder for when outsiders began recording it, not when it began. Related tusona drawings are practised by Luchazi and neighbouring peoples in Zambia. Describing sona as 'mathematics' is a modern reading; for practitioners they carry stories and knowledge.

sources.title: Sona, drawings and geometric figures on sand – UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage
Demaine et al., 'Properties of sona drawings', Journal of Mathematics and the Arts

points.heading: San knowledge of hoodia recognised in a benefit-sharing deal
points.text: For thousands of years the San ate the bitter flesh of the hoodia succulent to suppress appetite. After South Africa's CSIR patented an appetite-suppressing extract, CSIR acknowledged the San's traditional knowledge in 2002, and in March 2003 the San reached a benefit-sharing agreement with CSIR.
points.note: The agreement followed criticism by NGOs that CSIR had used San knowledge without consent or benefit-sharing. The event records the recognition of traditional knowledge; it does not claim that hoodia products are proven to work as slimming aids.

sources.title: Leveraging Economic Growth through Benefit Sharing – World Intellectual Property Organization

points.datasetTitle: Designing for Black and Mixed-heritage people
points.heading: The public sector equality duty applies to every function
points.text: Section 149 of the Equality Act 2010 requires public authorities to have due regard to the need to eliminate discrimination, advance equality of opportunity and foster good relations. It also applies to other organisations, including contractors, when they carry out public functions, so it covers policy, services, content and data decisions that affect Black and Mixed-heritage people.
points.note: Race is one of the protected characteristics listed in section 149(7). The duty is about the decision process (due regard); it does not dictate a particular outcome. Applies in England, Scotland and Wales.

sources.title: Equality Act 2010, section 149 (Public sector equality duty)
Equality and Human Rights Commission: Public Sector Equality Duty (PSED) (28 June 2022)

points.datasetTitle: Designing for Black and Mixed-heritage people
points.heading: Due regard means meeting different needs, not only avoiding harm
points.text: The duty is not only about avoiding discrimination. Section 149(3) says advancing equality includes taking steps to meet needs that differ between groups and encouraging participation where it is disproportionately low. Service Standard point 5 reflects this: it reminds teams designing public services that public sector organisations have a legal duty to consider everyone's needs.
points.note: Use this to justify targeted work, such as outreach to groups with low take-up. Section 149(6) says compliance may involve treating some people more favourably than others, but only where the Act otherwise permits it; take legal advice before positive action.

sources.title: Equality Act 2010, section 149 (Public sector equality duty)
GOV.UK Service Manual: Service Standard point 5, Make sure everyone can use the service

points.datasetTitle: Designing for Black and Mixed-heritage people
points.heading: Assess impact before you decide, and keep a record
points.text: UK government guidance says the equality assessment must happen before and at the time a decision is considered, and that written records from that time are the easiest way to show compliance. In Scotland and Wales, regulations go further and require listed authorities to assess the impact of new or revised policies.
points.note: In England there is no prescribed format for an equality impact assessment and no requirement to publish it. Scottish regulation 5 requires relevant evidence, including evidence from people who share the characteristic, and publication of the results; Welsh regulation 8 requires published reports where an assessment shows substantial impact. A form filled in after the decision does not show due regard.

sources.title: GOV.UK: Public sector equality duty: guidance for public authorities (18 December 2023)
legislation.gov.uk: The Equality Act 2010 (Specific Duties) (Scotland) Regulations 2012, regulation 5
legislation.gov.uk: The Equality Act 2010 (Statutory Duties) (Wales) Regulations 2011, regulation 8

points.datasetTitle: Designing for Black and Mixed-heritage people
points.heading: Involve the people affected, not only their data
points.text: Welsh regulations require listed authorities to involve people who represent the interests of those who share protected characteristics when carrying out certain duties. UK government guidance calls it good practice to ask about equality impacts in every public consultation, and the Consultation Principles say to consider targeting specific groups.
points.note: Wales regulation 5 is a legal requirement for listed Welsh authorities; the consultation question and targeting are good practice, not law, in England. Black and Mixed-heritage communities are not one group: involve Black African, Black Caribbean and Mixed White and Black Caribbean people and others specifically, and pay or support people for their time where possible.

sources.title: legislation.gov.uk: The Equality Act 2010 (Statutory Duties) (Wales) Regulations 2011, regulation 5 Engagement provisions
GOV.UK: Public sector equality duty: guidance for public authorities (18 December 2023)
GOV.UK (Cabinet Office): Consultation principles 2018

points.datasetTitle: Designing for Black and Mixed-heritage people
points.heading: Start from published ethnicity data before commissioning new research
points.text: The Race Disparity Unit publishes Ethnicity facts and figures, government data on how people from different ethnic groups fare across areas such as health, education, housing, work and crime. Policy teams can use it to build the evidence base for an impact assessment and to see where outcomes differ between specific groups.
points.note: Check the time period, geography and sample size of each measure: many are England-only or England and Wales, and some are several years old. Ethnicity facts and figures is an evidence source; it does not by itself explain the cause of a disparity.

sources.title: GOV.UK: Race Disparity Unit (organisation page)
Ethnicity facts and figures (GOV.UK)

points.datasetTitle: Designing for Black and Mixed-heritage people
points.heading: Plan evaluation that can show different effects for different groups
points.text: The Magenta Book, HM Treasury's guidance on evaluation, lists 'Have different groups been impacted in different ways, how and why?' as a typical impact evaluation question. It notes that experimental approaches are typically not strong at identifying different impacts on particular sub-groups. Separately, it says quota sampling can be used to over-sample minority groups that are not identified in the sampling frame.
points.note: Plan this at design stage: small sub-groups need enough sample size to detect differences. The Magenta Book was last updated in May 2026; it has no separate supplementary guide on equalities.

sources.title: GOV.UK (HM Treasury): The Magenta Book, central government guidance on evaluation (updated 15 May 2026)

points.datasetTitle: Designing for Black and Mixed-heritage people
points.heading: The Service Standard: solve whole problems and exclude no group
points.text: Service Standard point 5 says government services must work for everyone who needs them and teams should avoid excluding any group within their intended audience. Point 2 says users should not need to understand how government works to use a service, which matters for people facing several services at once.
points.note: Page accessed October 2026. These are assessment criteria for GOV.UK services in central government; other public bodies can use them as good practice. Include offline and assisted routes, not only the digital journey.

sources.title: GOV.UK Service Manual: Service Standard point 5, Make sure everyone can use the service
GOV.UK Service Manual: Service Standard point 2, Solve a whole problem for users

points.datasetTitle: Designing for Black and Mixed-heritage people
points.heading: Recruit research participants who reflect your actual users
points.text: The Service Manual tells teams to recruit research participants who represent the actual and likely users of a service, including a spread by ethnicity. Government Communication Service guidance warns that treating participants as homogeneous groups is limiting.
points.note: Recruit within groups as well as across them, for example Black African, Black Caribbean and Mixed White and Black Caribbean participants. Community groups and charities can help, but check that recruits still match your users.

sources.title: GOV.UK Service Manual: Find user research participants (updated 22 September 2026)
GOV.UK Service Manual: Service Standard point 5, Make sure everyone can use the service
Government Communication Service (communications.gov.uk): 4 tips to make your campaign imagery more diverse (undated)

points.datasetTitle: Designing for Black and Mixed-heritage people
points.heading: Recent internet use was not lower in Black or Mixed groups (UK, 2019)
points.text: In January to March 2019, 90.8% of UK adults had used the internet in the previous 3 months. The figure was 92.8% for the Black group and 96.0% for the Mixed group. Do not assume Black or Mixed-heritage users are digitally excluded; test for skills, device, cost and confidence barriers directly.
points.note: Base rate and limits: these are 2019 Labour Force Survey estimates for the UK and are now dated. Younger age profiles in the Black and Mixed groups may explain some of the difference. Recent use does not measure skills, data poverty or quality of access, and regional and age breakdowns are based on small samples.

sources.title: Ethnicity facts and figures: Internet use (last updated 17 July 2020)
GOV.UK Service Manual: Service Standard point 5, Make sure everyone can use the service

points.datasetTitle: Designing for Black and Mixed-heritage people
points.heading: Confidence in local police was lowest for some Black and Mixed groups
points.text: In England and Wales in the year ending March 2023, 68% of adults had confidence in their local police. It was 49% for Black Caribbean people, 49% for Mixed White and Black Caribbean people and 48% for Black 'other' people, but 65% for Black African people. Lower confidence can affect whether people use, or trust, a service.
points.figure: Black Caribbean 49%; Mixed White and Black Caribbean 49%; overall 68%
points.note: This measures confidence in local police only, from the Crime Survey for England and Wales. The ONS Trust in Government survey 2023 bulletin gives no ethnicity breakdown, so no official cross-service trust figure by ethnicity is cited here. Do not apply police figures to other services without your own research.

sources.title: Ethnicity facts and figures: Confidence in the local police (last updated 17 October 2024)

points.datasetTitle: Designing for Black and Mixed-heritage people
points.heading: Language needs vary widely within Black and Mixed groups
points.text: In 2021, 1.5% of usual residents aged 3 and over in England and Wales could not speak English well and 0.3% could not speak it at all. In 2011, English (or Welsh in Wales) was the main language for 98.5% of Black Caribbean people but 71.9% of Black African people. GOV.UK publishing guidance says to look for evidence of user need, such as search terms, contact centre calls and requests for translations, when deciding whether to translate.
points.figure: Black African 71.9%; Black Caribbean 98.5% (English main language, 2011)
points.note: The ethnic group breakdown is from the 2011 Census (England and Wales) and is dated; the overall 2021 figures are newer. Main language other than English does not mean poor English. Check contact centre data, search terms and requests for translations before translating.

sources.title: ONS: Language, England and Wales: Census 2021 (29 November 2022)
Ethnicity facts and figures: English language skills (last updated 26 March 2024)

points.datasetTitle: Designing for Black and Mixed-heritage people
points.heading: Do not use the acronyms that group everyone together
points.text: GOV.UK style and the Race Disparity Unit both say not to use the umbrella acronyms that group ethnic minorities together (quoted below). They emphasise Asian and Black groups and leave out others, including Mixed groups. Where grouping is truly needed, use 'ethnic minorities' or 'people from ethnic minority backgrounds'.
points.note: This is government style, not a legal rule. The NHS service manual gives the same advice.

sources.title: Ethnicity facts and figures: Writing about ethnicity
A to Z style guide - Writing to GOV.UK standards
NHS digital service manual: Inclusive content: ethnicity, religion and nationality (October 2023)

points.datasetTitle: Designing for Black and Mixed-heritage people
points.heading: Name specific groups, because broad groups hide differences
points.text: Guidance says to refer to ethnic minority groups individually rather than as a single group, and to be as specific as you can. Broad terms can mask disparities between groups and lead to misleading readings of data.
points.note: For example, Black Caribbean and Black African people often have different outcomes (see confidence in local police above). Name the groups your evidence covers, and say when you have had to combine groups.

sources.title: A to Z style guide - Writing to GOV.UK standards
Ethnicity facts and figures: Writing about ethnicity
NHS digital service manual: Inclusive content: ethnicity, religion and nationality (October 2023)

points.datasetTitle: Designing for Black and Mixed-heritage people
points.heading: Use phrases people accepted in research, with capital letters
points.text: In Race Disparity Unit research, 'people from a Black Caribbean background', 'the Black ethnic group' and 'Black people' were acceptable, but 'Blacks' was not. The RDU writes 'people with a Mixed ethnic background' and avoids 'non-White'. The NHS service manual says to use a capital letter when writing about ethnicity.
points.note: The GOV.UK A to Z style guide has no entry on capitalising Black; the capital-letter rule here comes from the NHS service manual and RDU practice. Describe people as they describe themselves where you can.

sources.title: Ethnicity facts and figures: Writing about ethnicity
NHS digital service manual: Inclusive content: ethnicity, religion and nationality (October 2023)

points.datasetTitle: Designing for Black and Mixed-heritage people
points.heading: Plain English is mandatory on GOV.UK
points.text: GOV.UK says plain English is mandatory because content must be understandable to everyone who needs it. It cites 1 in 6 adults in England with very poor literacy skills, and notes some users do not have English as their first language.
points.note: The literacy figure is quoted by GOV.UK without a date on the page; check the original survey before reusing it as a statistic. Plain English supports, but does not replace, translation where there is evidence of need.

sources.title: GOV.UK publishing guidance: Clear language
GOV.UK (Cabinet Office): Consultation principles: guidance (19 March 2018)

points.datasetTitle: Designing for Black and Mixed-heritage people
points.heading: Show a range of people in images, and avoid stereotypes
points.text: The GOV.UK Design System warns that only showing people of a particular age, gender or ethnicity can exclude people and reinforce negative stereotypes. Government Communication Service guidance adds that diversity for its own sake should not be the goal and suggests testing images with the audience.
points.note: The Design System advises avoiding people in illustrations. Avoid tokenism: show Black and Mixed-heritage people in ordinary, relevant roles rather than only in content about race. The GCS page is undated.

sources.title: GOV.UK Design System: Images
Government Communication Service (communications.gov.uk): 4 tips to make your campaign imagery more diverse (undated)

points.datasetTitle: Designing for Black and Mixed-heritage people
points.heading: Accessibility is a legal requirement for public sector websites
points.text: The 2018 accessibility regulations require most public sector websites and apps (there are exemptions and a disproportionate burden test) to meet accessibility standards and publish an accessibility statement. GOV.UK guidance says at least 1 in 5 people in the UK have a long term illness, impairment or disability.
points.figure: At least 1 in 5 people in the UK
points.note: GOV.UK guidance now points to WCAG 2.2 AA. Accessibility is not specific to ethnicity, but disabled Black and Mixed-heritage people can face both barriers, so test with them.

sources.title: Understanding accessibility requirements for public sector bodies
The Public Sector Bodies (Websites and Mobile Applications) (No. 2) Accessibility Regulations 2018 (SI 2018/952)

points.datasetTitle: Designing for Black and Mixed-heritage people
points.heading: Use the harmonised ethnicity standard so data can be compared
points.text: The Government Statistical Service harmonised standard lists Black, African, Caribbean and Black British options and Mixed options such as White and Black Caribbean and White and Black African. In the 2021 Census, 4.2% of people in England (2.4 million) identified as Black and 3.0% (1.7 million) as Mixed or Multiple.
points.note: The question wording differs slightly in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. Using the standard lets you compare your data with Census and survey data. See the hub's separate page on collecting ethnicity data for detail.

sources.title: Government Analysis Function: Ethnicity harmonised standard
ONS: Ethnic group, England and Wales, Census 2021

points.datasetTitle: Designing for Black and Mixed-heritage people
points.heading: Design forms for self-identification, choice and write-in answers
points.text: The Race Disparity Unit says the best way to collect ethnicity data is to ask people, with a 'prefer not to say' option and a clear explanation of why. Write-in options add detail: in the 2021 Census they showed 271,000 people identifying as Nigerian, 151,000 as Somali and 113,000 as Ghanaian.
points.note: Self-reported ethnicity is better than data recorded by a third party or proxy, which the RDU says is lower quality and may not reflect how people would describe themselves. Where possible, keep the detailed category and any write-in answer as well as the broad group (the hub's advice). Some people were offended when White was listed first, and others disliked inconsistent ordering, so use a consistent, tested order.

sources.title: Standards for ethnicity data (GOV.UK)
ONS: Ethnic group, England and Wales, Census 2021
Ethnicity facts and figures: Writing about ethnicity

points.datasetTitle: Designing for Black and Mixed-heritage people
points.heading: Leaving ethnicity out of a model does not stop bias
points.text: The Centre for Data Ethics and Innovation review in 2020 found that 'fairness through unawareness' is often not enough, because other data can act as proxies. It said data is needed to monitor outcomes and identify bias, but protected characteristic data is often not available.
points.note: The review covered policing, local government, financial services and recruitment. Collect ethnicity data lawfully and for a stated purpose so you can test outcomes by group; seek legal advice on any bias mitigation technique. Its recommendation on transparency applies to algorithms that have an impact on significant decisions affecting individuals.

sources.title: CDEI review into bias in algorithmic decision-making (27 Nov 2020)
GOV.UK (Centre for Data Ethics and Innovation): CDEI publishes review into bias in algorithmic decision-making (27 November 2020)

points.datasetTitle: Designing for Black and Mixed-heritage people
points.heading: Facial recognition accuracy for Black people depends on settings
points.text: note (last sentence replacement): The Home Office says a new algorithm has been procured and independently tested that can be used at settings with no significant demographic variation; it was due for operational testing in 2026.
points.figure: False positive identification rate (FPIR) 5.5% Black, 9.9% Black female, 0.04% White (threshold 0.8, test database ~180,000 images, NPL 2025)
points.note: Two different algorithms and uses: the 2023 figures are for live facial recognition, the 2025 figures for retrospective searches. The 0.8 threshold was chosen by NPL for testing, not stated as the setting police use. The Home Office says a new algorithm has been procured and independently tested and can be used at settings with no significant variation between groups; it was still due for operational testing.

points.datasetTitle: Designing for Black and Mixed-heritage people
points.heading: Publish how algorithmic tools work, including bias testing
points.text: The Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard is mandatory for all government departments and some arm's-length bodies. Its guidance asks organisations to describe any bias and fairness evaluation they have done. The CDEI review recommended a mandatory transparency obligation for the public sector in 2020.
points.note: The standard is recommended, not mandatory, for the wider public sector. The ATRS guidance does not mention the equality duty by name; link your record to your equality impact assessment yourself.

GOV.UK: Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard: guidance for public sector bodies (updated 8 May 2025)

points.datasetTitle: Designing for Black and Mixed-heritage people
points.heading: Protect small groups when you publish data
points.text: Black and Mixed groups can be small in local or service data, which raises the risk of identifying people. Government Analysis Function guidance says disclosure risk is higher where table cells have low counts, and the RDU standards say not to disclose data based on small numbers of people.
points.note: Small numbers also make estimates unreliable: report sample sizes and confidence intervals, and say when you have combined groups. Combining groups protects privacy but can hide differences, so explain the trade-off.

sources.title: Government Analysis Function: An introduction to Statistical Disclosure Control (SDC) (19 August 2026)
Standards for ethnicity data (GOV.UK)

points.heading: 1.7 million people in England and Wales are in a Mixed ethnic group
points.text: At Census 2021, 1,717,977 people in England and Wales (2.9% of the population) identified with one of the 'Mixed or Multiple' ethnic groups, up from 2.2% in 2011 and 1.3% in 2001. The share was 3.0% in England and 1.6% in Wales, so local services in Wales should not assume the England picture.
points.note: Census figures are self-identified. ONS rounds the England (3.0%) and Wales (1.6%) shares separately; the combined 2.9% comes from GOV.UK Ethnicity facts and figures. 2011 and 2001 shares are taken from the same GOV.UK table.

sources.title: Population of England and Wales
ONS: Ethnic group, England and Wales, Census 2021

points.heading: White and Black Caribbean is the largest Mixed group
points.text: In 2021, 513,040 people (0.9%) identified as Mixed White and Black Caribbean and 249,593 (0.4%) as Mixed White and Black African. The White and Black Caribbean share has risen from 0.5% in 2001 to 0.8% in 2011 and 0.9% in 2021, and White and Black African from 0.2% to 0.3% to 0.4%.
points.note: England and Wales only. Changes over time mix real population growth with people choosing different answers between censuses (see 'Words and identity').

sources.title: Population of England and Wales

points.heading: Mixed groups are the youngest in England and Wales
points.text: People in Mixed groups had a median age of 19 in 2021, against 40 for the whole population of England and Wales; the White and Black African and White and Asian groups had the lowest median age of the 19 groups, 16. Nearly half (48.6%) of people identifying as White and Black African were aged 0 to 15, against 18.5% of the whole population.
points.note: A young age profile partly drives some outcome gaps, so compare like-for-like age groups where possible.

sources.title: Office for National Statistics: Ethnic group by age and sex, England and Wales: Census 2021
Age groups

points.heading: Scotland: Mixed group tripled to about 61,000 people
points.text: Scotland's Census 2022 counted 60,899 people (1.12%) in the 'Mixed or multiple ethnic group' category, against 19,815 (0.37%) in 2011, an increase NRS reports as 41,100 people. Scotland uses a single write-in Mixed category, with no separate White and Black Caribbean or White and Black African boxes.
points.note: Counts are from the chart data published on the NRS page. Scotland's census was in 2022, a year after the rest of the UK, and its categories are not directly comparable with England and Wales.

sources.title: National Records of Scotland: Scotland's Census 2022 - Ethnic group, national identity, language and religion (21 May 2024)

points.heading: Northern Ireland: Mixed is the largest minority ethnic group
points.text: In Northern Ireland's Census 2021, 14,400 people (0.8%) were in the 'Mixed Ethnicities' output category, the largest of the minority ethnic groups. The NI question offered a single 'Mixed ethnic group' option.
points.note: NISRA rounds figures for display. The NI classification differs from England, Wales and Scotland.

sources.title: NISRA: Census 2021 Main statistics for Northern Ireland, statistical bulletin: Ethnic group (22 September 2022)
List of ethnic groups - GOV.UK

points.heading: One in ten households has members of different ethnic groups
points.text: In 2021, 10.1% of households in England and Wales (2.5 million) had members who identified with two or more ethnic groups, up from 8.7% in 2011. In 2011, 88% of people identifying as White and Black Caribbean who lived as part of a couple were in an inter-ethnic relationship.
points.note: The inter-ethnic relationships analysis uses 2011 data; ONS has not been found to publish the same analysis for 2021. Multi-ethnic households include, but are not limited to, Mixed families.

sources.title: ONS: Ethnic group, England and Wales, Census 2021
Office for National Statistics: What does the 2011 Census tell us about inter-ethnic relationships? (3 July 2014)

points.heading: Government style: 'people with a Mixed ethnic background'
points.text: The government's style guide refers to 'ethnicity' rather than 'race'. It avoids 'Mixed people' and 'Mixed race people' and usually says 'people with a Mixed ethnic background' or 'people from the Mixed ethnic group'.
points.note: This is a style for official statistics, not a rule for how people describe themselves. Many people call themselves mixed race (see next point).

sources.title: Ethnicity facts and figures: Writing about ethnicity

points.heading: Mixed race, mixed heritage, dual heritage: terms people use
points.text: Academic research found 'mixed race' was the term most people in this group chose for themselves, although it is contested because it relies on the idea of 'race'. 'Mixed heritage' and 'dual heritage' are also used, including in official reports, and some young people dislike 'dual heritage' because it refers to only two backgrounds.
points.note: The research dates from 2009 and preferences change. Ask people which term they prefer and use it.

sources.title: University of Kent (Kent Academic Repository): Aspinall, Mixed race, mixed origins or what? Anthropology Today 25(2) (2009)
Mixed Museum (Mix-d: Museum): What's in a name?
HM Inspectorate of Probation: The experiences of black and mixed heritage boys in the youth justice system (October 2021)

points.heading: Each UK nation asks the question differently
points.text: England and Wales use 'Mixed or Multiple ethnic groups' with tick boxes for White and Black Caribbean, White and Black African, White and Asian, and a write-in for any other Mixed background. Scotland uses one 'Mixed or multiple ethnic group' option where people write in their ethnic group, and Northern Ireland a single 'Mixed ethnic group' option. Figures from the 4 nations cannot be added together group by group.
points.note: Scotland figures come from its 2022 census; the others are from 2021.

sources.title: Government Analysis Function: Ethnicity harmonised standard
List of ethnic groups - GOV.UK

points.heading: Testing found some people uneasy with the word 'Mixed'
points.text: ONS question testing for Census 2021 found most people were comfortable with the colour terms, but a small proportion were uncomfortable with terms including 'Mixed'. In 2011, people identifying as Mixed were more likely to tick several boxes, so ONS tested 2 write-in lines on the paper form.
points.note: Findings come from ONS focus groups and testing, not a representative survey.

sources.title: Office for National Statistics: National identity, ethnic group, language and religion question development for Census 2021

points.heading: The same person may answer differently over time
points.text: Linking the same people across the 2001 and 2011 censuses showed that Mixed categories were less stable than most others: 43% of people who chose White and Black African in 2001 chose another category in 2011. White and Black Caribbean was more stable (76.4% gave the same answer), and ONS notes people in Mixed groups are more likely to have more than one ethnicity in their records.
points.note: Changes can reflect real changes in how people see themselves, who filled in the form, or errors and imputation. This is not evidence that anyone's answer is 'wrong'.

sources.title: University of Manchester, Centre on Dynamics of Ethnicity (CoDE): How have people's ethnic identities changed in England and Wales? (Census briefing, 2001-2011 data)
Office for National Statistics: Understanding consistency of ethnicity data recorded in health-related administrative datasets in England: 2011 to 2021 (16 January 2023)

points.heading: White and Black Caribbean pupils: suspension rate almost twice average
points.text: In England in the 2022 to 2023 school year, pupils in the Mixed White and Black Caribbean group had 1,736 suspensions for every 10,000 pupils, almost twice the national rate of 9.33 per 100. Only the Gypsy or Roma and Irish Traveller groups had higher rates.
points.note: Rates count suspensions, not pupils, so one pupil can be counted more than once. These are 2022 to 2023 figures from Ethnicity facts and figures; DfE has since published newer years on Explore education statistics, which are not covered here here. The data cannot show causes.

sources.title: Pupil exclusions (suspensions)

points.heading: Higher permanent exclusion rates, even after other factors
points.text: In 2022 to 2023 the permanent exclusion rate for Mixed White and Black Caribbean pupils in England was 0.24, against 0.11 for all pupils. The Timpson Review (2019) found these pupils were about 1.6 times as likely as White British pupils to be permanently excluded after controlling for factors such as poverty and special educational needs.
points.note: Small numbers (323 exclusions) make rates volatile. The Timpson analysis uses older data; it controls for recorded factors but cannot rule out unrecorded ones.

sources.title: Permanent exclusions
GOV.UK (Department for Education): Edward Timpson publishes landmark exclusions review (7 May 2019)

points.heading: Children from Mixed groups are over-represented in care
points.text: On 31 March 2025, 11% of children looked after by local authorities in England were from Mixed or Multiple ethnic groups. DfE says children from Mixed groups were over-represented compared with the overall child population.
points.note: DfE publishes this at the 5-group level only on the release page; it does not split out White and Black Caribbean or White and Black African there. Only one authoritative source verified.

sources.title: Children looked after in England including adoptions, reporting year 2025

points.heading: Mixed children are over-represented in youth custody
points.text: In the year ending March 2025, Mixed children were 18% of children in youth custody in England and Wales and 18% of those remanded in custody. An HM Inspectorate of Probation inspection (2021) found black and mixed heritage boys were consistently over-represented in custody and often received poorer services.
points.note: Youth justice data uses 5 broad groups, so Mixed subgroups cannot be separated. Over-representation alone does not show discrimination or cause.

sources.title: Youth Justice Statistics: 2024 to 2025
HM Inspectorate of Probation: The experiences of black and mixed heritage boys in the youth justice system (October 2021)

points.heading: Employment: 69% of people from Mixed groups were in work
points.text: In 2022, 69% of people aged 16 to 64 from Mixed ethnic groups in England, Scotland and Wales were employed, against 76% overall. The Mixed group is the only one where women had a higher employment rate (71%) than men (67%).
points.note: Survey estimate (Annual Population Survey). Mixed groups are aggregated, so the figure cannot show White and Black Caribbean or White and Black African separately. The younger age profile may affect the rate.

sources.title: Employment

points.heading: Higher detention rates under the Mental Health Act
points.text: In England in the year to March 2023, people from Mixed groups were detained under the Mental Health Act at a rate of 158 per 100,000, against 64 for White people. The rate for Mixed White and Black Caribbean was 102 and for Mixed White and Black African 139.
points.note: Standardised rates from the Mental Health Services Data Set, as published on Ethnicity facts and figures, which gives 158 in its summary and 157 in one table. The Mixed figure is driven mainly by the Mixed Other group (288 per 100,000). Rates fell sharply in 2022/23 partly because 2021 census population estimates replaced older ones. Ethnicity recording in health data is less reliable for Mixed groups (see 'Data quality'). One source; NHS England's newer years are not covered here.

sources.title: GOV.UK Ethnicity facts and figures: Detentions under the Mental Health Act (published 16 August 2024)

points.heading: Dido Elizabeth Belle (1761 to 1804), raised at Kenwood
points.text: Dido Elizabeth Belle was the daughter of Royal Navy officer Sir John Lindsay and an African woman, Maria Bell(e). She was raised by Lord Mansfield's family at Kenwood in north London, and her baptism in 1766 is recorded at St George's, Bloomsbury.
points.note: Much of her early life is uncertain; English Heritage notes conflicting accounts of how her mother came to England.

points.heading: Samuel Coleridge-Taylor (1875 to 1912), composer
points.text: Samuel Coleridge-Taylor was born in Holborn, London, in 1875. The National Archives records that his father was a medical student from Sierra Leone and his mother was English. He became famous for Hiawatha's Wedding Feast and died in 1912.

points.heading: The 1930 Fletcher Report stigmatised mixed families in Liverpool
points.text: In 1930 the “Liverpool Association for the Welfare of Half-Caste Children” published Muriel Fletcher's report on mixed families in Liverpool and other ports. The Mixed Museum describes it as biased and methodologically flawed but highly influential on how mixed race people and families were seen for many years.
points.note: The report uses offensive historic language; the University of Liverpool archive keeps the original terms only to describe the record accurately.

points.heading: About 2,000 'brown babies' born during the Second World War
points.text: Around 2,000 babies were born in Britain to Black American servicemen and white British women during the Second World War. Nearly half were given up to local authorities or children's homes, and the British government blocked their adoption by Americans, including their fathers, despite interest from hundreds of African Americans.
points.note: The total is an estimate. Most evidence comes from oral histories and government records gathered by Professor Lucy Bland (Anglia Ruskin University).

points.heading: Mixed categories first appeared in the England and Wales census in 2001
points.text: The census for England and Wales first asked about ethnicity in 1991, and 4 Mixed categories were added in 2001. ONS notes that Mixed groups largely reflect relationships formed since post-war migration. 660,000 people (1%) identified as Mixed in 2001, rising to 1.2 million (2%) in 2011.
points.note: Before 2001, people of mixed ancestry had to choose a single group or 'Other', so earlier counts are not comparable.

points.heading: Health records agree least with census for Mixed groups
points.text: When ONS linked 2011 Census answers to NHS records, agreement on ethnicity was below 67% for all Mixed groups, and below 21% for 'Other Mixed'. By comparison, White British and Bangladeshi had agreement of 92% or more.
points.note: Linked data covers people found in both sources, which may introduce bias. Disagreement may reflect how records were collected, as well as changes in how people identify.

points.heading: Admin data can undercount Mixed young adults
points.text: ONS's first admin-based ethnicity estimates for England under-represented the Asian, Black and Mixed groups among people aged 20 to 34, and the 'Other' group was much larger than expected compared with the 2011 Census. ONS has since revised its methods; it shows that admin records can give a different picture from the census for Mixed groups.
points.note: Research and experimental statistics; ONS has continued to change its methods.

sources.title: Office for National Statistics: Producing admin-based ethnicity statistics for England: changes to data and methods (23 May 2022)

points.heading: Aggregated 'Mixed' figures hide differences
points.text: Many surveys and administrative datasets publish only one 'Mixed' total, which can hide large differences between White and Black Caribbean, White and Black African, White and Asian and other Mixed groups. Government standards say to note this limit whenever groups are combined.
points.note: Some data on Ethnicity facts and figures still uses the older 2001 Census categories.

sources.title: Standards for ethnicity data (GOV.UK)
List of ethnic groups - GOV.UK

points.heading: What designers and analysts should do
points.text: Ask people to describe their own ethnicity rather than recording it for them, use the harmonised categories with a write-in option, and do not combine groups in non-standard ways. ONS advises using at least the 5 main ethnic groups, and analysts should flag small numbers and wide confidence intervals.
points.note: Self-reporting improves accuracy but cannot remove changes in how people identify over time.

points.heading: Latin America: about 134 million Afro-descendants (ECLAC estimate)
points.text: The UN Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC/CEPAL) estimates that Afro-descendants in Latin America number 134 million people, 21% of the region's population. This is a modelled regional estimate built from national censuses and surveys that ask the question differently, and ECLAC's 2020 presentation said more countries were expected to add an Afro-descendant question in the 2020 census round.
points.note: Modelled estimate by ECLAC, not a census count. The UNFPA page reports ECLAC's own launch of the figure, so the two sources are not independent. ECLAC's slide on census rounds lists 11 countries that asked an Afro-descendant question in the 2010 round; this count is taken from the list on the slide, not from a stated total.

points.heading: Brazil: 'pardo' (brown, mixed) became the largest group in 2022
points.text: Brazil's statistics office IBGE asks people to declare their own colour or race from five options: branca (white), preta (Black), parda (brown), amarela (yellow) or indígena (Indigenous). IBGE says people may understand these categories in different ways, drawing on family origin, skin colour, physical features, ethnicity or community belonging, and that it treats race as a social category, not a biological one. In the 2022 Census 92.1 million people (45.3%) declared themselves pardo and 20.7 million (10.2%) preto, while 88.3 million (43.5%) declared themselves branco. It is the first census in IBGE's comparable series, which runs from 1991, in which more people declared themselves pardo than branco: in 1991, 2000 and 2010 the white share was larger.
points.note: Figures are from IBGE's 2022 Census results on ethnic-racial identification (December 2023), with a newspaper report of the same release as a second source. 'Brown' is a direct translation of parda; it is often described in English as mixed, but that is not IBGE's definition. Some headlines say 'first time since 1872'; that compares with a nineteenth-century census whose categories are not comparable, so it is not used here.

points.heading: Colombia: one census option joins 'negro', 'mulato' and Afro-Colombian
points.text: Colombia's statistics office DANE asks people which group they recognise themselves as 'according to their culture, people or physical features' (de acuerdo con su cultura, pueblo o rasgos físicos). One answer option combines negro(a) (Black), mulato(a), afrodescendiente and afrocolombiano(a), with separate options for Raizal people of the San Andrés, Providencia and Santa Catalina archipelago and Palenquero people of San Basilio. In the 2018 census, answers in these groups fell 30.8% compared with 2005. DANE attributed this to incomplete answers, including the question not being asked, refusals and areas that could not be safely covered. Its official figure of 4,671,160 people (9.34%) therefore comes from a household survey estimate (the 2018 Quality of Life Survey) rather than the census count.
points.note: The 2018 census count itself was 2,982,224 (6.8%), down from 4,311,757 (10.4%) in 2005; DANE adopted the survey estimate as the official total. The fall was publicly contested, including a 2020 legal challenge (tutela) reported by La Silla Vacía. 'Mulato' is usually translated as mixed, but DANE does not define the term.

points.heading: Mexico: 2.6 million people identified as Afro-Mexican in 2020
points.text: Mexico's 2020 Census, run by INEGI, counted 2,576,213 people who identified as Afro-Mexican, Afro-descendant or Black (negra), about 2% of the population. Mexico's Constitution recognises Afro-Mexican peoples and communities 'whatever their self-designation', reflecting that people use several names for themselves.
points.note: Count and share from INEGI's presentation of 2020 Census results, also reported by the Mexico City Human Rights Commission and the Wilson Center. People were counted if they recognised themselves as Afro-Mexican or Afro-descendant; the Wilson Center describes the group as including people who identify as Black (negra).

points.heading: United States: 'Two or More Races' rose to 33.8 million in 2020
points.text: The US Census Bureau lets people choose more than one race. The 'Two or More Races' population was 33.8 million (10.2%) in 2020, up from 9 million in 2010, and 46.9 million people (14.2%) were Black or African American alone or in combination with another race. The Bureau says much of the rise reflects improved question design and coding, so 2010 to 2020 comparisons need caution.
points.figure: 33.8 million Two or More Races (10.2%); 46.9 million Black alone or in combination (14.2%)
points.note: The 276% increase is partly a measurement change, as the Census Bureau states. Pew's figure of a 295% rise in non-Hispanic multiracial Black people compares 2000 with 2024 using Census Bureau data, including the 2024 American Community Survey, so it is a different source and period. In 2020, 3.1 million people reported both White and Black or African American, the third-largest multiracial combination.

sources.title: US Census Bureau: Improved Race and Ethnicity Measures Reveal U.S. Population Is Much More Multiracial (2021)

points.heading: South Africa: 'Coloured' is a population group used in statistics
points.text: Statistics South Africa still publishes figures by population group, and in Census 2022 people in the 'Coloured' group made up 8.2% of the national population; the City of Cape Town's census profile puts the share in Cape Town at 35.0%. The categories come from apartheid-era legal race classification. Censuses have asked people to identify themselves since 1996, and Stats SA's Statistician-General explained that the question was kept so that progress in eradicating the consequences of apartheid could be measured and monitored. The figure records how people describe themselves in the census; it is a statistical category, not a judgement about anyone's ancestry.
points.note: Handle the term with care: it comes from apartheid race classification (a 2016 Stats SA presentation lists the pre-1994 legislated groups as including 'Coloured (Mixed)'). How far people today embrace or reject the label is not covered here. The Cape Town share is from the City of Cape Town, using Stats SA census data.

points.heading: Operational Delivery is over half the Civil Service
points.text: Operational Delivery is the largest Civil Service profession, with 300,080 civil servants at 31 March 2026. It accounts for 54.9% of civil servants with a recorded profession; the next largest are Policy (6.8%) and Digital and Data (5.8%).
points.note: 54.9% is of the 546,425 with a reported profession; of all 557,825 civil servants the share is 53.8%. Professions data reporting rate was 98.0%.

points.heading: Civil Service ethnic minority share at a record 19.2%
points.text: Of civil servants with a known ethnicity, 19.2% were from an ethnic minority background in 2026, up from 18.0% in 2025. Black civil servants numbered 26,655, the second largest ethnic minority group after Asian civil servants (46,310).
points.note: The 5.8% Black share is 26,655 of 459,540 civil servants with a known ethnicity (data browser totals); it is not a figure stated in the bulletin. Percentages exclude unknown and undeclared ethnicity, which together cover 98,285 people.

points.heading: Ethnicity pay gap reporting is still voluntary
points.text: No employer in Great Britain has to publish an ethnicity pay gap. Government guidance from April 2023 offers a voluntary, consistent method. In March 2026 the government published its consultation response and draft clauses for mandatory reporting by employers with 250 or more staff, but the Equality (Race and Disability) Bill had not been introduced to Parliament by October 2026.
points.note: Status as at 26 October 2026. The bill was not in the 13 May 2026 King's Speech, and the government's background briefing notes for that speech list no such bill (GOV.UK). One law firm's working assumption is that any duty would start no earlier than 2027. Proposed scope: private and voluntary employers in Great Britain and public bodies in England with 250 or more staff. The government response and draft clauses are covered on the DEEIA lens page; this point covers what it means for employers now.

points.heading: A Black pay gap may not show in published figures
points.text: The planned rules would require at least a two-group comparison (for example, White and all ethnic minority staff), with five broad groups 'where possible'. The 2023 voluntary guidance advises publishing a group only where it has at least 50 employees. Where Black staff are few, their figures may be merged into a wider group or left out.
points.note: The minimum group size for the mandatory scheme was still being decided in March 2026; the consultation had proposed at least 10 employees per group. The last sentence of the text is a reading of the two rules, not a finding from data.

points.heading: Most large employers already hold staff ethnicity data
points.text: The government's impact assessment estimates that 89% of employers with 250 or more staff already collect their employees' ethnicity, and 44% already publish an ethnicity pay gap. Both estimates rest mainly on a 2023 Business in the Community survey of employers that had signed its Race at Work Charter.
points.note: Scope: employers with 250 or more staff in England, Scotland and Wales. The survey covered nearly 250 employers already committed to action on race, so it may overstate practice across all large employers. The impact assessment treats the sample as 'relatively representative'. Its own 2025 business survey found lower figures: 82% collect ethnicity data, 27% calculate an ethnicity pay gap and 9% publish one. The impact assessment calls 44% 'a fair mid-point'. A 2024 CIPD survey found 40% of large employers carrying out ethnicity pay gap analysis. The Race at Work Charter itself is covered elsewhere in the hub.

points.heading: Social value in central government contracts
points.text: Since October 2025, central government buyers must use the Social Value Model in Procurement Policy Note 002 for contracts above the threshold. Social value must normally be worth at least 10% of the total score, with limited exceptions where it is 10% of the quality score. Buyers choose outcomes relevant to the contract. One listed example of fair pay practice is monitoring and reporting gender and ethnicity pay gaps.
points.note: The model has no outcome specific to race; ethnicity appears as an example under fair pay, and another outcome covers jobs for groups under-represented in the workforce. It applies to central government, not to every public body. Contracts and outcomes vary, so suppliers are not asked about ethnicity pay gaps in every tender.

points.heading: The equality duty follows public money into contracts
points.text: When a public body buys services, the equality duty stays with it: Cabinet Office guidance says the duty cannot be delegated and has no financial threshold. A contractor that exercises public functions must itself have due regard to the duty's aims when carrying them out. The duty itself is set out on The DEEIA lens page.
points.note: Section 149 extends to England, Scotland and Wales, not Northern Ireland. A private member's bill to repeal it is before Parliament and is not law; see the DEEIA lens page.

points.heading: Supplier diversity: local commitments, little national data
points.text: Some public bodies buy membership of supplier diversity networks to reach businesses owned by ethnic minority people. The City of London Corporation describes itself as the first governing body to join Minority Supplier Development UK. Westminster City Council and the Metropolitan Police joined later. Its own paper says data protection law limits how buyers can find diverse-owned suppliers. A 2021 report for that network called on government and public bodies to lead.
points.note: The sources give no national figure for public spending with Black-owned suppliers. 'Ethnic minority businesses' in these sources covers all ethnic minority groups, not Black-owned firms alone. The 2021 report was commissioned by the supplier diversity network itself. For business support and finance, see the Black enterprise page.

points.heading: Black trustees: 3% overall, 7% among under-60s
points.text: In the Charity Commission's 2024 survey, 3% of trustees were Black, compared with 4% of adults. Among trustees under 60 the picture reverses: 7% were Black, compared with 5% of the population of that age.
points.note: England and Wales, registered charities. Survey of 2,194 trustees, weighted by charity income, compared with Census 2021. The regulator's summary names Asian, mixed and other ethnic groups, not Black people, as less likely to be trustees; the report gives no significance test for the 3% against 4% gap. Mixed-ethnicity trustees were 1% against 2% of adults. One trade press report places a 1% Asian figure in the under-60 group; the regulator's report gives it for over-60s.

points.heading: Black staff are 3.8% of the voluntary sector workforce
points.text: In December 2023, 13% of people working in the UK voluntary sector were from Global Majority backgrounds, against 15% in the public sector and 16% in the private sector. Black employees made up 3.8% of the voluntary sector workforce.
points.note: UK, December 2023. NCVO puts the Global Majority share of the population at 18%. An earlier Almanac (2022) found charities less ethnically diverse than other sectors; the 2024 edition says the sector 'still lags behind slightly', with the recent rise driven mainly by Asian workers. 'Global Majority' is NCVO's term. Labour Force Survey estimates are now official statistics in development (ONS).

sources.title: NCVO: UK Civil Society Almanac 2024: who works in the voluntary sector? (2024)
Charity Times: Charities 'less ethnically diverse' than the private and public sectors, research finds (19 October 2022)

points.heading: Small groups with thin reserves
points.text: A spring 2020 survey by the Ubele Initiative found that most responding Black, Asian and minority ethnic-led groups were micro or small, with yearly income under £100,000, and most held no reserves. The authors estimated that 87% could stop operating if the crisis lasted beyond three months.
points.note: Self-selecting sample: 182 responses from 165 organisations, of which 137 were led by Black, Asian and minority ethnic people, and 62% of those were in London. It is not representative of the sector. The 87% figure is used in different ways: in the report for the share that could close (an author projection) and the share that were micro or small (61 of 70 Wave 2 respondents); in press coverage for the share without three months' reserves. The report found 68% held no reserves. The groups are not broken down into Black-led and others. No register counts Black-led charities.

sources.title: The Ubele Initiative: Impact of COVID-19 on the BAME community and voluntary sector, final report (April 2020; copy hosted by Diversity UK)

points.heading: Funding and commissioning barriers named by Black and minoritised-led groups
points.text: The 2021 Booska Paper, convened by the Ubele Initiative, gathered the views of Black and minoritised community leaders on funding and commissioning during the pandemic. It made nine calls to action for funders. Among the barriers reported were tenders weighted mostly on price.
points.note: Qualitative research: the price and quality split is an example from participants, not a national figure. The second source repeats Ubele's own summary.

points.heading: Black majority churches and London church growth
points.text: Sunday church attendance in London rose by 16% between 2005 and 2012, bucking a national downward trend, with growth especially among Black majority and immigrant churches. Two-thirds of new London churches were Pentecostal Black majority churches. A study of Southwark, reported in 2017, counted 240 Black majority churches in that borough alone.
points.note: London only; the London-wide figures date from 2012 and come from one study, the London Church Census (commissioned by London City Mission). The share of Inner London worshippers who are Black is covered elsewhere in the hub.

points.heading: Churches as partners in the vaccine rollout
points.text: In March 2021, leaders of sixty Black majority churches issued a joint statement backing the NHS COVID-19 vaccine rollout. Some church leaders offered their buildings as pop-up vaccination sites.
points.note: The sources give no count of vaccination clinics held in church buildings and no measure of the effect on uptake. Coverage is UK-wide but examples are mainly from London.

sources.title: The Voice: UK's black majority churches want their congregations to consider taking the COVID-19 vaccine (2 March 2021)
