points.heading: Funder audits: about 5% of funding reached minority-led groups
points.text: Twenty funders that audited over £271 million of grants with the Funders for Race Equality Alliance tool found that 5% of the money went to organisations both led by and working for Black, Asian and minority ethnic communities. An earlier group of 13 funders found that 6% of funded organisations were led by the communities they served.
points.note: UK. The two figures measure different things (share of money and share of funded organisations); the 13 funders were the first cohort of the 20. 'Led by' meant at least half of the board and senior team came from the communities served. The audit uses a combined Black, Asian and minority ethnic category with no Black-only figure. Funders chose to take part, so the results may not represent all grant-makers.

sources.title: Equally Ours (host of the Funders for Race Equality Alliance): Funding audit: current practice in racial justice funding (results to November 2021)
ACEVO (blog by Barrow Cadbury Trust for the Funders for Race Equality Alliance): Funding and racial justice: data driving change (20 May 2021)

points.heading: Foundations now publish their own racial equity figures
points.text: Some large foundations now report every year how much of their funding goes to groups led by people facing racial inequity. Paul Hamlyn Foundation put 17% of its audited 2024/25 UK funding into grants to organisations 'led by and for' those communities; Esmée Fairbairn Foundation reported 25.4% of its 2025 funding to organisations they lead.
points.note: UK. Definitions differ: Paul Hamlyn's 17% uses a majority of board and senior staff; on the stricter DEI Data Standard definition (at least 75% of the board and 50% of senior staff) its figure is 13%. Esmée's figure relies on organisations' own answers on a monitoring form and covers 93% of the grants it awarded in 2025. Neither report gives a Black-only figure. Figures from two foundations do not describe the sector.

sources.title: Paul Hamlyn Foundation: Racial justice audit analysis of PHF's UK grant-making 2024/25 (9 December 2025)
Esmée Fairbairn Foundation: Who our funding is reaching 2025 (undated web page)

points.heading: National Lottery grants for projects serving Black communities
points.text: The National Lottery Community Fund awarded £767 million in 2024/25. It reports grants by the communities a project will mostly benefit: 756 grants worth £73.9 million for African communities, 575 worth £61.0 million for Caribbean communities and 625 worth £67.2 million for Black British communities.
points.note: UK. Applicants tick the communities a project will mostly benefit and can tick more than one, so the groups overlap and must not be added together. The figures describe who a project serves, not who leads the organisation. A further 631 grants (£69.2 million) were for 'any other Black, African or Caribbean background'.

Civil Society News: National Lottery Community Fund's grants up by over £80m last year, accounts show (14 August 2025)

points.heading: The Phoenix Fund and Phoenix Way: community-led grant-making
points.text: The Phoenix Fund, launched in 2020 and designed by Black and racially minoritised community leaders, distributed £2.4 million to 184 groups across England from around 1,400 applications. In 2021 the National Lottery Community Fund and the Ubele Initiative announced a £50 million, five-year partnership, The Phoenix Way, with community panels shaping awards.
points.note: The Phoenix Fund covered England; The Phoenix Way's panels are drawn from across England, though its stated aims refer to groups across the UK. Announced figures; the sources do not report how much of the £50 million has been paid out. Charity Times reported that about 85% of the budget would go to activity directly supporting Black and minority-led organisations. The Learning, games and community page lists The Phoenix Way as a funding route.

points.heading: Social investment: blended loans and grants
points.text: In October 2026 Social Investment Business, the Ubele Initiative and Create Equity opened the Flexible Finance Fund for Black and racially minoritised charities and social enterprises in England; Charity Times reports it is worth £4 million. It offers loans of £50,000 to £1.5 million with a grant of 50% to 100% of the loan, up to £200,000.
points.note: England only. Applicants need at least two years' operation and a turnover of at least £200,000. Grant funding comes from Access – The Foundation for Social Investment, and the fund is supported by the government's Growth Guarantee Scheme. The £4 million total is reported by trade press, not by the fund's own page. It is new, so no results have been reported. Loans must be repaid; groups should take independent advice.

sources.title: Social Investment Business: Flexible Finance Fund (open October 2026)

points.heading: Black employees have the highest union membership rate
points.text: In 2025, 26.9% of Black or Black British employees in the UK were trade union members, the highest of any ethnic group and above the average of 22.4%. Over half of Black employees worked in health and social work, education or public administration and defence; these industries account for over three-quarters of Black union members.
points.note: UK employees, 2025. Based on the Labour Force Survey, now official statistics in development. The 95% confidence interval for Black employees (24.2% to 29.8%) lies above the intervals for every other ethnic group, including White (22.5% to 23.7%). The industry pattern describes where Black union members work; the source does not say it explains the higher rate.

points.heading: Insecure work among Black and minority ethnic workers
points.text: TUC analysis found that 16.3% of Black and minority ethnic workers were in insecure work in 2024, compared with 10.8% of White workers. Insecure work here means zero-hours contracts, agency, casual and seasonal work (not fixed-term contracts), and self-employment paid below two-thirds of median earnings.
points.note: UK. The TUC groups all Black and minority ethnic workers together, so there is no Black-only figure. Its release a year earlier gave 16.9% for 2023; figures differ between releases as data are updated. The TUC is a campaigning body and the analysis is its own, from Labour Force Survey and Family Resources Survey data. The Myths and facts page covers the TUC's 2022 poll on racism at work.

points.heading: Unions organise Black members in their own structures
points.text: Unions such as UNISON run groups for Black members, and the TUC holds a Black Workers' Conference, which in 2026 met in Bournemouth from 24 to 26 April. UNISON uses 'Black' in the political sense, as a shared term for people facing racism.
points.note: Union definitions of 'Black' are often wider than the Black or Black British group used in official statistics, so union figures and government figures may not count the same people. The page on what it means to be Black explains political blackness.

points.heading: Black barristers: 3.6% of the Bar, 1.2% of KCs
points.text: In December 2025, 3.6% of the practising Bar (including pupils) were Black or Black British, compared with 5.5% of the UK working-age population. The gap widens with seniority: 1.2% of King's Counsel were Black, against 3.9% of other barristers.
points.note: Barristers in England and Wales, compared with the UK working-age population. Percentages exclude those who did not give their ethnicity. The regulator notes the gap between King's Counsel and other barristers is widest for those of Black African background (0.4% of KCs against 2.2% of other barristers). The Professions point elsewhere in the hub uses Ministry of Justice figures on a different basis. Solicitors are covered on the Collecting ethnicity data page.

points.heading: Nursing and midwifery: a third from ethnic minority backgrounds
points.text: On 31 March 2026, 33.8% of the 867,935 nurses, midwives and nursing associates on the UK register were from Black, Asian and ethnic minority backgrounds, up from 32.5% a year earlier. The regulator's 2025 survey found 40% of responding professionals had faced discrimination in the previous year, most often on grounds of ethnicity or age.
points.note: UK. The register report gives no Black-only figure. The discrimination figure comes from a survey of registrants who chose to respond.

points.heading: Learie Constantine: first Black life peer
points.text: Sir Learie Constantine, the Trinidad-born cricketer and campaigner (died 1971), was the first Black life peer; he took his seat in the House of Lords on 26 March 1969.

points.text: Walter Tull (killed 25 March 1918), one of the first Black officers in the British Army, did not receive the Victoria Cross. Sources say he was recommended for the Military Cross, which was never awarded; MPs and campaigners have sought a posthumous award.
points.note: Corrects a common error. Evidence of the recommendation is reported, not documented in an official citation; no Ministry of Defence position was quoted in either source.

points.heading: William Hall: first Black recipient of the Victoria Cross, 1857
points.text: William Hall, a Nova Scotian sailor in the Royal Navy, won the Victoria Cross for action at Lucknow on 16 November 1857 and received it on 28 October 1859. Veterans Affairs Canada and the Canadian Encyclopedia both describe him as the first Black recipient.
points.note: No awarding body publishes a count of Black VC recipients. 'First' is as documented by the two sources.

points.heading: Samuel Hodge: first Black soldier awarded the VC, 1866
points.text: Lance Corporal Samuel Hodge of the 4th West India Regiment, from Tortola, won the Victoria Cross for action in the Gambia on 30 June 1866. Two independent sources describe him as the first Black soldier, or the first soldier of African-Caribbean descent, to receive the VC.
points.figure: First Black soldier awarded the VC (1866 action)
points.note: Hall (a sailor) came first. Hodge is the first soldier. The sources word this differently.

sources.title: Samuel Hodge, the West India Regiments & Britain's Forgotten African-Caribbean Soldiers – History of War

points.heading: William Gordon VC, West India Regiment, 1892
points.text: Lance Corporal William James Gordon of the West India Regiment, from Jamaica, won the Victoria Cross for shielding his commanding officer at Toniataba in the Gambia on 13 March 1892. The London Gazette published the award on 9 December 1892.
points.note: The award comes from the primary record (London Gazette). The sources do not say whether Gordon was Black. He is presented here only as a West India Regiment recipient documented in Caribbean military heritage sources.

points.heading: Johnson Beharry VC: first living VC recipient since 1965
points.text: Johnson Beharry, born in Grenada in 1979, was awarded the Victoria Cross in 2005 for two actions in Iraq in 2004. The National Portrait Gallery and History of War describe him as the first living recipient since 1965.
points.note: Neither source calls him the 'first Black' recipient of anything. Do not add that label. He is a living public recipient, named here in that role only.

points.heading: Caribbean volunteers in the Second World War: about 10,000
points.text: The West India Committee puts the number of Black West Indians who joined the armed forces in the Second World War at over 10,000. This includes over 5,500 RAF ground crew, over 400 airmen and over 600 women in the Auxiliary Territorial Service. points.heading: Topic choice explains part of the NIH gap: a contested reading
points.text: The 2019 NIH study argued that Black applicants cluster in topics (for example community and population health) with lower award rates, explaining part of the gap. points.note: The 69 and 1,021 totals are our sum of Pearn Kandola's four published category counts. Pearn Kandola does not explain how ethnicity was assigned. points.heading: Treat ethnicity as special category data with a Schedule 1 condition
points.text: Under UK GDPR, data revealing racial or ethnic origin needs both an Article 6 lawful basis and an Article 9 condition. Paragraph 8 of Schedule 1 to the Data Protection Act 2018 ('equality of opportunity or treatment') is the usual condition for monitoring, and requires an appropriate policy document. Public bodies such as the University of Cambridge rely on it and keep monitoring data separate.
points.note: The ICO says this guidance is under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025.

points.heading: Do not infer ethnicity from names, photos or appearance
points.text: The ICO says that if you intend to infer ethnicity, for example from a name or image, you are processing special category data however confident you are. ONS linkage shows records not based on self-report often disagree with the census: below 76% agreement for Mixed groups and below 72% for Other groups.
points.note: The ONS agreement figures compare health records with Census 2021 and do not show how each record was captured. The two ICO extracts come from one page.
