points.heading: Honours: share with unknown ethnicity is disputed
points.text: Ethnicity facts and figures says ethnicity was not known for 0.6% of recipients in December 2024 (7 of 1,177). The Honours and Appointments Secretariat says roughly 10% of recipients on any list do not provide it. 12.5% of December 2024 recipients were from Asian, Black, Mixed or Other groups.
points.note: The two figures may use different denominators or counting rules. Neither page explains the difference.

sources.title: Honours recipients — Ethnicity facts and figures
Honours and Appointments Secretariat: Diversity

points.heading: Arts and culture: large gaps outside permanent staff
points.text: In Arts Council England's 2021/22 data from 806 organisations, ethnicity was 'not known' for 21% of the workforce and 'prefer not to say' for 4%. Gaps were higher for artists (29% not known) and volunteers (29%). In museums, the source's 'Black, Asian or ethnically diverse' share was 7% in 2022/23.
points.note: 'Unknown' can mean the organisation did not ask the question.

sources.title: Equality, Diversity and Inclusion: A Data Report 2021-2022 (Arts Council England)
National portfolio museums are becoming more diverse, ACE report finds

points.heading: Health records: mostly complete now, but less accurate for some
points.text: A 2023 study found ethnicity recorded for 82.3% of currently registered patients in CPRD Aurum GP data. ONS found 89.9% agreement with Census 2021 in GP-derived data. In 2019/20, 13% of inpatients and 17% of outpatients had no known ethnicity recorded.
points.note: Completeness among all patients ever registered is much lower: 58.0% in Aurum and 36.5% in GOLD.

sources.title: Completeness, agreement, and representativeness of ethnicity recording in CPRD and linked HES (Population Health Metrics, March 2023)
Understanding consistency of ethnicity data recorded in health-related administrative datasets in England: 2011 to 2021 (ONS, November 2023)
Flawed NHS records distort our view of ethnic health gaps, study shows (Nuffield Trust with NHS Race and Health Observatory, June 2021)

points.heading: Police: self-defined ethnicity missing in about 1 in 5 searches
points.text: In the year ending March 2024, self-defined ethnicity was missing for 19.3% of stop and searches in England and Wales, up from 5.0% in 2014. It was 31.3% in the Metropolitan Police area. Suffolk reported 22% missing for local people searched in 2024–25.
points.note: Using officer-observed ethnicity as a fallback cuts the unknown share to 1.6%, but that is an inferred measure.

sources.title: Police powers and procedures: stop and search, year ending 31 March 2024 (Home Office)
Use of Police Powers report, 16 January 2026 (Suffolk Police and Crime Commissioner)

points.heading: Employers: collection has been patchy
points.text: In a CIPD survey of 250 HR practitioners (2019), 53% said their organisation collected some ethnicity data. In BITC's 2018 survey of 6,506 employees, 11% said their employer collected ethnicity pay gap data. By 2023, 44% of Race at Work Charter signatories published an ethnicity pay gap.
points.note: These are different samples. Charter signatories are likely to be more engaged than employers in general.

sources.title: Employers unable to report on ethnicity pay due to missing data (CIPD, February 2019)
Race at Work 2018: The Scorecard Report (Business in the Community)
44% of employers voluntarily publish their ethnicity pay gap (HR Review, October 2023, reporting BITC)

points.heading: Stated willingness is higher than recorded disclosure
points.text: In a 2022 OnePoll survey for INvolve of 1,500 employees, 95% said they were willing to disclose their ethnicity to their employer. In administrative data, about 18–19% of civil servants have no recorded ethnicity. Survey-based and qualitative evidence also differs: participants in the Understanding Patient Data research expressed mistrust.
points.note: Commercial poll; no breakdown by ethnic group was published. No large published UK survey breaking down willingness to disclose by ethnic group was found.

sources.title: Majority of employees are happy to share ethnicity data, poll finds (People Management, May 2022)
Civil Service workforce (Ethnicity facts and figures, October 2024)

points.heading: Public trust and the pay gap reporting law
points.text: In the government's 2024 tracker, 73% trusted the NHS to use data effectively. Adults of Asian or Black heritage were more likely to feel in control of who uses their data. The March 2026 response (857 replies) confirmed mandatory ethnicity pay gap reporting for employers with 250+ staff. The Equality (Race and Disability) Bill was not in the May 2026 King's Speech and had not been introduced.
points.note: Bill status checked against sources dated 12 to 13 May 2026; later changes are not covered here. The earlier 2018–19 consultation had 321 responses, and the 2023 response decided against mandatory reporting at that stage.

sources.title: Public attitudes to data and AI: Tracker survey (Wave 4) report (UK government, Responsible Technology Adoption Unit, December 2024)
Mandatory ethnicity and disability pay gap reporting: consultation response (UK Government, March 2026)
Is the government on course to introduce a new Race Equality Act?
Equality (Race and Disability) Bill absent from King's Speech (LNB News 13/05/2026)

points.datasetTitle: Science, engineering and the built environment
points.heading: Black workers are under-represented in engineering and technology jobs
points.text: EngineeringUK's analysis of the 2024 Labour Force Survey found 2.7% of people in UK engineering and technology occupations were Black/African/Caribbean/Black British, against 5.3% in all other occupations combined. Mixed/Multiple ethnic groups made up 1.3%, against 1.7% elsewhere. Overall, 13.7% of the engineering and technology workforce came from minority ethnic groups, compared with 17.5% in other occupations.
points.note: Labour Force Survey sample sizes limit the analysis to five broad ethnic groups. The April 2026 dashboard rounds the comparison (Black 3% vs 6%; Mixed 2% vs 2%; 15% minority ethnic) and does not state its reference year. Both sources come from the same publisher.

sources.title: EngineeringUK: The engineering and technology workforce (May 2025)
EngineeringUK: Engineering and technology workforce dashboard (April 2026)

points.datasetTitle: Science, engineering and the built environment
points.heading: Black women are under-represented among women in engineering roles
points.text: Among women working in UK engineering and technology occupations in 2024, 3.8% were Black/African/Caribbean/Black British, compared with 5.4% of women in all other occupations combined. Women from Mixed/Multiple ethnic groups were 2.0% of women in engineering and technology, against 1.7% elsewhere, a difference EngineeringUK describes as small or none.
points.note: Single publisher; based on EngineeringUK analysis of 2024 Labour Force Survey data for the UK. Women from minority ethnic groups overall were better represented (20.7% vs 16.7%), driven by Asian women, so the aggregate hides the Black gap.

sources.title: EngineeringUK: The engineering and technology workforce (May 2025)

points.datasetTitle: Science, engineering and the built environment
points.heading: About 1% of UK-registered architects are Black or Black British
points.text: The Architects Registration Board's analysis of the Register in 2022 found Black or Black British people made up 1% of architects, against 4% of the UK population, and Mixed ethnic groups 2%, against 3%. In 2021, 2% of new registrants were Black or Black British. 70% of Black or Black British architects were based in London and the South East.
points.note: Ethnicity comes from ARB's voluntary EDI survey, completed by over 70% of architects; 7% preferred not to say their ethnicity. The trade press source reproduces ARB's release, so it is not independent evidence.

sources.title: Architects Registration Board: Architects today, analysis of the architects' profession in 2022 (April 2023)
Specification Online: New data highlights under-represented groups in the architects' profession (13 April 2023)

points.datasetTitle: Science, engineering and the built environment
points.heading: About 5% of town planners are from racialised minorities
points.text: The Royal Town Planning Institute's State of the Profession 2023 estimates, from a five-year average of Annual Population Survey data (2016-2020), that 95% of town planning officers belong to a White ethnic group and 5% to a racialised ethnicity. The RTPI says sample sizes are too small for more detailed breakdowns, so no separate Black or Mixed figures are published. 19.50% of UK student members identified with a racialised minority ethnicity, with no data for 43.41%.
points.figure: 5% racialised minority (no Black or Mixed breakdown)
points.note: 'Racialised minority' is the RTPI's term. The planner estimate is a UK five-year average of Annual Population Survey data for 2016-2020; the comparison population (81% White, 19% racialised minorities) is the 2021 Census for England and Wales, so the two do not cover the same geography or period. Single publisher.

sources.title: Royal Town Planning Institute: State of the Profession 2023 (November 2023)

points.datasetTitle: Science, engineering and the built environment
points.heading: Black workers are 4% of the construction site workforce in CITB survey
points.text: CITB's 2025 Construction Workforce Mobility Survey of 3,611 UK site workers found 4% were of Black origin, up from 2% in 2022, and 1% Mixed, against 5% and 2% of the UK population aged 16-64. Separately, Annual Population Survey data for 2021 published by the Government show 3.5% of Black workers and 5.6% of workers of Mixed ethnicity were employed in construction, compared with 6.5% of all workers.
points.note: The two measures differ: CITB gives the ethnic make-up of an on-site interview sample; the APS figures give the share of each ethnic group's workers employed in the construction sector (UK, 2021).

sources.title: CITB: Construction Workforce Mobility 2025, full report (2025)
GOV.UK Ethnicity facts and figures: Employment by sector (data for 2021)

points.datasetTitle: Science, engineering and the built environment
points.heading: 1.7% of UK STEM academic staff were Black in 2018/19
points.text: Analysis of HESA records compiled by Jisc for the Royal Society found that in 2018/19, 18.7% of STEM academic staff in UK higher education were from ethnic minority groups, including 13.2% who were Asian and 1.7% who were Black. By comparison, 7.1% of STEM postgraduate entrants were Black. The report says there appears to be a drop-off of Black and Mixed ethnicity postgraduates entering STEM academic employment, and 3.5% of Black STEM academic staff held professor posts, against 11.9% of white staff.
points.note: Data are now several years old. The report warns that broad categories hide variation by subject, sex, age, nationality and institution.

sources.title: Royal Society: STEM sector must step up and end unacceptable disparities in Black staff and students academic progression and success (25 March 2021)
Royal Society / Jisc: Ethnicity STEM data for students and academic staff in higher education 2007/08 to 2018/19 (March 2021)

points.datasetTitle: Science, engineering and the built environment
points.heading: 8.1% of engineering and technology students were Black in 2020/21
points.text: EngineeringUK's 'Engineering in higher education' report, using 2020/21 HESA data, found 8.1% of engineering and technology students were Black and 4.9% were Mixed, similar to all subjects (8.3% and 4.8%). Asian students were better represented in engineering and technology than across all subjects (18% vs 12.7%).
points.note: Data are for 2020/21 and cover UK higher education students. The 2.7% Black share of the engineering and technology workforce (EngineeringUK, 2024 Labour Force Survey) covers a different population and year, so the two figures cannot be compared directly. The second source reproduces the first.

sources.title: EngineeringUK: EngineeringUK releases new report on engineering in higher education (16 March 2023)
Electronic Specifier: EngineeringUK releases report on engineering in higher education (2023)

points.datasetTitle: Science, engineering and the built environment
points.heading: Black STEM graduates half as likely as white peers to get a first
points.text: In 2018/19, 17.9% of Black UK-domiciled STEM first-degree qualifiers achieved first-class honours, compared with 35.7% of white qualifiers, and 9.5% of Black students left with a third, against 3.2% of white students. The Jisc report for the Royal Society found the 17.8 percentage point first-class gap statistically significant. Non-completion among Black STEM first-degree students was 4.7% in 2017/18, compared with 2.7% for white students.
points.note: Data are for 2018/19 (degree classes) and 2017/18 (non-completion). Raw gaps do not adjust for entry qualifications or age; the report shows older qualifiers in all groups get fewer good honours, and that after adjusting for POLAR4 participation area there is very little difference in first-degree non-completion between ethnic minority and white STEM students taken together. Mixed ethnicity STEM qualifiers are reported separately (45.8% achieved upper second class honours).

sources.title: Royal Society: STEM sector must step up and end unacceptable disparities in Black staff and students academic progression and success (25 March 2021)
Royal Society / Jisc: Ethnicity STEM data for students and academic staff in higher education 2007/08 to 2018/19 (March 2021)

points.datasetTitle: Science, engineering and the built environment
points.heading: Ethnic minority share of construction apprenticeship starts: about 9%
points.text: In England in 2024/25, apprentices from ethnic minorities (excluding white minorities) made up 18.0% of all apprenticeship starts. Calculated from the same Department for Education data, they made up about 9.3% of starts in Construction, Planning and the Built Environment (2,270 of 24,280 with known ethnicity) and 12.5% in Engineering and Manufacturing Technologies (5,670 of 45,330). Over the five years since 2019/20, starts grew 42.6% for Black learners and 52.0% for Mixed learners.
points.note: Sector percentages are calculated by this hub, not published by DfE, using DfE's own method for the 18.0% headline (62,880 of 348,530 starts with known ethnicity). Counts are rounded to the nearest 10. This data set does not split starts by sector for Black or Mixed learners separately; DfE also reports only 10.3% of 2023/24 leavers in Engineering and Manufacturing Technologies were from ethnic minorities.

sources.title: Department for Education: Apprenticeships, academic year 2024/25 (27 November 2025)
Department for Education: Subjects - Starts, Enrolments by Age, Sex, Ethnicity, LLDD, SSA, Detailed level, STEM (27 November 2025)

points.datasetTitle: Science, engineering and the built environment
points.heading: Black engineering graduates of 2009/10-2013/14 had lowest full-time work rate
points.text: A Royal Academy of Engineering study published in November 2016, using HESA DLHE data for UK-domiciled full-time first-degree graduates from 2009/10 to 2013/14, found 71% of white engineering graduates were in full-time employment six months after graduating, against 51% of black and minority ethnic graduates and 46% of Black graduates. Six months after graduating, 14% of Black engineering graduates were unemployed, compared with 7% of white engineering graduates.
points.note: Single source, and the data predate the current Graduate Outcomes survey. The report says the differences were significantly greater for engineering graduates than across all subjects.

sources.title: Royal Academy of Engineering: Employment outcomes of engineering graduates: key factors and diversity characteristics (November 2016)

points.datasetTitle: Science, engineering and the built environment
points.heading: Black representation in chemistry falls from 4.9% of undergraduates
points.text: The Royal Society of Chemistry's 2022 'Missing Elements' report found 4.9% of chemistry undergraduates identified as Black, but only 1.4% of PhD chemistry students and 0% of chemistry professors did. It also found Black and minoritised ethnic chemists were paid £6,000 less than White colleagues, and principal investigators from those groups were 7 percentage points less likely to win research funding.
points.note: The 0% reflects rounding: IOM3 reports that values under 2.5% were rounded down to zero to protect anonymity, and that the 0% applies to professors identifying as Black or Mixed Race. The RSC release says 'PhD' students where IOM3 says 'postgraduate'.

sources.title: Royal Society of Chemistry: New £1.5m unit to tackle racial inequalities in science (March 2022)
IOM3: Royal Society of Chemistry reports racial inequalities within chemical sciences (16 March 2022)

points.datasetTitle: Science, engineering and the built environment
points.heading: Engineers report race-related microaggressions and family barriers
points.text: The Royal Academy of Engineering's 2023 study (1,507 engineers surveyed, plus 26 focus groups and 50 interviews) found engineering was often a second choice for people from South Asian or Black African backgrounds whose families may favour more 'prestigious' professions. Engineers who reported bullying or harassment mostly experienced microaggressions related to gender and race, which often went unchallenged. King's College London notes Black students have lower attainment in maths and physics and are less likely to achieve a 2:1 or first.
points.note: Qualitative findings describe experiences, not prevalence by ethnic group. Seven in ten engineers in the same survey (69%) perceived the profession's culture as inclusive, so the evidence is mixed rather than one-directional. The King's College London statement comes from a 2022 funding announcement and gives no figures or reference year.

sources.title: Royal Academy of Engineering / DJS Research: Cultural inclusivity in engineering (March 2023)
King's College London: Equality programme, Success for Black Engineers awarded Royal Academy of Engineering funding (4 April 2022)

points.datasetTitle: Science, engineering and the built environment
points.heading: John Edmonstone taught Charles Darwin taxidermy in Edinburgh
points.text: The Natural History Museum describes John Edmonstone as 'a former enslaved Black man from Guyana' who, while living in Edinburgh, taught the young Charles Darwin taxidermy. The museum says he was born into slavery in Guyana in 1790 and by 1824 was working for the University of Edinburgh's zoological museum. The Linnean Society records that Darwin's Galápagos finches were preserved using techniques Edmonstone had taught him.
points.note: Dates differ between sources: the Linnean Society says he moved to Edinburgh in 1823 and that Darwin met him in 1826. The Natural History Museum refers to his death but says his burial place is not known; neither source gives a date of death. The museum notes that the Galapagos mockingbirds, rather than the finches, did most to prompt Darwin's thinking on evolution.

sources.title: Natural History Museum: John Edmonstone, the man who taught Darwin taxidermy (n.d.)
Linnean Society: The man who taught Charles Darwin taxidermy (2 October 2018)

points.datasetTitle: Science, engineering and the built environment
points.heading: Andrew Watson studied engineering at Glasgow before football fame
points.text: University of Glasgow Archives record that Andrew Watson, born in Georgetown, Guyana, enrolled at the University in November 1875 to study philosophy, mathematics and engineering, leaving in 1876 for a football career. The Institution of Civil Engineers describes him as 'an engineer and the first Black British international footballer', who spent 20 years working on ships and became a qualified engineer.
points.note: The University gives his birth year as 1857; other accounts give 1856. He died in Kew, Surrey, on 8 March 1921 (Scottish Football Association). His engineering career is less documented than his football career.

sources.title: University of Glasgow Archives & Special Collections: Guyana (n.d.)
Institution of Civil Engineers: Black excellence isn't new: finding the UK's examples (31 October 2024)
Scottish Football Association: Remembering Andrew Watson

points.datasetTitle: Science, engineering and the built environment
points.heading: George Bemand: UCL engineering student and artillery officer
points.text: Dulwich College's First World War archive records that George Edward Kingsley Bemand, born in Jamaica in 1892 to 'a white father, George, and a black mother, Minnie', went on from the College to University College London, where he studied engineering. Commissioned in the Royal Field Artillery in May 1915, he was, the College says, 'very possibly the first person of colour, outside of India' to hold such a commission in the modern British Army. He was killed on 26 December 1916.
points.note: Sources differ on his date of birth (19 March per Dulwich College; 9 March per the Western Front Association). The 'first' claim is hedged by its source.

sources.title: Dulwich College 1914-18: Bemand, GEK (n.d.)
Western Front Association: 26 December 1916, 2nd Lt George Edward Kingsley Bemand (n.d.)

points.datasetTitle: Science, engineering and the built environment
points.heading: Lilian Bader qualified among the first WAAF instrument repairers
points.text: The RAF Museum records that Lilian Bader, born in Liverpool in 1917 to a Barbadian father who had served in the Royal Navy and an Irish mother, joined the Women's Auxiliary Air Force in 1941 and trained as an Instrument Repairer. She became one of the first women in the air force to qualify in that trade, checked aircraft instruments for faults at RAF Shawbury and was promoted to Acting Corporal. She died on 14 March 2015.
points.note: Her trade was technical aircraft maintenance rather than professional engineering. The RAF Museum records that she was forced to leave a NAAFI canteen job in 1939 'because she was Black'.

sources.title: RAF Museum: Technician, Leading Aircraftwoman Lilian Bader (n.d.)
RAF Benevolent Fund: Black History Month, Lilian Bader, a trailblazer in the RAF (2 October 2025)

points.datasetTitle: Science, engineering and the built environment
points.heading: RIBA archives: earliest Black member found so far elected in 1950
points.text: RIBA's collections team identifies Reuben Johnson Oluwole Wright (1914-1990), an architect from Sierra Leone who trained in Edinburgh, as the earliest Black member it has found so far; he became an associate in 1950. Its search also surfaced Ransford Jarrett-Yaskey MBE (1924-2000), Chief Architect to the Sierra Leone Ministry of Works, who was elected an Associate Member in 1958.
points.note: RIBA stresses that nomination papers did not record ethnicity and that earlier Black members probably exist. Single institutional source.

sources.title: RIBA: Who was the first Black RIBA Member? (n.d.)

points.datasetTitle: Science, engineering and the built environment
points.heading: Government Science and Engineering: over 10,000 civil servants
points.text: The Government Science and Engineering (GSE) profession describes itself as over 10,000 civil servants with a background or interest in science and engineering, working in specialist, deep specialist, policy, analytical and operational roles. It is managed from within the Government Office for Science, and Crown and public servants are welcome to be members.
points.note: Membership of the GSE profession is open and is not the same as the 'Science and Engineering' profession recorded in Civil Service Statistics. The 10,000 figure comes from an undated GOV.UK page that sets out priorities for 2016 to 2017 and names Sir Patrick Vallance as Head of Profession, so it may be out of date.

sources.title: GOV.UK: About us, Government Science & Engineering Profession (n.d.)
GOV.UK GSE blog: Black History Month, contributions to science and engineering (1 October 2020)

points.datasetTitle: Science, engineering and the built environment
points.heading: Black staff are 3.1% of Civil Service science and engineering staff
points.text: Civil Service Statistics for 31 March 2025 record 395 Black and 320 Mixed civil servants in the Science and Engineering profession: about 3.1% and 2.5% of the 12,765 with known ethnicity, with 13.7% from ethnic minority groups overall, against 18.0% across the whole Civil Service. Median salary was £38,380 for Black staff in the profession and £45,290 for White staff. In 2020 the GSE profession's own blog put its ‘BAME’ share at around 4%, against around 10% of all civil servants.
points.note: Percentages calculated by this hub from rounded headcounts (nearest 5), excluding 2,845 staff with unknown or undeclared ethnicity, so they are approximate. The 2020 figure used a different survey basis and is not directly comparable. Salary gaps are not adjusted for grade.

sources.title: Cabinet Office: Civil Service Statistics data browser 2025, profession of post by ethnicity (generated 6 November 2025)
Cabinet Office: Civil Service Statistics 2025, statistical bulletin
GOV.UK GSE blog: Black History Month, contributions to science and engineering (1 October 2020)

points.datasetTitle: Science, engineering and the built environment
points.heading: Government Planning Profession: numbers too small for reliable shares
points.text: The Government Planning Profession supports planners and planning inspectors, most of whom work in the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government and the Planning Inspectorate. Civil Service Statistics for March 2025 record 10 Black and 5 Mixed civil servants in the Planning profession, against 330 White (headcounts rounded to the nearest 5). Black and Mixed counts for Planning Inspectors are suppressed because they are too small to publish.
points.note: Ethnicity is unknown or undeclared for 90 of the Planning profession headcount, so percentages would be unreliable. Most UK planners work in local government and the private sector, outside the Civil Service.

sources.title: GOV.UK: About us, Government Planning Profession (n.d.)
Cabinet Office: Civil Service Statistics data browser 2025, profession of post by ethnicity (generated 6 November 2025)

points.datasetTitle: Science, engineering and the built environment
points.heading: Royal Academy of Engineering funds university diversity projects
points.text: The Royal Academy of Engineering's Diversity Impact Programme, launched in October 2021, gives grants of up to £100,000 to university engineering departments to address unequal outcomes for students from under-represented groups; the Academy reports almost £2m awarded to 20 universities. A 2022 award went to King's College London's 'Success for Black Engineers' project, which aims to increase Black applicants and raise attainment and wellbeing for Black engineering students.
points.note: The 'almost £2m to 20 universities' total is a cumulative figure from an undated programme page. The Academy refers to an interim evaluation of the 2022 cohort, but its published programme pages give no outcome measures by ethnicity, so impact is not yet evidenced.

sources.title: Royal Academy of Engineering: Diversity Impact Programme (n.d.)
Royal Academy of Engineering: Academy awards grants totalling £1 million for innovative interventions to increase diversity and inclusion in engineering (30 March 2022)
King's College London: Equality programme, Success for Black Engineers awarded Royal Academy of Engineering funding (4 April 2022)

points.datasetTitle: Sport: taking part, leading and belonging
points.heading: Black adults' activity has not risen in nine years (England)
points.text: In the year to November 2025, 57.2% of Black adults in England did at least 150 minutes of activity a week, below White adults. Sport England reports that activity among Black adults, Asian (excluding Chinese) adults and adults from other ethnic groups has not increased since November 2015-16, so the gap to White British and White other adults has widened.
points.note: 'Active' means 150 or more minutes of moderate-intensity activity a week, adults aged 16 and over in England. Both sources are from Sport England, the official statistics producer for this survey.

sources.title: Sport England: Active Lives Adult Survey November 2024-25 release (23 April 2026)
Sport England: Active Lives Adult Survey November 2024-25 Report (April 2026)

points.datasetTitle: Sport: taking part, leading and belonging
points.heading: Mixed-heritage adults were the most active group in England, 2016 to 2022
points.text: Adults from Mixed ethnic backgrounds were the most likely of all ethnic groups in England to be physically active in each year from 2016 to 2022, at 70.8% in the year to November 2022, against 56.1% of Black adults. Sport England's 2016-18 sub-group analysis found 72.4% of White and Black African adults and 65.9% of White and Black Caribbean adults active, compared with 58.5% of African and 58.2% of Caribbean adults.
points.note: The sub-group figures combine two survey years (November 2016-18) and are older than the headline series. In the November 2024-25 report, adults from Mixed (69%) and White other (69%) backgrounds are the joint highest groups shown, rounded to whole numbers.

sources.title: GOV.UK Ethnicity facts and figures: Physical activity (9 January 2024)
Sport England: Sport for all? Why ethnicity and culture matters in sport and physical activity (February 2020)

points.datasetTitle: Sport: taking part, leading and belonging
points.heading: Black, Asian and 'other' children are the least likely to be active (England)
points.text: In the 2024-25 school year, 41% of Black children and young people in England (school Years 1-11) averaged 60 minutes or more of activity a day, compared with 52% of those from Mixed backgrounds. Sport England reports that children and young people from Asian (43%), Black and other (42%) ethnic backgrounds remain the least likely to be active, that there has been no long-term change for Black children and young people since 2017-18, and that the gender gap between Black boys and girls is 10.6%.
points.note: Sport England notes that Black children are 6% of the child population, so changes for this group have wider confidence intervals. The report does not rank the Asian, Black and other groups against each other.

sources.title: Sport England: Active Lives Children and Young People Survey, academic year 2024-25 (4 December 2025)
Sport England: Ethnicity research page (undated)

points.datasetTitle: Sport: taking part, leading and belonging
points.heading: Black adults and children are under-represented in swimming
points.text: Sport England's 2020 analysis found Black adults, 3.1% of England's adult population, under-represented in swimming, cycling and walking for leisure relative to their population share. Black children and young people, 4.6% of 5 to 16-year-olds, were over-represented in football and dance but under-represented in swimming, cycling and walking.
points.note: This compares each group's share of participants with its share of the population (adults November 2016-18; children and young people 2017-19). It is not a measure of swimming ability. Sport England's 2024-25 children's report gives its 25-metre swimming measure without an ethnicity breakdown. Both figures come from a single Sport England report.

sources.title: Sport England: Sport for all? Why ethnicity and culture matters in sport and physical activity (February 2020)

points.datasetTitle: Sport: taking part, leading and belonging
points.heading: Wales and Scotland: school sport by ethnicity, and limited data
points.text: In Wales in 2022, 38% of pupils who identified as Black, Black Welsh, Black British, Caribbean or African took part in organised sport outside the curriculum three or more times a week, compared with 43% of pupils from Mixed or Multiple ethnic groups and 41% of White pupils. sportscotland states that there is limited data on sports participation among ethnic minority people in Scotland because the populations are small.
points.note: Sport Wales estimates that about 2,000 Black pupils took part three or more times a week; this is a population estimate, not the number of pupils surveyed. Sport Wales' commentary says White and Mixed pupils were more likely to take part than Asian pupils or pupils from another ethnic group. It does not directly compare Black pupils' participation with White or Mixed pupils'. The sportscotland note is undated and relies on 2011 Census data.

sources.title: Sport Wales: School Sport Survey 2022 (2022)
sportscotland: Race and sport learning note (undated, cites 2011 Census)

points.datasetTitle: Sport: taking part, leading and belonging
points.heading: Sport boards: 15% ethnically diverse, few chairs or CEOs
points.text: Board members from culturally or ethnically diverse backgrounds in sport bodies surveyed by Sport England and UK Sport rose from 7.9% in 2020 to 15.11% in 2024, against 18.3% of the England and Wales population at the 2021 Census. Senior roles were less diverse: 4 of 76 chairs and 8 of 97 chief executives who answered were from culturally or ethnically diverse backgrounds, and all 29 performance directors were from a White background.
points.note: 'Culturally or ethnically diverse' groups all ethnic minority respondents together; no Black-specific figure is published. Figures come from 669 board responses across around 128 boards.

sources.title: Sport England and UK Sport: Diversity in Sport Governance, Annual Survey 2024 (November 2024)
UK Sport: Diversity in Sport Governance Report 2024 (19 December 2024)

points.datasetTitle: Sport: taking part, leading and belonging
points.heading: Football clubs: 13% of coaches Black, Asian or Mixed Heritage
points.text: Across the clubs signed up to the Football Leadership Diversity Code in 2022-23, 13% of coaches, 11% of senior coaches and 7% of senior leaders were Black, Asian or Mixed Heritage. The FA said this falls very short of its aim of representing what is seen on the pitch.
points.note: Figures cover the Code's 53 club signatories and combine Black, Asian and Mixed Heritage staff. In November 2023 the FA said a new rule making workforce diversity reporting mandatory for professional clubs had been approved in principle and, after consultation, would be introduced ahead of the 2024-25 season.

sources.title: The FA: Football Leadership Diversity Code results 2022/23 (November 2023)
The FA: FLDC year three report published (22 November 2023)
Premier League: Football Leadership Diversity Code - 2022/23 update (22 November 2023)

points.datasetTitle: Sport: taking part, leading and belonging
points.heading: England coaching staff: 23% in the men's game, 0% in the women's game
points.text: The FA reported that 23% of its England coaching staff in the men's game were from Black, Asian, Mixed or other ethnic backgrounds in October 2025, up from 19% in June 2024, against a 2028 target of 25%. For England coaching staff in the women's game the figure was 0%, down from 4%, against a 2028 target of 7%. Separately, the number of registered referees from Black, Asian and Mixed Heritage backgrounds rose by 17.5% in the 2024-25 season.
points.note: Both sources are published by the FA and use a combined Black, Asian, Mixed or other ethnic background category. The referee figure is a percentage increase, not a share of all referees.

sources.title: The FA: EDI End of Year Report 2025 (December 2025)
The FA: A review of our 2024-2028 EDI strategy, 'A Game Free From Discrimination' (2 December 2025)

points.datasetTitle: Sport: taking part, leading and belonging
points.heading: Black former players: fewer reach management, more are dismissed
points.text: A working paper tracking 3,420 players active in England's top two divisions between 1990 and 2010 identified 544 (16%) as Black or of mixed Black heritage; around 4% of them became first-team managers, compared with 11% of non-Black former players. The researchers found lower recruitment into junior managerial roles, slower progression and higher dismissal rates for Black former players.
points.note: This is a working paper by Peeters, Hoey and Szymanski, described by the University of Liverpool as commissioned by the Black Footballers Partnership. Erasmus gives the sample as 3,420 players; Liverpool says about 3,500. The two summaries describe the 4% differently. Erasmus gives it as the share of Black former players who became first-team managers. Liverpool gives it as Black former footballers' share of all Premier League and EFL managerial roles. Liverpool also reports that a Black manager is 41% more likely to be fired than a white manager when performance is equal.

sources.title: Erasmus University Rotterdam: Black former players get fewer chances at management (27 March 2024)
University of Liverpool Management School: Why are there so few black football managers? (16 September 2024)

points.datasetTitle: Sport: taking part, leading and belonging
points.heading: Volunteering: Black adults had the highest rate shown (England)
points.text: In the 12 months to November 2025, 24.0% of Black adults in England volunteered to support sport and physical activity, the highest of the ethnic groups shown, compared with 25.2% in November 2016-17. Volunteering among adults of Mixed ethnicity fell by 5.2% over the same period to 22.8%, and among children it fell by 9.2% for Black girls and 9.5% for Mixed girls since 2017-18.
points.note: Volunteering covers roles such as coaching, officiating and organising. The Black adult figures appear in the report's chart without commentary, and the change for Black adults is not marked as statistically reportable.

sources.title: Sport England: Active Lives Adult Survey November 2024-25 Report (April 2026)
Sport England: Active Lives Children and Young People Survey, academic year 2024-25 (4 December 2025)

points.datasetTitle: Sport: taking part, leading and belonging
points.heading: Arrests and other police actions for racist and indecent chanting rose to 33 (2024-25)
points.text: Police made 33 football-related arrests and other police actions for 'racist and indecent chanting' in the 2024-25 season, up from 9 in 2023-24, out of 2,037 in all, according to Home Office figures for England and Wales. The Home Office records racist and indecent chanting as a single offence category, so racist chanting cannot be counted on its own.
points.note: The July 2025 release gave 32 for the domestic season; the November 2025 update gives 33 for the full 2024-25 season. Since 2019-20 these figures have included other police actions such as Fixed Penalty Notices, which the Home Office now shows separately (293 of the 2,037 in 2024-25). The figures measure police action, not the number of incidents.

sources.title: Home Office: Football-related arrests and banning orders 2024 to 2025 season, data tables (13 November 2025)
Home Office: Football-related arrests and banning orders, England and Wales: 2024 to 2025 domestic football season (17 July 2025)

points.datasetTitle: Sport: taking part, leading and belonging
points.heading: Race is the most common hate crime incident at matches
points.text: Hate crime incidents were reported at 420 regulated football matches in the 2024-25 domestic season, and 287 of the incidents related to race, more than any other category. A further 212 online hate crimes connected to football were recorded in that season, a measure the Home Office classes as official statistics in development.
points.note: Incident figures come from post-match police reports for regulated matches. The online figure counts offences reported to bodies such as the FA, UEFA, Kick It Out or the police that meet threshold tests. It is designated official statistics in development and is not broken down by type in the summary.

sources.title: Home Office: Football-related arrests and banning orders, England and Wales: 2024 to 2025 domestic football season (17 July 2025)
Home Office: Football-related arrests and banning orders, 2024 to 2025 football season international update (13 November 2025)

points.datasetTitle: Sport: taking part, leading and belonging
points.heading: Kick It Out: 792 reports of racism in 2025-26
points.text: Kick It Out received 792 reports of racism across professional, grassroots and online football in the 2025-26 season, up 19% on the previous year and 45% of all reports it received. These are reports made to the charity rather than proven incidents; it says its figures track rises recorded by the UK Football Policing Unit and the FA.
points.note: Kick It Out is an anti-discrimination charity, and these are reports made to it, not proven incidents. Its 2024-25 summary gives a racism count for online reports only (268), so no like-for-like total for 2024-25 is shown here.

sources.title: Kick It Out: Reporting statistics, 2025/26 season (2026)

points.datasetTitle: Sport: taking part, leading and belonging
points.heading: Grassroots football: 1,147 race-related allegations (2025-26)
points.text: The FA recorded 1,147 serious case allegations relating to ethnicity, race or colour in grassroots football in England in the 2025-26 season (0.92 per 1,000 fixtures), up from 1,021 in 2024-25. Of 235 charges, 157 were proven and 57 not proven when the report was published, and race-related cases remain the largest category of discrimination.
points.note: Grassroots means Steps 5 and below of the men's pyramid and Tiers 5 and below of the women's pyramid, including youth football. Allegations are not findings, and some charges were unresolved at publication. The FA cites independent research estimating that, for every 100 serious incidents brought to its attention, a further 89 go unreported. This 'reporting gap' of 1.89 covers all serious incidents, not only race-related ones.

sources.title: The FA: Grassroots Football Behaviour and Discipline Review 2025-26 season (October 2026)
The FA: Annual Grassroots Discipline Review for the 2024-25 season published (9 December 2025)

points.datasetTitle: Sport: taking part, leading and belonging
points.heading: Cricket: 75% of Black respondents reported discrimination
points.text: The Independent Commission for Equity in Cricket, reporting in June 2023, found that 50% of more than 4,000 survey respondents had experienced discrimination in cricket in the past five years, rising to 75% of all Black respondents. The Commission concluded that 'cricket has failed Black communities'. The England and Wales Cricket Board apologised unreservedly and said the report's conclusions highlight that 'for too long women and Black people were neglected'.
points.note: The survey drew responses from people involved in cricket who chose to take part, and 79% classified themselves as White British, so it is not a random sample. The number of Black respondents is not given in these sources. Figures come from the ECB, Wisden and CNN's reporting of the Commission's report.

sources.title: CNN (syndicated by KVIA): Racism, sexism and class-based discrimination widespread in English cricket, independent report finds (27 June 2023)
England and Wales Cricket Board newsroom: ECB responds to ICEC report on equity in cricket (27 June 2023)
Wisden: The ICEC report – a game for all, Wisden Cricketers' Almanack 2024 (2024)

points.datasetTitle: Sport: taking part, leading and belonging
points.heading: Emma Clarke: the first recorded black woman footballer (1895)
points.text: Emma Clarke, born in Bootle in 1876, played for the South team in the British Ladies' Football Club match at Crouch End, north London, on 23 March 1895, watched by 10,000 people. Haringey Council describes her as considered to be the first known Black women's footballer in Britain, and a Nubian Jak blue plaque honouring her, her sister Jane and the 1895 team was unveiled in Hornsey in December 2019.
points.note: Haringey Council gives her dates as 1876 to 'after 1903'; her date of death is not recorded in these sources. Haringey places the match in Crouch End near Nightingale Lane; the Hornsey Historical Society says the exact field has not been confirmed.

sources.title: Haringey Council: Black History Haringey 365 – Plaques and monuments (undated)
Hornsey Historical Society: 1895 – Women's Football Makes its Official Debut in Hornsey (undated)

points.datasetTitle: Sport: taking part, leading and belonging
points.heading: Rugby pioneers: James Peters (1906) and Clive Sullivan (1972)
points.text: In 1906 James 'Jimmy' Peters became, in the Rugby Football Union's words, the first black player in England's international rugby union history, winning five caps to 1908; the RFU notes it would be 80 years before another black player represented England. In 1972 Cardiff-born Clive Sullivan captained Great Britain to the Rugby League World Cup, which the Dictionary of Welsh Biography records as making him the first Black person to captain a Great Britain team in any sport.
points.note: Peters died in 1954 and Sullivan in 1985. The RFU's '80 years' and the RFL's 'until 1988' differ slightly. The RFL also records Roy Francis as the first black player to play for Great Britain, in 1947.

sources.title: Rugby Football Union: Jimmy Peters – England Rugby's Black Pioneer (1 October 2021)
Dictionary of Welsh Biography: Sullivan, Clive (1943-1985), rugby league player (undated)
Rugby Football League: The Black Pioneers of Rugby League, by Tony Collins (27 August 2020)

points.datasetTitle: Sport: taking part, leading and belonging
points.heading: Harry Edward: Britain's first Black Olympic medallist (1920)
points.text: At the 1920 Antwerp Olympic Games Harry Edward won bronze medals in the 100m and 200m, and Team GB describes his as the tale of the first black athlete to compete and win medals in its history. At the 1922 AAA Championships he won the 100, 220 and 440-yard finals within one hour; he later emigrated to the United States and died in 1973.
points.note: Sources differ on his birth year: Team GB gives Berlin, 1895; DCMS gives Berlin, 1898.

sources.title: Team GB: Black History Month – The story of Harry Edward (1 October 2020)
Department for Culture, Media and Sport: Harry Edward – Britain's first Black Olympian (undated)

points.datasetTitle: Sport: taking part, leading and belonging
points.heading: Jack Leslie: called up for England in 1925, then dropped
points.text: Plymouth Argyle striker Jack Leslie (1901-1988) was called up as a reserve for England in October 1925, but the honour was rescinded shortly afterwards, which the FA says is thought to have been on the grounds of racial prejudice. His family received a posthumous England cap in 2022, and Historic England unveiled a national blue plaque at his former Plymouth home in May 2025.
points.note: The plaque, which gives his dates as 1901 to 1988, reads that he was 'the first Black footballer selected for England'. Viv Anderson was the first Black footballer to play for England at senior level, in 1978. The FA also describes Leslie as the first Black footballer to captain a Football League team, and gives 137 goals in 401 appearances for Plymouth Argyle.

sources.title: The FA: Jack Leslie honoured with blue plaque (21 May 2025)
Plymouth Argyle: Blue Plaque unveiled to honour Argyle legend Jack Leslie (19 May 2025)

points.datasetTitle: Sport: taking part, leading and belonging
points.heading: Learie Constantine: cricketer and Britain's first black peer
points.text: Trinidad-born cricketer Learie Constantine played as a professional for Nelson in the Lancashire League, which won the league eight times in his ten seasons. During the Second World War he won damages after a London hotel refused him and his family accommodation. English Heritage describes him as Britain's first black peer; his 1969 peerage is covered on the hub's recognition page.
points.note: Dates differ between sources: English Heritage gives 1929 for the Nelson contract and 1943 for the hotel refusal; the Inner Temple gives 1928 and 1944. He died in London on 1 July 1971.

sources.title: English Heritage: Blue plaques – Learie Constantine (undated)
The Inner Temple: Learie Constantine – Professional Cricketer, Activist, Britain's first Black Peer (undated)

points.heading: Black firefighters: 1.4% of firefighters in England, 2024
points.text: In March 2024, 1.4% of firefighters in England whose ethnicity was known were Black and 2.6% were from Mixed ethnic backgrounds, against 4.4% and 2.5% of the working-age population at the 2021 Census. Across all fire and rescue staff the Black share was 1.7%. By 31 March 2025, 5.6% of firefighters were from an ethnic minority overall, up from 3.5% in 2011.
points.note: Shares exclude staff whose ethnicity is not stated (8.8% of all staff in 2024; 8.5% of firefighters in 2025). On-call firefighters with more than one contract are counted more than once.

sources.title: GOV.UK Ethnicity facts and figures: Fire and rescue services workforce (4 June 2025)
Home Office: Fire and rescue workforce and pensions statistics: England, year ending March 2025 (4 December 2025)

points.heading: Wholetime crews more diverse than on-call crews, 2025
points.text: On 31 March 2025, 7.4% of wholetime firefighters in England were from an ethnic minority, compared with 2.2% of on-call firefighters, 4.1% of fire control staff and 9.3% of support staff. The published headcount table records 423 wholetime and 36 on-call firefighters as Black or Black British. Ethnic minorities made up 7.9% of firefighters recruited in the year.
points.note: Counts are headcounts of staff with a stated ethnicity, taken from table FIRE1104.

sources.title: Home Office: Fire and rescue workforce and pensions statistics: England, year ending March 2025 (4 December 2025)
Home Office: FIRE1104 Staff headcount by ethnicity, fire and rescue authority and role (4 December 2025)

points.heading: Senior fire ranks remain less diverse than the frontline, 2025
points.text: Firefighter, the most junior and most common rank, was the only rank in England where the ethnic minority share (6.7%) was above the all-firefighter figure of 5.6% in March 2025. Every rank above it, from crew manager to brigade manager, was lower. The rank table records no staff at brigade manager level as Black or Black British, and three at area manager level.
points.note: Rank headcounts are from Home Office table FIRE1104 (FIRE1104c) at 31 March 2025. Senior ranks are small groups (129 staff at brigade manager rank, of whom 11 did not state an ethnicity; 174 at area manager rank), so shares move sharply from year to year.

sources.title: Home Office: Fire and rescue workforce and pensions statistics: England, year ending March 2025 (4 December 2025)
Home Office: FIRE1104 Staff headcount by ethnicity, fire and rescue authority and role (4 December 2025)

points.heading: Inspectorate found racism in at least 11 services, 2023
points.text: His Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services reported in March 2023 that it found evidence of racism, sexism and homophobia in at least 11 fire and rescue services in England. In its staff survey, 62% of ethnic minority respondents who had experienced bullying or harassment had not reported it, compared with 41% of White respondents. The government's ethnicity statistics service cites the report alongside its fire workforce data.

sources.title: HMICFRS: Values and culture in fire and rescue services (30 March 2023)
GOV.UK Ethnicity facts and figures: Fire and rescue services workforce (4 June 2025)

points.heading: London Fire Brigade: 'institutionally misogynist and racist', 2022
points.text: An independent culture review of London Fire Brigade, chaired by Nazir Afzal and published in November 2022, described the brigade as institutionally misogynist and racist. The brigade itself states that the review found Black, Asian and minority ethnic staff experience poor treatment and do less well in their careers. The review recorded a Black firefighter who had a noose put above his locker.

sources.title: London Fire Brigade: Independent Culture Review of London Fire Brigade (published November 2022)
Fire Protection Association: Damning workplace culture report reveals severe shortcomings at London Fire Brigade (November 2022)

points.heading: 7.9% of prison and probation staff are Black, 2025
points.text: At 31 March 2025, 7.9% of HM Prison and Probation Service staff who reported their ethnicity identified as Black or Black British, up 1.7 percentage points in a year; 16.1% were from an ethnic minority overall. Ethnic minority representation was lowest among operational managers (bands 7 to 9), at 6.1%. By 30 June 2026 the ethnic minority share had risen to 18.6%.
points.note: 86.9% of staff had reported their ethnicity. Covers England and Wales.

sources.title: Ministry of Justice: HM Prison and Probation Service annual staff equalities report 2024 to 2025 (27 November 2025)
Ministry of Justice: HMPPS recruitment diversity statistics, June 2026 (20 August 2026)

points.heading: Black prison officers: from 2.6% to 4.4%, 2017 to 2023
points.text: In March 2023, 4.4% of prison officers in public sector prisons in England and Wales whose ethnicity was known were Black, matching the 4.4% Black share of the working-age population, up from 2.6% in 2017. In 2024 to 2025, band 3 to 5 prison officers were the grade with the highest share of ethnic minority recruits, at 53.4%, and 25.2% of all HMPPS joiners identified as Black.
points.note: Ethnicity was unknown for 16.6% of prison officers in 2023. Covers bands 3 to 5 in public sector prisons in England and Wales; excludes private prisons. The population comparison is the one published by the source; its working-age total is the same figure used on the England-only fire page, so treat the match as approximate.

sources.title: GOV.UK Ethnicity facts and figures: Prison officer workforce (24 September 2024)
Ministry of Justice: HM Prison and Probation Service annual staff equalities report 2024 to 2025 (27 November 2025)

points.heading: Black applicants: 40.3% of applications, 18.4% of accepted offers
points.text: Between July 2024 and June 2026, 40.3% of all applications to HMPPS recruitment campaigns came from Black applicants, but Black candidates made up 18.4% of formal offers accepted. For band 3 prison officer posts, the relative rate index for ethnic minority applicants was 0.72, meaning a higher proportion of White applicants progressed through the process.
points.note: Published as official statistics in development.

sources.title: Ministry of Justice: HMPPS recruitment diversity statistics, June 2026 (20 August 2026)

points.heading: Youth custody staff: 30.5% from ethnic minorities, 2026
points.text: At 30 June 2026, 30.5% of Youth Custody Service staff who reported their ethnicity were from an ethnic minority, the highest share in HMPPS, against 18.2% in public sector prisons and 19.8% in the Probation Service. The Youth Custody Service share has risen from 17.2% in March 2021.
points.note: Youth Custody Service figures are based on a small group (376 ethnic minority staff at 30 June 2026), so the share can move sharply. Covers England and Wales.

sources.title: Ministry of Justice: HMPPS recruitment diversity statistics, June 2026 (20 August 2026)
Ministry of Justice: HMPPS workforce statistics tables, June 2026, Table 5 (20 August 2026)

points.heading: Higher discipline rates, lower bonus rates for ethnic minority staff
points.text: In 2024 to 2025, ethnic minority HMPPS staff faced conduct and discipline cases at 2.6 per 100 staff, compared with 1.6 per 100 for White staff. Black or Black British staff had the lowest recognition bonus award rate of any ethnic group, at 29.8%. Black staff were also the least likely to receive temporary cover allowances (3.3%).
points.note: The report advises caution over small subgroup sizes, and says rising case numbers may partly reflect staff having more confidence to speak out. Differences in rates do not by themselves show why they arise.

sources.title: Ministry of Justice: HM Prison and Probation Service annual staff equalities report 2024 to 2025 (27 November 2025)

points.heading: Probation inspectors: 45% of minority ethnic staff do not feel safe raising race concerns, 2023
points.text: HM Inspectorate of Probation's 2023 follow-up to its 2021 race equality inspection found that 45% of minority ethnic probation staff surveyed did not feel safe raising issues of racial discrimination, and 41% did not believe staff recruitment offered equal opportunity. The Chief Inspector said there was still some way to go to reassure Black, Asian and minority ethnic staff that they would be treated equally.
points.note: The survey covered 97 minority ethnic probation staff.

sources.title: HM Inspectorate of Probation: Race equality in probation follow-up: a work in progress, summary (September 2023)
HM Inspectorate of Probation: Race equality in probation remains a work in progress (7 September 2023)

points.heading: Ambulance staff: 4.2% from ethnic minorities, 2022
points.text: In June 2022, staff from ethnic minority groups made up 4.2% of NHS ambulance staff in England, far below the share among nurses or hospital doctors. In the 2024 NHS Workforce Race Equality Standard report, operational ambulance staff reported the highest level of harassment, bullying or abuse from patients and the public (50.3%) and were the least likely profession to believe their trust acts fairly on career progression (48.1%; 43.1% among ‘BME’ men).
points.note: The 4.2% excludes White minority groups and comes from NHS staff records for England in June 2022, the latest year published on this measure. The survey figures come from a different source and year (the NHS Staff Survey, reported in the 2024 WRES report).

sources.title: NHS workforce (Ethnicity facts and figures, June 2022 data)
Workforce Race Equality Standard 2024 data analysis report (NHS England, 2025)

points.heading: Black NHS staff least likely to see fair progression
points.text: In the 2024 NHS Workforce Race Equality Standard report, just 42.3% of staff from a Black background believed their trust provides equal opportunities for career progression or promotion, a measure that has tracked below other ethnic groups since at least 2015. Women from Black backgrounds reported high levels of discrimination from managers or colleagues (17.9%).
points.note: Covers all NHS trusts in England, including ambulance trusts. Survey measures come from the 2023/24 NHS Staff Survey, as reported in the 2024 WRES report.

sources.title: Workforce Race Equality Standard 2024 data analysis report (NHS England, 2025)
NHS Workforce Race Equality Standard (WRES) 2024 data analysis report for NHS trusts

points.heading: PCSOs and special constables more diverse than officers, 2026
points.text: At 31 March 2026, 14.3% of police community support officers in England and Wales who stated their ethnicity were from an ethnic minority, against 18.3% of the resident population, making them the most ethnically diverse part of the police workforce. Special constables followed at 13.1%. A year earlier the figures were 14.0% and 12.9%.
points.note: Shares exclude White minorities and staff who did not state an ethnicity, and are based on full-time equivalents. Covers the 43 territorial forces in England and Wales, excluding British Transport Police. Black-only shares for these groups are published in the open data tables, not the bulletin.

sources.title: Police workforce, England and Wales: 31 March 2026 (Home Office)
Home Office: Police workforce, England and Wales: 31 March 2025, second edition (updated 9 October 2025)

points.heading: Home Office, including Border Force: 6.2% Black staff, 2025
points.text: At the end of March 2025, 6.2% of Home Office staff were Black or Black British and 24.7% were from ethnic minority backgrounds. Migration and borders operations, which includes Border Force, Immigration Enforcement, UK Visas and Immigration and HM Passport Office, employed 81% of Home Office staff in 2024. Ethnic minority representation was lower at senior grades: 9.6% in the Senior Civil Service, against 28.7% at the most junior grades (AA/AO).
points.note: No separate Border Force breakdown by ethnicity is published; 32% of staff records had unknown ethnicity in 2024.

sources.title: Home Office: Home Office workforce diversity statistics 2024 to 2025 (31 March 2026)
Home Office: Home Office workforce diversity statistics 2023 to 2024 (27 February 2025)

points.heading: Armed forces reserves: 7.0% from ethnic minorities, 2026
points.text: At 1 April 2026, 7.0% of the UK's Future Reserves 2020 volunteer reserve were from ethnic minorities (excluding White minorities), up from 6.8% a year earlier. The share was 4.9% among reserve officers and 7.7% among other ranks. Ethnic minorities made up 9.8% of reserve intake in the year to 31 March 2026.
points.note: Black-only shares for reserves are not given in the bulletin text.

sources.title: UK armed forces biannual diversity statistics: April 2026 (MOD)
Ministry of Defence: UK armed forces biannual diversity statistics: April 2025 (12 June 2025)

points.heading: West India Regiments: raised 1795, partly from enslaved men
points.text: Eight West India Regiments were embodied in 1795 as a formal part of the British Army. The National Army Museum records that estimates suggest 13,400 enslaved people were purchased for the regiments between 1795 and 1807, and that serving soldiers who had been enslaved when recruited were freed under the Mutiny Act of 1807. The National Archives notes the regiment was later deployed in colonial conflicts, particularly in Africa.
points.note: The 13,400 figure is given by the museum as an estimate.

sources.title: National Army Museum: West India Regiments
The National Archives: Caribbean ancestors, an overview (research guide)

points.heading: British West Indies Regiment: 15,600 men, 1915 to 1918
points.text: The British West Indies Regiment was established by Royal Warrant on 3 November 1915 and grew to 11 battalions and 15,600 men, two thirds of them from Jamaica. Military regulations prevented Black West Indian soldiers from holding a rank higher than warrant officer. By the end of the war, 185 men from the regiment had been killed in action and 1,071 had died of sickness.

sources.title: Imperial War Museums: How the West Indies helped the war effort in the First World War
Imperial War Museums: British West Indies Regiment

points.heading: Taranto, December 1918: protest against unequal treatment
points.text: British West Indies Regiment soldiers were denied a pay rise given to the rest of the British Army because they were classed as so-called 'native' troops. Gathered at Taranto in Italy for demobilisation in December 1918, they were badly mistreated. Imperial War Museums describes a riot suppressed by armed soldiers; historians refer to the mutiny of the regiment's battalions and have long regarded it as resistance to a racist military hierarchy and an early stirring of Caribbean nationalism, while recent research also points to the veterans' hopes for imperial reform.
points.note: The second source is the abstract of a paper presented at The National Archives' Voices of the Home Fronts conference, 19 October 2018.

sources.title: Imperial War Museums: The World War 1 Black British soldiers deliberately forgotten
Goldsmiths Research Online: Smith, The British West Indies Regiment mutiny at Taranto and multicultural memories of the First World War (2018)

points.heading: Caribbean and African aircrew in the RAF: about 450 flew, over 150 killed
points.text: Around 450 volunteers from the Caribbean and Africa served as RAF aircrew in the Second World War, flying with Bomber, Fighter, Coastal and Flying Training Commands; the RAF Museum records that over 150 were killed. About 100 volunteers were commissioned and 103 decorated. The National Archives notes that for the first half of the 20th century only white men were eligible for combatant roles or commissions, with notable wartime exceptions.
points.note: The RAF Museum's own pages differ slightly: one gives 150 killed, the other over 150. Ethnic origin was not recorded on RAF personnel files, so all totals are estimates.

sources.title: RAF Museum: Pilots of the Caribbean, The Second World War, 1939 to 1945: the record
RAF Museum: The Empire Windrush, Peter Devitt (22 June 2018)
The National Archives: Caribbean ancestors, an overview (research guide)

points.heading: Blitz firefighters: George Arthur Roberts and Black 'front liners'
points.text: London Fire Brigade records George Arthur Roberts, born in Trinidad, who fought on the Western Front in the First World War, as the first Black man to join the London Auxiliary Fire Service, in 1938. He served at New Cross Fire Station during the Blitz and was awarded the British Empire Medal in 1944; he died in 1970. In December 1940, A. A. Thompson, general secretary of the League of Coloured Peoples, praised the number of 'coloured men' in London working as wardens, Auxiliary Fire Service men, stretcher parties and first aid units.
points.note: Sources differ on his birth year: London Fire Brigade gives 1891, Southwark News gives 1890.

sources.title: London Fire Brigade Museum: George Arthur Roberts BEM
Southwark News: Blue plaque for first Black man to serve in army and fire brigade (15 September 2016)
London Fire Brigade Museum: Black 'front liners' and fire service personnel during the London Blitz, Stephen Bourne

points.heading: Early Black and mixed-heritage police officers: 1835 to 1968
points.text: John Kent, born in 1805, whose father had been enslaved, began policing at Maryport in 1835 and joined Carlisle City Police in 1837; the Police Federation and Cumbria Police describe him as Britain's first Black police officer. Robert Branford joined the Metropolitan Police in 1838 and became superintendent of Southwark's M Division in 1856; an 1893 memoir by a former Met chief inspector described him as of mixed race. He died in 1869. Sislin Fay Allen joined the Met in 1968, becoming the UK's first Black policewoman; she died in 2021.
points.note: Branford's heritage is known from an 1893 memoir cited by historian Jeffrey Green. 'First' claims rest on surviving records and may change as research continues.

sources.title: Police Federation of England and Wales: Remembering Britain's first black police officer (21 October 2021)
The Voice: Britain's first black police officer honoured with blue plaque (28 October 2019)
Jeffrey Green: Robert Branford, 1817-1869, London police superintendent
BBC News: Sislin Fay Allen, Britain's first black policewoman dies aged 83 (July 2021)
Police Professional: UK's first black female police officer dies aged 83 (7 July 2021)

points.datasetTitle: Intersections: age, disability, sexual orientation and gender identity
points.heading: Mixed-heritage groups are the youngest; few are aged 65 or over
points.text: At Census 2021, people in Mixed or Multiple ethnic groups had a median age of 19, against 40 for England and Wales as a whole. In the Mixed White and Black African group, 48.6% were aged under 16 and only 2.5% were 65 or over. The older age profile of the Black Caribbean group is covered in the older people figures above.
points.note: Census Day 21 March 2021, England and Wales. Age profile shapes most comparisons in this section: groups with few older people show lower rates of age-related conditions and benefits. Both sources present ONS census data, so there is effectively one publisher.

sources.title: Office for National Statistics: Ethnic group by age and sex, England and Wales: Census 2021
Ethnicity facts and figures (Cabinet Office): Age groups (31 March 2023)

points.datasetTitle: Intersections: age, disability, sexual orientation and gender identity
points.heading: The Windrush generation is now in later life
points.text: Many of the people who came to the UK from Commonwealth countries before 1973 are now in later life. By the end of July 2026, 1,717 of the 12,272 claims made to the Windrush Compensation Scheme (14%) had been made on behalf of the estate of someone who had died. In January 2024 a Home Office minister told Parliament that at least 53 claimants had died before receiving compensation, a figure Age UK highlighted in February 2024.
points.note: The estate-claim total is calculated by adding the monthly and quarterly counts in Home Office table WCS_02; one person can make several claims, and claims can change category. Estate claims count claims made by estates, not deaths while waiting. The 53 figure was given by a Home Office minister and counts claimants who died before receiving compensation; it does not say the scheme caused those deaths. The National Audit Office counted 118 estate claims (5%) by March 2021. The hub's Windrush pages cover the scandal and the scheme in full.

points.datasetTitle: Intersections: age, disability, sexual orientation and gender identity
points.heading: Black pensioners: more than twice the White rate of low income
points.text: In the three years from April 2022 to March 2025, 29% of UK pensioners in households headed by a Black adult were in relative low income after housing costs, against 12% of pensioners in White-headed households. In 2021, Age UK reported that 44% of Black older households received an occupational pension, against 61% of White older households. The hub's earlier 31% figure (April 2021 to March 2024) comes from DWP data published before DWP revised its method in March 2026. The two figures are not directly comparable, so the difference should not be read as a fall.
points.note: UK. Relative low income means below 60% of median household income after housing costs; ethnicity is that of the household head. DWP table 6.5db gives 28.9% and 12.4%. The comparison group is all White households, not White British as in the earlier figure. In March 2026 DWP revised its estimates for 2021/22 to 2023/24 using administrative benefit data, creating a break in the series. The Black pensioner group is small (about 139,000 people), so the estimate is uncertain. Not age-standardised. Age UK's pension figures were published in 2021.

points.datasetTitle: Intersections: age, disability, sexual orientation and gender identity
points.heading: Unpaid care: similar rates for Black Caribbean and White British women
points.text: Taking age into account, 10.3% of Black Caribbean women and 11.3% of Mixed White and Black Caribbean women in England gave unpaid care in 2021, close to 11.0% of White British women. Rates were lower for Black African women (7.6%) and men (5.0%). In a 2023 survey, ethnic minority carers were more likely than White carers to be struggling to make ends meet (34% against 29%).
points.note: Census figures are age-standardised percentages of usual residents aged 5 and over in England; they count who gives care, not how many hours. The Carers UK figures come from its State of Caring 2023 survey of carers across the UK and group all ethnic minority carers together, not Black carers alone; the briefing does not define the group but quotes a White Irish carer within it.

points.datasetTitle: Intersections: age, disability, sexual orientation and gender identity
points.heading: Black workers are 23% of the adult social care workforce
points.text: In 2025/26, 23% of the adult social care workforce in England were from Black, African, Caribbean or Black British ethnicities, against 6% of the economically active population and 4% of the whole population. Of adults receiving long-term care and support, 4.5% were from Black ethnic groups in 2021, and they made up a larger share of people supported in community or prison settings (5.3%) than in residential care (2.2%).
points.figure: 23% of workforce v 6% of economically active
points.note: England. Comparators are from Skills for Care's Chart 65: population from Census 2021, economically active from the Labour Force Survey 2025/26. The people-supported figures come from NHS data via Ethnicity facts and figures and are not age-standardised; the Black population is younger than average. Skills for Care's 2026 race equality report found global majority staff as a whole 50% more likely to enter formal disciplinary processes; it does not give a Black-only figure. The hub's earlier workforce point uses an older 'about a third ethnic minority' figure.

points.datasetTitle: Intersections: age, disability, sexual orientation and gender identity
points.heading: Dementia: higher diagnosis rates and younger deaths
points.text: A study of UK GP records for 2007 to 2015 found the rate of dementia diagnosis was 25% higher in Black women and 28% higher in Black men than in White women and men, after adjusting for age and other factors. A second study, of people aged 65 and over in England, found Black people with dementia died on average 2.7 years younger than White people with dementia. Alzheimer's Society says support is typically accessed later by Black communities in the UK.
points.note: Both studies measure recorded diagnoses, which depend on who is assessed; the first estimates that Black men developing dementia were less likely than White men to be diagnosed. The age-at-death gap is an average difference and may partly reflect the younger age profile of Black older people. The two studies share an author. The evidence is from research studies and a charity, not official statistics; the Alzheimer's Society page is undated. A higher rate is not evidence of cause.

points.datasetTitle: Intersections: age, disability, sexual orientation and gender identity
points.heading: Within each age group, Black African people report less disability
points.text: In England in 2021, 6.6% of Black African people aged 16 to 49 reported a disability, against 15.0% of White British people of the same age, and 30.9% against 35.3% at 65 and over. Black Caribbean rates were close to White British rates up to age 64 and higher at 65 and over (39.6%), and Mixed White and Black Caribbean rates were higher in every adult age group.
points.note: Census disability is self-reported against the Equality Act definition; figures are age-specific, England. A UK survey for 2024/25 gives a similar picture for ages 16 to 64: Black 17.7%, Mixed 25.5%, White 26.0% (calculated as disabled divided by disabled plus non-disabled from DWP table LMS007; not age-standardised). Differences in reported disability are not evidence of cause. See also the age-standardised 22.4% figure for Mixed White and Black Caribbean people above.

points.datasetTitle: Intersections: age, disability, sexual orientation and gender identity
points.heading: Disabled Black adults: 52.8% in work
points.text: In 2024/25, 52.8% of disabled Black adults aged 16 to 64 in the UK were in employment, against 74.5% of non-disabled Black adults, a gap of 21.7 percentage points. DWP notes the gap for White adults is wider (28.7 points), partly because non-disabled White adults have the highest employment rate (84.3%). For Mixed groups, 49.1% of disabled adults were in work.
points.note: Annual Population Survey, UK, ages 16 to 64; not age-standardised. The 'BME' combined figures from the TUC are covered by the hub's existing TUC point and are not Black-only.

points.datasetTitle: Intersections: age, disability, sexual orientation and gender identity
points.heading: Disability benefits by ethnicity; no ethnicity data for Access to Work
points.text: In the three years to 2024/25, 7% of benefit units headed by a Black adult received the daily living part of Personal Independence Payment, against 9% of White-headed units and 8% overall. Access to Work statistics are published by age, gender, medical condition, region, employer size and employment status, but not by ethnicity.
points.note: Family Resources Survey, UK, by ethnic group of the head of the benefit unit; not age-standardised, and White-headed units are older on average. Lower receipt is not evidence of lower need or of barriers to claiming. Without ethnicity in Access to Work data, it is not possible to say whether Black disabled workers use the scheme in proportion. Both sources are DWP; no other publisher produces these figures.

points.datasetTitle: Intersections: age, disability, sexual orientation and gender identity
points.heading: About 17,000 people in England live with sickle cell disease
points.text: Government and NHS England estimate that about 17,000 people in England live with sickle cell disease, with about 250 new cases a year. The national patient safety investigator puts the UK figure at about 15,000, with around 300 babies born with the condition each year and about 1 in 79 babies carrying the trait. It mainly affects people of African and Caribbean heritage, but anyone can inherit it.
points.note: The estimates differ in date, geography and source (the 15,000 UK figure cites the Sickle Cell Society), so treat both as approximate. The hub's DNA and genomes page covers sickle cell trait and malaria.

points.datasetTitle: Intersections: age, disability, sexual orientation and gender identity
points.heading: The NHS response: training, funding and a new gene therapy
points.text: In 2023 the national patient safety investigator recommended that NHS England set minimum training for staff caring for people in sickle cell crisis. In 2025 NICE made the gene-editing therapy exagamglogene autotemcel (Casgevy) available for severe sickle cell disease through a managed access agreement. NHS England also funded £9 million to expand apheresis (blood exchange) services.
points.note: Casgevy is for people aged 12 and over with severe sickle cell disease and is available while more evidence is collected. These are commitments and decisions; their effect on patients' experience of care is not shown by these sources.

points.datasetTitle: Intersections: age, disability, sexual orientation and gender identity
points.heading: Sexual orientation by ethnic group at Census 2021
points.text: In England and Wales in 2021, about 1.8% of Black African and 2.1% of Black Caribbean people aged 16 and over identified as gay, lesbian, bisexual or another minority sexual orientation, against about 3.1% of the whole population on the same basis (ONS's published overall figure is 3.2%). The figure was about 5.8% in the Mixed White and Black Caribbean group and 5.7% in the Mixed White and Black African group. ONS says the higher Mixed figures are likely to be related to these groups' younger age profiles.
points.note: Group figures are the sum of ONS's three rounded percentages (gay or lesbian, bisexual, other), so each may differ from the unrounded total by up to 0.15 points. The difference between the Black African and Black Caribbean figures is within that margin. Not age-standardised. Percentages are of all usual residents aged 16 and over, including the 7.5% who did not answer the question. Only ONS publishes census figures on sexual orientation by ethnic group.
