points.datasetTitle: Intersections: age, disability, sexual orientation and gender identity
points.heading: Gender identity by ethnicity: figures to treat with great caution
points.text: Census 2021 recorded 1.6% of people in Black ethnic groups as trans, against 0.3% of White British people. ONS later found patterns suggesting some people with lower English proficiency may not have understood the question as intended, and in 2024 the estimates became official statistics in development. ONS says it is less confident in breakdowns by characteristics linked to English proficiency, such as ethnicity.
points.note: ONS cannot say whether the census overestimates or underestimates the trans population. These ethnic breakdowns should not be used as estimates of the number of Black trans people. Sexual orientation estimates were not affected and remain accredited official statistics.

points.datasetTitle: Intersections: age, disability, sexual orientation and gender identity
points.heading: Racism in LGBT spaces and pressure to change
points.text: In a Stonewall survey of LGBT people in Britain carried out in 2017 and published in 2018, three in five Black LGBT respondents (61%) said they had faced discrimination or poor treatment in their local LGBT community because of their ethnicity. In the government's 2017 National LGBT Survey, 13% of Black cisgender respondents had undergone or been offered conversion therapy, against 7% of White respondents; among Black trans respondents the figure was 28%.
points.note: Both are online surveys, not representative samples. The National LGBT Survey had 108,100 valid responses, of whom 1% were Black, so the Black trans figure rests on a small number of people. The hub's existing 51% figure covers all Black, Asian and minority ethnic LGBT people.

sources.title: LGBT in Britain – Home and Communities (2018)

points.datasetTitle: Intersections: age, disability, sexual orientation and gender identity
points.heading: Hate crime: no official count where race and sexuality meet
points.text: Police in England and Wales recorded 21,407 sexual orientation and 3,955 transgender hate crimes in the year to March 2026. The Home Office reports victim ethnicity only for racially or religiously aggravated offences, so official figures cannot show how many victims were Black LGBT+ people. In Stonewall's 2017 survey, a third of Black, Asian and minority ethnic LGBT people had experienced a hate crime or incident in the previous year, against one in five White LGBT people.
points.note: Police recorded crime reflects reporting and recording practice as well as offending; a change to the Metropolitan Police's recording system in 2024 limits comparisons over time. The Stonewall figure combines all ethnic minority LGBT people, from a YouGov survey of more than 5,000 LGBT people in Britain carried out in 2017.

sources.title: Home Office: Hate crime, England and Wales, year ending March 2026 (8 October 2026)

points.datasetTitle: Intersections: age, disability, sexual orientation and gender identity
points.heading: UK Black Pride at 20
points.text: UK Black Pride marked 20 years in 2025 with an exhibition at Queer Britain, produced with the organisation and its co-founder, Phyll Opoku-Gyimah (Lady Phyll). London Museum describes her as 'a pioneering LGBTQ+ rights and anti-racism campaigner'.
points.note: The hub's existing points cover its start in 2005, the first event in Southend-on-Sea and its 'Europe's largest' self-description; UK Black Pride's own history also says it was officially launched in 2006. London Museum calls it the world's largest, a wider claim the organisation does not make. There is no official statistical source on the organisation.

points.datasetTitle: Intersections: age, disability, sexual orientation and gender identity
points.heading: Health: poorer mental health and gaps in HIV prevention
points.text: In a Stonewall survey carried out in 2017 and published in 2018, 62% of Black, Asian and minority ethnic LGBT respondents in Britain said they had experienced depression in the previous year, against 52% of all LGBT respondents. In 2024, 0.6% of gay and bisexual men of Black ethnicity tested for HIV in sexual health services in England tested positive, against 0.2% of all gay and bisexual men tested. Among those with a need for HIV prevention medicine (PrEP), uptake was similar for ethnic minority and White gay and bisexual men (77.8% and 79.4%).
points.note: Stonewall's YouGov survey is not a random sample, combines all ethnic minority LGBT people and records self-reported depression. HIV test positivity reflects who comes forward for testing, not how common HIV is in the population. The PrEP figure combines all ethnic minority gay and bisexual men. Government's PrEP roadmap (2024) sets out actions to widen fair access. Disparities are not evidence of cause.

points.heading: Black shares grew in Birmingham, Manchester, Leicester and Newcastle
points.text: Between 2011 and 2021, the Black share of residents rose from 9.0% to 11.0% in Birmingham, from 8.6% to 11.9% in Manchester, from 6.2% to 7.8% in Leicester and from 1.8% to 3.3% in Newcastle upon Tyne. points.text: At Census 2021, about 52,400 people living in rural settlements in England identified with a Black ethnic group. That is 0.6% of the rural population and 2.2% of all Black people in England. Allerdale, Mid Devon and Torridge had Black shares of 0.1%, the lowest of any local authority in England and Wales.

points.datasetTitle: Place: the four nations and the regions
points.heading: Liverpool's Black community dates back to the 18th century
points.text: National Museums Liverpool describes Liverpool's Black community as the oldest in Europe, with settlers in the 1750s including sailors, freed enslaved people and sons of African rulers studying in the city. The National Lottery Heritage Fund describes it as Britain's oldest Black community, dating to the 1730s. At Census 2021, 3.5% of Liverpool's residents identified with a Black ethnic group.
points.note: Claims to be the 'oldest' Black community are contested: the two sources differ on Europe or Britain and on the 1730s or 1750s, and neither sets out evidence comparing Liverpool with other places. National Museums Liverpool uses 'Black' in its trail to mean people with African heritage.

points.datasetTitle: Place: the four nations and the regions
points.heading: The Anti-racist Wales Action Plan sets a goal for 2030
points.text: The Welsh Government published the Anti-racist Wales Action Plan in 2022, with a vision for 2030, and refreshed it in November 2024. In its culture, heritage and sport chapter, the 2024 update sets actions to require funded organisations to meet anti-racism performance requirements, which may be set through remit letters, award letters and other conditions of grant, and to require public bodies to establish highly inclusive, anti-racist working environments with anti-racism training. Its health chapter reports that NHS Wales health boards, trusts and special health authorities have each formulated anti-racism action plans.
points.note: The plan is government policy, not legislation, and sits alongside the public sector equality duty in the Equality Act 2010. The plan's own page gives 20 July 2022 as its first publication date, while later documents say June 2022.

points.datasetTitle: Place: the four nations and the regions
points.heading: A Senedd committee found gaps in how the plan is delivered
points.text: A Senedd committee inquiry, held from March 2023 to February 2024, welcomed the plan's scale and vision. Several councils and other bodies said they were not clear about their role in delivering it, and the plan does not include key measurable targets. The committee concluded that the 2030 aim would be undermined if the plan did not bring together those who can drive change, provide the resources needed and set targets to measure progress.
points.note: Responding to the committee's recommendation to publish a yearly breakdown of funding, the Welsh Government said this was 'impossible' because the plan cuts across many policy areas.

points.heading: Tiger Bay in Cardiff is Wales' oldest multi-ethnic community
points.text: Cardiff's former docklands, once known as Tiger Bay, are described by the Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments of Wales as Wales' oldest multi-ethnic community, with sailors and workers from over 50 countries having settled there. A People's Collection Wales item about the Butetown History and Arts Centre states that research shows over 57 nationalities were living in Tiger Bay in the 1940s. During the race riots of 1919, violence occurred in the docks areas of Cardiff, Barry and Swansea.
points.note: Counts vary between sources: over 50 countries (Coflein) and over 57 nationalities in the 1940s (People's Collection Wales).

points.heading: About 65,400 people in Scotland were African, Caribbean or Black
points.text: Scotland's Census 2022 counted 58,636 people in African ethnic groups (1.08% of the population) and 6,778 in Caribbean or Black groups (0.12%). Together that is about 65,400 people, or 1.2%. In 2011 the figures were 29,638 (0.56%) and 6,540 (0.12%), so the African groups roughly doubled.
points.note: Calculated: the combined total adds the two published counts, and 'roughly doubled' compares the 2011 and 2022 African counts. Scotland's census was a year later than the 2021 censuses elsewhere in the UK, so the dates differ.

points.text: In Scotland's 2022 census, 'African, African Scottish or African British' and 'Caribbean or Black' were separate headings, unlike the single Black heading used in England and Wales. points.text: In 2022, African people were the largest ‘non-white’ ethnic group in Aberdeen, at about 4% of residents. In Glasgow, the number of people recording an African ethnic group rose from 1,257 in 2001 to 12,440 in 2011, while Caribbean or Black was the only group to fall between 2011 and 2022. points.heading: The Race Equality Framework sets Scotland's race equality aims to 2030
points.text: The Scottish Government's Race Equality Framework for Scotland 2016-2030 sets out six themed visions for race equality, shaped through engagement with grassroots community organisations, public sector practitioners and individuals. In 2020 a Scottish Parliament committee found that progress on race equality in employment had been slow or stalled, and that the ethnicity employment gap had gone backwards. Public bodies in Scotland are also bound by the Equality Act 2010, which forms part of Scots law.
points.note: The framework is government policy, not legislation. The framework is cited from an archived copy of the Scottish Government PDF (March 2016).

points.text: The Scottish Government is funding an Anti-Racism Observatory for Scotland (AROS), a new national organisation to work with government, public bodies and communities. points.heading: Scotland's economy was tied to empire and slavery for two centuries
points.text: An independent steering group, part of a project sponsored by the Scottish Government, reported in 2022 that for more than two centuries Scotland's economy was closely tied to imperial trade and conquest, including the enslavement of human beings. The Scottish Government accepted its recommendations, including a dedicated space to address Scotland's role in empire, colonialism and historic slavery, in January 2024. In 1778 the Court of Session decided the case of Joseph Knight, who claimed that, despite being purchased by Wedderburn in Jamaica, the act of landing in Scotland had freed him; he was partially successful in arguing that Scots law could not support the status of slavery.
points.note: The account of the Joseph Knight case is from National Records of Scotland, which holds the court papers.

points.text: Census 2021 counted about 11,000 Black people in Northern Ireland, 0.6% of the population: 8,069 recorded as Black African and 2,963 as Black Other. Black people were the second largest minority ethnic group in Northern Ireland.

points.text: The Executive Office's Racial Equality Strategy 2015-2025 set a framework for government departments to tackle racial inequalities, eradicate racism and hate crime, and promote good race relations. It set seven shared aims, with actions underscored by the Section 75 equality and good relations duties.

points.text: An independent review commissioned by the Executive Office, published in December 2024, found that the strategy's aims had been undermined by the lack of an action plan, of involvement of people with lived experience, and of a process for ethnic monitoring. points.heading: Section 75 differs from the public sector equality duty
points.text: In Northern Ireland, Section 75 of the Northern Ireland Act 1998 requires public authorities to have due regard to the need to promote equality of opportunity between people of different racial groups, among other groups, and regard to promoting good relations. The public sector equality duty in section 149 of the Equality Act 2010 does not extend to Northern Ireland. The main race discrimination law there is the Race Relations (Northern Ireland) Order 1997.
points.note: Derived from the Act's extent section: section 149 is not among the provisions that section 217(3) extends to Northern Ireland. Section 75 also covers religious belief, political opinion, age, marital status, sexual orientation, sex, disability and people with dependants.

points.heading: Recorded race hate in Northern Ireland reached record levels
points.text: In the 12 months to 31 March 2026, police in Northern Ireland recorded 2,367 race hate incidents and 1,507 race hate crimes, the highest since records began in 2004/05. NISRA links the rise to periods of civil unrest in August 2024 and June 2025. Figures for the 12 months to 30 June 2026 were higher again, at 2,561 incidents and 1,615 crimes.
points.note: The figures cover all race-motivated incidents and crimes, not only those against Black people, and do not show victims' ethnicity. They include only incidents and crimes reported to and recorded by the police. Both sets of figures are official statistics published by NISRA (14 May 2026 and 27 August 2026).

points.heading: Brazil's 2010 racial equality statute defines who counts as Black
points.text: A 2023 amendment (Law 14.553) requires the administrative records of public bodies, private employers and their workers, such as hiring and dismissal forms, to include self-classified ethnic and racial fields, and requires IBGE to survey the ethnic and racial make-up of the public sector every five years.
points.note: Applies to Brazil only. The hub's Latin America material covers the preto and pardo census categories and their counts. The results of the five-yearly public-sector survey are not reported here.

points.heading: Brazil reserves half of federal university places, with racial shares
points.text: Law 12.711 of 2012 requires federal universities to reserve at least 50% of places on each course for students who did all their secondary schooling in state schools. Within those places, the share for self-declared preto, pardo and Indigenous students must be at least their share of the state's population at the latest census. Law 14.723 of November 2023 added quilombola students (from communities descended from settlements of people who escaped slavery), lowered the income threshold and set an evaluation every ten years with an annual report.
points.note: Places are also reserved for disabled students. In April 2012 Brazil's Supreme Court unanimously upheld the University of Brasília's earlier race-based admissions policy (ADPF 186), in a case brought by a political party.

points.heading: Brazil: 30% of federal recruitment places reserved by quota law
points.text: From 2014, Law 12.990 reserved 20% of places in federal civil service recruitment competitions for Black (negro) candidates, for a term of ten years. In 2024 the Supreme Court extended that law until Congress passed a replacement. Law 15.142 of 3 June 2025 replaced it, reserving 30% of places in federal competitions and temporary recruitment for people who self-declare as preto or pardo, Indigenous people and quilombolas, wherever two or more places are offered. Self-declarations as preto or pardo go through a confirmation procedure that must involve specialists in ethnic and racial relations.
points.note: In Great Britain, government guidance for employers says positive discrimination is unlawful and that setting recruitment quotas, as opposed to targets, would probably be unlawful discrimination; sections 158 and 159 of the Equality Act 2010 allow only limited positive action, and the hub's positive action guidance explains what is allowed. Brazil's Supreme Court kept the 2014 quota in force in ADI 7654: a judge's injunction of 26 May 2024 was confirmed unanimously by the full court on 17 June 2024.

points.heading: Brazil treats racism as a crime with no time limit on prosecution
points.text: Brazil's 1988 Constitution makes the practice of racism a crime with no bail and no limitation period, punishable by imprisonment. In October 2021 the Supreme Court held by a majority that racial insult (injúria racial) is a form of racism and so has no limitation period. Law 14.532 of 11 January 2023 then moved racial insult into the racism law, with two to five years' imprisonment and a fine.
points.note: The 2021 ruling was debated among lawyers on the grounds that only Congress may define crimes and their limitation periods (the principle of legality) and on the separation of powers, according to an article by Douglas Strachicini in the Brazilian Senate's legal journal; the 2023 law put the point into statute.

points.heading: Colombia reserves two seats in its lower house for Afro-descendants
points.text: Article 176 of Colombia's Constitution creates special constituencies in the House of Representatives, two of whose seats are elected by the constituency of Afro-descendant communities. The seats were first contested in 1994; in 1996 the Constitutional Court struck down the law behind them, and they stayed empty until Law 649 of 2001 regulated them again. Under that law, candidates must be members of the community and endorsed by an organisation registered with the Ministry of the Interior.
points.note: An article by Ana Carolina Osorio in the journal of Colombia's national civil registry (Registraduría) records long-standing questions about how representative the elected members are, citing low votes and 'paper' organisations. Collective land rights under Law 70 of 1993 are covered on the hub's Latin America page.

points.heading: Colombia's equality ministry lost its legal basis in June 2026
points.text: Law 2281 of January 2023 created a Ministry of Equality and Equity whose priority groups included Afro-descendant, Black, Raizal and Palenquero peoples. In May 2024 the Constitutional Court struck the law down because Congress passed it without assessing its fiscal impact, but delayed the effect for two legislative years. A bill to re-create the ministry was not fully passed before 20 June 2026. Decrees of 19 June 2026 put the ministry into liquidation (Decree 0626) and returned the three agencies attached to it, including the family welfare institute ICBF, to their former sectors (Decree 0627).
points.note: The ministry served many groups, not only Afro-Colombians. The court's objection was to the law-making procedure, not to the ministry's aims.

points.heading: Uruguay sets an 8% public-job quota for Afro-descendants
points.text: Uruguay's Law 19.122 of 2013 recognises that Afro-descendants have historically suffered racism and discrimination, and requires state bodies to give 8% of the posts they fill each year to Afro-descendant candidates. The National Civil Service Office reports on this every year. In 2024, 415 people were recruited under the rule, 1.72% of recruitment in the bodies covered.
points.note: The 1.72% leaves out bodies whose intake was too small for 8% to make up one post. Seven bodies met the quota in 2024. The law also sets an 8% share in training programmes and shares in study grants. A 2024 report by Uruguay's national human rights institution and the Civil Service Office reviews its first ten years.

points.heading: The Americas have a regional anti-racism treaty, in force since 2017
points.text: The Inter-American Convention against Racism, Racial Discrimination and Related Forms of Intolerance was agreed at the Organization of American States in Antigua, Guatemala, on 5 June 2013 and came into force on 11 November 2017. Costa Rica and Uruguay were the first states to ratify. Brazil's Congress approved it by the procedure that gives human rights treaties the same standing as constitutional amendments, and it took effect for Brazil on 27 June 2021.
points.note: The OAS treaty register listed six states as having ratified as of 26 October 2026: Antigua and Barbuda, Brazil, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Mexico and Uruguay. The UK is not a member state of the OAS.

points.heading: India lists Siddi communities as Scheduled Tribes in named districts
points.text: India's Parliament sets lists of Scheduled Tribes state by state, sometimes limited to named districts. Siddi communities are listed in parts of Gujarat. An Act passed in 2002 (in force January 2003) added 'Siddi (in Uttar Kannada district)' to Karnataka's list, and an Act of March 2020 extended the Karnataka listing to Siddis in Belagavi and Dharwad districts.
points.note: Status depends on the district as well as the state. A 2019 press report cited estimates of 17,000 to 18,000 Siddis in Karnataka; this is not a census count. The hub's world page covers Siddi history.

points.heading: Pakistan's Sheedi community in UN race-equality reviews
points.text: In 2016 the UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD) regretted that Pakistan had given no information on the Sheedi, descendants of East Africans, and asked it to ensure they could take part in cultural life, including the Sheedi Mela festival. Pakistan's reply, received in 2021, said the Sheedi enjoy all rights as citizens and that no rights complaint about them had reached the Sindh Human Rights Commission. In its September 2024 findings the committee was concerned about high poverty and unemployment among ethnic minority groups including the Sheedi, and recommended better access to jobs, training and support for small businesses.
points.note: The government and the committee describe the situation differently. Pakistan's report also says the first Sheedi woman was elected to the Sindh Assembly in 2018. At the 2024 review a committee member asked whether Pakistan's census allows people of African descent, including the Siddi community, to identify themselves.

points.heading: UN reviews press Iraq on discrimination against Black Iraqis
points.text: In 2014 CERD noted that Black Iraqi and Roma communities were affected by poverty and social exclusion, and recommended special measures. In 2019 it was still concerned about structural discrimination against people of African descent. Iraq's 2023 report to the committee says its High Commission for Human Rights referred a complaint about people of African descent in Basra to prosecutors. In September 2024 the committee said Iraq had taken too few measures against structural discrimination targeting people of African descent and again recommended special measures on poverty, living conditions, education, health care and jobs.
points.note: Iraq's report says its laws, plans and policies are free from racial discrimination; the committee's findings rest partly on civil society reports, including an unofficial estimate that unemployment among Black Iraqis could be as high as 80%. The hub's world page covers population estimates and history.

points.heading: Israel set up a government anti-racism unit after a 2016 review
points.text: In 2016 Israel's government set up an inter-ministerial team, led by the Ministry of Justice's director general, to tackle racism against Israelis of Ethiopian origin. The government adopted its recommendations in July 2016, including a Government Unit to Coordinate the Fight Against Racism in the Ministry of Justice, which was set up in 2017. The unit's remit later widened to all groups facing institutional racism.
points.note: A 2023 assessment by the Institute for National Security Studies says the unit's authority was not set in law and its budget was inadequate. The same assessment cites a 2023 survey reporting that 90% of Israelis of Ethiopian origin had encountered institutional racism.

points.heading: The UN standard behind these reviews: General Recommendation 34
points.text: In 2011 CERD adopted General Recommendation 34 on racial discrimination against people of African descent. It asks states to identify communities of African descent, especially by collecting disaggregated data, and to run regular surveys of discrimination. The committee cites it when reviewing states in the region, for example Iraq in 2019.
points.note: The UK is reviewed by the same committee; the hub's law material covers the 2024 UK review.

points.heading: Civil Service Jobs is where you find and apply for roles
points.text: Civil Service Jobs is the Civil Service's own recruitment website, and you can apply there at any time without joining a talent scheme. Set up job alerts so new roles that match your skills come to you, and check whether each advert is open to everyone or only to existing civil servants.
points.note: Some vacancies are advertised only across government or inside one department, so not every role is visible to external candidates. Some organisations take applications on their own websites, linked from the advert.

points.heading: Fast Stream: the graduate leadership programme, closing 5 November
points.text: The Fast Stream is a leadership development programme with 18 specialist schemes, including digital, cyber security, statistics and economics. Most schemes need a 2:2 degree or above and many are open to degree apprentices; you start on £31,554 and move between postings in different departments.
points.note: The 2027 window closes at midday on 5 November 2026, so dates and pay will change for the next round. Competition is intense: about 1% of applicants were recommended for appointment in the 2024-25 cycle. The hub's Schemes and programmes section profiles the Fast Stream in more detail, including its diversity funnel.

points.heading: Apprenticeships: earn while you learn from age 16
points.text: Civil Service apprenticeships pay you while you study for a recognised qualification, at levels 2 (GCSE equivalent) to 7 (master's equivalent), in professions including digital, cyber security, finance and science and engineering. They are open from age 16 to anyone who meets the nationality rules, and mid-career apprenticeships are offered to people changing career.
points.note: The old Civil Service Fast Track Apprenticeship has closed and is not a current route; look on Civil Service Jobs for departmental apprenticeships instead. The Career Launch apprenticeship for school leavers launched in 2025. The hub's Recruitment and career routes section covers apprenticeships as an entry route.

points.heading: Summer Internship Programme: paid placements for students
points.text: The Summer Internship Programme (SIP) gives undergraduates from lower socio-economic backgrounds eight weeks of paid work in a department, at £475 a week. You need to be in your final two years of a degree, and a good appraisal can earn you a Fast Pass through the early Fast Stream stages.
points.note: SIP replaced the Summer Diversity Internship Programme (SDIP), which was open to ethnic minority and lower socio-economic background undergraduates and later also to disabled students. Since August 2025 SIP is for people from lower socio-economic backgrounds only, assessed using Office for National Statistics measures. You cannot apply for SIP and the Fast Stream in the same year. The hub's Schemes and programmes section also covers SIP; a separate Care Leavers Internship Scheme exists too.

points.heading: Supported routes for people facing barriers to work
points.text: Going Forward into Employment (GFiE) recruits people who face barriers to work, such as care leavers, carers, veterans and people with convictions, into real, ring-fenced roles with simpler applications. It runs under an exception to open competition that the Civil Service Commission allows for employment programmes.
points.note: The hub's circumstances section covers this in more depth. The GFiE page gives two different totals for people recruited since 2018 (over 3,050 and over 3,600), so no headline figure is used here.

points.heading: Join from outside government, or come in on a secondment
points.text: You do not need government experience to apply, and roles at every level up to the Senior Civil Service are advertised to external candidates, though not every vacancy is open to them. If you want to keep your current job, a secondment lets you work in government for a fixed period, usually up to two years, while staying employed by your own organisation.
points.note: Secondees go through the same pre-employment and security checks as new joiners. Schemes include GovXchange (local and central government) and a digital secondment programme.

points.heading: Grades run from administrative assistant to Senior Civil Service
points.text: There are seven broad grades: AA/AO, EO, HEO, SEO, Grade 7, Grade 6 and the Senior Civil Service. Civil Service Careers gives average starting salaries from about £23,000 at AA/AO to about £76,000 at SCS level, but pay depends on department, location and role.

points.heading: Digital, data and technology roles, including at GDS
points.text: Government employs product managers, developers, designers, data scientists, architects and user researchers, and the capability framework sets out each role and the skills needed at every level. The Government Digital Service (GDS) builds GOV.UK and GOV.UK One Login and recruits across these professions.
points.note: The framework was previously called the Digital, Data and Technology (DDaT) Profession Capability Framework and now sits on a new web address under a new name. GDS has moved into the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport; some GDS pages still name its former department.

points.text: Roles are assessed against up to five elements: behaviours, strengths, ability, experience and technical skills. Not every role uses all five; the job advert tells you which ones apply and how each will be tested.
points.note: The hub's Recognition section maps contributions to Success Profiles behaviours. The GOV.UK candidate overview gives the same wording for 'technical' as for behaviours; Civil Service Careers defines technical as the demonstration of specific professional skills, knowledge or qualifications.

points.heading: Write behaviour examples with the STAR method
points.text: When an advert asks for behaviour examples, describe a real situation, what you did and how, and the result: official guidance suggests the STAR method (situation, task, action, result). Examples can come from work, volunteering or a hobby, and the online form cuts off anything over 250 words per example.
points.note: Do not assume the panel knows your context: spell out how the example shows the behaviour being assessed.

points.heading: CVs and personal statements: match the essential criteria
points.text: Your CV and personal statement are scored against the essential criteria in the advert, so only include what is relevant. Use specific examples with facts and figures, stay within the word limit, and you may be asked to remove details such as your name, age or gender so the sift is anonymous.
points.note: Anonymised (name-blind) CVs are used by some recruiters, not all; the advert or form will say. Work history can include volunteering and work experience.

points.heading: The sift: aim for at least 4 out of 7 on each example
points.text: A sift panel reads and scores your written evidence before deciding who to interview. Many organisations use a seven-point scale, and you generally need at least 4, 'acceptable demonstration', for each example to go further.
points.note: Feedback is not usually available at sift stage. The same example can pass one sift and fail another, because each vacancy is a separate competition.

sources.title: GOV.UK (Government Recruitment Service and Civil Service Resourcing): Using the Civil Service Jobs website as a candidate (updated 27 January 2026)

points.heading: Online tests: practise first with the free official versions
points.text: You may be asked to take one or more online tests, such as verbal, numerical or judgement tests; the advert says which. Free practice tests are available on GOV.UK, no specialist knowledge is needed, and your answers must be your own.
points.note: GOV.UK lists eight tests after adding the Civil Service Styles Assessment in January 2026; the Civil Service Careers page still lists seven.

sources.title: GOV.UK (Civil Service Resourcing): Civil Service online tests (updated 27 January 2026)
Civil Service Careers: Assessments and interviews (undated page, read 29 October 2026)

points.heading: Use AI to prepare, never to answer for you
points.text: You can use AI tools to research a department, check spelling or practise interview questions. You must not use them to invent experience or to complete tests and live assessments, and applications can be rejected or withdrawn if you do.

sources.title: Civil Service Careers: A candidate's guide to artificial intelligence (AI) in recruitment (undated page, read 29 October 2026)
Civil Service Careers: Fast Stream guidance on the use of generative AI (undated page, read 29 October 2026)

points.heading: By law, appointments are on merit after fair and open competition
points.text: The Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010 requires Civil Service appointments to be made on merit after fair and open competition, and the independent Civil Service Commission sets the rules departments must follow. If you think a department has broken them, you can complain first to the department and then to the Commission.
points.note: The Commission cannot re-score a competition or rule on feedback, security vetting or internal promotions.

sources.title: Civil Service Commission: Recruitment Principles 2018 (in force; PDF re-issued in new branding 17 March 2026)
Civil Service Commission: Recruitment (last updated August 2026)

points.heading: When roles can be filled without open competition
points.text: The Recruitment Principles allow ten exceptions, including short temporary appointments, secondments, highly specialist skills and government employment programmes. Exceptions are meant to be rare, and senior or higher-paid appointments need the Commission's prior approval.
points.note: Temporary or programme appointees at junior grades can sometimes be made permanent after 12 months.

sources.title: Civil Service Commission: Exceptions (last updated August 2026)
Civil Service Commission: Recruitment Principles 2018 (in force; PDF re-issued in new branding 17 March 2026)

points.heading: Prepare real examples for behaviour questions
points.text: Before the interview, reread the job description and plan examples showing each behaviour listed. You can reuse examples from your application or choose stronger ones, and think about how you would handle similar situations in future. Interviews usually last 30 to 60 minutes.
points.note: Guidance gives slightly different lengths: GOV.UK says 30 to 60 minutes and Civil Service Careers says 45 to 60 minutes.

sources.title: GOV.UK (Government Recruitment Service and Civil Service Resourcing): Using the Civil Service Jobs website as a candidate (updated 27 January 2026)
Civil Service Careers: Assessments and interviews (undated page, read 29 October 2026)

points.heading: Strength questions: answer genuinely, do not rehearse
points.text: Strength questions ask what you enjoy and do well, and there are no right or wrong answers. The panel wants your first, honest response, so the best preparation is to reflect on your strengths and how you like to work rather than learning answers.
points.note: Strengths are not tied to grade, and you will never be expected to show every strength in the Civil Service Strengths Dictionary.

sources.title: Civil Service Careers: A guide to Civil Service Success Profiles (undated page, read 29 October 2026)
GOV.UK (Cabinet Office): Success Profiles, candidate overview (updated 29 January 2025)

points.heading: Technical interviews, presentations and exercises
points.text: For specialist roles, such as digital and data jobs, you may face technical questions, a presentation, a test or a work sample. The topic may be sent in advance or given on the day, and assessors usually ask follow-up questions about it.
points.note: Hiring managers can use the digital and data capability framework to write adverts and assess candidates at interview, so reading your role's page helps you see what level is expected.

points.heading: Video and pre-recorded interviews
points.text: Some interviews happen by video, either live or pre-recorded, where you record answers to questions shown on screen. Check your set-up beforehand and treat it with the same preparation as a face-to-face interview.
points.note: AI tools must not be used to produce answers during live or recorded interviews.

sources.title: Civil Service Careers: Assessments and interviews (undated page, read 29 October 2026)
GOV.UK (Cabinet Office): Success Profiles, candidate overview (updated 29 January 2025)

points.heading: Assessment centres combine several exercises
points.text: Some roles and schemes use an assessment centre with a mix of interview, presentation, written exercise or role play, lasting half a day or a full day. Your invitation explains what will happen; the Fast Stream's virtual centre includes a written advice exercise and a stakeholder exercise.
points.note: Ask for reasonable adjustments early if you need them, for example extra time or materials in another format.

points.heading: Bring your own questions: the interview works both ways
points.text: Use the interview to find out whether the team and organisation suit you, for example about the work, ways of working or development. Before applying, you can also contact the person named on the advert with questions about the job.

points.heading: Always ask for feedback, whatever the outcome
points.text: After the final stage you will be told the outcome, and you are encouraged to ask for feedback even if you are successful. Test feedback is available in your Civil Service Jobs account.
points.note: Feedback is generally not available at the sift stage.

sources.title: Civil Service Careers: Assessments and interviews (undated page, read 29 October 2026)

points.heading: Reserve lists: a near miss can still lead to a job
points.text: Panels rank appointable candidates in order of merit. If there are more good candidates than jobs, you can be placed on a reserve list and offered the same or a similar role for up to 12 months without being tested again.
points.note: Being on a reserve list is not a job offer; whether you are contacted depends on vacancies arising.

points.heading: Start with the vacancy's own identifiers: reference, department, grade
points.text: Record the vacancy reference number, the job title, the recruiting organisation, the grade and the closing date for every application. Grades are not identical across departments, so note the grade exactly as the advert words it. You can only apply once for each vacancy, so a clear record also stops you starting a duplicate application.
points.note: Grade names such as AO, EO, HEO, SEO, Grade 7 and Grade 6 are a guide only; each organisation may use its own structure.

points.heading: Save the advert and the exact version you submitted
points.text: Adverts are often taken down after they close, and you cannot change an application once it is submitted. Save a copy of the advert, the job description and the exact text, CV or statement you sent, and note which version went where. You will need them to prepare for interview and to reuse good material later.

points.heading: Note which Success Profiles elements each stage assesses
points.text: The Civil Service recruits using Success Profiles, which has five elements: Behaviours, Strengths, Ability, Experience and Technical. Each advert chooses which elements it assesses and at which stage, and behaviours are pitched at the grade of the role. Write down the elements and behaviours named in the advert so you can match your examples and your feedback to them.

points.heading: Log every stage, its date and its result
points.text: A campaign can include a sift, online tests, an interview, a presentation or an assessment centre, and not every campaign uses all of them. For each stage record the date you were invited, the date it took place, any score you were given and the outcome. A significant number of organisations use the Civil Service rating scale of 1 to 7, and generally a score of at least 4 is needed to progress.
points.note: Rating scales can vary between recruiting organisations; check the advert or your results email.

points.heading: If you are put on a reserve list, record the date and when it ends
points.text: When a panel finds more appointable candidates than jobs, it can hold the others on a reserve list and offer them the same or a similar role later without testing them again. Reserve lists last up to 12 months, so note the date you were told and the date the list will expire. A reserve list place is not a job offer.
points.note: Whether you are contacted depends on vacancies arising during the life of the list.

sources.title: Civil Service Commission: Recruitment Principles 2018 (in force; PDF re-issued in new branding 17 March 2026)

points.heading: Track the offer, each pre-employment check and the start date
points.text: A successful candidate first receives a provisional offer, and a formal offer only follows once pre-employment checks are complete. Record the date of the provisional offer, the documents you sent and when, each check and its outcome, the date of the formal offer and the agreed start date. The checks can take several weeks.
points.note: Higher security clearances add time; see the deadlines section.

sources.title: GOV.UK (Government Recruitment Service and Civil Service Resourcing): Using the Civil Service Jobs website as a candidate (updated 27 January 2026)
Scottish Government: Recruitment candidate guide, Pre-employment checks (last updated 31 August 2026)

points.heading: Use the Applications page in your Civil Service Jobs account
points.text: If you applied on the Civil Service Jobs site itself, you can follow the application from the Applications page of your account and open each job for more detail. Online test feedback is also held in your account. If your contact email changes after you apply, update it once in Account details and it carries through to your submitted applications.

sources.title: GOV.UK (Government Recruitment Service and Civil Service Resourcing): Using the Civil Service Jobs website as a candidate (updated 27 January 2026)
GOV.UK (Civil Service Resourcing): Civil Service online tests (updated 27 January 2026)

points.heading: Keep your own record for anything applied for elsewhere
points.text: Some organisations take applications on their own websites or by email, and those applications do not appear in your Civil Service Jobs account. Formal offers from those organisations are not shown there either. Your own record is the only place where every application sits together.

sources.title: GOV.UK (Government Recruitment Service and Civil Service Resourcing): Using the Civil Service Jobs website as a candidate (updated 27 January 2026)
Lancaster University Management School Careers: Managing your job search (12 February 2024)

points.heading: Let job alerts bring vacancies to you, and pause them when needed
points.text: Civil Service Jobs can email you new vacancies that match saved search criteria, as often as you choose. You can pause, restart, edit or delete alerts, or run a search from an alert. Closing your account withdraws applications in progress and stops alerts, so save copies of past applications first.
points.figure: First alert may arrive within 24 hours (daily setting)

points.heading: A spreadsheet tracker: one row per application
points.text: A spreadsheet with one row per application is a simple way to see everything at once: role, organisation, location, link, date applied, closing date, stage and status. University careers blogs suggest adding follow-up reminders and protecting the file with a password, because it holds personal information. Any spreadsheet program works; the hub endorses none.

points.heading: Calendar reminders and a task list for the steps in between
points.text: Put every closing date, test window, interview and document deadline in a calendar with a reminder. A short to-do list that breaks each application into smaller steps can help: the NHS says breaking tasks into manageable chunks and planning ahead can help relieve stress.

sources.title: GOV.UK (Cabinet Office): Success Profiles, candidate overview (updated 29 January 2025)
NHS Every Mind Matters: Stress (undated page, read 30 October 2026)

points.heading: One folder for adverts, applications and letters
points.text: Keep one main folder with subfolders for job descriptions, application materials, unfinished applications, offers and rejection emails. Name each file with the vacancy reference, title and organisation so it matches your tracker. If you claim Jobseeker's Allowance, the same record helps you show your work coach your applications and interviews.

points.heading: Closing times: often 23:55 on the closing date
points.text: Guidance for departments that publish adverts on Civil Service Jobs tells them to use 23:55 as the closing time, so many adverts close five minutes before midnight. Do not plan to submit in the last hour; check the closing date and time shown on the advert itself. If you need adjustments, contact the advert's named contact well before the closing date.
points.note: This rests on one source, GOV.UK (Civil Service Resourcing), guidance for advert-only departments last updated in June 2022; the advert's own closing time always takes precedence.

points.heading: Sift and interview dates vary by campaign
points.text: There is no standard time between the closing date and the sift result, or between sift and interview. The recruiting organisation tells you what to expect at each stage, and interviews usually last 30 to 60 minutes. Record the dates you are given so you can see when a stage is overdue and ask the named contact.

Civil Service Careers: About the application process (undated page, read 29 October 2026)

points.heading: Online tests have their own completion window
points.text: If you are invited to take an online test, you will be sent an email invitation with instructions, and it will usually say how many days you have to complete it. The test may be timed, so choose a time when you can give it your full attention. Put the window's last day in your calendar as soon as the email arrives.

sources.title: GOV.UK (Cabinet Office): Success Profiles, candidate overview (updated 29 January 2025)
GOV.UK (Civil Service Resourcing): Civil Service online tests (updated 27 January 2026)

points.heading: Reserve lists last up to 12 months
points.text: The Recruitment Principles allow a reserve list to be used for up to 12 months. The Scottish Government says its reserve lists typically operate for a maximum of one year and that candidates are contacted if a suitable post arises. Note the expiry date in your tracker.

points.heading: Pre-employment checks: several weeks, longer with vetting
points.text: Baseline checks can take several weeks, and roles needing national security vetting can take longer. United Kingdom Security Vetting says every clearance application is unique, its checks involve several agencies, and it cannot give exact timescales. Both GOV.UK and the vetting guidance say not to hand in your notice until you have a formal offer or a decision.
points.note: No official source publishes a standard number of days for checks or clearance; any figure you see elsewhere should be read as indicative.

points.heading: Notice periods: check your contract before you resign
points.text: Your contract or written statement sets the notice you must give your current employer. By law the minimum is one week once you have worked there for at least a month, but many contracts require more. Record your notice period so you can agree a realistic start date. This is general information, not legal advice.
points.note: Acas can advise on exceptions to the statutory minimum.

sources.title: GOV.UK: Handing in your notice, Giving notice (undated page, read 30 October 2026)
Acas: Notice when resigning (last updated 24 November 2025)

points.heading: Complaints about fair recruitment: within 12 months of closing
points.text: If you believe a department broke the Recruitment Principles, complain to the department first, following the steps in the advert. You can then take it to the Civil Service Commission, which expects complaints within 12 months of the closing date for applications. Keeping dated records makes this possible. This is general information, not legal advice.
points.note: The Commission may consider a complaint lodged after 12 months in exceptional circumstances. It does not re-score competitions and does not consider feedback, pre-employment checks or vetting, or internal promotions.

Civil Service Commission: Recruitment (last updated August 2026)

points.heading: Ask for feedback whatever the outcome
points.text: Civil Service Careers encourages every candidate to ask for feedback after the final stage, whether or not they were successful. Careers services say the same for any interview. Note in your tracker when you asked, who you asked and when it arrived.

points.heading: Know what feedback to expect at each stage
points.text: Feedback is generally not available after the sift, though some organisations give comments against the rating scale. Online test feedback appears in your Civil Service Jobs account, with a report for the Judgement Test and Styles Assessment. The guidance sets no deadline for asking, so ask promptly.
points.note: The Civil Service Commission does not consider complaints about the provision of feedback.

points.text: Write feedback down against the element or behaviour it refers to and, where given, the score on the 1 to 7 scale. Over several campaigns this shows which behaviours you score well on and which need stronger examples. Success Profiles is designed in part to give candidates standardised feedback to support their development.

points.heading: Build a bank of STAR examples and reuse the best
points.text: Keep your examples in one document, each written in the STAR shape: situation, task, action and result, with the behaviour it shows and where you used it. You can use the same example at interview as in your application, or a better one. Update the bank after each round of feedback.

points.heading: Treat setbacks as information, and set small goals
points.text: Being unsuccessful is a normal part of a search, and it is normal to apply for several roles before getting an interview. Reflect on what happened, use the feedback, and set yourself small goals so you can see progress, celebrating your achievements as you go.

points.heading: Look after your wellbeing during a long search
points.text: Job problems are among the possible causes of stress. Talk to people you trust, keep active, and try slow breathing before an interview. A low mood that lasts longer than about two weeks may be a sign of depression; if low mood or stress is affecting your daily life, call NHS 111 or talk to a GP. In England you can refer yourself to NHS talking therapies.
points.note: If you feel unable to cope or keep yourself safe, get urgent help straight away.

points.heading: You do not have to do it alone
points.text: Careers advisers, mentors, a manager or HR, or a Jobcentre Plus work coach if you are not in work, can help after a setback. Careers services such as the National Careers Service in England and Careers Wales offer advice on applications and interviews.

points.heading: No typical day: what digital and early careers staff describe
points.text: One GDS developer described a day that starts with a stand-up, then coding, code reviews, planning and meetings, some of them for staff clubs or networks. Fast streamers describe moving between departments and roles and taking on responsibility early.
points.note: The GDS developer accounts date from 2021, during pandemic remote working, so office patterns have since changed. These are individual experiences, not a standard day.

points.heading: Hybrid working: at least 60% of your time in the office
points.text: Most civil servants are expected to spend at least 60% of their time in a government building or on official business, with senior managers expected to do more. Within that, many roles offer flexible patterns such as part-time, compressed hours and job sharing.
points.note: Not every department can meet the rule because of office space, and the FDA union says most of its surveyed members think the mandate has not worked. Check each advert, as some roles differ.

points.heading: Pension: alpha, a career average defined benefit scheme
points.text: New joiners usually join alpha, which adds 2.32% of your pensionable pay to your pension each year, increased in line with inflation. Your own contributions depend on your pay band, starting at 4.6% on earnings up to £36,199 in 2026-27.
points.note: Contribution rates are reviewed each year, so check the current rates. A defined contribution option called Partnership is also available.

points.heading: Annual leave usually starts at 25 days and rises to 30
points.text: Many departments give 25 days' annual leave on joining, rising to 30 with length of service, plus public and privilege holidays. How quickly it rises differs between departments.
points.note: There is no single Civil Service rule here: GDS adds a day each year, while the Valuation Office Agency reaches 30 days after five years.

points.heading: Learning: at least 5 days a year, plus Civil Service Learning
points.text: Every civil servant is guaranteed five days a year for learning and development, with courses on Civil Service Learning, coaching, job shadowing and professional qualifications. Some organisations offer more, such as 10 days and a personal training budget at GDS.

points.heading: One Big Thing: a yearly learning push for every civil servant
points.text: One Big Thing is a shared learning activity that every civil servant is asked to join each year. The 2025 edition, 'AI for All', ran from October 2025 to February 2026 and covered using AI safely and responsibly at work.

points.heading: Staff networks and the Civil Service Race Champion
points.text: Departments have volunteer staff networks for wellbeing, equality and professions, and there are more than 20 cross-government networks for people from under-represented groups. The Civil Service also has a Race Champion, who marked Black History Month 2025 by setting out progress on representation.
points.note: The Race Champion role was held by the Civil Service Chief Operating Officer, Cat Little, in October 2025.

points.heading: Nationality rules decide which jobs you can apply for
points.text: UK nationals can apply for any Civil Service job, and about three quarters of posts are also open to Commonwealth and European Economic Area nationals. The rest, which need special allegiance to the state, are reserved for UK nationals; each advert states who is eligible.
points.note: The hub's circumstances section covers this in detail. Rules for European Economic Area nationals changed from 1 January 2021, so check the full rules and the advert for your own case.

points.heading: Baseline Personnel Security Standard (BPSS): four checks
points.text: Everyone joining government goes through the Baseline Personnel Security Standard: identity, right to work, employment history and unspent criminal convictions. Your employment, study or other activity is usually checked for at least the last three years.
points.note: Gaps of six months or more in the last three years need references or evidence, so keep records of study, caring or time abroad.

points.heading: Some roles need security clearance: CTC, SC or DV
points.text: Roles with regular access to sensitive information need national security vetting on top of BPSS. Security Check (SC) covers regular access to SECRET material and Developed Vetting (DV) covers TOP SECRET; both include criminal record, credit and Security Service checks, and DV adds an interview.
points.note: Clearance can add weeks or months before you start; the Summer Internship Programme warns SC can take up to 3 months.

points.heading: Clearance usually needs years of UK residence
points.text: Vetting normally expects a minimum period living in the UK: 3 years for CTC, 5 years for SC and 10 years for DV. If you have lived abroad, it may still be possible, but check with the recruiter before you apply.
points.note: These are 'normal' expectations set out in departmental candidate guidance, not fixed legal bars: the Home Office says a lack of UK residency is not necessarily a bar to clearance. UK Security Vetting says only that UK residency may affect the checks carried out.

points.heading: Prove your right to work before your first day
points.text: You must prove your right to work in the UK before you start. British and Irish citizens can use a passport (current or expired); other people can use a share code or eligible immigration documents.
points.note: If you are a Commonwealth citizen without documents, you may be able to get them through the Windrush Scheme.

points.heading: Do not resign until you have a formal offer
points.text: Successful candidates first get a provisional offer, which becomes formal only when all pre-employment checks are complete. These checks can take several weeks, so keep your current job until the formal offer arrives.
points.note: Secondees go through the same checks as any new joiner.

points.heading: Probation: a settling-in period for new joiners
points.text: New joiners usually serve a probation period to show their conduct, performance and attendance are suitable. Length varies between organisations (six months at the Food Standards Agency, for example) and should not usually be more than two years.
points.note: Check your contract for the length that applies to you.

points.heading: Who can work in the Civil Service: the nationality rules
points.text: The Civil Service Nationality Rules decide who can be employed. In general you are eligible if you are a UK, Irish or Commonwealth national with the right to work in the UK, and certain EU, EEA, Swiss and Turkish nationals are eligible too. Having a visa that lets you work is not enough on its own: your nationality must also fit the rules.
points.note: Stateless people are not eligible under the rules. The rules apply across the whole Civil Service, not just the Fast Stream. This is general information, not immigration advice. Always check the job advert and the current Home Office rules on GOV.UK, and get advice from a solicitor or an adviser regulated by the Immigration Advice Authority if your situation is not straightforward.

points.heading: Some posts are reserved for UK nationals only
points.text: A small number of sensitive posts are 'reserved' and open only to UK nationals. All posts in the Security Service, the Secret Intelligence Service and GCHQ are reserved, and so are posts in the Diplomatic Service and the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office unless a minister decides otherwise. Some schemes are also open to British citizens only, so read each scheme's page.
points.note: Other departments can reserve particular posts where a minister decides special allegiance to the Crown is needed. The job advert will say if a post is reserved.

points.heading: EU, EEA and Swiss nationals and the EU Settlement Scheme
points.text: Since free movement ended on 31 December 2020, most EU, EEA and Swiss nationals can work in non-reserved Civil Service posts if they have settled or pre-settled status, or a valid pending application, under the EU Settlement Scheme. Irish citizens do not need this status, and some people qualify in other ways, for example as Commonwealth citizens or with leave to remain if they were eligible for the scheme by 31 December 2020. You will be asked for evidence of your status before you start. Some people can still apply to the scheme late if they have reasonable grounds.
points.note: The deadline for most people to apply to the EU Settlement Scheme was 30 June 2021. Family members' eligibility depends on their own status. This is general information, not immigration advice. Always check the job advert and the current Home Office rules on GOV.UK, and get advice from a solicitor or an adviser regulated by the Immigration Advice Authority if your situation is not straightforward.

points.heading: Visa sponsorship is possible but limited by salary thresholds
points.text: Departments can sponsor Skilled Worker visas, but the job must be at an eligible skill level and usually pay at least £41,700 a year or the going rate for the role, whichever is higher. Entry-level salaries are often below this, and the Fast Stream starting salary does not meet the threshold for new sponsorship. Adverts should say if a role is not open to sponsorship, and sponsorship is only considered after a job offer.
points.note: Salary thresholds and eligible occupations change often; lower rates can apply in some cases, such as some extensions. A certificate of sponsorship does not guarantee a visa. Your nationality must still meet the Civil Service Nationality Rules. This is general information, not immigration advice. Always check the job advert and the current Home Office rules on GOV.UK, and get advice from a solicitor or an adviser regulated by the Immigration Advice Authority if your situation is not straightforward.

points.heading: Which departments hold a sponsor licence
points.text: The Home Office register of licensed sponsors lists many government bodies, including the Cabinet Office, HM Treasury, HM Revenue and Customs, the Department for Business and Trade, the Department for Culture, Media and Sport, the Department for Education, the Department for Transport, the Department for Work and Pensions, the Department of Health and Social Care, the Ministry of Justice and the Office for National Statistics. The Scottish Government, Welsh Government and Northern Ireland Civil Service are listed too. A licence only means a body can sponsor: it does not mean any particular vacancy offers sponsorship.
points.note: The register is updated almost daily and lists each organisation under its own licence name, so a department not shown here may still hold a licence, possibly under a different name. Always go by the advert. This is general information, not immigration advice. Always check the job advert and the current Home Office rules on GOV.UK, and get advice from a solicitor or an adviser regulated by the Immigration Advice Authority if your situation is not straightforward.

points.heading: Graduate visas, dependants and proving your right to work
points.text: A Graduate visa lets you work in most jobs, but for a Civil Service role your nationality must still meet the nationality rules. Graduate visas last 2 years if you apply on or before 31 December 2026 and 18 months if you apply from 1 January 2027 (3 years for a PhD). Every new starter must prove their right to work before starting, and it is one of the four baseline security checks.
points.note: The Graduate visa length is changing on 1 January 2027. Partners and children may be able to join or stay with a Skilled Worker as dependants, with stricter rules for some 'medium skilled' jobs. You cannot extend a Graduate visa, but you may be able to switch to another visa. This is general information, not immigration advice. Always check the job advert and the current Home Office rules on GOV.UK, and get advice from a solicitor or an adviser regulated by the Immigration Advice Authority if your situation is not straightforward.

points.heading: Where to get regulated immigration advice
points.text: If you need help with your own immigration situation, use a solicitor or an adviser registered with the Immigration Advice Authority. It was previously called the Office of the Immigration Services Commissioner (OISC) and is sponsored by the Home Office. Check an adviser is registered, and whether they charge, before you use them.
points.note: You cannot get your money back if an adviser is not regulated. Solicitors who give immigration advice can be found through the Law Society in England and Wales, the Law Society of Scotland or the Law Society of Northern Ireland.

points.heading: You can ask for flexible working from your first day
points.text: Every employee can make a statutory request for flexible working from day one, covering hours, times, days and where you work. You can make up to two requests in 12 months, and your employer must consult you before refusing and normally decide within two months. An employer can still refuse for a good business reason.
points.note: These rights come from the Employment Relations (Flexible Working) Act 2023 and the Flexible Working (Amendment) Regulations 2023. The Employment Rights Act 2025 makes further changes to how employers must handle requests; check GOV.UK and Acas for when they apply.

points.heading: Part-time work and job shares in the Civil Service
points.text: The Civil Service says it promotes all forms of flexible working, including part-time work and job sharing, where two people share one full-time role. Job shares exist right up to Director General level. Adverts say which working patterns a role can offer, so check before you apply.
points.note: Flexible working is offered 'where we can', so what is possible depends on the role. Office attendance expectations differ between departments and are set out in adverts.

points.heading: Maternity, adoption and shared parental leave
points.text: By law you can take up to 52 weeks of maternity or adoption leave, and parents can share up to 50 weeks of leave and 37 weeks of pay through Shared Parental Leave. As a civil servant you may have statutory maternity pay topped up to full pay for the first 26 weeks, and more in some departments. Shared parental pay can also be topped up to full pay, subject to conditions.
points.note: Statutory maternity pay is not a day-one right, and full pay depends on meeting your department's conditions. Check your department's own policy.

points.heading: Partners can take paternity leave from day one
points.text: Paternity leave is available from your first day of employment, although statutory paternity pay still needs 26 weeks' service. Most civil servants get full pay while on paternity leave. If your baby is born on or after 6 April 2026, you can take paternity leave before or after shared parental leave.
points.note: Check your department's paternity leave policy for the exact pay you will get.

points.heading: Carer's leave: one week a year from your first day
points.text: If someone depends on you for long-term care, you can take up to one week of unpaid carer's leave every 12 months, from your first day in a job. You can take it as a whole week, single days or half days, and you do not need to give evidence of the person's care needs. The dependant does not have to be a family member.
points.note: Carer's leave is unpaid by law; some employers offer more. It is separate from parental leave.

points.heading: Tax-Free Childcare: £2 for every £8 you pay
points.text: If you are working, Tax-Free Childcare adds £2 for every £8 you pay into a childcare account, up to £500 every 3 months (£2,000 a year) per child. It is up to £4,000 a year if your child is disabled. Your child must usually be 11 or under (16 or under if disabled) and your provider must be signed up.
points.note: You must reconfirm your details every 3 months. Other childcare support, such as free hours, has its own rules.

points.heading: A returnship pilot for software developers
points.text: In 2026 the government began piloting a paid 18-month returnship for senior software developers who had been away from work for 18 months or more. The Government Digital Service offered placements in the Home Office and the Ministry of Justice. Applications for the pilot closed on 13 May 2026, and the approach could be expanded if the pilot succeeds.
points.note: This is a pilot, not a permanent scheme. The length, seniority and closing date come from one source, the advert as republished by Manchester Digital. Watch Civil Service Jobs for any future returner opportunities.

points.heading: Experience from outside paid work counts
points.text: The Civil Service recruits using Success Profiles, which look at behaviours, strengths, ability, experience and technical skills. Skills gained through voluntary work or hobbies, such as teamwork or communication, can show the experience a role needs, so time away from paid work can still provide good evidence. Only the elements relevant to the role are assessed.
points.note: Each advert lists the behaviours and other elements it will assess; read it closely.

points.heading: Age is not a barrier
points.text: Age is a protected characteristic under the Equality Act 2010, and age discrimination can happen to people of any age. There is no default retirement age for most jobs, and the Civil Service says you can apply for the Fast Stream at any age.
points.note: A small number of jobs can have a compulsory retirement age if the employer can justify it.

points.heading: Changing career: no government background needed
points.text: You do not need to have worked in government before. Many roles need skills you may already have, such as project management, finance, data, digital and people management, and the Civil Service offers mid-career apprenticeships and professional qualifications in areas such as commercial, digital and finance. Apprenticeships run from level 2 to level 7.
points.note: Apprenticeships are paid jobs; in England at least 20% of normal working hours is spent on training.

points.heading: Great Place to Work for Veterans: get through to the next stage
points.text: If you opt into the Great Place to Work for Veterans scheme and meet the minimum criteria, you progress to the next stage for most Civil Service vacancies, usually an interview or online test. You opt in on Civil Service Jobs by confirming you served in the armed forces. Appointments are still made on merit.
points.note: The scheme began in 2020 as a guaranteed interview for veterans and now runs as Great Place to Work for Veterans. It covers most, not all, vacancies.

points.heading: Going Forward into Employment for veterans and military partners
points.text: Going Forward into Employment runs a life chance pathway for veterans, service leavers and military spouses and partners, with simplified applications and support once you start. Over the last three years it has helped more than 180 veterans and military spouses or partners into Civil Service careers. Service leavers can see its vacancies through the Career Transition Partnership.
points.note: Spouses and partners of serving personnel, or of someone who left the forces in the last 12 months, can usually apply.

points.heading: The Career Transition Partnership helps you plan the move
points.text: The Career Transition Partnership is the Ministry of Defence's resettlement programme. It offers workshops, training, one-to-one guidance, employer events and a jobs portal, tailored to how long you served. In most cases you can use it from 2 years before discharge until 2 years after.
points.note: Official pages currently name different delivery partners for the programme, so check the Career Transition Partnership website for the latest details.

points.heading: The Office for Veterans' Affairs and the Armed Forces Covenant
points.text: The Office for Veterans' Affairs leads government work to support veterans and is now part of the Ministry of Defence. The Armed Forces Covenant is a promise that people who serve or have served, and their families, are treated fairly. In law, certain public bodies must have due regard to the principles of the Covenant when carrying out some housing, education and healthcare functions.
points.note: The Covenant's legal duty covers housing, education and healthcare functions; it does not create a right to a job. VALOUR is the UK-wide veteran support system for wider help.

points.heading: Going Forward into Employment started with prison leavers
points.text: Going Forward into Employment began in 2018 to help prison leavers into Civil Service jobs and now covers several groups facing barriers to work. Its roles are real, ring-fenced jobs with simplified applications and support for you and your manager, and most are outside London. The Civil Service welcomes applications from recent prison leavers and people with unspent convictions.
points.note: The same page also gives a figure of over 3,050, so treat the total as approximate. Some offences, including life sentences, arson, sexual offences and hate and terror offences, are currently exceptions, and departments may weigh an offence against the role.

points.heading: 'Ban the Box': no conviction questions at the first stage
points.text: Many Civil Service departments do not ask about criminal convictions on the application form. The Civil Service says it only asks about convictions once a job offer is made and accepted, so your application is judged alongside everyone else's. This approach dates from February 2016.
points.note: The source says 'many' departments, not all. Roles with specific security requirements, such as prison officers, can be exempt, and roles working with children or vulnerable people still require certain disclosures. This is general information, not legal advice. Rules differ in Scotland and Northern Ireland. Use the GOV.UK checker or a specialist charity such as Unlock or Nacro to check whether your conviction is spent before you disclose.

points.heading: Spent convictions under the Rehabilitation of Offenders Act 1974
points.text: Most convictions and cautions become 'spent' after a set time, which can be months, years or immediately. Once spent, you are treated as if the offence had never been committed and you usually do not have to disclose it unless the role needs a standard or enhanced DBS check. You only need to tell an employer about an unspent conviction if they ask.
points.note: This is general information, not legal advice. Rules differ in Scotland and Northern Ireland. Use the GOV.UK checker or a specialist charity such as Unlock or Nacro to check whether your conviction is spent before you disclose.

points.heading: Security checks: unspent convictions are judged case by case
points.text: After you accept a provisional offer, the Baseline Personnel Security Standard checks your identity, right to work, employment history and unspent convictions. Its policy is that a criminal conviction should not be an automatic barrier to employment. Departments look at factors such as how relevant the offence is to the role, how long ago it was and how serious it was.
points.note: A conviction for fraud, for example, may rule you out of a finance role. Some posts need higher national security vetting. This is general information, not legal advice. Rules differ in Scotland and Northern Ireland. Use the GOV.UK checker or a specialist charity such as Unlock or Nacro to check whether your conviction is spent before you disclose.

points.heading: New Futures Network links prisons with employers
points.text: The New Futures Network is a specialist part of HM Prison and Probation Service that brokers partnerships between prisons and employers in England and Wales. If you are still in prison or recently released, ask your prison employment lead or probation practitioner about the opportunities it brokers.
points.year: People released from prison each year (approx.)
points.note: The network covers England and Wales only.

points.heading: Care Leavers Internship Scheme
points.text: Care leavers aged 18 to 30 can apply for a paid 18-month internship in a government department or agency, run by the Department for Education. No qualifications are required and you are paid the same as other civil servants. After the first 12 months you may be made permanent, depending on your performance and the department's headcount and funding. More than 880 care leavers have been offered roles, and around 80% were made permanent.
points.note: The 2026 campaign has closed; in 2026 the advert ran from 8 to 31 May. You must be entitled to a leaving care package (including at least 13 weeks in care, some of it after your 16th birthday) and meet the nationality rules.

points.heading: Refugees: eligibility depends on your nationality
points.text: Being a refugee does not automatically remove your nationality, so your eligibility depends on your nationality in the normal way. You will be asked to confirm in writing whether your nationality was taken away or renounced, and departments should not contact your country's embassy. People who are stateless are not eligible under the current rules.
points.note: Asylum seekers are only eligible if they meet the nationality rules and have been given permission to work. This rests on one source, the Civil Service Nationality Rules. It is general information, not immigration advice: check the job advert and the current Home Office rules on GOV.UK, and get advice from a solicitor or an adviser regulated by the Immigration Advice Authority if your situation is not straightforward.

points.heading: Disability Confident: an interview if you meet the minimum criteria
points.text: The Civil Service runs the Disability Confident scheme, offering an interview to a fair and proportionate number of disabled applicants who meet the minimum criteria for the job. To qualify you must have a condition with a substantial and long-term adverse effect on day-to-day activities, and show you meet the minimum criteria in the advert. It does not mean every disabled applicant gets an interview.
points.note: Employers may limit interview numbers in high-volume campaigns. You can ask for adjustments even if you do not use the scheme.

points.heading: Adjustments at every stage, Access to Work and the passport
points.text: You can ask for adjustments at any stage, such as extra time in tests, questions in writing or a sign language interpreter, and you can raise them later in the process if you need to. Once in work, Access to Work can fund practical support, and a Workplace Adjustment Passport records what you and your manager have agreed, which helps if you change manager. Employers must make reasonable adjustments by law.
points.note: Adjustments can cover physical and mental health conditions. Access to Work has its own eligibility rules.
