points.heading: Qualifications from overseas: UK ENIC
points.text: UK ENIC (previously UK NARIC) is the official organisation for comparing international qualifications with UK ones. A Statement of Comparability shows how your qualification compares, which can help when an advert asks for a particular level. It is a chargeable service, and only some roles ask for formal qualifications.
points.note: UK ENIC is managed by Ecctis for the UK government; Home Office visa guidance also refers applicants to Ecctis. Check whether the advert actually needs a qualification before paying.

points.heading: Faith and religious observance are protected
points.text: Religion or belief, including having no religion, is a protected characteristic under the Equality Act 2010. Acas advises employers to be flexible about time for prayer and to consider requests for time off for religious festivals. You can raise your needs at offer stage or with your manager.
points.note: Employers do not have to provide a dedicated prayer room but should consider a suitable space. Agreed prayer time is usually made up, so total hours stay the same.

points.heading: More jobs outside London: Places for Growth
points.text: Places for Growth is moving Civil Service roles out of London. The government aims for 50% of UK-based senior civil servants and 50% of Fast Stream roles to be outside London by 2030, and plans to cut London-based posts by 12,000 by 2030.
points.note: These are targets, not guarantees. The share of senior civil servants based in London fell from 68% in 2020 to 61% in 2024.

points.heading: Early careers and routes without a degree
points.text: You can apply for a Civil Service apprenticeship from age 16, with levels from 2 to 7, and you can apply for vacancies on Civil Service Jobs at any time without joining a talent programme. The Summer Internship Programme is for university students from lower socio-economic backgrounds, and the Fast Stream is for graduates of any age. Some schemes, such as the Care Leavers Internship Scheme, ask for no qualifications at all.
points.note: Each advert sets its own essential criteria, so check whether a qualification is needed.

points.heading: Black African Fast Stream applicants: 14% of applicants, 0.3% success
points.text: In the 2026 Fast Stream competition, applicants from a Black or Black British – African background made up 14.0% of applications but 3.9% of those recommended for appointment, a success rate of 0.3% against 1.0% overall. The pattern has persisted: in 2025 the figures were 15.3% of applicants and 2.8% of appointments (0.2%).
points.note: Fast Stream is a graduate leadership scheme with about 1% overall success; figures are by first-preference application. Black Caribbean and Other Black counts were suppressed (fewer than five).

points.heading: Ethnic minority Fast Stream success is just over half the white rate
points.text: Ethnic minority applicants made up 43.0% of 2026 Fast Stream applications but 29.7% of those recommended for appointment: a success rate of 0.7%, against 1.3% for white applicants. The gap widened in 2024, when ethnic minority candidates were 36% of applicants but 22% of those recommended.
points.note: Base rate: 703 of 69,046 applications (1.0%) were recommended in 2026. The data does not show what causes the gap; in 2024 an Institute for Government researcher, quoted by Civil Service World, said it was unclear what was driving it.

points.heading: Black women are 1.8% of the UK workforce but 0.7% of IT professionals
points.text: BCS and Coding Black Females estimated that at least 20,000 more Black women would need to work in IT for them to be proportionately represented. In the accompanying survey, 67% of respondents from the Coding Black Females network said they faced more barriers to entering tech than women from other ethnicities. Asked what puts them off applying for IT roles, individual respondents mentioned degree requirements, more than three rounds of interviews and a lack of part-time or flexible options.
points.note: Workforce figures are BCS analysis of the ONS Labour Force Survey for 2021, published in October 2022. The survey heard from over 350 Black women working in tech, reached through the Coding Black Females network, so the 67% is indicative rather than representative. The comments on what puts people off applying are individual responses, not measured shares. This rests on one source, BCS.

sources.title: BCS: Thousands of black women 'missing' from the IT industry, report warns (27 October 2022)

points.heading: Black people are 3% of IT specialists; ethnic minority IT unemployment is nearly three times the white rate
points.text: BCS analysis of the Labour Force Survey shows that in 2023 Black, African, Caribbean and Black British people made up 3% of IT specialists, against 4% of all occupations. The unemployment rate for Black, Asian and minority ethnic IT specialists was 4.0%, against 1.4% for white IT specialists, which BCS describes as more than three times higher. Black, Asian and minority ethnic IT specialists were also more likely to hold a higher education qualification (88% against 71%).
points.note: From the published rounded rates the ratio is about 2.9. Taken together, Black, Asian and minority ethnic groups are over-represented in IT (21% of IT specialists), largely because of the high share of people of Indian ethnicity (9%), so the combined figure hides lower Black representation. The unemployment rate is not published separately for Black IT specialists.

points.heading: 61% of Black graduates felt their ethnicity disadvantaged them in job applications
points.text: In the Prospects Early Careers Survey 2024, 54% of graduates from ethnic minority backgrounds said they felt disadvantaged in the job application process because of their ethnicity, up from 43% in 2023. Among graduates from Black, African, Caribbean or Black British backgrounds the figure was 61%, up from 51%; among Asian or Asian British graduates it was 53%.
points.note: Perception data from a survey of 6,102 students and graduates in January and February 2024, published by Prospects at Jisc and reported by HRreview and ITV News. It measures how people felt, not measured discrimination. It is the most recent published breakdown by ethnicity found.

points.heading: Ethnic minority civil servants report more discrimination, every year
points.text: King's College London's analysis of People Survey data found ethnic minority civil servants reported higher bullying and discrimination than white peers in every year, with a consistent gap. In 2024, 11% of ethnic minority staff reported discrimination against 8% of white staff, and inclusion scores have diverged since 2018.
points.note: Rates for all groups have fallen since the pandemic; the KCL data only separates 'White' and 'Ethnic Minority', so Black staff cannot be isolated in that analysis.

points.heading: Hidden 'unwritten rules' and London tilt slow progression
points.text: The Social Mobility Commission found Civil Service progression depends on mastering unwritten rules and access to senior 'organisational guides', often formed on cultural similarity. It also found senior roles concentrated in London, and cumulative barriers for working-class staff who are also from ethnic minority communities.
points.note: Based on around 300,000 survey responses and over 100 interviews; focused on socio-economic background, with race treated as an intersecting factor. This rests on one source, Social Mobility Commission.

points.heading: Ethnic minority staff are least represented in the Senior Civil Service
points.text: Ethnic minority representation in the Civil Service reached a record 19.2% at 31 March 2026, but was lowest in the Senior Civil Service, at 10.6%. There were 26,655 Black civil servants, the second-largest ethnic minority group after Asian civil servants.
points.note: Percentages exclude people whose ethnicity is unknown or undeclared. The senior grade figure covers all ethnic minority groups combined, not Black staff alone. Source: Civil Service Statistics 2026, Cabinet Office, published 29 July 2026. This rests on one source, Cabinet Office (GOV.UK).

sources.title: Statistical bulletin: Civil Service Statistics 2026 (Cabinet Office)

points.heading: Equality law protects applicants, not only employees
points.text: In England, Scotland and Wales, section 39 of the Equality Act 2010 stops an employer discriminating against or victimising a job applicant in how it decides who to offer a job to, in the terms offered, or by not offering the job. Race includes colour, nationality and ethnic or national origin. A claim can be brought against a potential employer as well as a current one.
points.note: Northern Ireland is covered by separate laws, including the Race Relations (Northern Ireland) Order 1997; see the Northern Ireland points. This is general information, not legal advice.

points.heading: Ask the recruiting department first, using the steps in the advert
points.text: Raise the concern with the department or agency that ran the campaign, using the complaints steps set out in the job advert, and ask for feedback and for the reasons for decisions. The Civil Service Commission will not look at a complaint until the department has had the chance to respond and has given a final answer. Asking specific questions, such as what the panel noted, can help either to resolve the matter or to decide on next steps.
points.note: The Commission does not itself deal with the provision of feedback, so feedback requests go to the department.

points.heading: The Civil Service Commission: who can complain and when
points.text: The Commission regulates the legal requirement that people are selected for the Civil Service on merit through fair and open competition, and it publishes the Recruitment Principles. Anyone, including a member of the public, can complain that a department breached those Principles once the department's own process is finished. Its guide says it considers complaints about competitions concluded in the past 12 months, and those concluded more than a year earlier only in exceptional circumstances.
points.figure: 12 months from the end of the competition
points.year: Guide last updated 2017; web page current at 30 October 2026
points.note: The guide dates from January 2017; the web page and complaint form (March 2026) are newer, so check the current form before submitting. The Commission aims to complete investigations within 3 months.

points.heading: What the Commission cannot look at
points.text: The Commission does not deal with internal competitions and promotions, scores, feedback, pre-employment checks and vetting, or HR matters such as a withdrawn offer. It does not 'replay' competitions and will not usually act while the same matter is before an employment tribunal. It cannot hear complaints about most non-departmental public bodies or the wider public sector, whose staff are not civil servants.
points.note: Discrimination in any of these excluded areas can still be raised with the employer and, where the law allows, at an employment tribunal. A small number of Crown non-departmental public bodies employ civil servants and are covered.

points.heading: Most complaints to the Commission are out of scope
points.text: The Commission publishes the outcomes of recruitment complaints. Of 212 complaints in its 2024-25 table, 182 were recorded as out of scope, 13 were referred back to the department and 11 closed with no response from the complainant; of the few investigated, 3 found a breach and 3 found no breach. Complaints about scoring and reasonable adjustments were usually out of scope or sent back to the department.
points.figure: 182 of 212 out of scope; 3 breach, 3 no breach (2024-25)
points.note: Figures are counted from the published table (converted from PDF), not stated as totals by the Commission, so treat them as approximate. The base rate is that very few complaints reach a finding, which is why the departmental and legal routes matter.

points.heading: If a reasonable adjustment is refused
points.text: Employers have a legal duty to make reasonable adjustments for disabled applicants, for example to application forms, tests and interviews. In Civil Service recruitment, ask for adjustments when you apply and, if a need appears later, contact the named person in the job advert. If an adjustment is refused, complain to the department first; a refusal can also be raised at an employment tribunal.
points.note: The Commission's 2024-25 table shows reasonable adjustment complaints treated as out of scope or referred back to the department. Race and disability can overlap; both can be included in one complaint.

points.heading: Northern Ireland: a separate Civil Service and separate laws
points.text: The Northern Ireland Civil Service is outside the Great Britain Civil Service Commission's legal remit. The Civil Service Commissioners for Northern Ireland uphold the merit principle through their Recruitment Code and by auditing recruitment, and expect complaints to be handled promptly. Race discrimination in employment, including recruitment, is unlawful under Northern Ireland law and advice is available from the Equality Commission for Northern Ireland.
points.note: The Northern Ireland Commissioners' published role covers the Recruitment Code, audit and Code of Ethics appeals; it does not describe an individual recruitment complaints route, so use the complaints steps in the job advert. Advice is available from the Equality Commission for Northern Ireland and Advice NI. This is general information, not legal advice.

points.heading: Scotland and Wales: same Commission, own codes
points.text: The merit requirement and the Commission's complaints route cover the civil service of the State, which includes the Scottish Government and Welsh Government; only listed parts such as the security and intelligence agencies and the Northern Ireland Civil Service are excluded. Each government has its own version of the Civil Service Code. Acas offers its services in Welsh on request, and the same employment tribunal time limits apply across Great Britain, except for breach of contract claims in Scotland until 9 November 2026.
points.note: Councils, NHS bodies and most other public bodies are not civil service employers, so the Commission's route does not apply to them; their own complaints procedures and the tribunal route do. Breach of contract claims in Scotland follow a different time-limit timetable (change from 9 November 2026).

points.heading: Start informally where it is safe to do so
points.text: Acas and GOV.UK both advise trying to sort the problem out informally first, with your manager, HR or someone senior. Informal resolution is usually quicker, but it is not suitable for every situation, and you can go straight to a formal complaint if the matter is serious.
points.note: If the person involved is your manager, raise it with someone else in the management chain or HR.

points.heading: Use the department's grievance and anti-bullying procedures
points.text: If informal steps do not work, make a formal grievance in writing. Every employer should have a written grievance procedure, and your department may also have a specific policy on bullying, harassment and discrimination, which may set its own time limits. Follow that policy where there is one.
points.note: Departmental policies differ; check the intranet or HR for the current version.

points.heading: The Acas Code sets the minimum standard
points.text: The Acas Code of Practice on disciplinary and grievance procedures says grievances should be raised in writing without unreasonable delay, heard at a meeting, decided in writing and open to appeal. Workers have a legal right to be accompanied by a colleague or trade union representative. A tribunal can adjust an award by up to 25% if either side unreasonably fails to follow the Code.
points.note: The Code applies in Great Britain. Northern Ireland has its own Labour Relations Agency Code of Practice.

points.heading: Civil Service Code concerns: nominated officers, then the Commission
points.text: If you are asked to act against the Civil Service Code's values (integrity, honesty, objectivity, impartiality), raise it with your line management chain or your department's nominated officers, then with the Civil Service Commission if the response is unreasonable. Only serving civil servants can use this route. The Code does not cover HR management issues, so a discrimination grievance normally goes through the grievance route instead.
points.note: In Northern Ireland, the Civil Service Commissioners for Northern Ireland hear appeals under the NICS Code of Ethics.

points.heading: Whistleblowing covers public-interest wrongdoing, not grievances
points.text: Whistleblowing law protects workers who report wrongdoing in the public interest, such as a crime or a breach of a legal obligation. A personal grievance, including about how you were treated, is normally not covered unless your case is in the public interest. Since 6 April 2026, reporting sexual harassment counts as a qualifying disclosure.
points.note: Victimisation for making a discrimination complaint is covered by equality law instead (see the victimisation point).

points.heading: Trade unions can advise, accompany and represent
points.text: If you are a member, a trade union representative can advise you, help you write a complaint or questions, and go with you to grievance and appeal meetings.
points.note: What a union can offer depends on its membership terms; check with the union.

points.heading: Staff networks and employee assistance
points.text: Departmental diversity and race networks, and cross-government networks such as the Civil Service Race Forum, can offer support and a safe place for discussion, and can help you find the right route. They are not formal complaint routes and cannot decide a grievance. Your employer may also offer counselling or mental health support through an employee assistance programme.
points.note: The Civil Service Race Forum description comes from a 2019 Civil Service blog post; check current network and race champion arrangements in your department.

points.heading: Protection from victimisation and third-party harassment
points.text: It is unlawful to treat someone badly because they made, supported or gave evidence about a discrimination complaint in good faith. From 30 October 2026, employers in Great Britain can also be liable for harassment of their staff by third parties, such as members of the public, unless they took all reasonable steps to prevent it.
points.note: The third-party harassment duty was brought into force on 30 October 2026 by S.I. 2026/1065, which commences section 21 of the Employment Rights Act 2025. The revised Equality Act text on legislation.gov.uk may not yet show the new wording. It applies in Great Britain only. This is general information, not legal advice.

points.heading: Acas early conciliation comes before most tribunal claims
points.text: In Great Britain you must notify Acas before making most employment tribunal claims. Acas offers voluntary early conciliation, which can last up to 12 weeks, and the tribunal time limit is put on hold while it runs. If it does not settle the matter, Acas issues a certificate whose number goes on the claim form; if you notified Acas within your time limit, you have at least 1 month from receiving the certificate to claim.
points.figure: Up to 12 weeks; at least 1 month after the certificate
points.note: Acas says early conciliation is very busy and can take around 9 weeks to start, so notify early. Interim relief claims after dismissal have a 7-day limit and may not need notification.

points.heading: Tribunal time limit: now 6 months minus 1 day in Great Britain
points.text: For problems on or after 1 October 2026, the time limit for most employment tribunal claims, including discrimination, is 6 months minus 1 day. For problems before that date the old limit of 3 months minus 1 day still applies; where conduct continued over a period, what counts is the date it ended. For discrimination the clock starts from the most recent act in the claim, and a tribunal can allow a later claim if it thinks it just and equitable.
points.figure: 6 months minus 1 day (acts from 1 October 2026); 3 months minus 1 day (earlier acts)
points.note: The change was made by the Employment Rights Act 2025 and commenced by S.I. 2026/954, which keeps the old limit where the act, or the end of conduct over a period, was before 1 October 2026. Some older Acas pages still mention 3 months minus 1 day. Northern Ireland is not covered by this change. This is general information, not legal advice.

points.heading: Northern Ireland: Labour Relations Agency and a 3-month limit
points.text: In Northern Ireland anyone wishing to claim to the Industrial Tribunal or Fair Employment Tribunal must first notify the Labour Relations Agency about early conciliation. Race discrimination claims to the Industrial Tribunal must usually be made within 3 months. Religious belief and political opinion claims go to the Fair Employment Tribunal, with a 3-month limit from knowledge of the act, capped at 6 months.
points.note: The 1 October 2026 extension applies to Great Britain only. Conciliation can pause the deadline for up to one calendar month in Northern Ireland.

points.heading: Equality Advisory and Support Service (EASS)
points.text: EASS is a helpline giving information about discrimination and human rights. It can explain the law, help resolve problems informally, refer to conciliation or mediation and help check eligibility for legal aid, but it cannot give legal advice or help once a claim has started. For employment disputes, the legal aid service asks people to speak to Acas before calling EASS.
points.note: Opening hours are Monday to Friday 9am to 7pm and Saturday 10am to 2pm. EASS covers England, Scotland and Wales; in Northern Ireland use the Equality Commission for Northern Ireland, the Labour Relations Agency or Advice NI.

points.heading: The equality commissions: Great Britain and Northern Ireland
points.text: The Equality and Human Rights Commission is the equality regulator for Great Britain; it no longer runs a public helpline (EASS replaced it) but has legal power to assist individuals in some proceedings. In Northern Ireland, the Equality Commission must give advice to a prospective complainant under fair employment law unless the request is frivolous, and may grant wider assistance, including in race cases. nidirect lists the Equality Commission and Advice NI as sources of free and impartial advice.
points.note: This rests on legislation and government websites rather than the commissions' own guidance, so how each commission chooses which cases to support is not described here. Commission assistance in individual cases is discretionary. This is general information, not legal advice.

points.heading: Ombudsmen do not handle appointments or personnel matters
points.text: The Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman cannot investigate action about appointments, pay, discipline or other personnel matters in Crown employment, so it is not a route for recruitment or workplace discrimination complaints against government departments. The Scottish Public Services Ombudsman has the same exclusion.
points.note: This is based on legislation. For Civil Service recruitment, the independent route is the Civil Service Commission. This is general information, not legal advice.

points.heading: Asking questions: no statutory form in Great Britain since 2014
points.text: The formal discrimination questionnaire in the Equality Act 2010 was abolished in Great Britain from 6 April 2014. You can still send your employer a statement and questions, but there is no law requiring an answer. In Northern Ireland the statutory questions procedure still exists in race discrimination law.
points.note: A data subject access request is a separate legal right to see your own personal data (see the evidence section).

points.heading: Keep a dated record from the start
points.text: Write down what happened, when, who was present and how it affected you, as soon as you can. Keep emails, messages and screenshots. Note the dates of key decisions, such as sift results, interview dates and offers.

points.heading: Keep the recruitment paper trail
points.text: Save the job advert, person specification, your application, test results, invitations, feedback and every message with the recruiting team. Departments only have to keep records of external competitions for two years, so act early.

points.heading: Ask for your own data with a subject access request
points.text: You have a legal right to ask for a copy of the personal information an organisation holds about you, which can show what was recorded about you during recruitment or at work. Organisations usually have one month to respond, and requests are usually free.
points.note: Organisations can withhold some information, for example about judicial or ministerial appointments, and do not have to say why.

points.heading: How to word a complaint
points.text: Put it in writing and set out what happened, when, who was involved, why you think it was discrimination and which protected characteristic it relates to. Ask clear questions and say what outcome you want. Keep it factual and concise.

points.heading: Name people in the complaint, use roles in public
points.text: A complaint to the employer should name the people involved so it can be investigated, and your own name will usually be shared with the department. In anything public, such as a network discussion, describing roles rather than naming individuals helps protect fairness and your own position.

points.heading: Do not let internal steps run down the clock
points.text: Raising a grievance or complaint inside the organisation does not stop the tribunal time limit. When you set a date for your employer to reply, allow for the deadline, and notify Acas in time if you may need to claim.

points.heading: Look after your wellbeing during a complaint
points.text: Race discrimination can be very distressing and, in some cases, seriously affect mental health. Support may be available through an employee assistance programme, mental health first aiders, health and wellbeing representatives, a trade union and helplines such as Acas and EASS. Keeping a record can also help if talking about the experience is distressing.

points.heading: Ethnic minority civil servants at a record 19.2%, SCS level at 10.6%
points.text: At 31 March 2026, 19.2% of civil servants with a known ethnicity were from an ethnic minority background, a record high and up from 18.0% in 2025. Representation falls with seniority: at SCS level it is 10.6%, up only slightly from 10.5% in 2025. Black civil servants numbered 26,655 by headcount, the second largest ethnic minority group. This is the baseline any 2026-27 or 2027-28 ambition will be measured against.
points.note: Percentages exclude people whose ethnicity is unknown or undeclared. The SCS level measure used here differs from the Cabinet Office SCS Database, which holds the official headline Senior Civil Service figures. Civil Service Statistics 2026 gives headcounts by ethnic group; the latest percentage split on Ethnicity facts and figures (March 2024 data) showed 4.5% Black and 2.4% Mixed among civil servants with known ethnicity.

points.heading: No current Civil Service-wide SCS ethnicity target
points.text: The Civil Service Diversity and Inclusion Strategy covered 2022 to 2025 and deliberately chose not to set standalone representation targets, embedding ambitions in other programmes instead. Its period has ended and no successor Civil Service-wide strategy or published Senior Civil Service ethnicity target is listed alongside it on GOV.UK at 30 October 2026. Organisations therefore have no central numeric target to report against in 2026-27; departmental objectives carry the weight.
points.note: No successor strategy or Senior Civil Service ethnicity target was listed on GOV.UK at 30 October 2026. A target set internally by a department, or published elsewhere, would change this picture.

points.heading: Places for Growth 2030: half of UK-based SCS outside London
points.text: The government aims to have 50% of UK-based Senior Civil Servants outside London by 2030, to cut London-based civil servants by 12,000 by 2030 and to offer half of Fast Stream places outside London. London has the highest share of ethnic minority civil servants of any region, so relocation can change who reaches senior roles. The 2022 to 2025 Civil Service strategy committed to monitor diversity data through the rollout, and staff networks can ask whether that monitoring continues.
points.figure: 50% of UK-based SCS outside London by 2030; London headcount down 12,000
points.note: A published government ambition, not a statutory duty. The 38.0% London figure for ethnic minority staff is from 2024 data. The Institute for Government notes the SCS relocation ambition is taking longer to achieve.

points.heading: Civil Service ethnicity pay gaps 2026: Black and Mixed groups
points.text: The Cabinet Office publishes Civil Service ethnicity pay gap statistics each year. In 2026 the median hourly earnings gap for Black civil servants compared with White civil servants widened to 5.3%, while the median bonus gap narrowed to 40.3% from 42.9%. For the Mixed or Multiple group the median earnings gap was 0% and the median bonus gap 7.7%. Departmental figures, published in the same release, are the starting point for any departmental pay action plan.
points.figure: Black: 5.3% earnings gap, 40.3% bonus gap; Mixed: 0% and 7.7% (2026)
points.note: This rests on one source, Cabinet Office. Earnings pay gaps vary widely by department, and part of the gap reflects the larger share of ethnic minority civil servants working in London, where pay is generally higher.

points.heading: People Survey: discrimination at 7%, ethnic background cited by 11%
points.text: In the 2025 Civil Service People Survey, the Civil Service benchmark score for experiencing discrimination at work in the previous 12 months was 7%, unchanged from 2024. Among those reporting discrimination, the median benchmark for citing ethnic background was 11%, up 2 percentage points. The Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport says it will measure progress on its bullying, harassment and discrimination objective through People Survey data, so results by ethnic group matter for 2026-27 reporting.
points.figure: 7% discriminated against; 11% of those cited ethnic background (2025)
points.note: The 2025 survey was shorter and some theme scores are not comparable with earlier years. The 11% figure is a median benchmark across organisations, read from Table 2 of the results highlights. Earlier analysis found Black (9.5%) and Mixed (11.4%) civil servants more likely than White colleagues (7.8%) to report bullying or harassment in 2023.

points.heading: DCMS equality objectives 2025 to 2030 include a sponsorship pilot
points.text: The Department for Culture, Media and Sport became the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport in July 2026, and GDS is now part of it. Its published equality objectives for 2025 to 2030 commit to eliminating bullying, harassment and discrimination, to improving senior representation for under-represented groups through career interventions and a sponsorship pilot, and to annual pay gap reports and equity audits. Progress is to be tracked through People Survey and workforce data.
points.note: The objectives do not name Black or Mixed-heritage staff and set no numeric targets. The page still lists the former department's documents; GDS has no separate equality page.

points.heading: Departmental pay gap reporting: gender published, ethnicity not listed
points.text: The department commits to annual pay gap reports and equity audits. Its equality page lists gender pay gap reports only, the latest listed being 2024, with a 2025 gender pay gap report published in December 2025. No departmental ethnicity pay gap report is listed. The Cabinet Office publishes ethnicity pay gap figures for each department alongside its Civil Service-wide statistics, and these are the published figures that cover the department's staff.
points.note: A department may hold ethnicity pay analysis it has not published. Read 'not listed' as 'not found on the equality page at 30 October 2026'.

points.heading: PSED: publish information yearly and objectives every four years
points.text: Public authorities listed in the 2017 specific duties regulations must publish information showing compliance with the public sector equality duty at intervals of not more than one year, including information on employees if they have 150 or more. They must publish one or more equality objectives at intervals of not more than four years, and each objective must be specific and measurable. The general duty requires due regard to eliminating discrimination, advancing equality of opportunity and fostering good relations.
points.figure: Information: at least yearly; objectives: at least every 4 years
points.note: General information, not legal advice. These regulations cover authorities listed in Schedule 2 (mainly England and some cross-border bodies); Scotland and Wales have their own specific duties. The Ministry of Justice page describes the earlier 2011 regulations, since replaced.

points.heading: Ethnicity pay gap law: proposed, not introduced at 30 October 2026
points.text: The government confirmed in March 2026 that it will legislate for mandatory ethnicity and disability pay gap reporting for employers with 250 or more staff, and published draft clauses alongside its consultation response. The Equality (Race and Disability) Bill had not been introduced before Parliament was prorogued in April 2026 and was absent from the King's Speech of 13 May 2026. No date for reporting to start has been published, so there is no statutory ethnicity pay gap duty in 2026-27 and none is confirmed for 2027-28.
points.note: Status can change quickly if a bill is introduced. Linklaters' working assumption, published in March 2026, is that mandatory reporting is unlikely before 2027 at the earliest and likely to be later.

points.heading: Proposed reporting would show Black and Mixed groups separately
points.text: Under the proposed model, employers would report a binary comparison of White (including White Other) with all other groups, and also report by five broad groups where numbers allow, including Black and Mixed or multiple groups. Public sector bodies in England, and certain public authorities working across Great Britain on non-devolved functions, would be in scope if they have 250 or more employees. The government intends that large employers also publish action plans to tackle any ethnicity pay gap.
points.note: Proposed, not law. The consultation proposed a minimum of 10 employees in each group reported on, but the government says work to set the threshold is ongoing.

points.heading: Equality action plans: voluntary to 30 March 2027, mandatory planned
points.text: Employers with 250 or more employees can publish a voluntary gender equality action plan in the 2026 to 2027 reporting year; for most public authority employers the deadline is 30 March 2027. Subject to legislation, action plans become mandatory from spring 2027. The government aims for a single equality action plan covering sex, race and disability once all reporting duties are in force, so building ethnicity into plans now is a practical step.
points.note: Action plans cover the gender pay gap and menopause, not ethnicity, though the guidance asks employers to consider how sex overlaps with characteristics such as ethnicity. Mandatory plans depend on legislation, and the single combined plan is an aim, not yet law.

points.heading: NHS WRES: tenth national report published April 2026
points.text: NHS England published the 2025 Workforce Race Equality Standard report on 7 April 2026, the tenth since the standard was mandated, covering nine indicators for NHS trusts. Representation of Black and minority ethnic staff continues to rise, but staff remain under-represented at senior and very senior levels. Trusts are expected to keep collecting WRES data and acting on it in 2026-27.
points.note: The WRES has been required through the NHS Standard Contract since 2015/16. Arrangements for national NHS bodies are changing, so check NHS England for the 2026 collection timetable.

points.heading: Mann review on NHS racism: progress reports due 2026 and 2027
points.text: In June 2026 the government accepted Lord Mann's review of antisemitism and other forms of racism in the NHS, including robust accountability for race equality metrics and better data and transparency. It committed to an initial update to Parliament by October 2026 and a detailed report within 12 months of the review's publication on 4 June 2026. NHS staff standards published in July 2026 set minimum requirements for employers, including on tackling racism.
points.figure: Initial update by October 2026; detailed report within 12 months
points.note: No October 2026 update had been published on GOV.UK by 30 October 2026. Some recommendations need consultation or legislation. These commitments and the staff standards apply to the NHS in England.

points.heading: Police Race Action Plan continues in a new form after 2026 review
points.text: The Police Race Action Plan was launched in May 2022 to address inequalities affecting Black people. Its Independent Scrutiny and Oversight Board published its final report in April 2026. The chair of the National Police Chiefs' Council said progress had been inconsistent and that the plan will continue in a new guise with an operational focus on anti-racism. The government has committed to include its data in future versions of the Police Performance Framework.
points.figure: Ethnic minority officers 8.5% of FTE workforce
points.note: Sector-led and voluntary, not statutory. The 8.5% figure excludes White minorities. No dated milestones for 2026-27 or 2027-28 were published in the sources used.

points.heading: Windrush Compensation Scheme: monthly data, no closing target
points.text: The Home Office publishes Windrush Compensation Scheme data every month; the August 2026 release was published on 29 October 2026. By the end of August 2026 the scheme had paid about £133.5 million across 4,221 claims. Under changes announced in October 2025, following recommendations from the independent Windrush Commissioner, claimants who request a review of their decision can be paid up to 75% of their award in advance.
points.note: This rests on one source, Home Office. The £133.5 million and 4,221 figures are from table WCS_03 of the August 2026 data tables. No numeric target or end date for 2026-27 or 2027-28 is published.

points.heading: No standalone UK race equality strategy; REEG and maternity pledge
points.text: No standalone UK government race equality strategy had been published by 30 October 2026, and the government has said there will be no separate Race Equality Act; its race equality legislation is planned as the Equality (Race and Disability) Bill. The Race Equality Engagement Group, set up in March 2025, reported on its first year in July 2026 and feeds community voices into government plans on policing, finance, maternal health and education. The manifesto commitment to set an explicit target to close the Black and Asian maternal mortality gap has not yet produced a published numeric target.
points.note: Absence of a strategy is unconfirmed and could change. The maternal mortality target is a commitment awaiting a national action plan from the maternity and neonatal taskforce.

points.heading: Wales aims to be an anti-racist nation by 2030
points.text: The Anti-racist Wales Action Plan, refreshed in 2024, commits the Welsh Government to making Wales an anti-racist nation by 2030. Senior leaders in the Welsh Government civil service will have clear anti-racism objectives and 360-degree feedback, and leaders in Welsh Government-funded bodies will have measurable anti-racism objectives. A maturity matrix for tracking progress was published by January 2026.
points.note: This rests on one source, Welsh Government. It is a government policy commitment, not a statutory duty, and applies to Wales only.

points.heading: Ask for data by Black and Mixed groups, not only 'ethnic minority'
points.text: Aggregate 'ethnic minority' figures can hide different outcomes for Black and Mixed-heritage staff, as the Civil Service pay gap statistics show. The proposed national reporting model uses five broad groups that separate Black and Mixed groups. Networks can ask departments to publish workforce, progression and pay data in the same five groups now, where numbers are large enough to protect anonymity.
points.note: Small numbers in some grades mean figures may need to be suppressed or combined to protect privacy.

points.heading: Press for published pay gap action plans with targets
points.text: The McGregor-Smith Review recommended that employers publish aspirational targets and report progress annually. The Race at Work Charter asks signatories to capture ethnicity data and publicise progress. The government intends to require large employers to publish action plans on ethnicity pay gaps, so networks can ask for a plan now rather than waiting for the law.
points.note: Targets recommended by McGregor-Smith are aspirational, not quotas. The legal duty for action plans on ethnicity does not yet exist.

points.heading: Turn mentoring into sponsorship that changes careers
points.text: Government guidance notes that women from ethnic minority backgrounds may be over-mentored but under-sponsored. Sponsorship means a senior person advocating for someone and opening up opportunities, not only giving advice. The department's own objectives include piloting a sponsorship programme, and earlier Civil Service schemes paired ethnic minority Grade 6 and 7 staff with senior sponsors to help them reach the Senior Civil Service.
points.note: The 2026 guidance was written for gender pay gap action plans but its sponsorship advice applies more widely. The current status of the earlier Civil Service scheme described in 2020 is unconfirmed.

points.heading: Ask for a stated ambition for progression to senior grades
points.text: Ethnic minority representation at SCS level (10.6%) is about half the overall Civil Service rate (19.2%). McGregor-Smith said every employer with more than 50 staff should set aspirational targets throughout the organisation, not just at the bottom. Networks can ask for a published, time-bound ambition for senior grades and for Black and Mixed-heritage staff in particular.
points.note: General information, not legal advice. Quotas or reserved posts are generally not lawful; aspirational targets and positive action within the Equality Act are.

points.heading: Use lawful positive action in development and recruitment
points.text: The Equality Act allows proportionate positive action where an employer reasonably thinks people who share a protected characteristic are disadvantaged or under-represented, for example targeted development schemes. In recruitment and promotion, an employer may treat a candidate more favourably only if they are as qualified as the other candidate, the employer has no policy of favouring that group, and the action is proportionate. The 2022 to 2025 Civil Service strategy committed to using positive action where needed.
points.note: General information, not legal advice. Specialist HR or legal advice is needed before designing any positive action scheme.

points.heading: Hold executive sponsors to account with objectives and reports
points.text: McGregor-Smith called for executive sponsorship of key targets and for diversity to be a key performance indicator. Business in the Community now builds executive sponsor leadership into every Race at Work Charter commitment. The Welsh Government gives its senior leaders clear anti-racism objectives with 360-degree feedback, a model networks can point to.
points.note: These are recommendations and voluntary commitments, not legal duties.

points.heading: Give networks a formal advisory voice
points.text: The Civil Service Race Forum brings together ethnic minority staff networks and aims to advise Civil Service leadership on racial diversity and equality. The Race Equality Engagement Group shows a similar model at national level, feeding lived experience directly into policy. Networks can ask for a standing place in workforce and equality objective decisions, with time and resources recognised.

points.heading: Executive sponsors: own the race agenda visibly
points.text: The Race at Work Charter's first original commitment was to appoint an executive sponsor for race. Senior sponsorship gives inclusion work momentum, and the McGregor-Smith Review said the sponsor should be held to account for delivering aspirational targets. Visible behaviours suggested in guidance include having race-inclusion objectives, discussing race at senior management meetings, sponsoring ethnic minority staff networks and taking part in events such as Black History Month.
points.note: Descriptions of behaviours are drawn from guidance, not from evaluation of outcomes.

points.heading: Take part in reverse mentoring and 360-degree feedback
points.text: McGregor-Smith recommended that all senior managers consider reverse mentoring with someone more junior, to understand what it is like to be an ethnic minority employee in their organisation. The CIPD and Business in the Community suggest reverse mentoring and 360-degree feedback as ways to make leaders own inclusion. Leaders should listen, act on what they hear and report back.
points.note: Reverse mentoring relies on junior colleagues' time and openness; it should be voluntary and recognised.

points.heading: Sponsor actively: advocate, open doors, find stretch work
points.text: Sponsorship is advocacy and opportunity, while mentoring is guidance and listening. Good sponsors use their influence, for example by finding high-profile projects, giving references, and raising the profile of the person they sponsor with senior networks. Guidance suggests training sponsors and setting a clear timeframe, such as 6 to 12 months.

points.heading: Be an active bystander and call out racism
points.text: Allies challenge racist remarks and microaggressions when they happen and make room for ethnic minority colleagues to be heard in meetings. Acas points to the Business in the Community guide, which lists recognising privilege, being an active bystander and being ready to be vulnerable. Allyship is one part of a wider race equality strategy, not a replacement for it.
points.note: The Acas source is a blog post by a named Acas official, not formal Acas guidance.

points.heading: Lead by example on zero tolerance of harassment
points.text: The Race at Work Charter asks boards to commit to zero tolerance of harassment and bullying. Leaders can introduce and enforce clear policies so people are held accountable for racism, and model inclusive behaviour in every interaction. The department's own objective gives leaders tools to tackle bullying, harassment and discrimination.

points.text: Good allies keep themselves informed about race and racism and are comfortable talking about it at work. points.heading: UK Youth Parliament: elected members aged 11 to 18
points.text: The UK Youth Parliament has around 300 elected Members of Youth Parliament aged 11 to 18 who carry young people's views to government and service providers. Elections are usually held every two years, often in schools. The National Youth Agency has run the programme since May 2024, after the British Youth Council closed in March 2024.
points.note: Elections are not held in every constituency: the government said in 2024 that they run in over 70% of constituencies. One council page counts 369 seats for elected members, so totals differ by source.

points.heading: Make Your Mark and the House of Commons sitting
points.text: Make Your Mark is the UK Youth Parliament's survey of young people's priorities, and members take the results into national debate. Members meet at an annual conference and hold a sitting in the House of Commons chamber. Awareness is still low: in the government's evaluation only about a quarter of young people who were not members had heard of the programme.

points.heading: Scottish Youth Parliament: vote at 12 to 25, stand at 14 to 25
points.text: Around 160 Members of the Scottish Youth Parliament, aged 14 to 25, are elected every two years to represent young people in every part of Scotland. Young people aged 12 to 25 can vote. The 2026 elections run from 2 to 15 November 2026, using the single transferable vote.
points.note: The candidate deadline for 2026 has passed; the next chance to stand is expected in 2028. Voting methods (paper or online with a Young Scot card) vary by council area.

points.heading: Welsh Youth Parliament (Senedd Ieuenctid): 60 members
points.text: The Welsh Youth Parliament has 60 members. Forty are elected by young people voting in constituency elections and 20 are elected through partner organisations, so that more groups of young people are represented. A term lasts two years, and young people aged 11 up to 18 can register to vote.
points.note: The current members' page gives their ages as 11 to 17. The voting age range comes from the 2018 launch announcement (updated 2024); check the Welsh Youth Parliament site for the next election timetable.

points.heading: Northern Ireland Youth Assembly: 90 members chosen at random
points.text: The Northern Ireland Youth Assembly has 90 members who were in school years 9 to 12 (about ages 12 to 16) when recruited. Members are chosen by an anonymised random selection, 54 by constituency and 36 to reflect groups such as gender, religion, race, care experience and disability. Committees meet monthly online and plenary sittings are held twice a year, usually in the Assembly chamber.
points.note: This rests on one source, the Northern Ireland Assembly Commission (two pages of its Youth Assembly site). The current members took their seats in November 2025; unsuccessful applicants can join a consultation forum list.

points.heading: Children's Commissioners' young advisers
points.text: Children's Commissioners recruit groups of young people to advise them. In England a new advisory board of up to 16 young people aged 16 to 18 meets every six weeks until December 2027 to advise on AI in education. In Scotland the Commissioner's Young Advisors are aged 12 to 17 and meet about once a month.
points.figure: England: up to 16 members aged 16 to 18; Scotland: ages 12 to 17
points.note: Applications for the England board closed on 21 June 2026. England's first Children's Advisory Board (2022) was a pilot with 10 schools for ages 10 to 13. The Wales and Northern Ireland Commissioners also involve young people; check their sites for current panels.

points.heading: Local youth councils and young mayors
points.text: Some councils run a youth council, youth cabinet or young mayor scheme, and local youth councils are the second most common way members of the UK Youth Parliament first heard of it. Lewisham Council says it has the longest established young mayor programme, begun in 2004, and its young mayor has a £25,000 budget in 2026-27. The national youth strategy promises more local youth ambassador networks.
points.note: Schemes are set locally, so ages, election methods and budgets vary; contact your council's youth service. In the UKYP evaluation, 31% of members first heard of the programme through their local youth council.

points.heading: School and college councils
points.text: In Wales the law requires the governing body of every maintained school, except nursery and infant schools, to set up a school council, and the head teacher must make sure it meets six times a school year. In England the Department for Education counts school and college democracy as part of civic engagement in its enrichment benchmarks.
points.figure: Wales: 6 meetings a year by law
points.note: The Welsh regulation is shown as originally made in 2005, and the six-meetings rule does not apply to community or foundation special schools. No statutory duty for school councils in England, Scotland or Northern Ireland is cited here; pupil councils there depend on each school.

points.heading: Voting age now: 16 in Scotland and Wales, 18 elsewhere
points.text: At 30 October 2026 you must be 18 to vote in UK Parliament elections and in local elections in England and Northern Ireland. In Scotland and Wales you can vote at 16 in Scottish Parliament, Senedd and local council elections. You can register from 14 in Scotland and Wales and from 16 in England and Northern Ireland.
points.note: These are the rules in force today. They will change if the Representation of the People Bill becomes law (next point).

points.heading: Votes at 16 for all UK elections: a Bill, not yet law
points.text: The Representation of the People Bill would extend the vote to 16 and 17 year olds in all UK elections and let people register from 14. At 30 October 2026 the Bill has passed the House of Commons and is at committee stage in the House of Lords, with sittings scheduled from 2 November to 14 December 2026. It is not yet law.
points.note: The Bill can still be amended, and the date the new age takes effect will depend on Royal Assent and commencement. The government's youth strategy says votes at 16 will be in place by the next elections; treat that as a stated aim until the Act is passed.

points.heading: Register to vote: about five minutes online
points.text: You register once, not for every election, and again only if you change name, address or nationality. Online registration usually takes about five minutes and asks for your National Insurance number, though you can still register without one. You can register up to two years before you reach voting age.
points.note: Some groups are less likely to be registered, including young people and Black and Mixed-heritage people; see the representation section. An anonymous registration route exists for people with safety concerns.

points.heading: Petitions: thresholds differ by parliament
points.text: UK Parliament petitions stay open for six months; at 10,000 signatures the government responds and at 100,000 Parliament may debate it. Senedd petitions are reviewed by a committee at over 250 signatures and may be put forward for debate at over 10,000. Anyone of any age can submit a Scottish Parliament petition, and the committee looks at every published one.
points.note: To start or sign a UK Parliament petition you must be a British citizen or UK resident; to create a Senedd petition you need an address in Wales. Rules for Northern Ireland Assembly petitions are not covered here.

points.heading: Give evidence to committees and answer consultations
points.text: Select committees in Parliament publish inquiries that invite views from the public. Government policy papers and consultations are listed together on GOV.UK. Taking part in a consultation about local services is one of the forms of civic engagement the government measures each year.
points.note: Consultations have closing dates; read the scope and how responses will be used before replying.

points.heading: Free education services and visits at each parliament
points.text: The UK Parliament education service offers free school visits, classroom workshops and teacher training, and organisations can sign up to run UK Parliament Week activities. The Northern Ireland Assembly and Scottish Parliament also run education services, tours and events.
points.note: UK Parliament Week dates for 2026 are not confirmed here. The Senedd also runs an education service; check its website for current visits and workshops.

points.heading: Magistrate: from 18, at least 13 days a year
points.text: Magistrates in England and Wales are volunteers aged 18 to 74 who hear cases in panels of three. You must sit for at least 13 full days (or 26 half days) a year and are normally expected to serve for at least five years. By law, employers must allow reasonable time off.
points.note: These rules apply in England and Wales. Scotland uses Justices of the Peace and Northern Ireland lay magistrates, with different rules not covered here.

points.heading: Special constable: volunteer police officer from 18
points.text: Special constables are volunteers with the same powers as police officers. You can apply at 17 but must be 18 to be offered the role. Specials usually commit to at least 16 hours a month after training.
points.note: Hours and recruitment rounds vary by force; Police Scotland runs its own special constabulary.

points.heading: Volunteer Police Cadets: a uniformed youth group
points.text: The Volunteer Police Cadets is the police uniformed youth group in England and Wales; in Scotland it is Police Scotland Youth Volunteers. Its aim is adventure and good citizenship, not recruiting future officers. Ages vary by force: Thames Valley Police, for example, takes 13 to 18 year olds, and some forces run junior units for 11 to 13 year olds.
points.note: Each police force runs its own units, so check your local force for ages, meeting nights and costs. The 13 to 18 range quoted is from Thames Valley Police.

points.heading: NHS youth voice and patient involvement
points.text: NHS England's Youth Forum is a group of 25 young people who work with NHS England policy leads. More broadly, local groups that make decisions about health or education services are one of the ways people take part in civic activism.
points.note: The NHS Youth Forum page gives no age range; recruitment is run with Barnardo's. Local NHS volunteering ages and roles vary by trust or health board.

points.heading: School or academy governor: from 18
points.text: Governors and trustees oversee schools' strategy, finance and standards as volunteers. In England governors must be 18 or over when elected or appointed. Being a school governor is one of the local roles the government counts as civic activism.
points.note: Age rule quoted is for maintained schools in England. Wales also has associate pupil governors; Scotland uses parent councils and Northern Ireland boards of governors, not covered here.

points.heading: Independent custody visitors and monitoring boards
points.text: Independent custody visitors are volunteers who visit police custody suites to check the welfare and rights of people held in police custody. Independent Monitoring Boards check day-to-day standards in each prison and immigration detention centre. Monitoring board volunteering usually takes two or three days a month.
points.note: Minimum ages are not stated on these pages; ask the local scheme. Monitoring boards cover every prison in England and Wales and immigration detention across the UK.

points.heading: Jury service: a civic duty from 18
points.text: Jury service is a legal duty, not a volunteer role. In England and Wales jurors are chosen at random from the electoral register, must be 18 to 75, and must reply to a summons within 7 days. Service usually lasts up to 10 working days.
points.figure: ages 18 to 75; up to 10 working days
points.note: Rules shown are for England and Wales. Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own jury rules and summons arrangements.

points.heading: Public appointments to boards of public bodies
points.text: Public bodies and advisory committees recruit chairs and members through open public appointment campaigns. Vacancies are listed on the Cabinet Office's public appointments service, where you can set up alerts. Government says boards work best when they reflect the society they serve.
points.note: Each advert sets out the experience needed and the time commitment. Diversity data are in the representation section.

points.heading: Civil Service routes from age 16
points.text: You can apply for a Civil Service apprenticeship from 16, an internship while at university, and the Fast Stream after graduating. Apprentices are paid employees who study for a recognised qualification. You can apply while still at school if you will be 16 by the end of the summer holidays.
points.note: See the hub's joining page for application steps. Apprenticeship systems differ in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

points.heading: Summer Internship Programme: apply by 5 November 2026
points.text: The Fast Stream Summer Internship Programme gives undergraduates from lower socio-economic backgrounds a paid eight-week placement in a government department. You must be in your final two years at university. Applications for summer 2027 close at midday on 5 November 2026, and the placement runs July to August 2027.
points.note: Eligibility is assessed using ONS measures of socio-economic background, plus Civil Service nationality rules. See the hub's joining page for how to apply.

points.heading: Care Leavers Internship Scheme: 18 months, ages 18 to 30
points.text: The Care Leavers Internship Scheme, run by the Department for Education, offers 18-month paid jobs in government departments and agencies. Applicants must be care leavers entitled to a leaving care package and aged 18 to 30. Interns can be made permanent after 12 months.
points.note: You must have been in care for at least 13 weeks, some of it after your 16th birthday. See the hub's joining page for more.

points.heading: Youth Select Committee: 12 members of the Youth Parliament
points.text: The Youth Select Committee copies the work of Commons select committees. It has 12 members drawn from the UK Youth Parliament, and the National Youth Agency runs it with support from Parliament. Its 2025/26 inquiry began with a meeting at Parliament in September 2025.
points.note: Sources give different upper ages: Parliament says 14 to 18 and a council news item says 14 to 19. The committee now continues under the National Youth Agency after the British Youth Council closed.

points.text: The Duke of Edinburgh's Award is open to anyone aged 14 to 24. The Department for Education's 2026 enrichment framework names the Award, debating, Model United Nations and mock magistrates' trials as ways schools build civic engagement. Ask your school or college what it offers.
points.note: Some enrichment activities have costs; the framework lists free resources alongside paid options. The hub endorses no provider.

points.heading: Cadet forces: over 137,000 young people
points.text: The Ministry of Defence sponsors five cadet forces: Sea Cadets, the Volunteer Cadet Corps, Army Cadets, Air Cadets and the school-based Combined Cadet Force. At 1 April 2026 there were 88,870 community cadets. The 2025 Strategic Defence Review recommended growing cadet forces by 30% by 2030.
points.note: Minimum joining ages differ: Sea Cadets and the Volunteer Cadet Corps from 9, Army Cadets from 12, Air Cadets from 12 and in school year 8, and the school-based Combined Cadet Force from school year 8. Membership usually ends at 18 or on leaving school. The 137,000 total includes 48,240 Combined Cadet Force members.

points.text: The National Citizen Service, which offered 16 and 17 year olds in England residential trips and social action projects, ended on 31 March 2025. The government is replacing it with a wider national youth strategy, including a Youth Guarantee and Young Futures Hubs. Older guides that still recommend NCS are out of date.
points.note: The NCS Trust website no longer operates. Programmes under the youth strategy are being rolled out over the next ten years.

points.text: The #iWill Movement supports young people to take part in social action such as campaigning, volunteering and fundraising. Its Festival of Social Action runs every November. The national youth strategy promises more chances to volunteer through schools, colleges and communities.
points.note: The #iWill site describes itself as for ages 10 to 25. The hub endorses no single organisation.

points.heading: Holiday Activities and Food programme (England)
points.text: The HAF programme gives children eligible for benefits-related free school meals free activities and a healthy meal in the Easter, summer and Christmas holidays. In 2026-27 councils may also run it in half-terms. From September 2026, eligibility stays at the targeted free school meals threshold, not the wider expanded free school meals group.
points.figure: half-term spend expected to stay within 5% of allocation
points.note: This applies to England only. Councils can use up to about 15% of funding for places for other children; ask your council. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland run their own holiday schemes.

points.text: Councils publish holiday play schemes and clubs, which can be run by schools, charities or private providers. Some councils fund free or low-cost places beyond the HAF-eligible group.
points.figure: up to 15% of HAF funding for wider places

points.text: On Takeover Day, museums, galleries, archives and heritage sites invite young people to take over jobs usually done by adults. The 2026 national Takeover Day is on Friday 20 November and its theme is careers, though venues can hold one at any time of year.
points.note: This rests on one source, Kids in Museums. The national date falls in term time; ask your school or local museum. Black History Month programmes are set by each venue.

points.text: A gap year can be paid. The Year in Industry places school and college leavers in paid STEM placements, typically for 12 months, and you apply in your final year of A levels, Highers or equivalents. Apprenticeships are paid jobs with training and are open from 16.
points.note: Year in Industry details rest on one source, the Engineering Development Trust. Placement numbers are limited and competitive. Apprentice pay follows age-based minimum wage rates.

points.text: The Civil Service Summer Internship Programme runs in the university summer holidays, July to August, for students from lower socio-economic backgrounds. points.text: Volunteers' Week runs across the UK from the first Monday in June, and the 2027 week is 7 to 13 June. In England, 18% of people aged 16 and over volunteered formally at least once a month in 2025/26. Local volunteer centres list roles that suit holidays and gap years.

points.heading: Working in the holidays if you are under 16
points.text: Children can work part-time from 14 (13 in some council areas). In school holidays, 14 year olds can work up to 25 hours a week and 15 to 16 year olds up to 35 hours. Every child must have a two-week break from work during the school holidays each year.

points.text: Holiday clubs, tuition and activity providers should follow the government's out-of-school settings safeguarding guidance, including DBS checks where needed. points.heading: UK Youth Parliament: Black members in line with population
points.text: In 2025, 7% of Members of the UK Youth Parliament were Black, compared with 6% of 11 to 17 year olds in England and Wales. Mixed-heritage members were 5%, compared with 6% of 11 to 17 year olds. Asian members were over-represented (18% compared with 12%) and White British members under-represented.
points.note: This rests on one source, the government's UKYP evaluation, using the National Youth Agency's 2025 member census. Members are UK-wide but the comparison population is England and Wales (2021 Census). Most decision makers interviewed felt members were mainly from middle-class backgrounds, though a few said this was an assumption rather than based on hard evidence.

points.heading: Magistrates: 5% Black, 2% Mixed in 2026
points.text: At 1 April 2026, 14% of magistrates in England and Wales were from an ethnic minority: 5% Black, 2% Mixed and 7% Asian. The Black share rose from 4% a year earlier. In 2025-26, 17% of new magistrates were from an ethnic minority, compared with 9% of those who left.
points.note: Shares are of magistrates who declared their ethnicity. 81% of magistrates are 50 or over, so younger people of all backgrounds are under-represented.

points.text: In 2025/26, 46% of adults in England took part in civic participation, consultation or activism. The rate for Black adults was also 46% (Black African 46%, Black Caribbean 46%), up from 37% in 2024/25. White and Black Caribbean adults were less likely to take part (41%), and 16 to 24 year olds were the least engaged age group (35%).

points.heading: Voter registration gaps for Black and Mixed-heritage people
points.text: The Electoral Commission's study of the December 2018 registers found 84% of eligible White people were correctly registered, compared with 75% of Black people and 69% of people from Mixed backgrounds. Young people, students and recent movers were the least likely to be registered.

points.heading: Council candidates in Wales: about 1% Black, 1% Mixed
points.text: In the 2022 Welsh local elections survey, 96% of candidates who responded were White, about 1% were Black and 1% were Mixed. The survey is repeated at each ordinary election.

points.heading: Cabinet Office with Government Skills: Government professions
points.text: Four types: operational delivery, policy, functional, specialist. Functional (21): Actuary, Commercial, Communications, Counter Fraud, Cyber, Debt, Digital and Data, Economics, Finance, Geography, Grants, Human Resources, Internal Audit, Legal, Project Delivery, Property, Operational Research, Risk Management, Security, Social research, Statistics. Specialist (10): Corporate Finance, Intelligence Analysis, Knowledge and Information Management, Clinical, Occupational Psychology, Planning, Planning Inspection, Science and Engineering, Tax, Veterinary.

sources.title: GOV.UK: Government professions (updated 30 September 2026)
